Model Output:
# Brainstorming ## Unpacking the prompt: "Gods wore sneakers." The line is deceptively rich. Several readings present themselves: **Reading 1 — Divine slumming.** Gods walk among us disguised, and the tell is footwear. The mythic detail (Hermes' winged sandals, Vishnu's footprints, Achilles' heel) collapses into Air Jordans, Chuck Taylors, knockoff Adidas from a market stall. The comedy and pathos of the eternal buying consumer goods. **Reading 2 — Gods as athletes/street kids.** A pantheon reincarnated as a basketball team, a running crew, a group of teenagers in a housing estate. Sneakers as uniform, as tribal marker, as the thing you'd die for. Sneaker culture already has priests, relics, pilgrimages, resale markets — a religion in miniature. **Reading 3 — Sneakers as the new relics.** What if worship migrated? Gods survive on attention, and attention now flows to brands. A god who becomes a shoe. A shoe that becomes a god. The swoosh as a sigil. "Just do it" as a commandment. This is the sharpest satirical angle. **Reading 4 — The literal Hermes/messenger angle.** Delivery couriers, bike messengers, gig-economy runners. Hermes as a DoorDash driver. Sneakers as the modern winged sandal. The god of thresholds and crossings now crossing city streets for $4.20 a drop plus tip. **Reading 5 — Elegiac/decline reading.** The gods are old now, diminished, and sneakers are what old men wear because their feet hurt. Zeus in orthopedic New Balances. A retirement home for deities. Bittersweet comedy. **Reading 6 — Mythology of the sneaker itself.** A pair of shoes passed down, each owner touched by something. Anthology structure. Risky over 8 chapters but interesting. **Reading 7 — The sweatshop reading.** Gods wore sneakers — made by children in a factory. The dark underside: the shoes that carry divinity were stitched by the unblessed. This gives moral weight and stakes; it's where the satire gets teeth. A god who discovers who made her shoes. **Reading 8 — Africa/diaspora angle.** Yoruba orisha in Lagos, Legba at a crossroads in Port-au-Prince, Anansi in Brooklyn. Sneakers as diasporic currency — the "kicks" economy, secondhand bales shipped from the West to Ghana (Kantamanto market). Rich, underused. ## Possible protagonists - **A shoe repairman / cobbler.** Old man in a shopping-mall kiosk who resoles shoes. Gods keep coming to him because he's the only one who can fix divine footwear. Lovely, quiet, contained premise. He becomes a kind of confessor. - **A teenage sneakerhead** who spots a god in the wild by the shoes: a pair that never existed, a colorway from no season, a sole with no wear pattern despite miles. - **A courier**, mortal, who becomes an unwitting messenger for the divine. Or who is *becoming* Hermes without knowing. - **A woman who works at a resale authentication warehouse** — she can tell real from fake by smell and stitch. Then a pair arrives that is *too* real. Authentication as a theological act: what makes a thing genuine? - **A god in decline** — first person. Nike (the actual goddess of victory) who signed away her name. This is almost too good: Nike, goddess of victory, and the brand. A god who sold her name to a shoe company and now survives on the residue of every logo, every ad, every "just do it," but has lost the *self* of it. She has infinite reach and no interiority. That's a genuine emotional engine. - **A sneaker designer** who realizes her sketches are being dictated to her. ## The Nike idea, expanded Nike — Νίκη — the winged goddess of victory. Samothrace. She was never a major god; she was a personification, an attendant, often at Athena's shoulder. Then in 1971 a design student named Carolyn Davidson drew a swoosh for $35, and a company took her name. Now she is the most-invoked deity in human history. Her name is on more feet than Christ has crosses. The tragedy: she is worshipped constantly and *known* by no one. Every invocation is empty. She's bloated with attention and starving for meaning. Meanwhile her old colleagues have withered — Hermes reduced to a scarf brand and a courier's patron, Ares thriving weirdly, Hephaestus in the factories. This gives me: satire, pathos, mythic literacy, and the prompt as a *literal* pun ("Gods wore sneakers" — one god *is* the sneaker). But I don't want it to be a one-joke story. It needs a mortal center. Who? ## Combining: the two-hander **Nike + a girl who makes the shoes.** Or: **Nike + the cobbler.** Or: **Nike + a runner.** I like: **a young woman in a stitching line** in Vietnam, Indonesia, or Ethiopia, who sews wings onto shoes. Or a **secondhand market trader in Accra** who unpacks bales of dead white men's clothes. But I should be careful — writing that culture requires care and I risk exoticizing or making a real, ongoing labor injustice into a set piece for a Greek goddess's redemption arc. Better to complicate it: let the mortal have her own agency and her own myth, not be a lesson for a god. Alternative that might be stronger and safer to execute well: **the shoe repair kiosk.** An old cobbler, or better — a young woman who inherited her grandfather's repair stall in a dying mall. Gods come to her. She doesn't know they're gods. This is warm, contained, character-driven, and lets me parade a whole pantheon through in vignettes while keeping one continuous emotional thread. Third option: **the runner.** A mortal girl who runs, who has no talent for it, who runs anyway. Nike is drawn to her because she is the only person on earth who *loses* and keeps going, and therefore is the only person who understands victory as something other than a purchase. That's thematically tight: the goddess of victory learning what victory actually is from someone who never wins. Slightly on-the-nose but emotionally legible and satisfying. ## Hybrid concept (leaning) **Setting:** A struggling city. A dead mall with one live corner: SOLE SURVIVOR, a sneaker repair and restoration stall. Also a public track behind a chain-link fence, floodlights half-broken. **Mortal protagonist:** **Mercy Adjei-Kowalski** (mixed heritage, Ghanaian father, Polish-American mother — gives me a natural diasporic texture without appropriating a single culture wholesale) — 17, restores sneakers in her late father's stall, runs badly at night on the cracked track, keeps a ledger of every shoe she's ever fixed and who wore it. Or simplify the name: **Mercy Okonjo**. Or **Nia**. Let's hold names loosely. **Divine protagonist:** **Nike**, appearing as a woman in her thirties, tall, with the marks of removed wings between her shoulder blades (scars, or two vertical seams like a shoe's stitching). She wears the same pair of white sneakers, unbranded, that are always immaculate no matter what — because she has never once walked toward anything she wanted. **Antagonist:** Options — - **The Brand** itself, personified. A god born from marketing: sleek, kind, terrifying. Call him **Kydos** (glory) or **Zelos** (rivalry/zeal — actually Nike's literal brother in myth, along with Bia (force) and Kratos (power), children of Styx and Pallas). *That's perfect.* Zelos, Kratos, Bia, Nike — the four siblings who sat at Zeus's throne. Kratos = Power. Bia = Violence. Zelos = Rivalry/Emulation. In the modern world: Kratos is a hedge fund, Bia is a private security contractor, Zelos is a marketing executive. They have all thrived. Only Nike sold her name and became hollow. - **Zelos** as the antagonist: the god of emulation, of *wanting what others have*, who profits from every drop, every resale market, every kid stabbed for shoes. He's the one who brokered Nike's deal. He is the true god of the sneaker economy. Excellent. **Stakes:** Nike is dissolving — too diffuse, too invoked, no longer coherent. Her name is a spell said ten million times a day by people who mean a shoe. To survive she must be *invoked properly once* — someone must want victory and mean it, and name her. Or: she must reclaim her name by refusing it. Or she must find the one pair of shoes that were made *for* her and not *of* her. **MacGuffin possibility:** A single pair of shoes stitched by Hephaestus (now an old man in a shoe factory, or a machinist) — the last handmade divine footwear. Winged sandals reforged as sneakers. Whoever wears them wins. Mercy could win with them. The whole point being that she shouldn't. That's a clean, mythic structure: the temptation of the magic shoes, refused. ## Tone options - **Wry urban-fantasy** (Gaiman-ish, *American Gods*). Risk: derivative. - **Lyrical, close-third, elegiac with humor.** Sentences that carry weight. Fewer jokes, better jokes. - **First person, Nike narrating.** Voice of an ancient thing trying out slang. Fun, risky, can become twee. - **Alternating POV** between Mercy and Nike. Gives both interiority. 8 chapters divides nicely. - **Anthology of feet.** Each chapter a different god's shoes coming into the repair shop, with a through-line. Risk: episodic, weak spine. I think a **close third, mostly Mercy, with two or three chapters in Nike's POV** would give the best of both. Or keep it entirely on Mercy for mystery and reveal, and give Nike one interstitial chapter. ## Structural sketches ### Option A — The Repair Shop (8 chapters) 1. Mercy at the stall; a strange customer brings in impossible shoes. 2. She restores them; something happens; she meets Nike properly. 3. The pantheon parade: Hermes (courier), Hephaestus (cobbler emeritus), Athena (school administrator). 4. Zelos arrives with an offer: sponsorship, a real store, money. 5. Nike's backstory: the $35 swoosh, the signing away. 6. Mercy takes the deal / or a kid gets hurt over shoes and it lands hard. 7. The race. Mercy runs. The winged sneakers. 8. Aftermath: what she chooses; Nike's fate. ### Option B — The Race Structure around a single race (a citywide 10K? a high school meet? a street race at midnight?) as the climax, with chapters counting down. More propulsive. ### Option C — Diasporic road story Mercy follows the shoes back to their making: mall → warehouse → port → factory. Physical journey mirrors moral one. Ambitious for 8,000 words. Probably too much. ### Option D — Seven gods, one shoe Each chapter one god, one pair of shoes, one lesson. Final chapter ties it. Elegant but risks feeling like a listicle. I lean toward a **blend of A and B**: the repair shop as home base, the race as the spine and climax. ## Chapter-by-chapter draft (blend) 1. **"Sole Survivor"** — Establish Mercy, the dead mall, the stall, her ledger, her dead father, her terrible running. A woman comes in with white sneakers that have no wear on the soles at all. Mercy notices this and it unsettles her. Hook: the woman asks Mercy to *make them worn*. 2. **"Wear Pattern"** — Mercy tries to age the shoes; they refuse. The woman returns and they talk. Reveal (partial) — the seams on her back. Mercy runs that night, badly, and the woman watches from the fence. 3. **"The Pantheon of Small Repairs"** — Word spreads in the divine underworld of the city. Gods arrive: Hermes on an e-bike with worn-through heels; a war god's spotless combat trainers; Hephaestus, old machinist, who recognizes what Mercy has. Establishes rules and lore, and the fact that gods now live on brand-attention. 4. **"Zelos"** — The antagonist. Slick, generous, appalling. He offers Mercy a deal: her shop becomes a flagship, she becomes a name. Also seeds the race — a "Legacy Mile," a sponsored event. Nike warns her, and in doing so reveals what happened to her name. 5. **"Thirty-Five Dollars"** — Nike POV. Samothrace, the temple, being an attendant, then the 1971 room with the design student and the check. What it feels like to be said a billion times and heard zero. Her siblings. Beautiful and sad. Ends with what she needs: to be wanted by name, once, by someone who could lose. 6. **"The Drop"** — Consequence chapter. A kid Mercy knows gets robbed/hurt for shoes at the drop, or she sees the resale mob and understands Zelos's economy. Mercy makes a bad choice (takes the deal, or takes the shoes). Hephaestus gives her the last true pair — winged sneakers — and tells her they will make her win, and warns her that's the trap. 7. **"The Legacy Mile"** — The race. Rain, floodlights, the city, the gods in the stands. Mercy has the winged shoes. She laces them. Decision point: she runs in her own beat-up trainers instead, or she takes off the winged ones mid-race. She loses. She *names* Nike — not for victory but for the will to finish. Nike is restored/changed. 8. **"Wear Pattern (Reprise)"** — Coda. Mercy re-soles Nike's white shoes and they finally take a wear pattern. Zelos diminished but not destroyed (he's too modern to kill). The stall reopens. Last image: two pairs of sneakers, both worn. Maybe: Nike's shoes now say something small and handwritten on the tongue — a name. That's a real shape. Rising action, midpoint reveal, dark night, climax, coda. Roughly 1000 words each is tight but workable if I keep the cast lean. ## Things to consider / risks - **Word budget.** 8 × 1000 = 8000 words. The pantheon parade (ch 3) could eat too much. Keep the divine cast to four or five named figures max. - **The brand-name problem.** Should I name Nike-the-corporation? Legally and artistically, better to keep it oblique: "the company," "the swoosh," "the check-mark." That obliqueness is also spookier and more mythic. Never say the corporate name; the goddess just says *my name*. Lovely effect: the reader supplies it. And it makes the pun land without being crass. - **On-the-nose theme.** "Learning what victory means from a loser" is a risk. Antidote: make Mercy prickly, funny, specific. Give her an actual goal that isn't uplift — she wants to keep the stall, she wants to make a shoe from scratch, she wants to beat one specific rival, she wants her father's ledger to have her own name in it. - **The magic shoes climax** could be corny. Fix: make the refusal cost something concrete. Maybe she doesn't refuse — maybe she wears them and wins and it's *hollow*, and the real climax is what she does after. That might be better and less preachy. Or: she wears them, and they work, and she realizes mid-race she's not moving — the world is moving around her — and she takes them off. Physical, visceral, showable. - **Sneaker culture authenticity.** Use real texture: yellowed midsoles, icy soles, sole swaps, acetone, Barge cement, deoxidizing with hydrogen peroxide and UV, heat guns, insole shanks, crease guards, "beaters," "deadstock," "GR" vs "PE," Kantamanto and secondhand bales, resale bots, StockX-like authentication. This grounds the fantasy. Craft detail is the story's biggest asset — the cobbler's-bench specificity. - **The wear pattern as central image.** A shoe's sole records everything about the person: gait, weight, pronation, the miles. A god with no wear pattern has never gone anywhere. This is the story's best single metaphor and should recur in every chapter. Title could be "Wear Pattern." - **Names.** Mercy is nice (grace, mercy vs. victory — good thematic rhyme). Her father: Kwame? The rival runner: someone with a great name. Zelos could go by "Zell." Hephaestus as "Mr. Festus" or "Vulcan Shoe Repair." Hermes as "Herm," a courier. Athena maybe skip. Bia and Kratos as a pair of security guards at the drop — nice deep-cut joke for the mythologically literate. - **Ending tone.** Avoid tidy triumph. Best ending: quiet, working, hands busy. The gods keep coming. The stall stays open. Nike walks somewhere on purpose. ## Alternate concepts I could still pivot to - **The retirement home.** *Elysium Gardens*, assisted living, gods in Velcro sneakers. A nurse's aide POV. Funny and sad. Less propulsive; probably better as a 2,000-word piece than 8,000. - **The courier.** Hermes gig-economy story. Strong but narrower thematically. - **The authenticator.** Woman in a warehouse who can tell fake from real. Theological. Cold. Could be great but more cerebral, less heart. - **The sweatshop reversal.** Gods stitching the shoes; the factory floor as Olympus. Bleak, powerful, hard to sustain warmth. Elements from these can be folded in: Hermes-as-courier appears in ch 3; the factory/making thread comes through Hephaestus; the authentication motif can be Mercy's *skill* (she can tell what's real by hand, which is why she can see gods). # Reflection Looking over all this, the ideas that generate genuine heat are the ones where the pun and the pathos are the same thing. "Gods wore sneakers" is funny as a sight gag — Zeus in Velcro orthopedics — but that joke exhausts itself in a paragraph. What has legs (feet) is the double meaning: gods *wore* sneakers, past tense, meaning they used to be here and now they're only on the shoes. That's the version with an engine in it. **The Nike conceit is the single strongest asset.** The goddess of victory whose name was bought for thirty-five dollars and is now spoken more than any prayer in history, yet never *meant* — that is a complete tragedy in one sentence. It is mythologically accurate (she was a minor personification, a winged attendant), it is historically real (Carolyn Davidson, the $35 swoosh, 1971), and it makes the prompt literal without being cheap. I should absolutely build on this. The key discipline: **never name the corporation.** Let the goddess say "my name" and let the reader do the work. That restraint will make the story feel mythic rather than like brand-snark, and it sidesteps both legal awkwardness and the tonal trap of satire-for-its-own-sake. **The Styx siblings are a gift I shouldn't waste.** Nike, Zelos, Kratos, Bia — Victory, Rivalry, Power, Violence — the four who sat at Zeus's throne. Mapping them onto the sneaker economy is almost too neat: Zelos is the hype and the resale market and the wanting; Kratos and Bia are the security detail at the drop, the muscle, and also, glancingly, the things that happen to kids over shoes. Zelos as antagonist is much better than a corporate villain or a generic Olympian, because he's Nike's *brother*, which makes the conflict familial and therefore emotional rather than abstract. He can also be genuinely charming and half-right, which is what a good antagonist needs. The one caution: Kratos and Bia as a deadpan pair of enforcers is a good joke but they must not become comic relief that deflates the threat. Keep them silent, keep them brief. **The repair shop is the right center of gravity.** Of all the mortal-POV options — runner, courier, authenticator, factory worker — the cobbler/restorer is best because it is *hands-on*, it generates constant sensory specificity, and it makes the protagonist's skill the same as her supernatural perception. She reads soles the way an augur reads entrails. She can see gods because she can see wear. That's not a coincidence I have to explain; it's a structural rhyme that does its work silently. It also gives me a fixed location where the divine can arrive, which solves pacing: I don't need a quest, I need a doorway. The **wear pattern** image is the best thing in all this brainstorming and should be load-bearing. A sole records a life: pronation, weight, the miles, the way you push off, whether you drag. A god whose sneakers are pristine after three thousand years has never once walked toward something she chose. The whole story can be the process of getting a wear pattern onto one pair of shoes. That gives me an object-level goal, a metaphor, and a final image, all at once. It also gives me a title candidate stronger than anything else I've generated. **Where I'm worried:** *The theme is on the nose.* "The goddess of Victory learns what victory means from a girl who always loses" is legible to the point of being schematic. If I write it straight, it will read like a parable and the reader will be a page ahead of me for 8,000 words. Mitigations I trust: (a) give Mercy a want that is concrete, small, and slightly unlikable — she wants to beat one specific girl, she wants the stall's lease, she wants her own name in her father's ledger — rather than a want that is *about* the theme; (b) make Zelos persuasive enough that the sponsorship offer is genuinely the right choice by any sane accounting; (c) do not let anyone state the theme aloud, especially not Nike. The moment a character says "maybe winning isn't everything," the story dies. *The magic-shoes climax is the weakest structural element.* "She's offered enchanted footwear and nobly declines" is the most predictable version and I should resist it. The alternative I sketched — she *does* wear them, they *do* work, and the horror is that she isn't running, the world is being moved around her — is far better. It's physical, it's showable, it turns the wish-fulfilment inside out, and it means her heroic act is *taking something off mid-race*, which is an image rather than a speech. Losing after having briefly held winning is more interesting than never touching it. I'm fairly confident that's the move. *The pantheon parade could bloat.* At 1,000 words a chapter I cannot afford a page of cameos. Four divine figures maximum: Nike, Zelos, Hephaestus, Hermes — with Kratos and Bia as wordless furniture. Athena, Zeus, Ares, and the retirement-home gags are darlings I should kill early, or reduce to a single line of texture (a customer, a shoe left unclaimed, a name in the ledger). *The labor/factory thread is morally the most serious material here and also the easiest to botch.* Making a real, ongoing injustice — who stitches the shoes — into a scenic backdrop for a Greek goddess's redemption would be tacky. But ignoring it entirely, in a story about sneakers and gods, feels
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention ## What I'm writing A short story in eight chapters, roughly 1,000 words each, built on the double meaning of the prompt: gods *wore* sneakers — past tense — because worship migrated to the shoe and left them behind. The spine is Nike. Not the corporation, which I will never name, but the goddess: a minor winged personification, an attendant at Athena's shoulder, whose name was purchased in 1971 for thirty-five dollars and is now spoken more often than any prayer in human history and meant not once. She is enormous and hollow. Her sneakers, after three thousand years, have no wear pattern on the soles, because she has never walked anywhere she chose. The mortal center is **Mercy Boateng**, seventeen, who runs her dead father's sneaker restoration stall in a dying mall. Her craft is reading soles — pronation, drag, push-off, miles — and that is also why she can see gods: she can see what's real by hand. I want her want to be small, concrete, and slightly unattractive: she wants the lease renewed, she wants her name written in her father's ledger as a maker and not just a repairer, and she wants, badly and pettily, to beat one specific girl on the track. Nothing she wants is thematic. The theme will have to arrive sideways or not at all. The antagonist is **Zelos** — Rivalry — Nike's actual brother in myth, one of the four children of Styx who sat at Zeus's throne alongside Kratos (Power) and Bia (Violence). He is the true god of the modern sneaker economy: the hype, the drop, the resale market, the wanting. He brokered his sister's deal. He will be charming, generous, and substantially correct, and the offer he makes Mercy will be, by any sane accounting, the right one to take. Kratos and Bia appear as two silent men in black windbreakers and are never funny. **Hephaestus** is an old machinist in a shuttered factory outbuilding, and **Hermes** is a courier on an e-bike with his heels worn through to the foam. Those are the only other gods with lines. Athena, Zeus, Ares, the retirement home, the Velcro orthopedics gag — all cut. ## Choices **Central image and title: the wear pattern.** A sole is a record of a life. It is load-bearing in every chapter and it is the last image of the story. Working title: **Wear Pattern**. **The climax.** Mercy is given the last true divine footwear — winged sandals reforged as sneakers — and she *wears them*. They work. And the horror is that she isn't running; the world is being moved around her, the track sliding past like a walkway, and she is standing still inside a victory. Her heroic act is taking them off mid-race, barefoot on wet rubber, and losing. Not a refusal, a divestment. An image, not a speech. **Voice.** Close third, past tense, mostly Mercy — plain, tactile, dry, unsentimental, heavy on the physical vocabulary of the craft (Barge cement, acetone, yellowed midsoles, heat gun, insole shank, crease, beater, deadstock). One chapter (five) shifts to Nike's first person for the origin: Samothrace, the temple, the room in 1971, the check. That chapter is allowed to be beautiful; the others are not. **Restraint I'm committing to.** No character states the theme. Nike especially never explains what victory means. The corporation is never named — only "my name," "the mark," "the check-mark," "the company." No wisecracking gods. The mythology is never lectured; readers who know Styx's children get a gift, readers who don't lose nothing. **The labor question.** I will not build a factory set piece and I will not pretend the shoes make themselves. It enters through Hephaestus, who made things by hand and was replaced, and through one hard image Mercy already carries: her father's ledger has the names of everyone whose shoes he fixed, and she knows the name of nobody who made them. One line, not a chapter. Enough to be honest, not enough to be tourism. **What I'm avoiding.** Cameo bloat. Gaiman pastiche. Brand snark. Uplift. A tidy triumph. Any sentence in which a character learns a lesson out loud. The word "hype" in the narration. Nike being wise. **Ending.** Quiet, hands busy. Mercy resoles the white sneakers and they finally take a wear pattern. Zelos is diminished but not destroyed, because he is too modern to kill. The stall stays open. A name written on a tongue in ballpoint. # Chapter Planning **1. Sole Survivor** (~1,000) Mercy at the stall in Pinewood Court, a mall with four surviving tenants. Establish the craft in loving detail, her father's ledger, the lease notice, the cracked public track behind the mall where she runs badly at night. A tall woman brings in a pair of plain white sneakers, no branding, no logo, and asks for something odd: not a clean, not a restoration. She wants them *worn*. Mercy turns them over and the outsoles are factory-perfect — no drag, no pronation, no miles — though the uppers have creases like a thing walked in for centuries. Mercy names the price. The woman doesn't blink. Hook: Mercy writes her in the ledger and the pen won't take the name. **2. Wear Pattern** (~1,000) Mercy tries everything — sandpaper, heat gun, a mile on the sidewalk in them herself — and the soles reset overnight. The woman returns. They talk while Mercy works; she is bad at small talk and good at questions about gait. Mercy sees, when the woman shrugs off her jacket, two vertical seams down her back like the stitching on a heel counter. That night Mercy runs; the woman watches from the chain-link, doesn't cheer, just watches, and Mercy runs the last two hundred meters harder than she meant to. Establish rival: Dinah Achebe, who beats Mercy by eleven seconds every single time, and whom Mercy loathes with real specificity. **3. The Ledger of Small Repairs** (~1,000) Word travels. A courier, Herm, drops off two pairs with the heels worn through to nothing — messengers ruin heels — and pays in something Mercy can't quite account for. Establish the rules obliquely through his chatter and Nike's corrections: gods live on attention, and attention moved. Mercy takes a bus to an outbuilding behind a closed plant to source a rare midsole and meets an old machinist who calls himself Festus, hands ruined, who looks at her thumbs and says she has the calluses of a maker, not a fixer. He asks what she's ever made from scratch. She has never finished a pair. Ends with the woman finally giving a name — Nike — and Mercy laughing, because obviously, it's on eleven pairs in the shop. **4. Zelos** (~1,000) A man in beautiful sneakers arrives with two silent men in black windbreakers. Zell. He is warm, funny, and has already paid the mall's arrears. His offer: her stall becomes a real store, her name on the door, and he'll put her in the Legacy Mile — a sponsored street race with a purse that covers the lease for three years. He is right about everything: nobody gets a shop by loving shoes. Nike, watching, says almost nothing until he leaves, and then tells Mercy how she knows him, and it is the first time Mercy understands that "my name" means the mark on the wall behind her. **5. Thirty-Five Dollars** (~1,000) Nike, first person. Samothrace. Being an attendant, a decoration on other gods' shoulders, an abstraction with wings. The slow centuries of thinning. Then the room in 1971: the design student, the sketch, the check written for thirty-five dollars, and Zelos with the pen. What it is to be spoken a billion times a day by people who mean rubber. She has reach without interior; she can be everywhere and arrive nowhere. Ends on what she has come to Mercy for, stated in the flattest possible terms: she wants to walk somewhere on purpose, and she needs a wear pattern to prove she did. **6. The Drop** (~1,000) Mercy signs. Consequence chapter. She goes to a release at Zell's flagship: the line around the block, the bots, the resale prices, Kratos and Bia at the door. A boy she has repaired shoes for since he was eleven gets his taken off him in the lot, and she finds him sitting on the curb in his socks, and the shoes are worth more than the boy is to anyone in that line. Afterward she goes to Festus, who gives her a shoebox: the last pair he ever made by hand, uppers stitched with something that was once feathers, and tells her plainly they will make her win, and that he is giving them to her anyway because he is tired of being the only one who knows what they cost. **7. The Legacy Mile** (~1,000) Rain, floodlights, closed streets, Dinah on the line, gods in the crowd. Mercy laces the winged shoes. The gun. And she is not running — the city is sliding past her, the road unspooling, other runners becoming scenery, the sensation of a moving walkway, no burn in her lungs, no wear on her soles. Standing still inside a victory. At three-quarters she stops, sits down on wet asphalt with the leaders' spray in her face, and takes them off. Runs the last four hundred barefoot. Comes fifth. Dinah wins. Mercy, hands on knees, throwing up on the finish line, says the name out loud — not for the win, for the last four hundred meters — and it is the first time in three thousand years anyone has meant it. **8. Wear Pattern (Reprise)** (~1,000) Coda, weeks later. The purse is gone; the lease is not renewed but a smaller unit near the loading dock is cheap. Zelos is still in business, because he is too modern to kill, and he sends a gift she doesn't open. Herm still comes. The boy has new shoes. Mercy resoles the white sneakers — and this time, when Nike comes back three days later from wherever she chose to walk, the outsoles have drag on the left, a heel strike, forty miles of somewhere. Mercy writes a name in the ledger and the pen takes it. Last beat: she finishes her own first pair from scratch, and on the tongue, in ballpoint, in her own handwriting, is a name that is not a brand.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a human writer might actually come at this A human who got the prompt "Gods wore sneakers" probably wouldn't build a cathedral. They'd start from something they personally know — the smell of a shoe repair shop, the specific humiliation of being the slow kid on a team, the aunt who wore the same white Reeboks for eleven years, the guy at the market who sold "Nikke" trainers with four stripes. The piece would grow outward from a lump of real texture rather than downward from a thesis. They'd also probably resist the pun for a while and then give in to it sideways. The Nike/Nike gag is the first thing anyone thinks of. A good human writer either avoids it entirely or uses it so late and so quietly that it feels like an accident. My plan uses it as the *entire engine*, which is a choice, but it's the obvious choice, and obviousness is a real cost. A human writer would allow the story to be about something they're actually irritated about. Irritation is the most reliable engine in short fiction. What's the irritation here? Maybe: that craft has become content. That the people who make things are anonymous and the people who *want* things are the whole economy. That nostalgia is a retail category. My plan gestures at these but keeps them in a headlock — "one line, not a chapter" — which is disciplined but may also be cowardly. A human would probably also let the story be *smaller* than eight chapters of mythic architecture. Eight thousand words is not long. Human short stories at that length usually have one location, two or three people, and one event. My plan has four gods, two locations plus a factory plus a race course plus a flagship store, an origin flashback, a signed contract, a mugging, a magic object, and a coda. That's a novella's inventory poured into a short story's cup. # Telltale LLM habits and why they'd hurt this piece **1. Thesis-first construction.** LLMs build stories as arguments with illustrations attached. Every element earns its keep by servicing the theme. Humans leave junk in. The junk is what makes it feel lived. My plan is *conspicuously* well-organised: every god maps to an economic function, every image maps to a meaning, the central metaphor is declared "load-bearing." Load-bearing metaphors are a construction concept, not a fiction concept. Readers can smell scaffolding. **2. The symmetrical metaphor.** "A sole records a life; a god with no wear pattern has never walked anywhere she chose." That's a *beautiful* idea. It is also completely closed. There's no slack in it, no residue, nothing that doesn't resolve. Real metaphors in good fiction are lopsided — they fit in one place and chafe in another, and the chafing is interesting. Mine fits everywhere, which means it will start to feel like a keychain being jangled. **3. Naming as meaning-delivery.** Mercy Boateng. Mercy versus Victory. The plan even flags the "thematic rhyme." A human might well name her Mercy — it's a real name — but wouldn't *design* it. And the reader who notices the rhyme will feel handled. Same with "Sole Survivor" as the shop name (a pun a real shop would absolutely have, to be fair) and "Pinewood Court" (perfectly plausible, slightly generic-American-mall). **4. Compulsive competence.** LLM protagonists are gifted. Mercy is a savant of soles who can perceive divinity through craft. That's a superhero origin dressed as blue-collar realism. Humans write protagonists who are *okay* at things, or good at one thing and bad at the surrounding life. The plan hedges by making her a bad runner, but bad-at-running-but-spiritually-magnificent-at-cobbling is still flattering. **5. Antagonist who is "charming and substantially correct."** This is now itself a cliché — the LLM-approved sophisticated villain. Zelos being right about the money and warm about it is a good instinct, but "charming, funny, has already paid the arrears, and everything he says is true" is a *type*. Real Rivalry isn't a slick guy in nice shoes. Real rivalry is your friend not congratulating you. It's checking someone's story. It's the ache in your chest when someone you know gets what you wanted. A god of that would be much stranger and much more intimate than a marketing executive with two silent bodyguards. The windbreaker bodyguards are, honestly, a Marvel bit. **6. The tasteful restraint that becomes evasion.** My plan is proud of what it won't do: never name the corporation, never state the theme, no wisecracking gods, one line about labour. Some of this is genuine discipline. But there's a difference between restraint and hedging. "Never name the brand" is partly craft and partly liability-management, and the story will feel it if the reason is timidity. Similarly, "one line, not a chapter" about who makes the shoes: that's not restraint, that's a shrug with good manners. Either the story cares about that or it doesn't. Deciding in advance to touch it exactly once, with exactly the right weight, is the most LLM sentence in the whole plan. **7. The impressive climax.** The moving-walkway victory is genuinely a good image, and I'm still fond of it. But look at its shape: a visually striking, thematically perfect, physically legible act of noble divestment, followed by vomiting on the finish line and speaking the goddess's name for the first time in three thousand years. That is a *set piece*. It's cinematic. It resolves the mythic plot and the emotional plot and the metaphor in one gesture. Humans rarely get climaxes that tidy, and readers don't fully believe them. **8. The bow.** Chapter 8 as planned is a stack of resolutions: purse gone but new unit found, boy has new shoes, Herm still comes, Zelos too modern to kill (a *knowing* non-resolution, which is its own bow), soles finally worn, pen finally takes the name, first handmade pair completed, name in ballpoint on the tongue. That's seven closures in a thousand words. It reads as a checklist of emotional debts being settled. **9. Rhythmic sameness and aphorism.** The plan's own prose has the tell: "She is enormous and hollow." "Not a refusal, a divestment. An image, not a speech." Short declarative punches. In the story itself this becomes a drumbeat — every paragraph ending on a zinger. Humans write long baggy sentences, then a short one, then a sentence that doesn't quite land, then a joke that isn't funny to anyone but the narrator. **10. No dead time, no boredom, no weather that isn't meaningful.** Everything in the plan happens *for a reason*. Rain in chapter 7 is dramatic rain. Human stories have Tuesdays. **11. Emotional legibility.** Characters in LLM stories feel one clear thing at a time and the reader always knows what it is. Mercy loathes Dinah "with real specificity" — good instinct — but the plan will probably render that as a clean, describable resentment rather than the actual sludge: admiration, wanting to be friends, wanting her to get injured, being ashamed of wanting that, being nice to her at the water table. **12. Dialogue as information transfer or theme delivery.** Herm's "chatter" exists to explain the rules. Festus asks "what have you ever made from scratch?" — a question no human asks except in fiction. Nike's flat declaration of her need at the end of chapter 5 is a mission statement. **13. Research-flavoured texture as garnish.** Barge cement, acetone, heat gun, midsole shank, deoxidising. Good stuff. But LLMs sprinkle it evenly, like seasoning, at the same density in every chapter. Real craft knowledge in fiction clumps — a character will go on for half a page about one obsessive thing and then say nothing technical for pages, because that's how enthusiasts talk. # Deeper critique of specific plan elements **The Nike concept.** Still the strongest asset, but it has a structural problem: she is a *concept-shaped* character. Her want is abstract (to be meant), her lack is abstract (interiority), her proof is symbolic (a wear pattern). Everything about her is allegory. In chapter 5 she gets a whole first-person origin, which will be the most beautifully written chapter and possibly the most inert, because backstory-as-explanation is exactly what a hollow character needs least. Better if she's just *weird* — a woman with an unnerving quality of attention, who doesn't understand certain ordinary things, and whose sadness is never explained by her, only inferred by Mercy. Also: the thirty-five dollars. It's a real fact, it's a great fact, and it's been in a hundred think pieces. Using it as the tragic core risks the story feeling like a dramatisation of a fact I read. **The wear-pattern quest.** "Make my shoes look worn" is a wonderful opening ask — genuinely strange, immediately concrete, exactly the sort of request a real shop would get and refuse. But once it becomes the *goal of the book*, and the final image is the soles finally showing drag on the left, it's a fable. The gap between "odd request" and "metaphysical proof of selfhood" is where the story becomes an LLM story. **Chapter 6's mugging.** This is the plan's most dangerous move. A boy Mercy has known since he was eleven has his shoes stolen and sits on the curb in his socks, so that Mercy can understand the economy. That is a real thing that happens to real kids, deployed as a moral beat for a middle-class-adjacent protagonist's arc. It's the exact instrumentalisation the plan claims to be avoiding with the factory. If it stays, the boy needs to be a person with his own opinion about it — possibly an unimpressed one, possibly he thinks Mercy's reaction is embarrassing. **Kratos and Bia.** Cut them or transform them entirely. Two silent enforcers in black windbreakers is a genre reflex. Bia as a woman who does crowd control at events and is very good at her job and quite kind is stranger. Or they're not present at all and Zelos's power is purely social. **Dinah Achebe.** "Beats her by eleven seconds every time" is a nicely specific detail. But the rival-who-wins-and-is-therefore-thematically-relevant is a slot. What if Dinah is barely aware Mercy exists? What if the rivalry is entirely one-directional and slightly pathetic? That's more human and funnier and sadder. **Hephaestus/Festus.** Old craftsman who gives the young protagonist the magic object and a warning is the oldest slot in the box. And "Festus" as a name is cute in the bad way. Consider: he doesn't want to give her anything, he wants her to do a boring favour, and the shoes are just sitting there and she takes them. **The ledger.** The pen that won't take a god's name is a lovely small piece of magic — genuinely good. But it's also a device that will get used three times (won't take it, still won't take it, finally takes it) and that three-beat structure is very tidy. **The Legacy Mile.** A sponsored street race with a purse that exactly covers three years' rent. That's plot machinery humming. # Ideas for making it more human **Reduce the inventory.** One location and its immediate surroundings. Cut the flagship store, cut the factory outbuilding, cut the origin flashback as its own chapter, cut either Hermes or Hephaestus. Let the gods come to the shop, because that's the best joke and the best structure. **Let it be funnier and lower.** Not wisecracking gods — the opposite: gods who are boring, who have annoying opinions, who get the terminology wrong, who leave their shoes for eight months and never pick them up. A rack of unclaimed divine footwear at the back with dusty tickets on it is funnier and sadder than any speech. **Make the mundane problem the actual problem.** The lease. The card reader that doesn't work. Her mother wanting her to do something else. A story where a goddess appears and the protagonist is mostly worried about rent is more human than one where the rent is a plot device that gets solved by a race purse. **Give Mercy a bad habit and a real flaw.** She lies about turnaround times. She keeps a pair someone never picked up and wears them. She's contemptuous of customers. She's been quietly not opening her father's mail. **Let something be unresolved and not knowingly unresolved.** Not "Zelos survives because he's too modern to kill" (which is a thesis). Something that just doesn't come back: a customer who never returns, a question Nike asks that Mercy never answers, a pair of shoes she can't fix. **Let the pun be a joke inside the story.** Mercy should absolutely find the name thing funny and say so. "That's your name? Like the—" "Yes." "Okay." Letting the characters be as sceptical as the reader defuses the cleverness. **Undercut the climax.** Options: she wears the winged shoes and they don't work at all, or work badly, or she never gets to race because the event's cancelled/rained out/she's not eligible. Or she wins and it's fine, actually, and the problem was never the winning. Or the race happens off-page and the chapter is about her getting home afterward. Something that refuses the set piece. **Let the labour question be handled by a character who has an axe to grind and is somewhat annoying about it,** rather than by the narration's tasteful single line. A customer, a cousin, a guy at the market. Real politics enters fiction through people being tedious about it, not through elegant restraint. **Allow bad writing in the good sense.** A paragraph about resoling that goes on too long. A description of the mall's food court that has no thematic function. Mercy's texts. A digression about her father that contradicts something said earlier. **Change the ending's shape.** Instead of seven closures: one small thing, unremarked. Maybe just the shop opening again on a Tuesday, and Nike's shoes are gone from the rack, and Mercy doesn't know when that happened. **Consider first person for Mercy** — it invites idiosyncrasy, digression, unreliability, and jokes, all of which fight the plan's stateliness. **Kill at least one thing I love.** The moving-walkway image, probably. Or the wear pattern as final image. Keeping both is greedy and both are doing the same job.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention ## The story One location, three months, a small cast. **Mercy Boateng**, nineteen, runs her late father's shoe repair unit in a mostly dead shopping centre. The prompt is honoured literally and structurally: gods come into her shop with sneakers, and the shop is where the whole story happens, apart from two short trips outside it. The central relationship is Mercy and a woman who calls herself **Nike** — yes, that Nike, and yes, Mercy finds it stupid and says so. Nike's request in chapter one is the story's engine and it stays small: she wants a pair of plain white sneakers made to look worn. Not enchanted. Not restored. Worn. Mercy takes the job because it pays and because it's interesting, and she never fully solves it, and that's fine. The antagonist is **Zelos**, her brother, and I'm stripping him of the slick-executive costume entirely. No bodyguards, no flagship, no windbreakers. He's a man who sits in the food court most afternoons with a coffee, who is friendly, who remembers everyone's business, who tells Mercy things about other people that she shouldn't know and can't unknow, and who ruins her relationship with running by making her aware of where she stands. He is the god of comparison. His weapon is information. He never makes an offer that's a contract; he makes remarks. ## Choices **No race climax.** The Legacy Mile is cut. There is a race in chapter seven but it happens at 6:40 a.m. on a Sunday at a municipal track, it's a time trial with eleven people at it, and it's the most ordinary event in the story. The winged shoes are cut too. There is no magic object that makes anyone win. **What replaces it:** the thing Nike actually wants turns out to be duller and stranger than proof-of-selfhood. She wants to know what a person's soles say about them, because she has three thousand years of standing at other people's shoulders and no idea how to tell one life from another. Mercy is the only person she's found who reads soles. That's it. That's the whole divine crisis: a specialist who's forgotten what she's a specialist in. **Wear pattern:** stays as a working detail, demoted from load-bearing symbol. Mercy talks about soles because it's her job. It is never explained as a metaphor and the story does not end on it. **Voice:** first person, Mercy, past tense, close and slightly grudging. Digressive. Funny when she isn't trying. Long sentences about Barge cement and heat guns, clumped where she's interested and absent where she isn't. She lies to customers about turnaround times. She has not opened her father's mail since April. **The gods are boring.** This is the main comic engine and the main sad one. A rack of unclaimed shoes at the back with tickets on them going yellow — some of those tickets are two thousand years old. Gods leave things and don't come back. Hermes is a courier called **Herm** who is a bad tipper and talks too much about brake pads. There is no Hephaestus, no Athena, no Ares. Nobody explains the rules of divinity to anybody. **The name.** The corporation is never named. Mercy makes the joke; Nike doesn't laugh; it's dropped. The thirty-five dollars appears once, as a bitter aside in a conversation about something else, not as a tragic origin. **No flashback chapter.** **Labour:** carried by **Adjoa**, Mercy's cousin, who works in fulfilment and is tediously and correctly angry about it, and who Mercy finds exhausting, and who is right. **The mugging is cut.** Replaced by something smaller and less exploitable: a regular customer, a fourteen-year-old called **Tobi**, who wants his beaters made to look new because he's ashamed of them, which is the exact inverse of Nike's request. Mercy is not moved by this. She just notices it. **What I'm avoiding:** thesis delivery, aphoristic paragraph-endings, symmetry, the wise mentor, the sophisticated villain, seven closures in the coda, weather that means something, any character saying anything about what victory is. **Ending:** the shop opens on a Tuesday. Nike's shoes are gone off the rack and Mercy doesn't know when. One unresolved thing stays unresolved and is not commented on. # Chapter Planning **1. Turnaround Time** Mercy, the unit, the centre — four surviving tenants, a Costa, a phone repair kiosk, a place that sells crystals. The craft, at length and with pleasure. Her father, glancingly. The lease letter she hasn't opened. A tall woman comes in with plain white sneakers, no branding, and asks Mercy to make them look worn. Mercy quotes her double and lies about turnaround. The woman pays cash and gives her name and Mercy makes the joke. The woman says "Yes." Ends with Mercy turning them over: the soles are factory-clean, but the uppers have creases like decades. **2. Rack of Unclaimed** Mercy works on the whites — sandpaper, acetone, a mile round the car park in them herself — and they come back clean overnight. Not dramatically; she just notices on Thursday that Tuesday's work is gone. Introduce the rack at the back: forty pairs nobody collected, some tickets so old the ink's gone. Herm arrives with heels worn to foam, talks about brake pads, tips badly, says something offhand that tells us he's known the rack a long time. Adjoa comes by on her break and is annoying about warehouse quotas. Mercy runs at the municipal track that evening because she always has, and is slow, and likes it. **3. Zelos in the Food Court** Nike starts coming in and sitting. She doesn't chat well. She watches Mercy's hands. Meanwhile Mercy notices the man in the food court who knows her name. He's nice. He mentions, casually, that the phone repair man's turnover, and that Dinah from the running club has a coach now, and that a girl Mercy went to school with has a shop on the high street. Mercy leaves the conversation feeling worse than she has in months and cannot locate why. First hint Nike is avoiding the food court. **4. What the Soles Say** The actual reveal, undramatic. Nike asks Mercy to read a stranger's soles — a pair on the bench — and Mercy does it easily: heel striker, drags the right, works standing up, ten stone something, walks on grass on weekends. Nike listens like it's music she can't hear. She admits, flatly, that she can't tell people apart, that she has stood at shoulders for three thousand years and remembers no faces. The thirty-five dollars comes out here as an aside and Mercy doesn't understand it until later. Tobi's beaters come in; he wants them made new. Mercy takes the job. **5. Adjoa** The chapter that isn't about gods. Adjoa at Mercy's flat, Mercy's mother on speakerphone, the unopened mail finally opened: the unit's going, the whole east wing is going. Adjoa says the obvious thing about how the shoes Mercy loves are made by people on her shift rate and Mercy says something cruel and true back. They don't resolve it. Mercy walks home past the centre at midnight and the whites are sitting on her workbench, immaculate again, and she puts them on the rack out of spite. **6. Nine Seconds** Zelos again, and this time he does the real damage: he tells Mercy her times, all of them, going back four years, and where she'd place at county, and what Dinah ran last Sunday. He's not cruel. He's admiring. Afterwards Mercy can't run without doing arithmetic. Nike finds her at the track not running, and this is the closest they come to an argument — Nike says something bluntly unhelpful about her brother. Mercy takes the whites back off the rack. **7. Sunday, 6:40 a.m.** The time trial. Eleven people, a man with a clipboard, frost on the infield. Dinah barely knows Mercy's name, which is worse than a rivalry. Mercy runs it in the whites — not because they're magic, they aren't, they're just a good fit and hers are shot — and she runs badly, four seconds off her own best, and finishes fifth of eleven. Nothing happens. Nike is at the fence and has walked there, three miles, on her own legs, on purpose, because she wanted to see. Afterwards Mercy sits on the kerb and Nike sits next to her and asks a question about hamstrings. **8. Tuesday** Coda. New unit near the loading bay, cheaper, worse light. Mercy moves the rack. Tobi picks up his beaters and they look new and he's happy and Mercy privately thinks she's ruined them. Zelos is still in the food court and she still says hello. Adjoa helps her carry things and neither of them mentions it. Mercy goes to check the whites and they're gone off the rack; she doesn't know when, and she checks the ticket book and there's no note. Last beat: she turns over the pair she's currently working on — hers, the shot ones, being resoled — and looks at the sole, and the chapter ends on the shop opening, not on a symbol.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Mercy Boateng Nineteen. Born in Coventry, raised in Coventry, has been to London eleven times and hated four of them. Her father, Kwaku Boateng, came over in 1989 and worked at a cobbler's on Far Gosford Street for six years before taking over the unit in the Cranbrook Centre in 1997, which everyone including him thought was a step up at the time. He died in April of the year the story opens — a stroke, at the bench, and the awful comedy of it is that he was found by the woman who runs the crystal shop, who has never stopped mentioning it. Mercy sat her A-levels eleven days later out of spite and got two Bs and a C and has done nothing with them. She is not a savant. She's competent, and she's been doing it since she was eight, which is a different thing. What she genuinely has is a good eye for soles, which came from a childhood game her dad invented to shut her up on slow afternoons: he'd hand her a pair off the rack, cover the ticket, and she'd guess the customer. She got good at it. It's not mystical. It's the same as a barber knowing what your hair does. She's slightly embarrassed by how proud of it she is. Flaws, specifically: she lies about turnaround times, always, as policy — quotes ten days for a job she'll do Thursday, then rings them Wednesday and lets them be delighted. She's contemptuous of about a third of her customers and it leaks. She hasn't opened her father's post since April; it's in a Tesco bag under the bench, and she's aware that this has moved from procrastination into something else, and she manages this awareness by not looking at the bag. She keeps a pair of size-6 Sambas that a woman never collected and she wears them to the pub. She is unkind about Adjoa behind Adjoa's back and knows Adjoa is a better person than she is. She runs. Has done since Year 9, with the Coundon Road club, three sessions a week, and she is genuinely and permanently mediocre — 5k in the low 22s, which is respectable and will never be anything else. This is the thing she'd defend hardest if pushed: she likes running badly. She likes the specific pleasure of the last 400 when it hurts and you're not going to do anything special. She has never articulated this and would be annoyed if someone did it for her. Physically: five foot four, broad through the shoulders from the bench work, hands that look older than she is — glue-stained, a permanent burn scar on the left thumb pad from a heat gun at fifteen. Hair in a scarf when she's working because of the dust. She sits hunched to one side. She has a habit of turning any shoe she's handed sole-up first, before she looks at the upper, which people find rude. She doesn't smile at customers on principle; she smiles a lot at Herm, who doesn't notice. Wants: the unit to stay open, which it won't. Her name on something. To not have to move back in with her mum in Radford. Nothing grand. > "Ten days," I said, which was a lie, and she said that was fine, which meant she'd have paid more, which is the sort of thing I notice and then think about at eleven at night." > "Everyone thinks a sole is the bit that wears out. The sole's the bit that tells you. Uppers lie. People stuff uppers with cedar and pray over them. Nobody's ever cleaned an outsole in their life." --- # Nike She has been called Nike for as long as there has been anyone to call her anything, which is the least interesting fact about her. What she is: an attendant. She stood at shoulders. Athena's, mostly, and before that at the shoulders of people whose names have gone. Her job was to be the thing that arrived at the moment of the outcome — she was never the outcome, she was the *arrival* of it. Three thousand years of being present at the most important second of somebody's life and then not being there for any of the rest. The consequence, and this is her actual problem: she cannot tell people apart. Not won't — can't. She has stood beside ten million faces at their single best moment and retained none of them, because she was never issued the equipment for it. She remembers outcomes. She remembers the *shape* of a win from the inside. She could not describe her own mother. She sold the name in 1971 and Zelos handled it, and the sum was thirty-five dollars, and she mentions this exactly once in the story and not as tragedy — as an irrelevance she can't stop returning to, the way you'd mention a bad haircut from decades ago. The name being everywhere hasn't hollowed her out in some cosmic way; it's just noise. Being said ten million times a day by people who mean rubber is like living next to a motorway. You stop hearing it and you sleep badly. She's not wise. She's not enigmatic. She's a poor conversationalist — she doesn't do reciprocity, doesn't ask follow-ups unless she's actually curious, will sit in silence for forty minutes and not register it as strange. She misses jokes and doesn't mind. She has some very specific incompetences: she can't gauge how long a thing takes, she doesn't understand queueing at the counter versus standing near it, and she has no small talk whatsoever. She's also capable of being extremely blunt about people in a way Mercy finds funny and then slightly frightening. The white sneakers: unbranded, canvas, plain, and she has had them for a while — vague on how long. She wants them worn because she has noticed that everyone else's shoes have information on them and hers don't, and she'd like some. That's the whole of it. She doesn't say it that way. She says "I want these to look like I've been somewhere." Physically: tall, six-one, long-boned, flat-footed in her stance, stands with her weight even on both feet in a way that reads as odd once you see it — nobody stands like that, everybody favours a side. Hair cropped close. Ageless in the annoying way, could be thirty-two or forty-eight. Two vertical lines down her back which Mercy sees once and never asks about. She watches hands. When Mercy works, Nike watches her hands and not her face, and it takes Mercy three weeks to find that comforting rather than creepy. # 1. Turnaround Time The Cranbrook Centre has four tenants left, and one of them is a Costa, which I don't count because a Costa is a fact of nature, like weather. So: three. There's the phone repair place, run by a man called Sami who I like and who is going under. There's Crystal Visions, which sells rocks and dreamcatchers and is somehow doing fine, run by Denise, who found my father, and who mentions it. And there's us. Boateng Shoe Repair, unit 14, east wing, opposite where the Clintons used to be and next to a shutter with a laminated sign on it saying EXCITING PLANS FOR THIS SPACE, which has been there since I was in Year 8. The light in the east wing is bad because the skylights went green with algae about a decade ago and nobody has ever cleaned them, so the whole wing is lit like the bottom of a pond. I've got two Anglepoises and a strip light and I still take the pale ones out to the car park to check the colour. What I do, mostly, is soles. People think it's heels — heels are the bread, heels are ninety seconds and eight quid and you can do them talking — but the interesting money is soles. A Vibram half-sole on a decent boot, that's a proper job. Stitch-down repair, that's a proper job. And then there's the trainers, which is what's kept us alive since about 2016, because it turns out a generation of men in their thirties will pay forty quid to have the midsoles of a shoe deyellowed rather than spend seventy on a new pair, and I do not question this, I just make sure I've got hydrogen peroxide in. Deyellowing is boring. You cling-film them, you paint it on, you put them in the window and let the UV do it, and the window in unit 14 faces the food court so you use a lamp. It's slow and it smells and it works. What actually takes skill is a sole swap — cutting the old outsole off a shoe that was never designed to come apart, cleaning the midsole down without gouging it, getting the new one on with Barge cement so the seam sits flush. Barge is the good stuff. It comes in a yellow tin and it smells like a decision you can't take back and if you get it on your fingers you'll be picking at it for three days. Dad used to say you can tell a bad cobbler by his thumbs. His thumbs were terrible. Mine are getting there. I've got a shiny patch on the left one from a heat gun when I was fifteen, and I remember him not being sympathetic in the slightest, and I remember it as a nice afternoon. He's been dead since April. That's not a thing I'm going to keep doing, mentioning it, but it's relevant to the state of the paperwork, which is: there's a Tesco bag under the bench with about four months of post in it, including two things from the centre management with the Cranbrook logo on the window of the envelope, and I know roughly what they say, and I have decided that I will open them when I have a free afternoon, and I have not had a free afternoon since April. She came in on a Tuesday, about half four, which is when the centre starts making the noise it makes when it's giving up for the day. I heard her before I saw her because the mat inside the door has a bad edge and everybody catches it. Tall. Really tall, six-one maybe, and holding a pair of white canvas trainers by the heels, one in each hand, the way you'd carry two fish. "Are you the one who fixes them," she said. "Depends what's wrong with them." She put them on the counter and I turned them over. I always do that. Sole up, first. Customers hate it — they've brought you the shoe to show you the scuff on the toe, and they want you to look at the scuff, and instead you flip it and study the bottom like a vet. But the sole's the only honest part. Uppers lie. People stuff uppers with cedar and steam the creases and pray over them. Nobody in the history of the world has cleaned an outsole. These were clean. Not cleaned — clean. Factory. There was still a faint mould line on the rubber where it came out of the press, that little raised seam you only ever see on deadstock, and I put my thumb on it and it was sharp. No polish on the ball of the foot. No feather at the outer heel. Nothing at all. I looked at the uppers then and the uppers were creased to hell. Deep across the toe box, both, the leather-look canvas gone soft and grey in the folds, the eyelets slightly pulled. That's ten years of wear on the top of a shoe that has never once touched the ground. Which is impossible, and I want to be clear that I noticed it was impossible, and that I did the thing you do, which is decide it's a manufacturing story you can't be bothered to hear. Insurance job. Prop from a film. Someone's weird uncle. "What do you want doing?" "I want them to look worn." "They do look worn." "Not there." She touched the toe box, dismissive, like the top of the shoe was a wig. "There." And she turned the left one over herself and put one long finger on the outsole, on the flat middle of it, where nothing was. I've been asked for a lot of things. I get asked to make new shoes look old about twice a year — costume people, mostly, and once a man who wanted a pair of work boots to look like he'd worked in them, which I did and charged him for and have never fully recovered from morally. It's a job. It's sandpaper and a wire brush and a bit of shoe cream in the seams and a mile of pavement. It's not hard. "Sixty," I said, which was double. "Fine." "And it's ten days." It wasn't ten days. It was Thursday. I do this, and I'm not going to justify it, except to say that when you tell someone ten days and then ring them on day two, they think you're a magician, and when you tell them Thursday and it's Friday, they think you're a shop that's closing down. "Fine," she said again, and she got a fold of twenties out of her coat, and she didn't look at them while she counted, which is a rich thing to do or a stupid one. I got the book out. "Name for the ticket?" "Nike." I laughed. I did actually laugh, a proper one, out loud, and I gestured at the shelf behind me where there were — I counted afterwards, because I'm like that — eleven pairs with the tick on them, in for various indignities. "Like the —" "Yes." And she stood there and let it be exactly as stupid as it was, and didn't help, and after a second I stopped laughing and wrote it down, and she watched my hand while I did it rather than my face, which I clocked and didn't like. "Tuesday week," I said. "Thursday," she said, and left, and caught the mat on the way out.

The line "you can tell a bad cobbler by his thumbs" and the follow-up about the heat gun scar is the chapter's best small moment: it introduces the father, establishes the relationship, and does it in two sentences without sentimentality. The impossible shoe — factory-clean soles, decade-worn uppers — is introduced with exactly the right narrative restraint. # 2. Rack of Unclaimed I started them Wednesday morning because Wednesday morning is dead. Sami came over about ten with two coffees and we did the thing we do where he tells me his footfall and I tell him mine and we both pretend we're comparing notes rather than checking who's going first. Then I put the whites on the bench and had a proper go. The correct method, if you actually want to age a sole, is not to attack it. Amateurs go at it with a wire brush and you get scratching — you get lines, and lines look like a wire brush, not like walking. What you want is polish and loss. A worn outsole is smoother than a new one, not rougher. The tread goes shiny where the foot rolls, it feathers off at the outer heel where you land, it shears at the ball where you push. So you use fine paper, 400 then 800, worked in the direction of travel, and you take the mould line off first because the mould line is the tell, and then you go at the landing zone with your thumb behind the paper so it wears in a dish, not a flat. I did all that. It took an hour and twenty and it was, I'll admit, satisfying. I took the seam off, I dished the outer heel, I feathered the ball, I rubbed a little black shoe cream into the sidewall stitching and wiped it back so it sat in the seams like grime does. Then I put them on — they were a six and a half, close enough, my toes touched — and did four circuits of the multi-storey, second level, because the concrete up there is coarse and does in about ten minutes what pavement does in a week. Came back sweating with them scuffed at the toe bumper and the tread properly grey. They looked worn. I stood them on the shelf and looked at them from the doorway and they looked like a pair of shoes somebody owned. Thursday I came in at half eight and they were clean. Here's the thing, and it matters: I didn't have a moment. There was no cold-down-the-spine, no stepping back. I picked one up and turned it over and thought *oh, I've put the wrong one out*, and looked behind me for the other, and there wasn't another, and then I thought *Sami's had a laugh*, which was ridiculous, and then I stood there for about forty seconds holding it. The mould line was back. Sharp under the thumb, the way it had been Tuesday. And what I did next, which I think is the honest response and not the film response, was put them in the cupboard under the sink and do three pairs of heels and a zip replacement and not think about it, because a woman had paid me sixty quid and if I let myself have a proper think about it I'd have to give her the sixty back. The rack's at the back, past the sink, on the wall the fire officer doesn't like. It's the unclaimed. Every repair shop has one. You do the job, you ring them, you ring them again, and then eventually the ticket goes yellow and the shoes stay. Dad's rule was six months and then charity, and Dad broke his own rule constantly, so there are things on there I've known my whole life. There's a pair of brogues, tan, size eleven, resoled and dubbined and beautiful, ticket says BENNETT and 1998. There's a single white court shoe. There's some children's Clarks, done, polished, never picked up, which I don't like looking at. And down the far end, low, where the damp gets at the wall, there are four or five pairs where the ticket is not yellow but *brown*, and thin like an old receipt, and the writing on them isn't Dad's and isn't anything I can read. Not a language thing. The ink's just gone, or nearly. One of them has a shape on it that might be a T. The shoes are sandals — that's the wrong word, they're a sort of laced leather thing, no heel, and the leather has gone the colour and texture of a dog chew. They've been there since before us. They were there when Dad took the unit over in ninety-seven and he never moved them and when I asked him once he said "they're somebody's," which is the least useful sentence in the trade. Herm came in Thursday afternoon. He does about every six weeks, and he always comes in mid-sentence. "—sixty quid for pads. Sixty. I said to him, mate. They're *pads*." "Hiya." He put his trainers on the counter, both heels worn clean through the rubber, through the foam, one of them into the actual lining, so there was a hole you could put a finger in. Every time. He's a courier, e-bike, and he does something with his heels — drags them, scoots them off kerbs, I don't know, I've asked to watch him ride and he thinks I'm joking. I've told him four times to buy a shoe with a rubber heel plug and he nods and comes back with the same last. "Can you do them?" "I can build the heel up. It'll never be right." "You always say that." He was pleased. He leaned on the counter, helmet under one arm, still in his hi-vis, and he does that thing of looking round the whole shop while he talks to you, like a dog in a new room. He was quiet for a second, which is rare. He'd gone still looking down the back wall. "That's still there, is it," he said. I turned round. He was looking at the leather things with the brown tickets. "They've always been there." "Right." He nodded slowly, like I'd told him a mate of his was still in the same job. "Right, yeah. She'll be back for them." "Who will?" "Oh —" and he had his phone out, and he was already gone, thumb going, and he said "she's like that, bit of a — you know," and then he said "here, do you know the one-way's changed by the Ikea?" and told me about that for eleven minutes. He paid twelve pounds. It was twelve pounds forty. He said "call it twelve," which he always says, and I always let him, and I'm not sure why except that he's the only customer I actually like seeing. Adjoa came at half five, on her break, which makes no sense because her shift starts at eight and the warehouse is off the A45, but she does it two or three times a month and I've stopped asking. She had her coat on and she sat on my stool and scrolled. "They've put it up to nine eighty," she said. "What's nine eighty." "Picks. An hour. That's the target." She looked up. "You want to know what happens if you do nine seventy-five?" "No." "Nothing happens. That's the thing. Nothing happens for weeks and then it happens all at once." She went back to her phone. "There's a bag under your bench." "There's a lot under my bench." "Mercy." "I'm working." She stayed till twenty past six and ate a Twix and told me about a man on her line who'd started a spreadsheet, and she was warm and she was funny and by the end of it I wanted her gone so badly my teeth hurt. I locked up and went to the track. Coundon Road, Tuesday and Thursday, and Thursday's reps — six times eight hundred with two minutes, which is a session designed by somebody who hates you. It was dark and the floodlights only do the home straight properly so you run the back straight on faith. I ran the fourth one badly and the fifth one worse and on the sixth, coming off the bend with about a hundred and fifty to go, it went how it goes: everything shuts down to a tunnel and your arms take over and there's nothing in your head at all. Not victory. There were eight of us and I was seventh. There's just the last hundred and fifty and the specific relief of not having anything left to protect. I got home at half nine and there was a text from a number I didn't have. *Thursday. It's Thursday. I've counted.*
