# Low Water It rained from three in the morning. Nobody had considered rain. It rains eleven days a year on that coast and it rained on the twenty-sixth, a fine cold drizzle off the sea that made the sand hold together and the fish slick, and it went on until nine. They started at 03:40 with headlamps and the pickup lights and two generators from the ice plant that Marisol's sons had driven down from Lima and left without saying much. Four hundred and ten people, or near it. Rosa did not count them and later regretted this. Old men. Children with the plastic buckets you use at the beach in summer. Meche Ccorahua, out of hospital eight days, on a chair at the top of the sand with a whistle and the master drawing in a plastic sleeve, calling the lines. Yenifer running the length of it with a laser rangefinder and a can of marker paint. Arno in his enormous boots with a printout going to pulp in his hand. They had a hundred and forty metres of beach and six hours and about eleven hundred tonnes of anchoveta, none of it fresh, all of it from the eleventh onward. That was the whole point and it was the thing hardest to explain to the people who had come — that they were not to gather anything new, that the material was to be the material that was already there, that if a bird fell during the work they were to leave it. Some of them understood. Some of them did it anyway because Rosa said so. It was raking. That was all it was. Flat-tined rakes, forty of them, and shovels, and hands. You dragged the mass into a band and then you cut the band to the line with the edge of the rake and then you went back along it and cleaned the edge, and the edge was the only thing that mattered, and the rain kept softening the edge. Rosa worked the third band from the water for two hours and then her knees went and she moved to the top of the beach and did the thing she was for, which was counting. Sixty-one metres done at five. Eighty-eight at six. The light came at half five and they could see what they had and it was not enough. Beto came at seven. She had not asked him. He had not said he would. He came down the sand in a waterproof she did not recognise with two thermoses and a pair of gloves from the school and he took a rake off a boy who was too small for it and got in the second band and worked until eleven without saying anything to her at all, and at some point she looked up from the tally and saw him down there at the far end and had to put the clipboard down and stand for a moment with her hands on her hips like someone catching their breath. --- Namibia went at 05:12 GMT with about nine hundred people at Walvis Bay and a road that flooded. Chile went at 11:40 with two hundred and sixty at Mejillones and no rain and got further than anyone. The other beaches did not go. Not from cowardice — from tide tables, and equipment, and a decision in one national government that arrived four days late, and a dispute in another about whether volunteers were insured. Forty had been talked about. Three happened. --- The tide turned at 09:50. They had two thirds of it. Ninety-four metres of a hundred and forty. Everything up to the fourth element of part two and none of part three, which was the part that did not change, which was the part Arno thought was the closing frame, which might have meant it was not a sentence at all but only the start of one. They kept going for fifty minutes with the water in it. Then the outer band went, and once the outer band went the second band lost its edge, and Meche blew the whistle three times, which was the signal, and the four hundred and ten people came up the sand. The sea took it in the wrong order. That was the thing Rosa watched and could not stop watching: it took part two first, the enumeration, the count, and then it took the end of part one, and the middle of part one went last, so that whatever had been written there was read out backwards and with the middle at the end. Somebody near her said, "Is it ruined?" "Probably," said Rosa. "So what do we do?" "We come back on the eleventh," she said. "There's a tide on the eleventh." --- The pulse did not stop. That is the part people got wrong afterwards, in the documentaries and in the book by the man from London who interviewed Yenifer twice and Rosa not at all. Seven hertz, continuous, through the night of the twenty-sixth and the day after and the week after. Nothing changed at 04:12 or at any other hour. The strandings thinned in February. Then in the first week of March there were four days that took the sardine fishery in Chile apart, and then it thinned again, and by April it was — Rosa checked the figures every Monday — running at about eleven per cent of the December baseline, which was still an ecological catastrophe and was, by the standards of the previous year, nothing at all. Nobody could say whether it worked. There was no method by which anybody could say. They did it again on the eleventh of February and got a hundred and twenty metres, and again in March, and the March one was very well organised and hardly anybody came. Fat Nancy's calf, B-0231, was photographed alive off Isla San Gallán in June. Rosa had the email printed out. She still could not open the folder on the old drive; the cable had never turned up; she had ordered one online in April and it had been the wrong one. --- In August she was on the beach at Sanjuanito with the frame, on the transect, because the transect was still scheduled. Down. The hand on the aluminium, the sound she would deny. There were fish in the quadrat. Not many. Eleven, and a crab. She picked one up. Twelve centimetres, second year, taken by something with a beak. And she read it — not the length, not the year class, but the other thing, the way the body was lying and which way the head was and where the damage was and what all of that was next to — and she did it before she had decided to, in the half second before deciding, the way you cannot look at a word in your own language and see a shape. She put it down and wrote *11* in the column. She was not frightened. That was what she noticed, kneeling there with the sea doing what it does and her knees full of ground glass and the molars standing out past the horizon exactly where they had been for two hundred and eighty days. She had been frightened in December, badly, for about three weeks. She was not frightened now. She had learned the language and it had gone quiet inside her, the way a language does, and now it was simply how the beach read. *That's the worse thing,* she thought, and got up, and moved the frame two metres north. --- Beto had made the fish stew he made, with no fish in it. "Julia's roof's done," he said. "Since when?" "Thursday. The cousin did it in the end. Three-forty, which is not three-twenty, but he did the flashing as well, which the nephew wasn't going to." "Is it good?" "It's good," said Beto. "It's the same sheet, Rosa. It was always the same sheet." She said that she was glad, and she was, and she let him tell her the rest of it — the nephew, the aunt, who was speaking to whom now — and outside the window it was dark over the water and there was nothing out there, and the seven hertz came up through the floor and the chair and her jaw, the way it had every day since November, patient, unhurried, still asking.

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of speculative fiction that demonstrates rare command of voice, structure, and restraint. Let me examine it carefully across multiple dimensions. VOICE AND STYLE: The prose operates in a mode of compressed, observational realism that earns its occasional lyrical moments. The opening chapter establishes Rosa's character through action and detail rather than exposition — the gloves she doesn't wear, the pencil hovering over the notes field, the filing cabinet drawer. The style is Sebaldian in its accumulation of precise, unglamorous detail, and it consistently lands. The "poetic leaps" are almost always grounded: "The smell had stopped being a smell around day nine. It had become a condition, like altitude." This is not purple prose — it's exact. The metaphor works because it describes a real phenomenon (olfactory adaptation) through a real comparison (altitude sickness as environmental condition rather than acute event). STRUCTURE: The formal experimentation is genuinely impressive and purposeful. The necropsy report, the email chain, the WhatsApp group, the government incident report — these are not gimmicks. They serve the story's central concern: how institutions process the incomprehensible through bureaucratic form, and how meaning leaks through the cracks of official language. The penciled marginalia on the necropsy report ("they landed. they didn't fall. every one of them landed first") is one of the story's finest moments — it conveys Rosa's dawning understanding without stating it, and the physical act of pressing hard enough to score the paper tells us everything about her emotional state. CHARACTER: Rosa is one of the more fully realized protagonists in this kind of fiction. Her thirty-one years of data, her failed reports, her bad knee, her relationship with Beto (rendered almost entirely through absence and small acts), her professional pride and its costs — all of this is built through accumulation rather than statement. The moment where she wants to slap Yenifer for doing the arithmetic out loud, and knows the wanting is unfair, is psychologically precise. Yenifer herself is well-drawn as a foil — younger, less burdened by institutional defeat, doing exactly what she was trained to do. Arno functions well as the acoustics counterpart, his verbal tics ("It's very clean") characterizing him efficiently. PLOT AND CONCEPT: The central conceit — that the megastructures have been reading the catch records, that the fish die in patterns that encode the history of human extraction, that the message is an inventory — is genuinely original and intellectually coherent. The escalation from anchoveta to squid to birds to the whale to Marisol Chumpitaz follows a logic that is both scientifically grounded and emotionally devastating. The response (raking patterns in dead fish on the beach) is the right kind of desperate, imperfect, human answer. The ambiguity of whether it worked is exactly correct. PACING: The story moves well across its eight chapters. The early chapters establish the scientific mystery with appropriate patience; the middle chapters accelerate through the escalating anomalies; the final chapters handle the response and aftermath with appropriate restraint. The WhatsApp group chapter is a structural masterstroke — it grounds the cosmic in the mundane and provides tonal relief without undercutting the stakes. WEAKNESSES: There are a few moments where the prose reaches slightly beyond what it earns. "The sea went white from the shore to the horizon and stayed white" is effective, but the chapter 6 mass mortality sequence is slightly more conventionally apocalyptic than the rest of the story's register. The Teo subplot (what he saw out at sea) is introduced and then deliberately left unresolved, which is a valid choice but feels slightly like a loose thread rather than a purposeful gap. The ending is very good but the final image ("patient, unhurried, still asking") is perhaps the story's most conventional moment — it's the kind of closing line that many writers would reach for, and this story has been doing better than that throughout. DIALOGUE: The dialogue is sparse and functional, which is appropriate. The exchanges between Rosa and Yenifer, Rosa and Arno, Rosa and Beto — all feel true. The Beto scenes are particularly well-handled; his presence is defined almost entirely by what he doesn't say and what he does instead. EARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: Rosa's final state — not frightened, having "learned the language," finding it simply how the beach reads, and recognizing that this is "the worse thing" — is genuinely earned. The story has built to this through thirty-one years of her professional life, through the specific texture of her relationship to data and bodies, through the accumulation of everything she has witnessed. The transformation is not dramatic; it's the quiet horror of adaptation, which is exactly right. FAITHFULNESS TO PROMPT: The story is entirely faithful to the prompt. The megastructures arrived a month ago, the fish started dying, and they spoke — but the story finds the most interesting possible interpretation of "they spoke," which is that the speaking was happening all along in the dying, and that understanding it required the specific expertise of a marine biologist who had spent thirty years converting bodies into numbers. OVERALL: This is a genuinely excellent piece of speculative fiction. It is not perfect — the mass mortality chapter is slightly less controlled than the rest, and the final line is the story's weakest — but it demonstrates consistent craft, genuine originality, and emotional intelligence throughout. It reads like the work of a serious writer who has thought carefully about both the science and the human stakes. # Brainstorming ## Unpacking the prompt Three blood-drop emojis, sent just after midnight. Immediately the question is: who sent it, and what does it mean? The emoji is a code — which implies a pre-existing arrangement between sender and receiver. That's the interesting bit. Someone has agreed, at some prior point, that 🩸🩸🩸 means *something specific*. A summons. A distress signal. A confession. A count. Options for what it means: - **Period tracking.** Comic misdirection: the protagonist panics thinking it's murder, it's her mate announcing she's finally come on. Darkly comic but thin unless it escalates. - **Distress code.** A friend's safeword for "come get me, something has gone wrong." Three drops = severity level three, the worst. - **Body count.** Three. Which is horrifying and funny in a very British way if the sender is, say, a fifteen-year-old with a spreadsheet. - **A hunt/game.** A group of teens playing an escalating dare game where the emoji is the call to assemble. - **Blood pact / blood oath.** Kids who did a stupid ritual at eleven and one of them is now calling it in. - **Miscarriage / medical emergency.** Too grim for comic, unless handled with black wit. - **Deer/roadkill.** Someone hit something with a car. Comedy of disposal. - **Vampire/supernatural.** Probably too genre-shifty; the prompt reads more grounded. But a *fake* vampire, a kid who's convinced himself, could be very funny and very sad. - **Butchery.** Sender works at a butcher's; it's a code for "I've nicked us some meat" and the story spirals from there. - **Cult/school ritual.** Sixth form society, initiation. ## Tone touchstones Darkly comic British YA — think Jenny Downham crossed with Bunny by Mona Awad crossed with Skins crossed with Kevin Barry's rhythm. Also: *Vernon God Little*'s voice, *Slaughterhouse Rulez* absurdism, Kate Weston, Holly Bourne's grit, Malorie Blackman's edge, Melvin Burgess. Key texture: deadpan narration, gallows humour, extremely specific British details (Greggs, Lucozade, a Wilko carrier bag, the 43 bus, Argos pen, a Vauxhall Corsa full of vape smoke, PE kit, "Miss", GCSE mocks, a Wetherspoons that smells of bleach and gravy). Rain. Retail parks. A canal. The particular melancholy of a town where the biggest employer closed in 2009. Voice: first person, present tense probably, teenage narrator with a fast, funny, defended interiority. The humour should be a shield over grief or fear. The comedy comes from the mismatch between catastrophic events and mundane logistics — you can't get an Uber at 1am in a town like this; the corner shop is shut; her mum's car has no petrol. ## Character sketches - **Narrator:** Wren Okonjo-Hallam? Or simpler: **Nia Vaughan**, 16, Welsh-borders town. Sharp, anxious, keeps lists. Diagnosed with nothing but self-diagnosed with everything. Works Saturdays at a garden centre café. Her defining trait: she is the one who *deals with things*. The friend group's designated adult. This is a burden and she's furious about it and also it's her entire identity. - Alternative narrator: a boy, **Dylan**, funnier, less capable, panics beautifully. Might make the comedy easier but the emotional undertow harder. - I like a girl narrator with a very dry voice. Let's say **Marnie Quinn**, 16. Or **Bethan**. Or **Cass**. - **The sender:** best friend. **Priya**? **Immy**? Let's think — the sender should be charismatic, chaotic, adored, exhausting. The kind of friend who's a weather system. Name options: **Saskia "Sass" Boyle**, **Immy Pryce**, **Row (Rowan)**. I like **Immy**. - Or subvert: the sender is not the best friend but the *estranged* friend — the one the narrator cut off six months ago, which makes answering the text a moral problem rather than a reflex. That's much better. Guilt engine. - **Third party:** a boy, ex or almost, whose presence complicates. **Kaden**. Or a younger sibling who tags along and is the moral centre. A little brother, 11, called **Bug**, who won't stay in the car. Kids in dark comedies are great. - **Adults:** mostly absent or useless. A mum working nights at the hospital (nicely ironic). A stepdad who does taxidermy. A teacher who's too invested. A police liaison officer with a lanyard and a vape. ## Plot directions ### Direction A: "The Third One" Three blood drops = three deaths. The narrator's estranged best friend has been keeping a tally of people she believes she's killed — not literally, but by omission, by cruelty, by being the last person to text them. Third one just happened. The night is a journey across town while the narrator tries to work out if her friend is a murderer, mentally ill, or just guilty. Ends with the reveal: the third one is the friend herself, in process. Devastating. Comic on the way there. Maybe too heavy on suicide content for the register — needs care, but YA does handle this. ### Direction B: "Blood Pact" Four years ago, four kids pricked their thumbs behind the leisure centre and swore an oath: if any of us ever needs the others, we send three drops and everyone comes, no questions. It's a joke. It's never been used. Then it's used. The story is one night: the narrator gathering the scattered, now-awkward, now-estranged four, and the slow revelation of why the sender called it in. Great structure — a gathering-the-team caper with a black heart. Each chapter can pick up a member and characterise them fast. Comedy in the reluctance ("I've got a mock at nine"), dread in the accumulation. ### Direction C: "The Deer" Immy has hit something with her mum's car. Or someone. Three blood drops = "there is blood, come." The night becomes a body-disposal farce that turns out to be a cover for something else. Very Coen. Risk: seen it. ### Direction D: "The Butcher's Daughter" Literal blood: the sender works at an abattoir/butcher's, and the code means something transgressive. Fun texture but hard to build 8 chapters. ### Direction E: "The Game" An app-based dare game in the town, escalating. Three drops means you've been nominated. Too Black Mirror. ### Direction F: Combination — B as spine, A as the truth underneath, C as the middle-act crisis. The pact gathers them; the reason is an accident (blood, a body, or nearly-a-body); the real reason underneath is that the sender has been drowning for months and nobody noticed. The night ends not with a corpse but with a hospital waiting room and a vending machine and someone finally saying the thing. ## Possible story beats (Direction F) 1. Midnight text. Narrator in bed, phone face-down, mock exam tomorrow. The drops arrive. Establish the pact via flashback and the fact she deleted this person's number but knows it by heart. Establish the town. She goes. 2. She gets to the location — not what she expected. Empty. A second text. She has to fetch someone else first: the boy. Rules of the pact: *all* of us or none. 3. Collect member two. Comedy of extraction (climbing through a window, a dog, a stepdad). Now two of them arguing in a car. 4. Collect member three — the one who moved on hardest, now a "nice" girl with a boyfriend and a future, who does *not* want to be reminded. Refuses. Comes anyway. 5. They find Immy. Blood is real. Situation revealed: she's been living somewhere she shouldn't; something has happened; there is a person hurt or dead. 6. The crisis and the farce: the practical problem. Do they call an ambulance? Police? The specific, ugly logistics. The friendship fractures. 7. Consequences. Hospital/police station/dawn. The truth of the three drops: not three victims — three *chances*, three times she's tried to ask. Or: the three drops were sent to three people and only one came. 8. Aftermath. Weeks later. The exam she failed. A visit. The pact renegotiated. Ending that is funny and bruised and hopeful-ish, not tidy. ## Alternative structural ideas - **Countdown structure:** each chapter headed with a time (00:04, 00:41, 01:15...). Very propulsive, suits one-night story. Chapters 1–7 are the night; chapter 8 jumps forward. I like this a lot. - **Non-linear:** intercut the night with the day the pact was made. Risky at 1000 words a chapter. - **Multiple POV:** no — first person single POV keeps the voice. - **Group chat interstitials:** text messages as scene breaks. Very YA, very readable, good for comedy timing. ## Comic set-pieces to consider - Trying to order an Uber; nearest driver is 34 minutes away in a different county. - Stealing a mobility scooter. Too silly? - A vicar's son who won't come out because he's on a fast. - Climbing over a fence into the wrong garden; a security light; a man in Y-fronts with a cricket bat who turns out to be their Geography teacher. - The blood turns out to be, in part, from a burst bag of beetroot / a nosebleed / a chicken from the reduced aisle — a fake-out that makes the real blood worse. - Someone insisting on stopping at a 24-hour garage for snacks mid-crisis. Meal deal in an emergency. - A first-aid course flashback used disastrously. - Everyone's phone dying at different, escalating moments. - The narrator's mother texting increasingly ominous messages from her nightshift. ## Darker textures - The town has a bridge everyone knows about and no one names. - A boy who died last year — Tom? — whose absence sits under everything. The pact was five, not four. The fifth is dead. That's why the drops are so loaded. Oh, that's good. The pact was made by five kids; one died (accident? overdose? bridge?) eighteen months ago; nobody has spoken since. The three drops arriving now is unbearable *because* of him. - The sender might be re-enacting something. - Self-harm content: three drops is chillingly literal. Need to handle carefully — implied, not detailed. - The dark comedy must not mock the pain; it should be the characters' armour, and it should fail at the right moment. ## Endings - Everyone survives; nothing is fixed; they eat chips at dawn on a roundabout. Understated. - The sender survives; the narrator finally tells the truth about why she cut her off (she was in love with her / she blamed her for the death / she was drowning too and couldn't carry another person). - Coda: the pact is remade with better terms. "New rule: you can send one drop. You can send it for nothing. You can send it because it's Tuesday." - Last line potential: a single 🩸 arriving weeks later and the narrator getting up and going. ## Names/places Town: **Cwm Ffynnon**? Too Welsh-specific maybe. **Barrowfield**. **Hensford**. **Pellchurch**. **Nant-y-Gaer**. I like a Welsh-borders or Midlands post-industrial town: **Aberthin**, **Mold-adjacent**, **Coldbrook**. Let's say **Coldbrook** — invented, generic-north-Midlands, good name. Landmarks: the Aldi roundabout, Bryson's Meats, the Beacon (a hill), the viaduct, the old fibreglass factory, Speedy Snax, the Iceland car park, Lidl. # Reflection The prompt's strength is its compression: three symbols, a timestamp, and an implied contract. Whatever I do, the story has to honour that the emoji is *code* — pre-agreed, loaded, and dreadful precisely because it's silly. A blood emoji is a stupid little cartoon; the fact that a group of teenagers made it mean life-or-death is exactly the darkly comic register the prompt is asking for. So Direction B/F — the blood pact — feels most native to the prompt. Direction A (a kill tally) is punchy but risks tipping into thriller, which loses the YA social texture. Direction C (roadkill farce) is fun but has been done and doesn't earn eight chapters. Direction E is too high-concept. What I keep returning to is **the pact made by children being called in by teenagers**. That's the engine: the gap between who they were at twelve and who they are at sixteen. Twelve-year-olds swearing an oath behind the leisure centre with a compass point and a bag of Haribo is funny; sixteen-year-olds having to honour it at 12:04am is both funny and awful. It gives me an automatic structure — a gathering — which suits eight short chapters brilliantly, because each collected member is a self-contained comic scene with a slice of characterisation and a step-down into darkness. The dead fifth member is the best idea I've had here. It solves several problems at once. It explains why the group fractured; it makes the emoji unbearable rather than just alarming; it gives the narrator guilt and the sender motive; and it lets me withhold something in the first half without cheating the reader. But I need to be careful: two crises (a dead boy in the past, a bleeding girl in the present) could overload a 8,000-word story. I think the past death should be handled lightly and obliquely — mentioned, circled, never fully explained until late — while the present night carries the plot. On the nature of the blood: I'm wary of making the reveal a self-harm scene, both because of duty of care in YA and because it can feel like the story's using it for shock. But avoiding it entirely might be evasive. A middle path: the immediate emergency is something messier and more absurd — an injury, an accident, someone else's blood, a genuinely ridiculous cause — while the *reason* she sent the code, the reason she's been so far gone, is quietly about not coping. That keeps the comedy alive through the middle chapters and lets the last third land emotionally without exploitation. A fake-out where the blood is partly comic (a smashed jar, a nosebleed, a burst bag of something red) and partly horribly real is a good structural trick: it makes the reader laugh and then take the laugh back. The one-night, timestamped structure is very appealing. It gives momentum, it makes each chapter's job obvious, and it lets a 1000-word chapter feel complete. My worry is that seven chapters of one night plus one epilogue might feel rushed at the climax — I'd want chapters 5, 6, 7 to slow the clock right down, so the timestamps go 00:04, 00:31, 01:02, 01:40, 02:05, 02:19, 02:47 — the gaps closing as things get worse. That's a nice formal effect and easy to sustain. Voice is the make-or-break. First person, present tense, a narrator who's funny because she's terrified and organised because she's terrified. The comedy has to be in the specificity: brand names, bus routes, the physical comedy of getting a friend out of a bedroom window, the appalling banality of a meal deal during a crisis. British YA lives or dies on texture. And crucially, the jokes should belong to the characters, not the author — they should be *deflections*, and the moment someone can't make a joke should hit like a slap. Cast size: five original pact members, one dead, leaves four for the night — narrator, sender, and two to collect. That's manageable. Any more and 1000-word chapters can't hold them. I want the two collected members to be maximally different: one who's kept the faith and is delighted to be summoned (dangerous, chaotic, comic engine), and one who's built a new respectable life and is horrified to be dragged back (conflict engine, and eventually the one who says the hardest true thing). That contrast will do a lot of work quickly. The narrator's own culpability matters. It's too easy to make her a rescuer. She should have blocked the sender, or ignored earlier, smaller signals — a single blood drop months ago that she read as attention-seeking. That's the wound: she's not coming to save her friend, she's coming to be forgiven. That gives chapter 7 its confrontation and chapter 8 its resolution — the renegotiated pact where a smaller signal counts. Risks to manage: sentimentality at the end (guard against it with a joke in the last paragraph, an unresolved practical detail, the flatness of aftermath); the mystery being either too obvious or too withheld (drip clues — the location, the missing fifth member, the sender's recent behaviour); and the dark comedy curdling into flippancy about serious harm (keep the harm real and the jokes aimed at logistics, adults, the town, and themselves). Finally, the ending image. I like a final 🩸 — a single drop — arriving later, and the narrator getting her shoes on without hesitating. It closes the loop, it's earned, and it's quietly devastating and hopeful at once. That's the target.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Premise.** Five kids made a blood pact behind the leisure centre when they were twelve: three drops means come, no questions, whatever it costs. Four years later, one of them is dead, the rest haven't spoken properly since the funeral, and at 00:04 on a Tuesday in February the code goes out. The story is one night — a gathering, a farce, and then a reckoning. **Plot spine.** Nell (narrator, 16) receives 🩸🩸🩸 from Saskia Boyle, whose number she deleted eight months ago and still knows by heart. The pact's rule is *all of us or none*, so before she can reach Sass she has to collect the other two survivors: Dilly Okoro (chaotic, delighted, dangerous, still believes in the pact) and Ffion Rees (respectable now, revising, engaged to a future, appalled). They find Sass at the old fibreglass works with a lot of blood, some of which is comically not hers. The immediate emergency resolves into a worse, quieter one: Sass has been sleeping rough for nine days, and she sent one drop in October that Nell ignored. The night ends in a hospital corridor. Chapter 8 jumps six weeks forward. **The dead boy.** Tomos "Tosh" Rees — Ffion's brother — died eighteen months ago. I'll keep his death oblique for most of the story: named early, circled, the manner of it withheld until chapter 6 or 7 (a hit-and-run on the Beacon road that was probably not an accident, never resolved, and Sass was the last person with him). He is the reason the emoji is unbearable and the reason the group shattered. He's atmosphere and load-bearing, not a second plot. **Voice and style.** First person, present tense, Nell — dry, fast, list-making, competent because terrified. Humour is armour and must fail at the right moments. Jokes belong to the characters, aimed at logistics, adults, the town and themselves — never at the pain itself. Heavy specificity of place: Coldbrook, a Midlands/borders town with a dead factory, an Aldi roundabout, a viaduct, Speedy Snax, the 43 bus. Short paragraphs. Sentence fragments for panic. Texts rendered plainly on their own lines. Each chapter headed with a timestamp, gaps narrowing as the night worsens: 00:04, 00:31, 01:02, 01:40, 02:05, 02:19, 02:47, then "Six Weeks Later." **What I'm aiming for.** Momentum: every chapter has a task. Comedy of extraction and logistics in the middle. A fake-out with the blood — genuinely funny, then retracted. A narrator who is not a rescuer but a supplicant seeking forgiveness. Adults absent or useless (Nell's mum on a hospital nightshift, ironically unreachable). An unsentimental ending: nothing fixed, one thing renegotiated, and a final single 🩸. **What I'm avoiding.** Thriller mechanics; a murder-tally reading; supernatural drift; graphic self-harm description (harm is real, present, and referred to, not staged for shock); a redemptive group hug; adults arriving to solve it; tidy explanation of Tosh's death; flippancy about serious harm; and any line that sounds like the author being clever over the characters' heads. # Chapter Planning **1. 00:04 — Three Drops** (~1000w) Nell in bed, phone face-down, Geography mock at nine. Three blood emojis from an unsaved number she recognises instantly. Establish the pact in flashback: five kids, a compass point from a maths set, a Haribo Tangfastic bag, the rules recited (three drops means come; all of us or none; no questions; whatever it costs). Establish Coldbrook. Establish that Nell blocked Sass in June. She texts back: *where*. Reply: a pin. The fibreglass works. She gets dressed. Last line: she also knows she has to fetch the others first, and that's the worst part. **2. 00:31 — Dilly** (~1000w) Extraction comedy. Dilly Okoro's bedroom window, a security light, a Staffie called Nutmeg, Dilly's nan awake watching QVC. Dilly comes out in a coat over pyjamas, thrilled — she's been waiting four years for this. She has a car (her brother's Corsa, no MOT, quarter tank). Bickering that establishes the eight months of silence and the rule they can't break: all of us or none. Which means Ffion. Dilly stops for petrol and a meal deal. First hint of Tosh: a sticker still on the dashboard. **3. 01:02 — Ffion Says No** (~1000w) The Rees house, new-build estate, motion lights, revision timetable visible through the window. Ffion at the door in a dressing gown, furious, whispering. She has a Chemistry mock, a boyfriend, a plan, a mother who cannot take one more thing. She says no. Nell shows her the screenshot. Beat: Ffion is Tosh's sister; three drops is the last thing he ever sent anyone. She gets in the car. Nobody talks. Second text from Sass arrives: *hurry* — then a photo, too dark to read except for something wet. **4. 01:40 — The Works** (~1000w) The fibreglass factory. Fence, torchlight, comic terror (a fox, a mattress, Dilly narrating like a nature documentary to stop herself crying). They find Sass in the old canteen with a camping lamp and a horrifying amount of red. Fake-out: much of it is a smashed jar of beetroot and a burst carrier bag of reduced-aisle chicken, which is grotesquely funny for about nine seconds. Then Nell sees Sass's arm, and the nine days of tinned food, and the sleeping bag, and stops laughing. End on Sass saying, cheerfully, that she's fine, and asking if anyone brought crisps. **5. 02:05 — Triage** (~1000w) Slowing down. The practical horror: the wound needs stitches, the nearest A&E is Hensford, twelve miles, the Corsa has no MOT and Dilly's had two ciders. Sass refuses hospital, refuses police, refuses her mum's name being said. Nell's mum is working the very ward they'd end up in and won't answer her phone. Argument that splits the room: Ffion wants to call 999 and go home; Dilly wants to obey the pact literally, whatever it costs; Nell wants to fix it herself. First aid attempted badly with a Speedy Snax napkin and a clean-ish T-shirt. Sass reveals she's been here nine days and that nobody has noticed, which nobody can answer. **6. 02:19 — One Drop** (~1000w) The confrontation. Sass produces her phone and shows Nell a message sent in October: a single 🩸. Delivered, read, never answered — then blocked. Nell's culpability lands. Ffion says the hardest true thing: that Sass was the last one with Tosh on the Beacon road and none of them have ever been able to ask her about it. Sass answers, partly. Tosh's last message to her was three drops, and she was asleep. The pact turns out to have failed already, once, fatally. Grief comes out sideways, as jokes that die. Ffion, of all people, is the one who picks up Sass's coat and says: get in the car. **7. 02:47 — Hensford** (~1000w) The drive: headlights, a fox, Dilly doing 40 in a 60 with immense concentration, Sass in the back with her arm up on a bag of frozen peas Dilly bought at the garage for reasons she cannot explain. A&E at three in the morning: plastic chairs, a vending machine that takes the money, a triage nurse with a lanyard. Nell's mum comes round the corner in scrubs, and the collision of worlds is both a relief and the end of Nell's control. Sass gives a fake surname; the nurse doesn't buy it. Nell, finally, tells the truth to an adult — one clean, flat paragraph of it. Chapter ends with the four of them asleep in a row of chairs at dawn, and Nell not letting go of Sass's coat sleeve. **8. Six Weeks Later** (~1000w) Aftermath, unsentimental. Nell failed the Geography mock (D, and a comment about "unrealised potential"). Sass is at her aunt's in Hensford with a social worker called Pauline and eleven stitches' worth of scar and a phone contract in her own name. Ffion smashed the Chemistry mock and still can't look at anyone. Dilly's Corsa is dead. They meet on the viaduct steps with chips because nothing else has been invented for this. The pact is renegotiated out loud, badly, with argument: one drop counts. One drop for nothing. One drop because it's Tuesday. Somebody says Tosh's name without flinching, once. Final beat: weeks later, late, Nell's phone lights up with a single 🩸 — from Ffion, of all people — and Nell is putting her shoes on before she's fully awake.

# How a human writer would come at this A human writer who's actually good at British YA would probably start not from structure but from a voice in their ear and one image they can't shake. The 🩸🩸🩸 prompt is *sound* before it's plot — the tiny absurdity of a cartoon blood drop carrying a life. A human would sit with that joke and let it get worse. They'd probably write the first chapter before knowing what the blood was, and then be stuck with whatever they'd committed to, and the story would bend around that accident. That accidental quality is what reads as human. They'd also write from a real town. Not "Coldbrook, a Midlands/borders town with a dead factory" — that's a composite, a stock set. They'd write from the town they left, and the details would be wrong-shaped and over-specific in ways no one would invent: the swimming baths that smelled of chips because the café shared an extractor with the pool; the phone box that still had a dial tone; the roundabout with the sculpture everyone called The Thing. Human specificity is *unbalanced*. It over-invests in one weird detail and forgets to describe the sky. A human would let the characters be worse people. Teenagers in real crises are selfish, bored, hungry, competitive about who's most upset, and briefly hilarious at exactly the wrong moment. They check their phones during other people's confessions. They think about whether they look good while someone bleeds. A human writer with a mean streak — which dark comedy requires — would let Nell resent Sass, actively, right up to the end, and not resolve that resentment. And a human would leave things unexplained not as a technique but because they genuinely don't know, or because it's none of the reader's business. The plan currently *decides* to withhold Tosh's death. A human would more likely have simply never worked it out, and that absence would feel different — less like a curtain, more like a hole. # Telltale LLM habits and why they'd hurt this piece **Structural over-tidiness.** The narrowing timestamps (00:04, 00:31, 01:02, 01:40, 02:05, 02:19, 02:47) are the most obviously machine-made thing in the plan. They're a *display* of craft: look, the gaps are closing, the tension is rising formally. A human might use timestamps, but they'd be sloppier — two chapters at the same time, one at 04:11 when the story's supposed to be over, one just headed "still Tuesday." The current scheme announces its own cleverness and, worse, it makes every chapter feel like a scheduled event rather than a thing happening. **One task per chapter.** "Every chapter has a task" is stated as a virtue in the intention. It's also a screenwriting-workshop tic. Real chapters have dead air, digression, a two-page argument about something irrelevant, a chapter that's mostly one girl in a car park thinking about her mother. If all eight chapters efficiently advance, the story will read as competent and airless. **Thematic legibility.** The plan has a *thesis*: the pact failed once fatally, therefore it must be renegotiated to allow smaller signals, therefore the ending is a single drop answered. That's very neat. It's a TED talk about mental health with teenagers in it. The final beat — 🩸 from Ffion, shoes on before fully awake — is well-constructed and will read as constructed. LLMs love a closing image that rhymes with the opening. Humans sometimes end on something that doesn't fit at all. **The safety instinct.** The plan explicitly avoids graphic self-harm and explicitly refuses to explain Tosh's death, and says so in the language of duty of care. Care is right. But there's a version of care that's actually *evasion*, and readers feel it as a soft spot. The plan also fake-outs the blood with beetroot and reduced chicken — which is a good joke — but the fake-out also functions as a flinch: it lets the reader (and author) laugh their way past the actual sight of an arm. The real thing needs to be seen, once, plainly, without adjectives. **Everyone gets a redemptive gesture.** Ffion, "of all people," picks up the coat and says get in the car. That's the LLM's compulsion to reward every character. Ffion could just as truthfully stay in the car with her hood up, or say the cruel thing and never take it back, or leave and get the bus home and be right to. **Balanced conflict.** Chapter 5's argument is described as a clean three-way split: Ffion wants 999, Dilly wants the pact, Nell wants to fix it. That's a debate-club arrangement of positions. Real arguments are lopsided, repetitive, badly aimed; people argue about the wrong thing (the car, the peas, who's got signal) because they can't argue about the real thing. **Uniform prose competence.** LLM prose tends to a steady, pleasant rhythm with regularly-spaced good lines. Human prose lurches — a flat functional paragraph, then something startling, then a bad joke the narrator's clearly proud of, then a sentence that runs on too long because she's panicking. The plan mentions fragments for panic, which is right, but it's the *unevenness* that matters, not the technique. **The wise adult.** Nell's mum appearing in scrubs and Nell telling the truth in "one clean, flat paragraph" is a beautiful beat and also exactly where an LLM reaches for catharsis-via-authority. The intention says adults are useless, then gives us a nurse mother who arrives at the perfect moment and absorbs the confession. That contradiction is worth interrogating. **Symbol maintenance.** The emoji risks becoming a Motif that gets Serviced. Once it's the title, the opening, the mid-point revelation (one drop in October), Tosh's last message, *and* the closing image, it's doing four jobs and each one weakens the others. Especially: Tosh's last message also being three drops is a very LLM move — the tragic backstory that mirrors the present with perfect symmetry. # Deep dive: where this specific plan goes wrong **The gathering structure is too pleasing.** Collect Dilly (chaotic comic engine), collect Ffion (respectable conflict engine), find Sass. Two extractions, two contrasted personalities, maximally different by design. You can see the design. Also: "all of us or none" is a rule invented purely to force this structure, and readers can smell a plot-shaped rule. If it stays, it needs to be a rule that *hurts* — one they resent, argue about, and possibly break. Or better: nobody insists on it. Nell just can't face Sass alone, and the pact is her excuse. That's a human reason. **Dilly is currently a function.** "Chaotic, delighted, dangerous, still believes in the pact." That's a slot. Nature-documentary narration to stop herself crying is a nice bit but it's also the manic-comic-relief-with-hidden-depths default. What if Dilly is the one who's genuinely a bit frightening — not lovable-chaotic but actually unstable, the one who'd hurt someone on Sass's behalf, whose loyalty is the scariest thing in the car? Or what if she's not funny at all, just *keen*, in a way that's embarrassing, because she's had no friends since the funeral? **Ffion's arc is pre-approved.** Revising, boyfriend, future, appalled → gets in the car → says the hard true thing → picks up the coat. That's the full three-act mini-arc of the reluctant friend, and it's the shape the reader expects from the moment she opens the door in a dressing gown. Alternatives: she never softens; she comes for entirely selfish reasons (she needs to hear what Sass says about Tosh, and doesn't care about Sass at all); she's actually the one who's been quietly paying Sass's phone bill and has known where she was all week and said nothing. **Sass is at risk of being The Beautiful Wreck.** Charismatic, chaotic, adored, exhausting, bleeding, cheerful, asks for crisps. That's a type — the Manic Pixie Casualty. The line "asks if anyone brought crisps" is exactly the kind of gallows-quip that LLMs and mid-tier YA both reach for. What would make her human: being *boring* about it. Flat, irritable, unimpressed by their arrival, faintly contemptuous that they took two hours, and not grateful. Or telling a long pointless story about a man in the Co-op while her arm is wrapped in a tea towel. Or — hardest — being furious at Nell not for the blocked message but for something petty and unrelated from Year 9. **The beetroot joke is one gag too many.** Beetroot *and* reduced-aisle chicken is over-egged; it becomes zany. One wrong red thing is funnier and more plausible. **Nine days sleeping rough at the old works** is slightly implausible in February in a town where everyone knows everyone, and "nobody noticed" is doing thematic work. Either lean into the implausibility (she has been noticed, by two adults, both of whom did nothing useful) or shrink it — three nights, since Friday, since the row. **Nell's culpability is stated rather than dramatised.** "She's not coming to save her friend, she's coming to be forgiven" is a great engine but it's currently delivered via a single revealed screenshot in chapter 6. The single 🩸 in October, read and unanswered and then blocked, is very clean. Humans are guilty in messier ways: she answered it with "u ok? x" and then went to sleep. She replied three days later. She screenshotted it and sent it to Ffion with "she's off again." That last one is genuinely ugly and would make the story much better and much braver. **The ending is the biggest risk.** Chips on the viaduct steps, pact renegotiated out loud, Tosh's name said once without flinching, then the closing 🩸. Every element is a resolution. "Somebody says Tosh's name without flinching, once" is the kind of stage direction that reads as authorial healing being administered. And "the pact is renegotiated out loud, badly, with argument" — the word *badly* is the plan trying to inoculate itself against neatness while still doing the neat thing. **"Nothing is fixed" as a stated intention often produces a story where quite a lot is fixed.** Sass has an aunt, a social worker called Pauline, a phone contract, eleven stitches. That's a good outcome. Ffion aced her mock. Dilly's car died (mild comic loss). Nell got a D. The only real cost is a grade. That's a very low price for a night like that. # Ideas for making it more human **Rough up the form.** Drop the narrowing-timestamp scheme. Head chapters with whatever Nell would notice: "00:04," "later," "still the car park," "I don't know, three-ish," "Tuesday, technically." Let one chapter be out of sequence because she can't remember the order. Let one chapter be almost entirely a conversation with nothing happening. **Let a chapter waste itself.** Somewhere in the middle, a chapter where they're driving and get lost and argue about whether the works has a back entrance and Dilly plays a song and Nell thinks about a completely unrelated humiliation from Year 10 and they don't get anywhere. The story should be allowed to be as inefficient as the night would actually be. **Give the town one unreasonable detail and repeat it.** Not five atmospheric details — one. The fibreglass works with the twelve-foot fibreglass cow outside it that was never removed, and which they all keep referring to, and which is the last image of the story instead of an emoji. Something ugly and stupid and unforgettable. **Make the narrator less likeable.** Nell should think one genuinely unforgivable thought — e.g. that it would be easier if Sass were dead, and the relief that thought brings, and how fast she puts it away. Not confessed, not resolved. Just there in the middle of chapter 5 and never mentioned again. **Let the humour misfire on the page.** Someone makes a joke and nobody laughs and they say it again, louder, and it's worse. That's the truest thing about teenage comedy and it's rarely written. **Don't let Sass be grateful, and don't let her be saved by them.** What if the actual intervention comes from somewhere stupid — a security guard, a taxi driver, a woman walking a dog at 3am who takes one look and calls it in over their protests, and they all resent her for it? The pact fails again, differently. They came, and it wasn't enough, and someone random did the useful thing. That's much more human and much funnier and much sadder. **Cut the Tosh-sent-three-drops symmetry.** Make his last message something banal and unbearable instead: a photo of a dog, a "you up," nothing. The pact wasn't used the night he died — that's the horror. Nobody called it in. Which is exactly why using it now is so enormous. **Reduce the moral clarity of the renegotiation.** Instead of a rule-change scene, let it be one line, in passing, months later, that nobody acknowledges. Or let the pact simply not be mentioned again, and the final action speak for it. **Consider ending mid-scene, or on something irrelevant.** The last paragraph could be about the fibreglass cow, or about Nell's mum leaving a note about the immersion heater, or about a bus. Something that isn't the theme. The theme should be visible through it, not in it. **Let the prose be uneven on purpose.** Some paragraphs deliberately flat and admin-like ("The 43 doesn't run after eleven. I knew that. I checked anyway."). One long unpunctuated run when she's running. A chapter where she's tired and the sentences get shorter and duller and slightly worse, and that's the point. **Allow one thing to be simply never explained** — not withheld artfully, just absent. Why Sass had a bag of frozen peas already. Who the man in the car park was. Something the reader will notice and the narrator will not return to. **Cost, properly.** Something should be genuinely lost that can't be got back. Dilly gets charged (no MOT, no insurance, and she's the one who drove, so it's her, not the group). Or Nell's mum is in trouble at work. Or Ffion tells her mother, and Sass's family situation gets *worse* because of their intervention, and everybody knows they made it worse and did it anyway.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The story.** Five kids made a pact behind the leisure centre in Year 7: three drops means come, no arguing, whatever it costs. It was a joke you'd die for at twelve. One of them, Tosh Rees, died eighteen months ago and nobody used the code that night — which is the wound under everything. At 00:04 on a Tuesday in February, Sass Boyle sends 🩸🩸🩸 to Nell, who blocked her in October. Nell goes. She collects Dilly (who has a car and no licence-shaped scruples) because she can't face Sass on her own, and Ffion (Tosh's sister) because Ffion has known where Sass was all week and said nothing. They find Sass at the old fibreglass works — under the twelve-foot fibreglass cow that nobody ever took away — with a cut arm and three nights of tinned food. They argue, waste time, get in each other's way, and in the end it isn't them who does the useful thing: a woman walking a dog at half three sees the blood and calls it in over their objections, and they all resent her for it. The cost lands on Dilly, who drove. Six weeks later something is slightly better and something is permanently worse. **Voice.** First person, present tense, Nell: dry, admin-brained, funny as a defence mechanism, and not especially nice. She thinks one unforgivable thing about Sass in the middle of the night and never mentions it again. Her guilt is ugly and specific: she didn't ignore Sass's single drop in October, she screenshotted it and sent it to Ffion with a caption. That's the thing she can't say. **Style.** Uneven on purpose. Flat admin sentences beside long panicked run-ons. Jokes that die on the page and get repeated worse. Chapter headings as Nell would give them — clock times where she checked, vague where she didn't ("later," "still the car park"). Texts on their own lines, unpunctuated. One unreasonable recurring detail: the cow. Adults absent, useless, or actively unhelpful. The blood seen once, plainly, without adjectives. **Choices made against the obvious version.** No narrowing-timestamp scheme. No one-task-per-chapter efficiency — chapter 4 wastes itself getting lost. No Manic Pixie Casualty: Sass is flat, irritable, ungrateful and boring about her own crisis. No redemptive gesture for Ffion; she says the cruel thing and doesn't take it back. Tosh's last message was nothing at all — no symmetry with the emoji. No wise adult absorbing a confession; Nell's mum is on shift twelve miles away and doesn't pick up. No renegotiated-pact speech. The final image is not the emoji — the emoji comes second-to-last, glancingly, and the story ends on the cow. **Avoiding:** graphic self-harm staging; the group-hug resolution; explanation of Tosh's death (it's a hit-and-run on the Beacon road, unsolved, and nobody in this story finds out anything); thematic summary in dialogue; the author being cleverer than the narrator. # Chapter Planning **1. 00:04** — Nell in bed, Geography mock at nine, phone face-down. Three drops from a number she deleted and knows by heart. The pact in flashback: compass point, Tangfastics, five thumbs, the rules chanted. Coldbrook established through two details only — the 43 doesn't run after eleven, and the cow. She texts *where*, gets a pin: the works. She could go alone. She admits, flatly, that she can't. Ends: she needs Dilly's car, and she needs somebody else there when she looks at Sass's face. **2. 00:31, ish** — Getting Dilly out. Nan awake downstairs with QVC on; a coat over pyjamas; the Corsa that's her brother's and shouldn't be moved. Dilly isn't comic relief — she's *keen*, embarrassingly, because she's had nobody since the funeral, and she's the only one who never stopped believing the pact was real. That eagerness is unnerving. She asks what Sass has done. Nell says she doesn't know. Dilly says "good" and means it. Tosh's sticker still on the dash; neither mentions it. **3. still the car park** — They should go straight to the works. Instead Nell makes Dilly drive to Ffion's, and admits why: in October Sass sent one drop, and Nell screenshotted it and sent it to Ffion captioned *she's off again*, and Ffion replied *lol*. Ffion comes to the door in a dressing gown, furious, mock at nine, and lets slip she's known Sass was at the works since Friday. She gets in the car. Not for Sass. To hear what Sass says. **4. later** — The wasted chapter. Wrong gate, no back entrance, ten minutes arguing about the towpath, Dilly playing one song too loud, Nell remembering a Year 10 humiliation with total clarity while a girl bleeds a mile away. Sass texts *are you coming or not*. Nobody answers it. A joke about the cow dies twice. They park in the wrong place. Nothing has happened and forty minutes are gone. **5. I don't know. Three-ish** — Inside. The canteen, a camping lamp, a sleeping bag, tins. Sass unimpressed that they took three hours. One wrong red thing — a smashed jar of pickled beetroot on the tiles — is funny for exactly as long as it takes Nell to see the arm. Plain sentence, no adjectives. Sass is boring about it: irritable, tells a long pointless story about a man in the Co-op, won't discuss hospitals, won't say her mum's name. Nell tries her own mum's mobile. Voicemail. Twice. **6. same** — The argument, lopsided and badly aimed: about the car, the peas Dilly bought at the garage for no reason, whose fault the towpath was. Ffion finally asks the actual question — what happened on the Beacon road — and Sass says she doesn't know and never did, and Ffion says the cruel thing: *he texted you nothing that night and you were still the last person who saw him*. Nobody takes anything back. Mid-argument, Nell thinks: it would be easier if she'd just died. Then puts it away. Nobody rings 999. **7. half three** — A woman with a dog on the towpath, hi-vis, sees the light and the blood through the doorway and calls it in while they're all shouting at her not to. Ambulance, then police, because of the address. Nell watches Dilly be spoken to beside the Corsa. Hospital corridor, four plastic chairs, a vending machine that works. Nell's mum is on shift at Hensford and never comes down. Sass gives a false surname; nobody believes her. Nell holds the sleeve of Sass's coat and says nothing at all. **8. Six weeks** — Aftermath, uneven. Nell got a D and a comment about unrealised potential. Sass is at an aunt's in Hensford, worse before better; Ffion told her mother, and Sass's mother found out from a police liaison officer, and that has made things badly worse in a way nobody can undo. Dilly has a court date and won't talk about it and isn't allowed in the Corsa, which is gone. No pact speech; nobody mentions the rules. They sit on the steps by the works because there's nowhere else. Late that night, glancingly, a single 🩸 arrives from Ffion — of all people — and Nell has her shoes on before she's decided anything. Last paragraph: walking past the cow, which is still there, still enormous, still nobody's problem.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Nell Vaughan Sixteen and a half. Lives with her mum in a two-bed above what used to be a florist's on Chapel Street; her mum is a healthcare assistant on nights at Hensford General, which means the flat is either a library or a mortuary depending on whether she's home and asleep. Nell has been quiet since Year 8 in the particular way that gets you called "sensible" on reports and never invited anywhere. She got sensible in self-defence, then found it was the only thing she was reliably good at, and now it's a personality. She keeps a Notes app list called **things to do before Thursday** which she updates at half two in the morning. She has never once done everything on it. Her flaw, and it's a real one: she manages people instead of liking them. She'll sort your bus fare, remember your appointment, know your mum's shift pattern, and privately keep a ledger. She's the friend everyone tells things to and nobody rings for a laugh. She resents this and cultivates it, in that order, over and over. The ugly thing: in October, Sass sent her a single blood drop at ten past eleven on a Sunday. Nell screenshotted it, sent it to Ffion with *she's off again*, and Ffion sent back *lol*. Then Nell blocked the number. She has thought about this maybe four hundred times and has never once said it aloud, and the fact that she can recite the timestamp is worse than anything else about her. Idiosyncrasies: eats the crusts first. Cannot leave a room where a light's been left on. Says "no worries" when there are worries. Reads the ingredients on things. Has a habit of narrating logistics out loud in a crisis — *the 43 doesn't run after eleven, the works is two miles, that's twenty-five minutes if I don't stop* — which she thinks is competence and is actually a way of not looking at anything. Once cried in a Home Bargains and told the woman it was hay fever, in February. **Physicality.** Not tall. Solid, slightly hunched, walks fast with her arms crossed in front of her like she's carrying something. Brown hair scraped back so hard it changes her face; a bobble on her wrist at all times, three of them. Chewed thumbnails, the sides bitten raw. Wears her mum's old fleece and a school coat she's had since Year 9 with the toggles gone. Doesn't gesture when she talks. Goes very still when she's frightened, and people mistake the stillness for calm, which is useful. **Motives and allegiances.** She tells herself she's going because you go. Underneath, she's going to be forgiven, which is not the same as helping, and some part of her knows it. Her allegiance is to the version of herself that would have answered in October. She's loyal to her mum in a bruised, tired way — protects her from knowing things, then rages that she doesn't know things. Regarding Sass: love, exhaustion, and something close to disgust, sitting in one place at one time. Regarding Ffion: they made each other complicit, and she can't be near her without seeing *lol*. > "I check the 43 timetable even though I know the 43 doesn't run after eleven. I know it in my body. I check anyway, and it doesn't run after eleven, and I sit there for a second like the app might have a think about it." > "Everyone always says I'm good in a crisis. What they mean is I'll do the ringing round. Nobody's ever said I was good, full stop." --- # Saskia "Sass" Boyle Sixteen. Mother works at the garden centre and has a boyfriend called Ste who is not a monster, which somehow makes it harder to explain why Sass can't be in the house. There was a row on the Friday, the details of which she gives differently each time she's asked, none of them the real one. She has been sleeping in the old canteen at the fibreglass works for three nights on a Regatta sleeping bag her nan bought for a Guides trip in 2018. Here's the thing about Sass: she is not tragic and she is not charming. She was the funny one at twelve — genuinely, the funniest of the five — and something in her has gone flat and mean and impossible to reach. She's irritable rather than sad. She talks about the wrong things at length. She has a real gift for making you feel like you've turned up late to a party you were on time for. When Nell arrives she doesn't cry and she doesn't say thank you; she says *three hours*, and it's an accusation, and it's fair. She's contemptuous of fuss and will not be helped in any way that involves an adult, a form, or a room she can't leave. She lies constantly about small things (she's eaten, she's fine, that's ketchup) and tells the truth about enormous ones with no warning, in a bored voice, and then changes the subject. Idiosyncrasies: keeps a lighter she doesn't use for anything. Bites the skin off the inside of her lip. Calls everyone by their surname when she's angry. Tells long stories with no punchline — the man in the Co-op, twelve minutes, no ending. Cold all the time and refuses to say so. Steals things she doesn't want. Has Tosh's number still in her phone and has never texted it, not once, which she thinks nobody has noticed. **Physicality.** Tall, gone thin in a way that shows in her wrists and her jaw. Bleached hair grown out four inches at the roots, done herself in September, badly, on purpose. Chipped black nail varnish, a signet ring from a market. Sits sprawled and takes up room; leans against things rather than standing. Very direct eye contact, held slightly too long. Smells of cold and smoke and something sweet. Her left forearm is wrapped in a tea towel with pheasants on it. **Motives and allegiances.** She sent three drops because she'd run out of other ideas and because she wanted to see whether it still worked. She did not think about what would happen if it did. She wanted Nell specifically. Her allegiance is to the five of them as they were in Year 7, which is not a group that exists, and to Tosh, whose death she doesn't discuss because she genuinely doesn't know anything and the not-knowing is the thing she can't survive being asked about. She'd deny needing any of them under oath. > "Three hours. I could've walked to Hensford in three hours. I could've bled to death and got up and had a wash." > "There was a man in the Co-op with a full trolley, right, and he had four of them big multipacks of Wotsits, four, and I stood there and I watched him put a fifth one in and I thought — no. Hang on. Anyway. Have you got any crisps?" --- # Dilly Okoro Sixteen. Short for Adaeze; nobody's called her that since primary. Lives with her nan on the Fernhill estate, has done since she was nine, and her nan is up at all hours with QVC on because of her hip. Dilly's older brother Ez left the Corsa on the drive when he went to Telford and said don't touch it, which she interpreted generously. Dilly is the one people expect to be the comic relief and she isn't, quite. She's *keen*. Since the funeral she has had nobody — not a falling-out, just a slow drift where she kept texting the group chat after everyone stopped, three, four messages in a row, no replies, for about five months. She still has the chat pinned. When the three drops go out she doesn't ask why, she asks *when*, and there's something in her face that Nell doesn't like: she has been waiting. Her loyalty is total and unexamined and slightly frightening. She would hurt someone on Sass's behalf and would not consider it a decision. Flaws: no brakes, socially. Says the thing. Laughs a beat too long and too loud, and then says the joke again, louder, when nobody joins in. Takes charge of the wrong tasks with enormous competence (she has a torch, a blanket, a first aid kit from Ez's boot, and a bag of frozen peas she bought at the garage for reasons she cannot articulate) and none of the right ones. Cannot drive well. Drove anyway. Idiosyncrasies: says "listen, listen" before every sentence when excited. Keeps her nan's spare glasses in her coat for no reason. Names things — the Corsa is Deborah. Absolutely cannot be quiet in a tense situation; narrates. Has one song she plays at volume as a form of first aid. **Physicality.** Small, wiry, all shoulders and elbows, in constant motion — knee going, thumb on the wheel, up and down off a wall. Box braids pulled into a bun, a wave cap in her coat pocket. Puffer coat over pyjama bottoms and school socks in slides, all night, in February. Grins with her whole face, including when nothing is funny. Touches people — a hand on your arm, your shoulder, hard — which Nell finds unbearable and needs. **Motives and allegiances.** The pact is not a memory to her, it's a live document. She wants it to be real because if it's real then she wasn't dropped, she was just waiting. She is loyal, in order, to: Sass, Nell, Ffion, and Deborah. She is also the one who'll pay for tonight, and she'll pay it without complaining, and that's the worst thing in the story. > "Listen, listen — I've got peas. Don't laugh. In an emergency you want cold. Everyone knows that. Everyone knows that. Why's nobody saying anything?" > "Four years I've had that chat pinned. Four years. And I never once thought, oh, she'll be dead by now. I just thought, right. Whenever." --- # Ffion Rees Seventeen in April. Lives on the Meadowvale new-build estate in a house that smells of Zoflora, with a mother who has been unwell in a diffuse, permanent, unnameable way since Tosh died. Ffion's response to her brother's death was to become excellent. Predicted straight nines, five A-levels planned, a boyfriend called Alfie who plays rugby and has never had a bad week, a revision timetable on the wall in four colours. Everyone in Coldbrook is proud of her in a way that operates like a hand on the back of the neck. She is not warm. She was never warm — that's the thing people forget about her, they think grief made her cold. She's precise, controlled, and cruel with accuracy rather than volume. She will find the one true sentence that ends a conversation and say it quietly and not take it back. She does not believe in the pact and never did; she went along with it at twelve because Tosh was doing it. Her secret is worse than Nell's in one way and better in another: she has known Sass was at the works since Friday. Someone told her. She did nothing, and she has a reason, and the reason is *I cannot bring one more thing into that house*, and it's a real reason and it's also cowardice, and she knows both. She replied *lol* to Nell's screenshot in October and thinks about it as often as Nell does. Idiosyncrasies: whispers when she's angriest. Keeps her phone face-down. Cannot bear to be touched by Dilly. Corrects facts mid-argument. Wears Tosh's old hoodie under her coat and will deny it's his if asked. Sanitises her hands. Says "right" as a full sentence, in about nine different meanings. **Physicality.** Tall like her brother was, straight-backed, holds herself as if being assessed. Dark hair in a low bun even at one in the morning. Comes to the door in a dressing gown over leggings and a school PE top, slippers, and doesn't apologise for it. Very still; she and Nell are still in different ways — Nell freezes, Ffion composes. Doesn't blink much. Arms folded high, hands tucked in. **Motives and allegiances.** She gets in the car for one reason: Sass was the last person to see Tosh alive and Ffion has never been allowed to ask her, and tonight there are no adults and Sass is cornered. That's it. Her allegiance is to her mother, absolutely and destructively. She loves Nell, a bit, in the way you love a co-conspirator you'd like to never see again. She does not like Dilly. She does not know what she feels about Sass and is frightened to find out. > "Right. So we're doing this. And when my mum wakes up at six and I'm not there, that's mine, that is. That's mine to carry. Not yours. So don't tell me about the rules." > "You were the last one with him. That's not an accusation, it's just where you were. You were the last one with him and he texted you nothing and you've never once said his name in front of me." --- # Tomos "Tosh" Rees (absent) Died eighteen months ago, aged fifteen, on the Beacon road. Hit-and-run. Nobody was ever charged. Nobody in this story finds out anything more than that, including the reader. He was the fifth thumb behind the leisure centre. He was the one who *made* it real — he'd read something about blood brothers and brought the compass and a bag of Tangfastics and a straight face, and the reason the pact stuck is that he was the sort of person you didn't laugh at when he was serious. Ffion's brother, Sass's — something; not a boyfriend, something less formal and more permanent. He was funny like Sass was funny; they were funny at each other for four years. His last message to anyone was to Sass at 21:40 that night: a photo of somebody's dog, tied up outside the Nisa. No caption. She didn't reply because she was watching something. Nobody used the code that night. Nobody thought to. That's the hole in the middle of all four of them, and it's shaped exactly like three little cartoon drops of blood. **Traces:** a sticker on the dashboard of the Corsa that Dilly won't remove and won't mention. A hoodie. A number still in Sass's phone. A road everyone drives a different way to avoid.

Chapter 1

Model Output:
# 1. 00:04 The phone lights up the ceiling before it makes any noise, and I know. That's the stupid thing. I know before I've read it. I've got the Geography mock at nine. Paper two, physical, which is the one I'm fine at, and I'd been lying there running through the hydrograph stuff the way you do — lag time, peak discharge, urbanisation, impermeable surfaces — and I'd got to the bit where I always get to, which is thinking about how many other people in Coldbrook are awake, and whether that number is going up or down. 🩸🩸🩸 Unsaved number. 07 something, ends 449. I know it like I know my own. I deleted it in October. Deleted and blocked, and then unblocked in November so I could see if she'd tried, and she hadn't, and I never saved it again because saving it would mean I'd done something. I sit up. The duvet slides off and the cold comes at my legs like a hand. Three drops. Three. Here's what it means, and I need to say it properly or it'll sound like nothing. Year Seven, the June of Year Seven, behind the leisure centre where the bins are and the wall's got that dip in it you can sit on. Five of us. Tosh had read something in a book about blood brothers and he'd brought his maths set and a bag of Tangfastics and he had that face on where you didn't take the mick, because he was serious about about four things in his whole life and when he was serious you shut up. He did the compass point on his own thumb first. Barely a mark. Then Sass, who said it was pathetic and did it too hard and bled all down her thumb and looked delighted. Then Ffion, because Tosh was doing it and she wasn't going to be the one who didn't. Then Dilly, who said "listen, listen, is it clean, that," and did it anyway. Then me. Last. I remember the point going in and thinking that it didn't hurt and being disappointed. And Tosh said the rules and we said them after him like a register. Three drops means come. No arguing. No questions till after. Whatever it costs. And then Ffion said we should have a word instead because a word's easier to say, and Tosh said no, because you might not be able to say anything, and that shut us all up for about four seconds. Then Dilly said what if you're on the toilet and we all laughed for so long that a woman came out and told us to move. We were twelve. We were twelve and we thought we were being ridiculous, and we were, and it stuck anyway. Nobody has ever used it. In four years. Not once. Not when Dilly's brother got done over outside the Nisa, not when Ffion's mum went in the second time, not — and this is the bit — not that night. Nobody used it that night. Tosh died on the Beacon road eighteen months ago and not one of us sent three drops, not before, not after, we just found out the normal way, off Facebook and off mums, and I have thought about that so often that it's gone smooth, like a coin. Then there's blue coming through the gap in the fence, going round and round on the shed wall, and the ambulance can't get in, obviously, so two of them come across the concrete with a bag each and a torch, and one of them says "hiya, I'm Gav," and it's over. That's the moment. I remember thinking that in the room: it's over, and I've got no job now. They ask her name and she says Saskia Prosser. The one who isn't Gav writes it down and says "and your date of birth, Saskia," and she gives it, and it's right, and I watch him not believe a word of it. Then the police come. Because of the address, because it's a derelict site, because someone's called it in at four in the morning — I don't know which. Two of them, a man and a woman, and the woman goes off with Gav and Sass, and the man stands out on the apron with a torch and asks whose car is on the verge. I watch it from the gap in the fence. That's all I do. I stand at the gap in the fence with my arms crossed and I watch Dilly Okoro stand on Bridge Lane next to Ez's Corsa with her puffer coat over her dog pyjamas and school socks in slides, at four in the morning, in February, and I watch her say things, and I watch him write. She doesn't look over at us once. Not once. Whatever she's saying, she's saying all of it herself. Ffion, next to me, says: "She'll be alright." "Will she." "No," Ffion says. — Hensford A&E at twenty past four is: a corridor, a row of chairs with the arms between them, a vending machine, and a man asleep sitting up with a towel round his hand. We get there in a police car, which I never told my mum, and which is the single most embarrassing thing I have ever done. Sass goes through with Gav and then a nurse and then a curtain. We get sent to the chairs. The vending machine works. That's the thing about Hensford — the machine works. I put in £1.20 and I get a Fanta out and I don't want it, and I hold it, and it's still shut when we leave. Mum's on that unit. Ward 6, which is two floors up and a different building, and I know her shift, and I know she's on till seven, and I could go up. There's a lift. I could get in the lift. I get my phone out at about half four and I ring her and it goes to the locker and to her saying the old landline number wrong, and I listen to the whole thing this time, right to the beep, and then I hang up without leaving anything, and I put the phone face-down on my knee like Ffion does. I don't go up. I want to say something about why but I haven't got anything. At about five a woman with a lanyard comes and sits on the chair opposite and says, "Is one of you family?" "No," Ffion says. "Do you know who is?" And we all sit there. Sass has given the wrong surname to four separate people, and they've all written it down, and none of them believed it, and at some point somebody is going to ring somebody, and it isn't going to be one of us, and everybody in that corridor knows it. They let us see her at about ten to six. Curtain, trolley, a blue paper sheet, her arm dressed and taped and up on a pillow, and she's got a hospital gown on over her own T-shirt because she wouldn't take it off. Eleven stitches. They said the number and Dilly said "eleven" out loud like a score. Sass says, "Did somebody move me peas?" Dilly starts laughing and can't stop and has to go out into the corridor. Then it's just me stood there, and she's looking at me, direct, too long, and I don't say sorry. I don't say anything about October. I don't say his name. I put my hand on her coat, which is folded on the end of the trolley, and I hold the sleeve of it, and I stand there like that for a bit. She lets me.
