# 8. Six weeks I got a D. Paper two, physical, the one I'm fine at. There's a comment on the front in green pen from Mr Aldiss: *Well below your usual standard, Nell — a lot of unrealised potential here. Come and see me.* I have not been to see him. I've got the paper in the front of my folder where I have to look at it every lesson, which I could stop doing at any time. Mum found out about the police car in the third week, off Chloe Prosser's mum, obviously, because that's how anybody finds out anything in Coldbrook. She didn't shout. She sat on the end of my bed with her coat still on and asked why I didn't come up to Ward 6, and I said I don't know, and she looked at me for a while and said "no." Then she said if I ever do that again I'm to come up to Ward 6. Then she went and had a bath. Sass is at her Auntie Bev's in Hensford. She's not fine. It got worse first, quite badly worse, in a way I can't put down neatly. Ffion told her mum on the Wednesday — she said she was going to and she did, which is Ffion — and Ffion's mum rang Sass's mum, and by then there was already a woman from the council involved because of the hospital, and Sass's mum found out that her daughter had been sleeping in the Kelloe works for four nights from a police liaison officer in her own front room with Ste standing in the doorway. Sass has not spoken to her mother since the 4th of March. I know that's our fault. Not the sleeping in the works — the way she found out. I've gone round it a lot of times: if nobody had told anybody, then nothing would have got sorted, and if we'd told it properly, ourselves, first, then maybe it wouldn't have arrived like that. But we didn't tell it. We shouted at a woman with a dog not to phone, and then a system did it for us in the worst possible order, and there's no version of me that gets to feel good about any of it. There's a social worker called Pauline. Sass says Pauline is alright, which from Sass is a reference you could put on a CV. Dilly's got a court date. The 14th of May, Hensford Magistrates. No insurance, which is the big one, and no MOT and no tax, and driving otherwise than in accordance with a licence, which she read out to me off the letter in a really flat voice like she was doing a shopping list. Six points minimum. She's sixteen. She hasn't got a licence to put them on so they go on the one she gets, which means she'll have six points before she's ever driven a mile legally, and she can't get insured for anything for years, and Ez has to sit there in the room with her. She won't talk about it. Genuinely won't — I've tried twice and she does this thing where she goes "yep" and then asks me something about somebody else. Ez took the Corsa away on a trailer on a Sunday. I watched it go past the end of Chapel Street and I couldn't tell you why I stood there for it. Ffion got 96 in the Chemistry. — We're on the steps by the works. Not inside. There's steps going down to the towpath by the bridge, concrete, and there's a bit where the wall's low enough to sit on, and it's where you sit if you've got chips and nowhere. Nobody arranged it. Dilly put *chips?* in the chat, the pinned one, the five of us, and three of us said yeah, and that was the first time anybody had put anything in it since the 9th of October. Sass came on the bus from Hensford. The 43 does run in the daytime. She's got a scar that's about as long as my little finger and still pink and shiny, and she doesn't cover it up, and Dilly asked to look at it and she let her, and Dilly said "eleven" again, exactly the same way, and Sass said "yeah, alright." Nobody says anything about the pact. I keep waiting for it. I've got a version in my head where somebody makes a speech about it, about how it should have been one drop, or how you should be able to send it for nothing, on a Tuesday, because you feel like it — I've had that whole speech drafted since about the second week of March. Nobody makes it. Dilly doesn't even say the word. What we talk about is: whether the chip shop's changed its oil (Ffion says no, Sass says obviously not), Pauline's car, whether Bandit the collie belongs to the woman or she was walking it for someone, which nobody knows and nobody's ever going to find out. Dilly tells us there's a bloke on Fernhill selling a Nissan Micra for £300 and Ffion says "Dilly" and Dilly says "I'm not saying I'd buy it." Ffion says, at one point, looking at the water: "Tosh'd have gone in there for a fiver." And Sass says, "He went in there for nothing. He went in there in Year Nine for absolutely nothing." And that's it. That's all of it. Nobody cries, nobody says anything about how good it is to say his name, and then Dilly asks if anyone wants the last of her chips and Ffion says they've gone cold and Dilly says they're better cold, and they argue about that for about four minutes. — Two weeks after that, it's ten to twelve on a Sunday and I've got my phone on the pillow and it lights up the ceiling. One drop. 🩸 From Ffion. That's all. No message, no pin, nothing after it. And I'm honestly not sure she meant anything by it — Ffion Rees does not send things by accident, but there's about four things it could mean and one of them is nothing. I've got my shoes on before I've decided anything. I'm in the hall doing my laces in the dark and I'm already saying it in my head, the logistics: Meadowvale's twenty minutes uphill, the 43 doesn't run after eleven, Mum's on till seven. I text her *coming* and I go. And on the way, because you have to go past it, there's the cow. Twelve foot of it on the verge, black and white, going green up the legs, with the hole in its side you can put your arm in. It's got a bag of something caught on one of its ears. Twenty-odd years it's been stood there and nobody has ever come for it. Not the council, not the site, not whoever made it. There's no plan for it. There's no form anywhere with that cow on it. I walk past it and it's just there, enormous, in the dark, being nobody's problem.

Every major beat is hit. **Character Consistency** Each character behaves exactly as their profile demands. The cow has been established throughout the story as an unreasonable recurring detail, and here it becomes something without being forced into symbolism. "There's no plan for it. There's no form anywhere with that cow on it." This is Nell's voice — the admin-brain finding the administrative absurdity — and it resonates with everything unresolved in the story (Tosh's death, Dilly's court date, Sass's relationship with her mother, Ffion's single drop) without the author reaching in to make the connection explicit. These are genuinely minor. **What's Particularly Impressive** The chapter manages grief without sentimentality, consequence without melodrama, and resolution without resolution. The "something is slightly better and something is permanently worse" structure from the plan is delivered without ever being stated. The guilt about October — Nell's specific, ugly guilt — is present in the chapter's silences. She never confesses. The story doesn't require her to. The chips scene is the best scene in the chapter: it's funny and sad and completely true to how people actually are with each other after something terrible, and it doesn't announce itself as such. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of darkly comic British YA fiction. Let me work through its qualities and failings systematically. STRENGTHS: The voice is the piece's greatest achievement. Nell's narration is pitch-perfect: dry, self-aware, digressive in the way actual teenage thought works, and consistently funny without ever undercutting the emotional weight. The logistics voice she describes — running through hydrograph terms, checking the 43 bus timetable she already knows won't run — is a beautifully observed coping mechanism that recurs naturally throughout. The parenthetical self-corrections ("I should explain the cow") feel genuinely earned rather than affectedly quirky. The characters are genuinely differentiated. Dilly's compulsive loudness that goes "a beat past the end of it," her bringing frozen peas, her refusal to discuss the court date — these are consistent, specific, and revealing. Ffion's quietness-as-anger, her Chemistry score of 96, her decision to tell Sass's mum on the Wednesday because she said she would — these details accumulate into a real person. Sass's flat affect, her giving a wrong surname to four people, her letting the dog onto the sleeping bag — all consistent. The dead Tosh is rendered with remarkable economy: the Sheffield United sticker, the compass pact, the dog emoji he sent before dying. The pact itself is a superb piece of world-building. The rules are established with total credibility — the specificity of the leisure centre bins, the Tangfastics, the maths set compass — and the story then systematically interrogates what the pact means and what it failed to do. The revelation that nobody sent three drops when Tosh died is devastating and arrives at exactly the right moment. The beetroot reveal is the piece's comic masterstroke. It's genuinely funny, it's earned (the smell detail is perfect), and it doesn't defuse the tension — it redirects it, because the real wound is revealed immediately after. This is sophisticated comic timing. The "it would be easier if she'd just died" moment is the piece's darkest beat, and it's handled with extraordinary restraint. The narrator puts it away "the way you'd put a phone in your pocket" and never returns to it explicitly. This is exactly right — it's not explained, not apologized for, not resolved. It just sits there. The cow is used well throughout — introduced with the right amount of detail, recurring at the climax and the ending. The final image of it being "nobody's problem" resonates without being over-explained. The dialogue is excellent. The argument about the peas, the argument about the car, the argument about whether it's a cow or a bull — these are funny and character-revealing simultaneously. "That's not a lay-by that's a passing place" is exactly the kind of argument people have in crisis. WEAKNESSES: The piece occasionally over-explains its own emotional logic. "I understand something about myself that I don't especially want" is slightly too neat a formulation. The narrator's self-analysis is generally a strength but occasionally tips into telling us what to feel rather than letting the scene do it. The Year Ten Christmas party digression in Chapter 4 is the clearest example — it's well-written but the narrator's commentary ("You'd think you'd be better than that. You're not.") is slightly too tidy. The thirty-eight-minute detour in Chapter 4 is structurally clever but slightly overlong. The barrier/passing place/skip sequence is funny but the joke runs a beat too long, which is ironic given that the piece is otherwise so precise about comic timing. The woman with the dog is a slightly convenient deus ex machina, though the piece is self-aware enough about systems and adults intervening that it doesn't feel entirely unearned. The detail of Sass immediately obeying her instruction to raise her arm — for a stranger, when she'd refused everything from her friends — is a sharp observation. The final chapter (six weeks later) is mostly excellent but the Ffion one-drop ending, while emotionally satisfying, is slightly too neat a mirror of the opening. It works, but it's the one moment where the piece's structural cleverness becomes slightly visible. The "darkly comic" element is well-balanced throughout — the comedy never trivializes the darkness, and the darkness never overwhelms the comedy. This is genuinely difficult to achieve and the piece manages it consistently. Overall this is a very high-quality piece of YA fiction with a distinctive, sustained voice, genuine emotional intelligence, and real craft in its construction. Its failings are minor and mostly involve occasional over-explanation of emotional states that the scenes themselves have already communicated. + Planning Phase (5 Steps)

The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. Model Output:
# Brainstorming ## The Prompt Itself "Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up." — Space Western. Immediately we have: a ship, a crew, cargo they shouldn't have taken, and a reveal. The line implies the speaker is nervous, deferential, and that the crate was picked up (salvaged? contracted? stolen?) with insufficient due diligence. The ellipsis does a lot of work — hesitation, disbelief, maybe the speaker has been staring at it a while before saying anything. Space Western as a genre gives me: frontier morality, hardscrabble economics, debts, bounty hunters, corporate railroads-in-space, indigenous/colonial tension, dust, cattle-analogues, saloons, gunfights measured in seconds, laconic dialogue, big skies (here: big vacuum), and the fundamental Western question — what does a person owe a stranger when the law is three weeks away? ## What's in the crate? (Casting wide) 1. **A child.** Cryo-stasis smuggling. Cheapest emotional hook, most reliable. Could be a genetically engineered child, a clone, a witness, an heir. 2. **A person, adult** — a stowaway who paid the shipper, or a prisoner being illegally transported. Maybe a bounty who faked their own transit. 3. **An animal** — something valuable, an alien beast, a xenofauna specimen. Could be a "calf" — the last of a breeding stock. Very Western: cattle rustling. The MacGuffin is livestock. 4. **A weapon that is alive** — bio-engineered killer, a "hound," a thing in a box that should not be opened. Horror-inflected. 5. **Something incorporeal** — a swarm, a spore, nanites. Body-horror direction. 6. **An AI substrate / a mind in a jar** that is physically twitching its housing. 7. **A pregnant creature** — the movement is birth. 8. **Nothing** — the crate is a trap, a beacon, a lure. The "movement" is a mechanism arming itself. 9. **A dead thing that isn't** — resurrection tech, a revenant. 10. **Seeds/eggs** — terraforming contraband, an ecology in a box, which is worth more than the ship. **Most Western-feeling options:** the child (orphan under protection = *Shane*, *True Grit*, *Lone Wolf and Cub*), the livestock (rustling, water rights, the last herd), and the prisoner (bounty, hanging, the marshal escorting a man to a rope). The child + livestock hybrid: something that is *both* a beast and a person, and the crew must decide which it is. That's rich, because the Western is fundamentally about deciding who counts as a person. **Strong idea:** the crate contains a juvenile of a native species — an animal to the corporation, a child to the people whose planet it came from. That fuses the cattle plot with the frontier-colonial plot and makes the moral question load-bearing. ## Crew concepts - **Captain** — needs to be the fulcrum. Options: grizzled ex-lawman; a woman running from a marriage/company contract; a former corporate pilot with a debt; a preacher-turned-smuggler. The Western captain should be laconic, competent, morally compromised but with a floor. - I like: **Captain Ysolde "Sol" Marchetti** — no. Let's go plainer, more frontier: **Captain Ada Renn**, or **Captain Marisol Vance**, or **Captain Ott**. Something with grit. Let's try **Captain Imogen "Gen" Cull** — hm, or a single hard name: **Captain Dray**. - Actually a great Western-flavored name set: **Vessel** *Bittermouth*, *Coyote's Word*, *Pale Mare*, *The Long Reckoning*, *Sundowner*, *Hardpan*, *Dust Devil*, *The Persistent*. - **The one who says the line** — should be the youngest, greenest, or the most anxious. A kid engineer. A cook. A newly hired hand. Good candidate for POV. - **The mechanic/xeno-hand** — knowledgeable, dry, the one who figures out what it is. - **The one who wants to sell it anyway** — internal antagonist, someone with a debt or a sick family, or just plain greed. Necessary for conflict inside the hull. - **The medic/former company person** — knows what the buyer is. Small crew, 4–5, so 1000-word chapters can hold them. ## Antagonists - **The Consignor** — a corporate agent who hired them, cold, polite, appears mid-story via comms and later in person. Company man in a clean coat. Very Western: the railroad man, the cattle baron's lawyer. - **A bounty hunter / retrieval specialist** — the gunslinger foil. Someone with a reputation, maybe a former associate of the Captain. "The Undertaker." Should feel like Angel Eyes or the Judge. - **The law** — a marshal ship, corrupt or merely bureaucratic, or genuinely decent but slow. - **Environment** — a dust-belt, an asteroid storm, a station with no fuel, a planet with a three-day night. The Western landscape is a character; in space, it's the deep black, a wildcat mining moon, a dry world. ## Setting texture - The Verge / the Dust Line / the Rimrock / the Trailhead. Frontier terminology: "the drift," "cattle stations," "waystations," "claim jumping," "the Company," "the Combine," "the Concern." - Refueling at a dirtside town: **Hollow Ford**, **Perdition Wells**, **Last Chance Station**, **Tallow**, **Ash Hollow**, **Cordwood**. - Ships as horses: the ship needs feeding, has a bad knee, is old. Salvage-built. - Money: scrip, chits, company credit. Debt as the engine — the crew is one bad job from losing the ship. ## Plot shapes (8 chapters) **Shape A: The Escort Western** (*Lone Wolf and Cub* / *The Mandalorian* / *3:10 to Yuma*) 1. Job accepted, crate loaded. 2. Something moves; open it; find the creature/child. 3. Debate: sell, dump, or protect. Buyer contact reveals stakes. 4. Refuel stop, near-discovery, first violence. 5. Bounty hunter arrives; chase. 6. Betrayal from within the crew. 7. Showdown at the destination. 8. Delivery to the true home / cost paid. **Shape B: The Siege** (*Assault on Precinct 13* western style) The crate's contents attract something; the ship is besieged in a rock field or on a dead moon. More claustrophobic, more horror. **Shape C: The Trial** The crew effectively holds a trial for the thing in the crate, with the corporate contract as prosecution. Talky; less Western. **Shape D: The Rustling Western** The crate is the last breeding female of a species the Combine wiped out to control a planet's water. Returning her = restoring a way of life. Cattle-drive structure: get from A to B across hostile territory. **Shape E: Horror turn** — the thing in the crate is genuinely dangerous and the humane instinct gets people killed. Bleak, subversive, *The Thing* by way of Sergio Leone. Risky but memorable. Could be split: it *is* dangerous, and also a person, and both are true. Shape A crossed with D feels strongest and most Western: an escort/drive across the black, with a creature that is both livestock and child. ## Possible twists - The crate wasn't picked up by accident — a crew member arranged it. - The creature imprints on the youngest crew member. - The creature is not a baby but a *seed carrier* — the movement is it hatching. - The buyer wants it not as a specimen but as a template — to build a weapon or a labor stock. - The captain has history: she once ran a cargo like this and didn't ask questions, and the guilt is the spine. - The "law" turns out to be the worst outcome — handing it over legally destroys it. - The creature can speak, badly, and its first words recontextualize everything. - The creature is dying and the whole run becomes a race to keep it alive. - The last beat: the crew burns their transponder, loses their livelihood, becomes outlaws. The classic Western ending — the frontier closes, and they ride out ahead of it. ## Tone options - **Laconic and dusty** — short sentences, understatement, weather. Cormac McCarthy-lite but not so far as to lose readability. - **Warm ensemble banter** — *Firefly* mode. Risky: could get cute. - **Grim horror-western** — atmospheric, tense. Best is probably laconic-with-warmth: hard people, sparse dialogue, a couple of dry jokes, and real tenderness earned late. ## POV options - Third limited on the Captain: most direct, gives us the decision-maker. - Third limited on the kid who speaks the opening line: lets us discover with them, keeps the Captain mythic and unreadable. - Alternating: risky in 8k words. - First person retrospective, old-timer telling it: very Western, very charming. "I was seventeen the year we hauled the Fenwright crate." First-person retrospective is tempting for voice, but third limited on the youngest crew member with the Captain as the object of study might be cleanest. Or — third limited on the Captain, since her moral arc is the story, and let the kid be the conscience externalized. ## Chapter beat drafts (Shape A/D fusion) 1. **The Hire.** Debt, a station, a bad contract. Load the crate. Establish crew, ship, and the rule "we don't open cargo." End on the line. 2. **The Opening.** They open it. Reveal. First contact. Captain's cold decision to seal it back up. 3. **The Owner Calls.** Comms with the consignor. Learn what it's worth and what it's for. Crew fractures. The thing gets out / is fed. 4. **Hollow Ford / the refuel.** Dirtside. Encounter with someone who knows what it is — an old woman, a native trader, a priest. Exposition delivered dramatically. Near-miss with company men. 5. **The Hunter.** The retrieval specialist boards or pursues. Violence. A crew member wounded or killed. Escape damaged. 6. **The Betrayal.** Someone sold their position. Confrontation. The creature does something that decides the matter — protects, or speaks, or mourns. 7. **The Reckoning.** Showdown at the destination — the creature's home, a moon the Combine has claimed. Gunfight/ship fight. Cost paid. 8. **The Ride Out.** Aftermath, delivery, elegiac close. Crew is outlawed but whole. Final image echoing the opening line. That's tight and each beat is a real 1000-word scene. ## Alternative darker plan The crate contains a man — a witness the Combine wants dead, sealed in a shipping coffin, still alive. Simpler, more noir, less mythic. Less interesting to me than the creature, but more grounded. ## Or: the crate contains a girl who isn't human Half-and-half: a hybrid child, product of an illegal program, the only survivor. Movement = she's waking from stasis. Combines child-pathos with the personhood question. Very *Logan*. ## Names, textures, lines - The ship: *Bittermouth* — good, harsh, memorable. - Captain: **Ilsa Rook**? **Captain Marlowe Ott**? I like **Captain Nadia Quill**... Let's try **Captain Wren Dahl**. Or a mononym: **Captain Sarsen**. Hmm — **Captain Odessa "Dess" Hale**. Something plain and hard: **Captain Marrow**? Too on-the-nose. - The kid: **Pim**, **Tobin**, **Ellis**, **June**, **Sparrow**. - The mechanic: **Otis Fen**, **Bram**, **Hoke**. - The medic/gunhand: **Sister Cass**, **Delacroix**, **Vega**. - The hunter: **Mr. Amaranth**, **The Tallyman**, **Corvo Kest**, **Mr. Sheaf**. - The Combine: **Ardent-Kell**, **The Pallas Concern**, **Meridian Combine**, **Vaunt & Sons**. - Places: **Hollow Ford**, **Tarn**, **Cassiopeia's Rest**, **the Drovers' Belt**, **Perdition**, **the Sump**. - Recurring motif: dust in everything. Water as wealth. The creature associated with water or rain. A song. A hat. A debt-ledger. ## Sensory / Western transplant ideas - Ships "watered" at fuel stops; fuel called "water." - Cargo manifests as brands. - "Rustlers" who cut transponders. - A stampede analogue: a migration of drifting organisms. - A funeral with a body committed to vacuum, someone reading badly from a book. - Boot Hill = a rock with names scratched into it at a waystation. # Reflection Looking back over all of this, a few things clarify. **The prompt's energy is discovery and dread, then obligation.** The line is spoken by a subordinate to a captain, which tells me the story wants hierarchy, and a captain who has to *decide*. So the story's spine should be a decision made under economic pressure. The Western does this better than almost any genre: the frontier is a place where law is absent and therefore character is exposed. If I write a story where the crew never really has a choice — where the creature is unambiguously innocent and the buyers unambiguously evil — I lose the tension. The debt has to be real. The crew has to have something genuine to lose. The moral choice should cost them their livelihood, not merely their comfort. **What's in the crate matters less than what it means.** I brainstormed a lot of options, but the ones that stay Western are: a child, a prisoner, or livestock. The idea that fuses them — a juvenile of a native species, treated as a beast by the Combine and as a person by the people it was taken from — is the strongest, because it makes the crew's argument about *what counts as a person* rather than *should we be nice to a baby*. That argument is inherently more dramatic and less sentimental. It also lets me have a creature that's genuinely alien and a bit frightening: it should not be cute. If readers are unsure whether it's dangerous for a while, the story has more voltage. And if it eventually does something both terrible and understandable, better still. Actually, I want to be careful not to over-engineer the alien. If I spend too many of my 8,000 words on xenobiology, the Western evaporates. The creature should be described physically and behaviorally, with restraint, and its meaning should come through the humans who look at it. Less taxonomy, more awe and unease. **The "cattle" angle is very strong for the Western texture.** The Combine harvesting a native species to control a planet — that's the water-rights plot, the cattle-baron plot, the buffalo-extermination plot, all of which are the beating heart of the genre. It gives me a villain who isn't a mustache-twirler but a *policy*. And a corporate agent who is polite and reasonable and perfectly willing to kill is more chilling and more Western (the company man, the Pinkerton, the hired lawyer) than a snarling brute. I want the antagonist's argument to be almost persuasive: *you signed a contract; the animal is Company property; we are the only thing standing between the frontier and chaos.* **Two antagonists may be one too many.** I brainstormed both a corporate consignor and a bounty hunter. In 8,000 words, that risks crowding. But I think it works if the consignor is mostly a *voice* — comms, a face on a screen, an inevitability — and the hunter is the body, the physical threat. The hunter should be the one with a face and a history. Ideally the hunter is someone the Captain knows. That gives me a scene in chapter 5 or 6 that is a conversation as much as a fight, which is very Leone, and cheaper in wordcount than an extended action set piece. **POV.** I keep circling. The retrospective first-person old-timer voice is delicious but risks arch cuteness and eats words on framing. Third limited on the youngest crew member preserves mystery around the Captain, but the story's central decision belongs to the Captain and I'd be watching it from outside. I think third limited on the Captain is right — but I should give the youngest crew member (the one who speaks the opening line) enough presence to function as the story's conscience and to carry the ending's emotional weight. The Captain decides; the kid is the reason. Also worth noting: the opening line should land at the end of chapter one, not chapter two, and it should be the chapter's last beat. That gives the first chapter a real shape — hire, load, unease, hook. Hmm, one risk: opening with the line as a chapter-one closer means chapter one is all setup. I need that setup to be interesting on its own — the hire scene should have friction, the debt should be concrete, there should be a reason they took a job they shouldn't have. Maybe the crate is not the only cargo; maybe it's the one item they weren't supposed to notice. Or maybe they salvaged it — "picked up" can mean scavenged, which is more Western (finders keepers on the frontier) and removes the need for a formal contract scene. Actually — best of both: they take a legitimate freight run, and the crate is an unmanifested addition, or they lift it off a derelict during the run and add it to the load because salvage is how they stay solvent. Salvage makes them complicit but not villains. I like that. Wait — if they salvaged it, the "buyer" doesn't know they have it, which weakens the ticking clock. Unless the crate has a tracker, which the Combine follows. That's clean: they lift it off a wreck, it pings home, and the Combine comes. Their greed causes the whole thing. That's good Western causality: the sin is small and ordinary, and the consequences are enormous. **Pacing worries.** Eight chapters at 1000 words is not much room. I should limit locations: the ship, one dirtside stop, one final destination. Three settings maximum. And the crew should be four people, not six — Captain, the kid, an engineer/xeno-hand, and one who wants to sell. Four is enough for a betrayal, a death, and a survivor. If someone dies, it should be around chapter 5–6 and it should cost. I'm also wary of the ending being too neat. The classic Western ending is bittersweet: the right thing is done, the doers are exiled by it. I don't want a triumphant firefight where the Combine is defeated — that's not credible against a corporation. Better: they get the creature home, and that's all they get. They lose the ship's registry, or the ship itself, or a crew member, and they ride out into worse country than they came from. And a final image that rhymes with the opening line — maybe the kid says something similar about a different container, or the Captain listens at a bulkhead out of habit, or something moves and this time nobody is afraid. **Tone.** Laconic, weather-and-dust, dry humor, restrained sentiment. Dialogue should be clipped. I should resist quipping. The prose can be a little lyrical about the black and the dust, but the people should talk plain. And I should honor the specific texture of the line: the ellipsis, the deference, the fear. That kid's voice should be characterized from the first sentence he speaks. **One more consideration.** There's an ethical texture here — a species harvested, a homeworld, dispossession — that maps onto real colonial history. I should handle it with some seriousness rather than as set dressing, but I also shouldn't make the story a lecture. Keeping the focus on four people in a small hull making a hard choice is the way to keep it honest and human-scaled. Let the larger horror stay in the background where it's most effective. So: I'm converging on a four-hander aboard a salvage-hauling ship in a frontier belt; a crate lifted off a wreck; a juvenile of a native species inside; a tracker calling the Combine home; a dirtside stop where they learn what they're carrying; a hunter with history; a betrayal born of debt; a run to a dead-looking world; a cost paid; and an ending where doing right makes them outlaws. That's a story I can tell in eight thousand words, and it fits the prompt's dread, its hierarchy, and its promise of something alive in the dark.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The story.** Four people on a salvage-hauling ship in a frontier belt lift an unmarked crate off a derelict because salvage is how they eat. The crate contains a juvenile of a native species the Meridian Combine has been harvesting to extinction in order to control a planet's water cycle. The crate has a beacon. The Combine comes. The crew's small, ordinary greed sets a large, terrible thing in motion, and the story is about what four indebted people do when the right choice will cost them everything they own. **Structure.** Three locations only — the ship, one dirtside stop, one final destination — so that 8,000 words go into people rather than travel. Chapter one ends on the prompt line, delivered as the chapter's last beat. Chapters two through six escalate inside the hull and at the stop. Chapter seven is the reckoning. Chapter eight is the ride out. No triumphant defeat of the corporation; they get the creature home and nothing else, and that is enough and not enough. **POV and voice.** Third person limited, past tense, on Captain Odessa Hale. She makes the decision, so the camera stays with her. The youngest crew member, Pim, speaks the prompt line and functions as the story's conscience; I'll give him a distinct verbal tic (over-explaining when frightened) so he's characterized instantly and can carry the ending's emotional weight. Prose: laconic, weathered, concrete. Short declaratives with occasional long breath-out sentences about the black and the dust. Dialogue clipped, plain, unquipped. I want dryness, not banter. **Crew of four.** Hale (captain, ex-Combine pilot, carries a specific old sin). Pim Arday (nineteen, cargo hand, over-talker, conscience). Otis Fen (engineer, sixty-odd, dry, has handled Combine cargo before and knows what it is). Renata Vega (pilot/gun, hard-nosed, real debt — a sister in a Combine work-hold — and therefore the one who sells them out for a reason I want readers to half-forgive). **The creature.** Not cute. Not a taxonomy lecture. Described sparingly through what the humans see and how they react: something long-limbed and dust-colored, wet-eyed, that hums in a register that makes the hull ring, that is frightening before it is pitiable. Ambiguously dangerous for two chapters. It kills once, understandably, and the story does not excuse it. Its meaning arrives through the humans looking at it, especially a dirtside woman who names it. **Antagonists.** The Combine agent, Mr. Sheaf, is mostly a voice on comms — polite, reasonable, contractual, chilling. The physical threat is Corvo Kest, a retrieval specialist who once flew with Hale; their confrontation is more conversation than gunfight, which is both more Western and cheaper in wordcount. **What I'm aiming for.** Dread that becomes obligation. A moral choice with a real price. Restraint. One good death that costs. An ending that rhymes with the opening line — something moving in the dark, and this time nobody afraid. **What I'm avoiding.** Quippy ensemble banter. Cute alien. Xenobiology exposition. A sixth crew member. Two full-bodied antagonists. Sentimentality unearned. Corporate villain monologues. A victory that a corporation would not plausibly permit. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — "Salvage" (~1000w).** The *Bittermouth* runs a legitimate freight leg through the Drover's Belt, hauling seed-stock to a wildcat moon. Establish debt: Hale's ship is one bad quarter from a Combine reclamation notice. They find a broken Combine tender, dead crew, and strip it. Vega wants the coolant; Pim finds a sealed crate, unmanifested, cold-bonded, heavy. Fen says leave it. Hale, doing arithmetic against her ledger, says take it. Loading, tension, the hold gone quiet. Final beat: Pim at the bulkhead, over-explaining, then — *"Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up."* **Ch. 2 — "What's Inside" (~1000w).** They open it. Stasis foam, a beacon light Fen doesn't see yet, and the thing: long-limbed, dust-colored, waking badly. It gets loose, panics, breaks Pim's wrist and nearly kills Vega before Hale corners it with a cargo net rather than a gun — the first sign of her floor. Sealed in an empty water tank. Fen finds the beacon and pulls it, too late; it's been pinging four hours. Hale's cold decision: run the freight leg, deliver, decide dirtside. Nobody sleeps. **Ch. 3 — "The Consignor" (~1000w).** Comms hail: Mr. Sheaf, Meridian Combine, unfailingly polite. He calls it *stock*, offers a finder's fee that would clear Hale's debt entirely, and makes clear the alternative. Crew fractures along honest lines: Vega wants the money (reveals the sister, obliquely); Fen won't say; Pim, wrist in a splint, won't stop feeding it. Hale stalls Sheaf, buys forty hours. Interstitial: the thing hums, and the whole hull rings with it, and Hale can't sleep for the sound. **Ch. 4 — "Hollow Ford" (~1000w).** Dirtside at a dust-choked waystation to water the ship. Hale offloads the seed-stock; the town is dying because the rains stopped. An old woman, Nakuthi Aro, sees the creature's blood on Pim's sleeve, and names it — a *stonebird*, or their word for it — and tells them plainly what the Combine did: harvested the migration to break the water cycle, and the world dried. Hale learns she once flew these routes for the Combine and never asked what she was hauling. That's the old sin, stated once, not dwelt on. **Ch. 5 — "Kest" (~1000w).** Corvo Kest is already at Hollow Ford, drinking, waiting — because Vega called ahead. He and Hale talk: old history, the arithmetic of survival, an offer. It is nearly reasonable. Violence when it comes is quick and ugly and off-balance: Fen takes a round covering their run to the ship. They lift off with the town's fuel bill unpaid and Fen dying in the galley. He tells Hale where the creature's people gather, and how he knows, and it's the worst thing he's ever admitted. **Ch. 6 — "The Price of a Sister" (~1000w).** Fen dies; vacuum committal, badly read. Vega confesses before she's accused — the sister, the work-hold, Sheaf's terms. Hale doesn't shoot her and doesn't forgive her. The creature, loose again, comes to Fen's empty bunk and hums, and Pim understands it is grieving, and Vega breaks. Decision made: they run for Tarn, the dry world, where the migration used to end. Vega chooses to stay aboard. Kest is behind them. **Ch. 7 — "Tarn" (~1000w).** The dry world, a salt basin where the stonebirds once came to breed. Kest's cutter on their tail; a running descent, the *Bittermouth* taking damage she won't recover from. They set down on the pan, open the ramp. The creature won't leave the hold. Pim walks it out. Kest lands and comes across the salt on foot, and the confrontation is short: Hale wins it and it is not clean, and Vega pays part of the bill. Then the hum — answered, from the rocks, from a remnant nobody knew survived. Rain smell. Nothing more. **Ch. 8 — "Outlaws" (~1000w).** Aftermath. The *Bittermouth* won't fly far; transponder burned, registry void, Sheaf's polite final message logged and deleted unheard. They are, formally, outlaws now, and poorer than when they started. Hale sits in the dark hold that used to hold cargo. Something moves in it — Pim, or a stonebird chick that stayed, or both. Pim starts over-explaining. Hale tells him it's all right. Final image: dust, the black, a ship with no name on the manifest, riding out ahead of the closing frontier.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a human writer might actually approach this A human writing to "Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up" would probably not start by building a moral architecture. They'd start with the *feeling* of the line — someone standing in a cold hold, hand not quite touching metal, and the awful intimacy of hearing something alive where nothing should be. They'd chase that image. Then they'd ask, selfishly, *what would be fun and horrible to write?* The plan I've made is competent, but it was built from the outside in — theme first, characters assigned roles to serve theme. That's the tell. A human would also probably get bored of their own plan halfway through and let the story go somewhere the plan didn't allow. They'd fall in love with a minor character. They'd let a scene run long because the dialogue was working. They'd forget to resolve something. Those "failures" are what make prose feel written by a person with a pulse and a deadline rather than assembled by a system optimizing for coverage. And critically: a human with taste would be *suspicious* of how neatly this all fits. Corporate extinction-harvesting causing a planet to dry out, the beacon that punishes their greed, the sister in the work-hold that motivates the betrayal, the dying engineer's deathbed confession — every element is load-bearing for the theme. Real stories have slack in them. They have a crew member whose backstory never comes up. They have a subplot that goes nowhere because life goes nowhere. The plan has zero slack, and slack is where humanity lives. --- # General LLM failure modes, and how they'd bite this piece **1. Thematic over-determination.** Everything means something. The creature isn't just an animal — it's a symbol of dispossession. The rain isn't weather — it's ecological restitution. The engineer doesn't just die — he confesses complicity first. LLMs do this because we're trained to be legible, and legibility reads as *quality* in the abstract but as *thesis* on the page. Human stories have inert matter in them. The best Westerns are full of stuff that's just there: a bad tooth, a horse that won't ford water, a joke nobody laughs at. **2. The moral thermostat.** LLMs write morality plays with the temperature pre-set. The plan says the creature "kills once, understandably, and the story does not excuse it" — but that's already a managed outcome. It's the *appearance* of moral risk with the risk removed. A human would let the creature do something genuinely unforgivable, or let Hale do something the reader can't square, and not put a little velvet rope around it. **3. Compulsive resolution.** Every thread tied. Vega confesses *before she's accused* — which is emotionally tidy and psychologically false; people deny, deflect, and get caught. Fen tells Hale exactly where the creature's people gather, which is convenient exactly when needed. The ending gives them poverty and outlawry but also moral vindication, rain, and a surviving chick. That's a bow, just tied in rope instead of ribbon. **4. Ensemble symmetry.** Four crew, each with exactly one function: authority, conscience, knowledge, betrayal. Named "Hale, Pim, Fen, Vega" — one syllable, one syllable, one syllable, two. Too balanced. Real crews are lopsided: two people who've worked together forever and barely speak, one who's only been aboard six weeks and nobody likes, someone whose job is unclear. **5. Exposition delivered by wise elder.** Nakuthi Aro exists to explain the plot. She's an Indigenous-coded figure whose narrative purpose is to inform white-coded protagonists about the atrocity. This is a well-known trap and the plan walks straight into it while congratulating itself on "handling it with seriousness." **6. Prose that performs.** "Laconic, weathered, concrete" is the stated aim, but LLM laconic tends toward *aphoristic* — every third sentence sounds like it wants to be quoted. Real McCarthy-adjacent prose is often boring and physical for long stretches. The danger is a story where every paragraph ends on a beat. **7. Dialogue as position-statement.** Sheaf will be "polite, reasonable, contractual, chilling," Kest's offer "nearly reasonable." That's LLM antagonism: the villain who articulates the counter-argument cleanly. Real menace is usually inarticulate, distracted, bored, or talking about something else entirely. **8. Sensory checklist.** Dust in everything, water as wealth, ships as horses, fuel called "water." All fine individually; as a system it's a genre-transposition exercise. A human would pick two and forget the rest, and would include one detail that doesn't fit the scheme at all. **9. Over-signposting emotion.** "Pim understands it is grieving, and Vega breaks." LLMs name the emotion and then dramatize it. Humans dramatize and let the reader name it — or don't let them name it. **10. Chapter titles as thesis statements.** "The Price of a Sister." "Outlaws." These tell the reader what the chapter means before it happens. --- # Deep dive: specific problems in this plan **The beacon.** Elegant, and that's the problem. It converts an ordinary bad decision into cosmic justice with a mechanical explanation. It also removes agency — the Combine finds them because of physics, not because someone talked. Human version: someone *talks*. At Hollow Ford, drunk, showing off. Or the crate's original owner isn't a corporation at all and the plot is smaller and stranger. **The extinction-ecology plot.** "Combine harvested the migration and the world dried" is an enormous claim requiring exposition I've already promised not to deliver. It also makes the story about Policy, which is the least Western thing available. The Western is small: this man, that fence, my water. Scaling to planetary ecocide inflates the stakes and deflates the intimacy. And it makes the crew's choice easy — nobody is torn about whether to abet ecocide. **Vega's sister.** The single most common motivation-patch in genre fiction. Sympathetic, unfalsifiable, and it does the reader's forgiving for them. A human might make Vega's reason smaller and worse: she's tired, she's forty-eight, she wants a house, she doesn't think the thing is a person and is *not stupid* for thinking so. **Fen's deathbed confession.** Two problems. One, he dies to deliver information. Two, "the worst thing he's ever admitted" is doing double duty as pathos and plot. Also: the wise old engineer who knows about the cargo, dies covering the retreat, and confesses complicity — this is three tropes stacked. **Kest as Hale's old flying partner.** The "we used to ride together" antagonist is a good Western move but here it's doing the same work as Hale's Combine past. Redundant backstory. And "the confrontation is more conversation than gunfight" is my plan admitting it wants to save wordcount, which readers will feel as anticlimax. **Hale's "old sin."** "She flew these routes for the Combine and never asked what she was hauling." That's generic. It's the shape of a sin without a sin in it. A human would give her something specific, dated, with a name attached, and would let her be *unrepentant about parts of it*. **Pim's "over-explaining when frightened."** A verbal tic assigned as a characterization shortcut. It'll read as a tic. Better if his nervousness manifests physically or in what he *does* rather than a speech pattern I can deploy on cue. **The ending.** Rain smell, answering hum, ship dying, outlaws riding out, "something moves in the hold and this time nobody is afraid." That last line is the plan's most LLM sentence — the deliberate rhyme, the reassurance, the closed circle. It's *pretty*. It's also a bow. **Three locations, four crew, eight chapters, one death.** The whole architecture is optimized for coverage. It'll read as well-managed. Well-managed is the enemy. --- # Ideas toward something more human **On the crate:** - What if the crate's contents are never fully explained? They see it, they deal with it, they never learn what it was. That's more frightening and more true to salvage work. - What if it's smaller than expected — the crate is huge and the thing inside is the size of a dog, and the horror is that it was packed for something much bigger, and the rest of the space is *used*. - What if it's not the last of anything. There are thousands. That doesn't make it less worth saving; it makes the saving *pointless*, which is more interesting. - What if the movement is not the creature but a mechanism, and the creature is discovered later, and the crew's first theory is wrong for two chapters. Wrong theories are very human. **On the moral situation:** - Give the crew a *good* reason to hand it over that isn't money. It's dangerous. It's already hurt someone. There's a legitimate quarantine argument. - Let the humane choice be actively wrong in one measurable way — someone innocent dies downstream because they didn't hand it over. - Let Hale not be the moral center. Let her be the one who wants to sell it, and lose the argument, and be *right* that it ruined them. - Remove the villain's argument entirely. Sheaf doesn't argue. He says "sixty hours" and hangs up. Menace by indifference. **On the crew:** - Make one of them boring and useless and beloved. No arc. Dies or doesn't, doesn't matter. - Two crew who are ex-married and won't discuss it. Silence as texture, never resolved. - Give someone a physical problem unrelated to plot: a bad hip, a rash, a tooth. Let it recur and annoy. - Cut Nakuthi Aro entirely. Let the information come from a Combine document, a manifest, a bill of lading with a species code on it. Bureaucracy is more chilling than a wise elder and doesn't require me to ventriloquize an Indigenous voice. - Or: keep a dirtside character but make them useless, wrong, a liar, or interested only in getting paid. **On prose:** - Deliberately include flat, functional paragraphs. Let some pages be about fixing a pump. - Ban the ending-on-a-beat habit for at least three chapters. Let chapters end mid-motion, unresolved, boring. - One long ugly run-on sentence somewhere, because someone's panicking. - Let the creature be described inconsistently by different characters. No consensus description. - Include one joke that isn't funny and one that is, and don't flag which. **On structure:** - Skip a chapter of expected plot. Jump from Hollow Ford to Tarn and let the reader assemble the missing days. - Put the biggest violence in chapter 3, not 5 or 7. Fold the escalation curve. - Let chapter 8 not be an ending. Let it be a Tuesday. - Cut the vacuum funeral. Everyone writes the vacuum funeral. **On the ending specifically:** - No rain. No answering hum. They let it out on the salt and it walks off and that's all, and they don't know if it lived. - Or: it dies on the way, and they finish the trip anyway, and bury it, and the story is about what they became rather than what they achieved. - Or: the last chapter is Hale filing a false manifest, doing paperwork, and the emotion is entirely in what the form does not have a field for. - Cut the final line-rhyme. End on something small, physical, and unresolved — a hand on a bulkhead, a bill unpaid, a name misspelled. **On slack:** - Include a thread that goes nowhere: a passenger they were supposed to pick up and don't, mentioned twice, never explained. - Someone's radio program. A recurring song they're sick of. A card game with a running score. - One chapter where the crate is barely mentioned. The through-line of all of this: **stop making everything count.** The current plan is a machine where every part turns another part. A human story is a room with some furniture in it that nobody chose.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The core.** Five people on a hauler in a frontier belt take a crate off a wreck because salvage is how they eat. Something is alive in it. That's the whole engine. I'm keeping the story small — no ecocide, no last-of-its-kind, no planetary destiny. The crate holds a juvenile animal of a species the Meridian Combine breeds for its glandular secretion, which is the base of a drug. There are thousands of them. Saving this one accomplishes almost nothing, and the crew does it anyway, and it costs them the ship. That pointlessness is the point, and it's more human than significance. **Plot changes from the draft plan.** No beacon — the Combine finds them because Hoyt gets drunk at the waystation and talks. Human error, not cosmic justice. No wise elder delivering the atrocity; the information comes from a bill of lading with a species code and a bonus schedule on it, and from a woman at the fuel yard who only wants to be paid. No sister in a work-hold. Vega's reason for selling them out is small and bad: she's forty-eight, she's tired, she wants out, and she genuinely does not think the thing is a person. She's not wrong to think that. No deathbed confession. No vacuum funeral. No answering hum, no rain, no rescue by nature. They let it out on the salt and walk away and don't know. **Hale is not the conscience.** She's the one who wants to sell it. She loses the argument, and she's right that it ruins them. Her arc is not redemption; it's being outvoted by people she's responsible for and living with the bill. She has a specific old sin — a name, a date, a shipment — mentioned once, briefly, and never explained. **Slack, deliberately.** Bo Ottway is aboard and mostly useless and everybody likes him. He has a bad tooth for the whole story. There's a passenger they were supposed to collect at Perdition and never do; it's mentioned twice, never explained. There's a card game with a running score. Hoyt and Vega used to be married and won't discuss it. One chapter barely mentions the crate. **Structure.** Big violence lands in chapter four, not seven. I skip time between chapters six and seven without narrating the run. Chapter eight is paperwork and a Tuesday. The prompt line closes chapter one. **Voice.** Third limited, past tense, Hale. Plain, physical, occasionally flat. I will let paragraphs be about pumps. I will let three chapters end mid-motion without a beat. One panicked run-on. The creature is described differently by everyone and never authoritatively; no taxonomy. Dialogue clipped, mostly unclever, and Sheaf does not argue — he states terms and hangs up. **Avoiding.** Bows, thesis-statement chapter titles, ending line-rhymes, aphorism-per-paragraph prose, symbolism doing the work of feeling, and any moment where a character names the emotion the scene is already producing. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — Wreck** (~1000w). *Bittermouth* hauling pipe to a wildcat moon, four days behind, engine-mount cracked. They come on a broken Combine tender, crew dead of decompression weeks ago. Strip it: coolant, a spool of cable, and one cold-bonded crate in a hold otherwise empty — packed for something six times its size, the rest of the space wadded with insulation. Fen says leave it, Vega says weigh it, Hale does arithmetic against her reclamation notice and says take it. Ottway's tooth. Hoyt mentions the passenger they're due to collect at Perdition. Last beat: Pim in the hold, hand not quite on the metal — *"Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up."* **Ch. 2 — Opening** (~1000w). They open it, badly. Two hours of the wrong theory first: they think it's a mechanism, a mine, a pressure relay. Then it comes out — nobody agrees what it looks like; Pim says dog, Vega says spider, Hale doesn't say. It's hurt and terrified and it opens Vega's forearm to the bone. Hale gets it into an empty water tank with a net and a boat hook. Nobody sleeps. The chapter ends with Hale hosing blood off the deck plates, mid-motion, no closing line. **Ch. 3 — Paper** (~1000w). Fen finds the bill of lading pouch welded inside the crate lid: Combine form, species code, live-weight bonus schedule, extraction interval. Not a rescue document, an inventory line. Ottway reads the bonus rates aloud and it's the worst thing in the story. Argument in the galley: Hale wants to sell it back — the finder's fee clears the notice — Pim won't, Fen won't say, Vega sides with Hale and means it. Vote deferred. Card game continues; Ottway is winning. Hoyt takes the tooth business seriously for two paragraphs. Crate barely mentioned in the last third. **Ch. 4 — Perdition** (~1000w). Dirtside to water the ship. Yard woman Meg Cassity wants the bill paid in advance and has no interest in anything else. Hale spends most of the chapter on the engine mount. Hoyt drinks and talks — one line, overheard, to strangers. Combine men arrive faster than anyone expected. It goes wrong in a fuel yard: short, ugly, badly lit. Hoyt is killed. Ottway shoots a man and is not fine about it. They lift with the bill unpaid and half a tank. **Ch. 5 — Sixty Hours** (~1000w). Sheaf's hail: name, terms, sixty hours, coordinates. He does not argue. He hangs up. Vega admits she called ahead from the yard, before Hoyt ever opened his mouth, and doesn't apologize; her reasons are small and honest and land badly. Hale doesn't shoot her, doesn't forgive her, and privately agrees with her. Hoyt's things get bagged; no funeral, just a bag and a locker. The animal is loose in the hold; Pim has been feeding it protein paste, which he didn't mention. **Ch. 6 — Vote** (~1000w). The crate is barely present. Ottway's tooth abscesses; Fen pulls it in the galley with pliers and gin and this takes most of the chapter. Around it, the vote happens sideways, in fragments — Fen finally speaks, briefly, about hauling for the Combine at nineteen. Hale loses four to one, or three to one with Vega abstaining. She says fine. She logs the course. Chapter ends on her hand on the ledger, not on a line. **Ch. 7 — Salt** (~1000w). Time-skip: they're already descending on Tarn, damage narrated as fact, not dramatized. Kest's cutter on them; the descent costs them the port nacelle permanently. On the pan, the animal won't come out. Pim walks it out on a cable. Kest crosses the salt; the exchange is brief, mostly logistics, then fast and unclean. Vega is shot. The animal goes off across the salt and does not look back. No hum, no rain. They watch it go for a while and then stop watching. **Ch. 8 — Manifest** (~1000w). Ninety days later. Registry void, transponder burned, *Bittermouth* on one nacelle running unlicensed short-haul out of a rock nobody names. Vega alive, arm bad, still aboard, still unforgiven and still crew. Ottway's mouth healed crooked. Hale filling out a false manifest, which has no field for any of it. Pim asks if she thinks it lived and she says she doesn't know, because she doesn't. The passenger from Perdition is mentioned once more and left alone. Ends on something small: the bill from Meg Cassity's yard, still unpaid, folded in the ledger, and Hale putting the ledger away.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Odessa Hale **Background.** Fifty-one. Born on a company world she doesn't name because the name is a company name. Flew for Meridian Combine from twenty-two to thirty-four — freight, not enforcement, though that distinction mattered more to her then. Left after the Cavender run. She won't say what the Cavender run was. She bought *Bittermouth* at a Combine surplus auction with severance money and eleven years of accumulated back-pay she had to sue for, which is a fact she's proud of in a way that has curdled. Nineteen years captaining. Never made money. Never quite lost the ship. She carries a reclamation notice in the ledger, second page, dated. She has read it enough times to know the clause numbers. What she cannot make anyone understand — including herself, some nights — is that the ship is not the point of the ship. Four people eat because it flies. Five, before Perdition. **Personality.** Practical to the edge of coldness, and past it, occasionally. She does arithmetic under pressure the way other people pray. She is not a good liar but she is an excellent withholder — she can let a silence stand for so long that people fill it themselves and then blame themselves for what they filled it with. She's fair, which is not the same as kind. She has never once raised her voice on her own ship, and everyone finds this more frightening than shouting. Her real flaw isn't hardness. It's that she believes responsibility and authority are the same object, and so being outvoted feels to her like a moral failure rather than a democratic outcome. When she loses the vote in chapter six, the sting isn't the money. It's that they took the weight off her and she doesn't know what to do with her hands. **Idiosyncrasies.** Keeps a paper ledger in a plastic sleeve because she doesn't trust anything a Combine auditor could reach. Writes in pencil. Sharpens the pencil with a knife, badly, so there's always shavings in the ledger's gutter. Won't sit with her back to a hatch — not from paranoia, she says, just habit, and it *is* just habit, which is worse. Drinks the last of the coffee and then makes a fresh pot immediately, so that nobody ever finds the pot empty; nobody has noticed her doing this in nineteen years. Hums exactly two bars of something and stops. Never more than two bars. **Physicality.** Tall, gone lean the way rope goes lean. Gray coming in at the temples in a streak she doesn't dye and doesn't cut short either. Face that photographs badly and reads well. Broad flat hands with a permanently split right thumbnail from a hatch dog in '39. Moves slow, and it isn't age; she moves slow because moving slow in a small hull means you never have to say sorry. When she's thinking she goes very still and looks at a point about two feet above whoever's talking. Wears the same coat inside and out, and there is a Combine crest on the left breast where someone has cut the stitching out, leaving a paler patch shaped like a hexagon. **Motives and allegiances.** The crew, in the abstract, unsentimentally. The ship, as instrument. She does not owe the Combine anything and does not hate them, which unsettles Pim more than hatred would. Her private position on the animal is straightforward: it is an animal, it is worth eleven thousand in finder's fee, eleven thousand clears the notice, and none of the rest of it is her business. She will hold that position honestly, lose, comply, and never pretend she was persuaded. She likes Ottway and can't say why. She respects Fen and never tells him. She thinks Pim is soft and is not sure that's a defect. Vega she has flown with for nine years and understands completely, which is why she can't forgive her — there was nothing to misunderstand. **Voice.** "Weigh it, then. If it's under four hundred we take it, and if it's over four hundred we take it anyway and complain about the mount. Don't look at me like I said something." *Eleven thousand and the notice went away. That was the whole sum of it. She had done worse arithmetic and slept fine, and she'd do this arithmetic and sleep fine, and the fact that it was Pim's face she saw doing it was not a reason, it was just a face.* --- # Renata Vega **Background.** Forty-eight. Grew up in a fuel yard on Tarn's neighbor moon, which is the last coincidence in her life; she will point this out on Tarn and nobody will care. Certified pilot at nineteen, flew ore tenders, flew mail, flew a company shuttle for a Combine survey office for six years and quit because it was boring, not because it was wrong. Married Hoyt Ridley for four years and eight months. Divorced eleven years ago, and they've crewed together for nine of those, which tells you something neither of them will discuss. She is a better pilot than the *Bittermouth* deserves and knows it, and has never left, and the reason she hasn't left is the thing she cannot look at directly. **Personality.** Blunt, funny in a flat way, absolutely without malice and absolutely without illusion. She's the one who says the true thing at the wrong time. She does not romanticize the ship, the crew, the frontier, or herself. Her sin is not greed — eleven thousand isn't what she wanted. What she wanted was *out*: a room with a door on a world with weather, and to stop being forty-eight in a hull that smells like other people. She called the Combine from the fuel yard because it was a way out and because she looked at the thing in the water tank and saw an animal, and she was not stupid to see that. She does not apologize. This is not pride. She's genuinely puzzled by the expectation, because she thinks she's the only one aboard being honest. **Idiosyncrasies.** Cleans her nails with a multitool at the galley table, which drives Fen quietly insane. Keeps score of the card game in grease pencil on a bulkhead and has never once cheated, and when Ottway wins she writes it larger. Talks to the ship in Portuguese-inflected mechanical curses she learned from her mother and doesn't translate. Has a bad habit of eating standing up. Wears a wedding band on a chain, and if you notice it she will tell you it's not what you think, and it isn't; she just doesn't have anywhere else to keep it. **Physicality.** Short, thick through the shoulders, forearms like a person who has hauled things. Black hair cut level with her jaw with sewing scissors. Broad face, deep laugh lines, and an expression at rest that reads as contempt but is just how her mouth sits. Sits with her boots up on things. Chews the inside of her cheek when she's flying. After chapter two her left forearm is a long puckered scar she doesn't cover, and she will show it to people, and the showing is not bravado — it's evidence. **Motives and allegiances.** Herself, first, admitted openly. Hale second, which she'd deny. Hoyt, obscurely, permanently, and his death does not produce grief so much as a low continuous inability to finish sentences for about a week. She stays aboard after her betrayal not to atone but because she is a pilot and this is a ship, and also because leaving would concede that what she did was disqualifying, and she doesn't believe it was. **Voice.** "It bit me. To the bone. I got no position on its soul, Pim, I got a position on my arm." "You want me to say sorry. Fine — I'm sorry it went the way it went. I'm not sorry I called. Those are two different sentences and you can have both of them." --- # Bo Ottway **Background.** Thirty-six or thirty-nine; he's given both. Came aboard six years ago as temporary help loading grain sacks at a station Hale can no longer remember the name of, and simply did not get off. His job title has never been established. He loads, he cooks badly, he sits with people, he's very good at the one thing nobody else can do, which is be in a room without making the room worse. He's not stupid. He's incurious. There is a difference and Fen is the only one who's clocked it. Ottway has never in six years asked what was in a crate, and this is not virtue, it's temperament, and it means when he finally *does* care about something he has no experience carrying it. **Personality.** Placid, agreeable, extremely funny by accident and never on purpose. Genuinely likes everyone, including people who have done nothing to earn it, including Combine men, which is why what happens in chapter four ruins him — he shoots a man he'd have bought a drink for, and the arithmetic other people can do, he can't. He does not become dark. He becomes *quiet*, which from Ottway is a klaxon. He wins at cards constantly and has no idea why and refuses all instruction on strategy. **Idiosyncrasies.** The tooth. Lower left, back, cracked eating something at Perdition — no, earlier, he doesn't know when. He has been managing it with gin, with cloves, with a wire, with pressing his thumb against his jaw and going still mid-sentence. He mentions it constantly and is never once dramatic about it. He hums along to the same three songs on the shortwave and doesn't know the words, so he hums the words too. Keeps a dead man's boot from the tender because it fit and boots cost money, and nobody can convince him this is grotesque. **Physicality.** Big, soft-bodied, freckled across the shoulders. Sandy hair going thin at the crown, which he's unbothered by. Sits down heavily. Fills doorways without meaning to. Broad open face that shows everything, which after Perdition is hard to be around. Halfway through the story he's holding his jaw with two fingers whenever he stops talking; by the end his mouth is healed crooked and he lisps slightly on *s* and doesn't mind. **Motives and allegiances.** The crew, uncomplicatedly, the way weather is uncomplicated. He does not have a position on the animal until chapter six and then he has one and it's immovable, and he cannot explain it, and he doesn't try. He wants his tooth to stop. He wants Hoyt back. He wants somebody to deal the next hand. **Voice.** "I'm not saying it's a person. I'm saying I ain't selling it. Those aren't the same and I don't got to make 'em the same." "Nine cents. Nine cents a gram, live weight, plus interval bonus. That's — hold on." *(pressing his jaw)* "That's what they wrote down. Somebody typed that." --- # Marius Fen **Background.** Sixty-three. Engineer, *Bittermouth*, fourteen years. Before that: eleven ships, three of them Combine. He was nineteen the first time he loaded live cargo for the Combine and he understood exactly what he was doing at the time, which is the part he'll say in chapter six, in about nine words, and then he'll change the subject and Hale will let him. He has a wife on Ceres Waystation he calls every ninety days for six minutes. Nobody knows anything about her. He's mentioned her twice in fourteen years and both times in the context of a birthday. **Personality.** Dry to the point of desiccation. Answers questions with the shortest true sentence available. He is the ship's actual center of gravity and everyone would deny this including him. He doesn't moralize and he despises moralizing, and so when the vote comes he says his nine words and votes and that's it — the fact that it lands like a hammer is not his intention and he'd be annoyed to hear it did. His flaw is a kind of withholding that shades into cowardice: he knew what the crate probably was from the moment he saw the packing, and he said "leave it" and nothing more, and when Hale overruled him he shrugged, and five people's lives went sideways in the space of that shrug. He'll carry that and never mention it. **Idiosyncrasies.** Eats the same thing every day — rice, oil, salt — and will accept nothing else, and has been offered nothing else in eleven years. Keeps the tools immaculate and the galley filthy. Reads paper westerns, actual paper, the same six, over and over, and doesn't consider this ironic because he doesn't consider it. Hates Vega's nail-cleaning with a fury he expresses only by relocating himself. **Physicality.** Small, dense, bandy. Hands like a set of pliers that learned a trade. Bald, sunspotted skull, white stubble he shaves twice a week whether it needs it or not. Wears reading glasses he refuses to keep on a cord and therefore loses eleven times a day. Squats rather than kneels. Never leans on anything. When he's angry he wipes his hands on a rag for much longer than the rag requires. **Motives and allegiances.** The ship, mechanically. Hale, absolutely, unstated, and she has no idea. He wants to make it to sixty-eight and Ceres. He pulls Ottway's tooth in chapter six because someone has to, and does it well, and does not comfort him during, and that's the most affection he shows anyone in the story. **Voice.** "Leave it." "They packed that box for something six times bigger. That's all I'm going to say about the box." *He'd been nineteen. That was true and it was also nothing, and he'd learned young that you could hold a thing that was true and nothing and it would still weigh.* --- # Pim Arday **Background.** Nineteen. From a farm on a moon where the crop failed twice, which is the whole of his biography and he tells it too often. Signed on eight months ago at Hollow Ford for a berth and food. He has never been off-ship at a place with weather. He is careful, honest, physically brave in ways that surprise people, and has almost no understanding of money — genuinely does not grasp what eleven thousand means, which is why his position on the animal costs him nothing and he knows it, and that shames him. **Personality.** Earnest without being sweet. He argues badly and won't stop. When he's frightened he doesn't babble — he *works*: rechecks a latch four times, coils a line that's already coiled, and it's Hale who reads the coiling. He is the one who touched the crate first and heard it first and afterward he cannot stop being the person who's responsible for that. His flaw: he mistakes his own certainty for other people's obligation. He is baffled and then furious that Hale can see what he sees and reach a different sum. He has not yet learned that people can be honest and still not agree with you. **Idiosyncrasies.** Bites his thumbnail, then apologizes to no one for it. Cannot leave a hatch half-dogged. Feeds the animal protein paste for four days without telling anybody, not out of deception but because he assumed everyone knew and it was fine. Calls it "it" the whole story and never names it, which one might expect him to do, and he doesn't, and that's deliberate: naming it would be claiming it. **Physicality.** Thin, long-wristed, growing still. Dark hair he cuts himself in the head. Bad posture that improves to a soldier's when he's scared. Bruises easily and is embarrassed about it. Hands too big for his arms. He stands very close to people when he's making a point and doesn't know he does it. After the salt, a rope burn across both palms that he never mentions again. **Motives and allegiances.** Hale, worshipfully at first, and the erosion of that worship is the story's quiet second engine. He wants the animal to live and he wants Hale to want it too, and only one of those is achievable. He does not hate Vega, which annoys her. **Voice.** "Captain. Something's — " *(and then the correct sentence, the one he'd been building for four minutes, went out of him)* " — something's moving in that crate we picked up." "You keep saying it's an animal like that settles it. Fine. It's an animal. Now what."
