Model Output:
# Chapter One ## Wreck The mount had been cracked since Hollow Ford and Fen wanted eleven hundred to weld it, which was eleven hundred they didn't have, so they were running at three-quarter burn and four days behind on a load of drill pipe that paid on delivery and not before. Hale did the arithmetic again anyway. She had the ledger open on her knee in the pilot seat, the plastic sleeve slid halfway off, pencil shavings in the gutter of the page. Fuel to the wildcat moon. Fuel back. Fen's eleven hundred. The reclamation notice on the second page, dated, which she did not need to reread and reread anyway, the way you press a bruise. "Debris field," Vega said. "Two hundred klicks, off the lane. Tender-class." "Beacon?" "Nothing." "How long's it been dead?" Vega chewed the inside of her cheek. "Cold. Weeks. Month, maybe." Hale closed the ledger. "Take us over." --- It was a Combine tender, the little kind that ran station-to-station and never went far, and it had come apart at the seam where the drive section married the hull. Something had gone through her — a rock, a bad valve, God — and she'd let go all at once. There were four bodies. Two still strapped in. Hale had Ottway leave them where they were. They took the coolant first because coolant was money, forty liters of it in sealed cans, and then a spool of shielded cable that Fen looked at for a long time before he said it was worth having. Hoyt worked the cutter. Pim stacked. Ottway carried, and every fourth or fifth trip he stopped in the lock and pressed two fingers under his jaw and stood there breathing until it passed. "You want gin," Vega said. "I had gin." "Have more gin." "It's a nerve," Ottway said. "It's the nerve of it. Gin don't get down where the nerve is." He shouldered the can and went out. Hoyt found the boots. Dead man's, size eleven, good soles. He held them up in the lockway with an expression of straightforward pleasure and Ottway said he'd take them if nobody else wanted them, and nobody else wanted them, and that was that. "Perdition's still on for the fourteenth," Hoyt said. "For the passenger." "I know." "Because if we're four days behind on the pipe—" "I know, Hoyt." The cargo hold of the tender was ninety percent empty and that was the first thing wrong with it. A tender that size ran full or it didn't run. This one had racking for maybe sixty containers and it held one, cold-bonded to the deck in the exact center, and the whole rest of the volume was wadded out with insulation batting, meters of it, gray and puffed, jammed floor to ceiling like packing in a jeweler's box. "Huh," said Pim. Fen came in behind them with his lamp and stood in the hatch and did not come further in. The crate was maybe a meter and a half on the long side. Steel, no markings, no manifest strip, cold-bonded at all four corners with the good bonds, the kind that came off with a charge and a spanner and not otherwise. The insulation had been packed around it out to two meters in every direction and then kept going, out and out, filling the room. "They built the padding for something six times bigger," Fen said. "Meaning?" "Meaning either they loaded the wrong crate or they unloaded the right one somewhere and didn't restow." He wiped his hands on his rag. "Leave it." Vega already had the strain gauge on it. "Four twenty." "Four twenty," Hale said. "Give or take. That's with the crate." "Leave it," Fen said again, and then didn't say anything else, and later Hale would think about the exact length of that silence and the exact shape of his shrug and how much both of them had turned out to weigh. Because here was the arithmetic. An unmarked crate off a dead Combine tender, cold-bonded, packed like a reliquary, meant somebody had cared about it. Somebody who cared about it would want it back, or somebody else would want it more. Salvage law in the Belt was two sentences long and both of them said *finders*. And she had a notice in her ledger with clause numbers she could recite, and eleven hundred owed to her own engineer, and four days of pipe money bleeding out behind her. "Take it," she said. "Captain—" "If it's under four hundred we take it and if it's over four hundred we take it anyway and complain about the mount." She was already turning for the hatch. "Don't look at me like I said something." Fen wiped his hands on the rag. --- It took three hours and cost them a charge, a spanner, and the skin off two of Hoyt's knuckles. They walked it out on the powered dolly with the batting shoved aside in drifts, and Hale stood in her own hold and watched it come down the ramp and thought that it looked like nothing. That was the thing worth remembering afterward. It looked like a crate. It looked like every crate. They netted it to the deck aft of the pipe. Ottway put a hand on the lid the way you'd pat a horse, out of pure habit, and took the hand off again, and pressed his fingers under his jaw. They ran the shortwave through supper. Ottway hummed the words to a song he did not know the words to. Vega cleaned her nails at the table with the multitool and Fen got up and ate his rice standing in the corridor. The card score on the bulkhead read OTT 41, VEG 33, HOYT 29, PIM 12, and Vega added a stroke to Ottway's tally and wrote the four larger than it needed to be. "Fourteenth," Hoyt said, to nobody. Hale went forward and sat with her back to the bulkhead and the hatch in her sightline and drank the last of the coffee and put a fresh pot on. She was reading the notice again when Pim came up. She heard him before she saw him because he stopped twice in the corridor. When he got to the hatchway he stood in it holding the frame with both hands and Hale looked at his hands and not his face. "Captain." "Mm." "I was doing the aft latches." He said it as though the latches were the point. "I do them at the end of watch, all of them, twice, and I was doing the ones aft of the pipe, and I did them twice, and then I did them again." Hale put the pencil down. "Captain. Something's—" He had built a sentence somewhere back in the corridor, four minutes of sentence, and it went out of him. "—something's moving in that crate we picked up."
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished opening chapter that demonstrates genuine craft and discipline. Let me work through its qualities systematically. **Voice and Prose Style** The prose is exactly what the plan promised: plain, physical, occasionally flat, and deeply controlled. It came up off the flats every afternoon at about the fifteenth hour and got into the fuel yard and the mouths of the pumps and the seams of everything, and there was a man whose whole job was walking the yard with a brush. The town sat in a shallow bowl with a cracked salt pan north of it and forty years of tailings south, and it existed because ships needed water and water needed pumping and nobody had thought of anywhere better. Meg Cassity ran the yard. She was maybe sixty and she came out of the office with a slate and did not look at the ship. "Four hundred cubic. In advance." "On delivery of the pipe," Hale said. "Payment clears at Dessin on the nineteenth." "In advance." "It's a hundred and sixty and I've watered here nine times." "You've watered here nine times on credit," Cassity said, "and it's cleared eight of them, and I'm not in the mood to run the average." She turned the slate around. "I'll take half in advance. Rest against the pipe. That's the whole of it and I've got a queue." Hale paid half in advance and it was most of what she had loose, and Cassity chalked the balance and went back inside, and that was the last she was interested in any of them. --- Hale spent nearly the whole of that day under the ship on her back on a mat in the dust with the mount above her face. The crack had run. It had been eleven centimeters at Hollow Ford and it was fourteen now and it had turned at the end, hooked up toward the web, which was the direction you did not want. Fen came down and looked at it and squatted beside her and said nothing for a while. "Weld won't hold at fourteen." "I know." "You want it plated, and plating's a shop, and a shop's four days and two thousand." "I know." "So what are you doing." "I'm looking at it," Hale said. She had the ledger up on the landing gear strut where she could reach it. She did the arithmetic four times and got the same answer four times, which was that the numbers did not close in any arrangement, and there was one number that closed them, and it was in a water tank forty meters over her head. She lay in the dust with grit in her collar and did the sum and did not feel anything about it except tired. Pim came down twice, once with water and once with nothing, and stood at the edge of the mat and did not say what he'd come to say either time. --- Hoyt and Ottway went into town for the dentist and the dentist was a man with pliers and a chair and Ottway looked at the chair and said he'd think about it, and then they went to the place across from the yard because that was what there was. # Chapter Seven ## Salt The mount let go at forty kilometers. It had held through the burn out of the Belt and through nine days of transit and through the whole of the deceleration, and then at forty kilometers above the salt pan the crack ran the rest of the way up into the web and the port nacelle came off its bearing and went over about eleven degrees and stayed there, thrusting into the airframe instead of past it, and the *Bittermouth* began to fly like a thing being dragged. Vega flew it anyway. That was the last piece of piloting she ever did that would have impressed anybody who knew, and there was nobody watching but Hale, and Hale knew. "Cutter's at nine hundred and closing," Fen said, over the noise. He was aft with his hands in the housing and it was nothing he could fix from there and he had his hands in it anyway. "Ignore him." "He's got—" "He's not going to shoot us down over the pan, Marius, he wants the animal. Ignore him." The cutter came down parallel at four hundred meters and stayed there, matching, patient, and did not fire, and that was worse. They came onto the salt at eleven degrees off, on one and a half nacelles, and the port gear folded on contact and put them down on the housing with a noise like a building falling, and slid, and stopped. Nobody was hurt. That was luck and Vega, in that order. --- Tarn's pan went out flat to the curve of the world in every direction, white going gray going white, and there was nothing on it. Rock outcrops away to the north at some distance the eye could not fix. The sky was the color of dishwater. It was very cold and the air was thin and you could take it if you didn't hurry. They put the ramp down. The animal would not come out. It had been out of the tank for eleven days by then and living aft of the pipe, and it knew the hold, and the hold was the third place it had ever known and the other two had been a crate and a tank. Pim went in and got down on the deck four meters off it, the way he did, and talked to it, and it folded itself smaller. "It won't." "Then it won't," Hale said. "Get out of there. He's on the ground." The cutter had set down eight hundred meters north and a man had got out of it and started walking, and he was not hurrying either. Pim came out. Then he went back in, and got a length of cable off Fen's spool — the shielded cable, off the tender, the thing Fen had looked at so long — and he made a loop in it, a big soft loop, and he took it in and knelt in the dust and foam and he was in there eleven or twelve minutes and Hale would not stand at the top of the ramp and watch because if she watched she'd stop it. He came out backward, walking backward down the ramp, holding the cable in both bare hands with the loop out ahead of him, and it came after the loop. Not on the loop. It never once took the loop. It came after it the way a thing comes after the only object in a room it has decided about, four points of contact and then six, dragging the straight leg, out into the light it couldn't see in, onto the salt. The cable went through Pim's hands twice and took the skin off both palms and he did not let go and he never mentioned it afterward, ever, not once. --- Kest came up to about thirty meters and stopped. He was a narrow man in a good coat with the collar up and he had a long gun broken over his forearm the way you carry one when you don't expect to close it. He looked at the ship for a while, at the nacelle over on its bearing, at the folded gear. "That's done," he said. "It is." "Sheaf sent me a window. Sixty hours. You're outside it by nineteen." "I know what I'm outside of." Kest nodded. He looked past her at the animal standing on the salt with its head sweeping slow across all of them, and he looked at it without any expression at all, the way you look at freight. "Class two, live," he said. "That's the whole of my paper. I'm not empowered on anything else. Not on the yard at Perdition, not on your man. That's a different file and it isn't mine." "Is that supposed to help." "It's supposed to be accurate." He shifted the gun. "I'll take it off you. You'll sign a recovery, you'll get the eight percent because the schedule says eight percent and the schedule doesn't care what happened in a fuel yard, and I'll leave you a beacon so somebody comes for you inside a week. That's the offer and it's the whole offer and I'd take it." "No." Kest let out a breath. "You know I've got two more in the cutter." "I figured." "Then what are you doing, Hale." "I'm standing here," she said. He closed the gun. --- It was six seconds and it was ugly and it was nothing like anything anybody would want to tell. Vega shot him from the top of the ramp with the hatch gun before he had it up, which was not clean and was not fair and did not matter, and the two out of the cutter opened up from three hundred meters and one of them was good. Vega went down on the ramp plate on her side in the same place Hoyt had been. Ottway got her by the collar of her coat and dragged her in through the lock exactly the way Pim had done at Perdition and Fen got the hatch gun going and put forty rounds up the pan at nothing until the two of them broke and ran back for the cutter, and the cutter lifted in about ninety seconds and went north and did not come back. Kest lay out on the salt at thirty meters with his coat open. --- The animal had gone during it. Nobody saw it go. They found it a hundred and fifty meters out, going, not fast — the straight leg dragging, folding and unfolding, four points and then six — and it did not stop and it did not turn its head and there was nothing behind it that would have made it want to. Pim walked out about twenty meters and stood there with his hands hanging open at his sides and the blood on them going tacky in the cold. There was no sound. There was no rain and nothing came out of the rocks to the north and the pan stayed exactly as empty as it had been all afternoon, and the animal got smaller and then became a mark and then became a thing you had to decide you were still seeing. They watched it for a while. Then Fen said Vega was bleeding out on the galley table and they stopped watching and went in.

"The Bittermouth began to fly like a thing being dragged" — this is a clean, earned simile, not a reach. "That was luck and Vega, in that order" — this is the kind of compression that takes real skill. The description of the sky as "the color of dishwater" is plain and right. The animal's movement — "four points of contact and then six, dragging the straight leg, out into the light it couldn't see in" — is precise and physical without being overwrought. The prose maintains the planned voice: third limited past tense, plain, physical, occasionally flat. Paragraphs are allowed to be about mechanics. Three sections end mid-motion. The violence is handled with the planned brevity: "It was six seconds and it was ugly and it was nothing like anything anybody would want to tell." This is exactly the right register — it refuses to dramatize what the plan said should be fast and unclean. **Character Consistency** Hale is consistent: she does arithmetic, she's practical, she stands her ground with Kest in a way that's neither heroic nor stupid, just stubborn. Her "I'm standing here" is perfect — it's not a thesis statement, it's a fact. Vega shooting Kest from the ramp is consistent with her character: not clean, not fair, and she doesn't wait for permission. Pim's cable sequence is beautifully rendered — the detail that the animal never takes the loop but follows it, and that Pim loses skin from both palms and never mentions it, is exactly what the profile promised. Fen's practicality at the end ("Vega was bleeding out on the galley table") is perfectly in character. **The Animal** The plan specified the animal should be described differently by everyone and never authoritatively. Here it's rendered through behavior and movement rather than appearance, which is the right call for this chapter. The description of its movement — "four points and then six" — is consistent with the earlier chapters' approach of physical fact over taxonomy. **Dialogue** The Kest exchange is exactly what was planned: brief, mostly logistics, accurate rather than menacing. "It's supposed to be accurate" is a good line. "I'm standing here" is better. The dialogue is clipped, unclever in the best sense, and nobody makes a speech. Kest is a bureaucrat with a gun, not a villain, and the exchange treats him that way. **Emotional Register** The chapter earns its darkness. The watching-the-animal-go sequence is handled with the planned restraint: "They watched it for a while. Then Fen said Vega was bleeding out on the galley table and they stopped watching and went in." This is the correct ending — not the animal disappearing as a transcendent moment, but as a thing that happened and then life continued. The refusal to give it weight is what gives it weight. Pim's rope-burn detail — "the blood on them going tacky in the cold" — and the note that he never mentioned it afterward is quietly devastating and earns its place. **Minor Criticisms** The phrase "a thing you had to decide you were still seeing" is slightly precious — it's the one moment where the prose reaches for something poetic in a way that's marginally self-conscious. It works, but it's the closest the chapter comes to overreaching. The Vega shooting sequence is handled well but the phrase "which was not clean and was not fair and did not matter" is doing a lot of telling — though in context it reads as the narrator's deliberate refusal to dramatize, which is consistent with the voice. It's a borderline case. The chapter is not amateurish in any detectable way. The structure is confident, the pacing is controlled, and the restraint is genuine rather than performed. **Overall** This is a chapter that does exactly what it sets out to do, does it with real craft, and resists every temptation to make the ending mean more than it does. The pointlessness is the point, and the prose earns that pointlessness without winking at it. # Chapter Eight ## Manifest Ninety-one days later, Hale sat in the galley of a ship with no name on her and filled out a false manifest. The form was a Braid Interior short-haul C-2, which was the shortest legal form there was, and it wanted eleven things. Master. Vessel. Registry. Port of origin. Port of destination. Cargo, described. Cargo, weight. Consignor. Consignee. Certificate number. Signature. She wrote *O. Marchand* on the master line, which was her mother's name, and she wrote a registry that belonged to a hull broken up at Dessin four years ago, and she wrote *drill collar, assorted, 900kg* which was accurate, and she wrote a certificate number she had bought off a man on the rock for forty dollars and which would pass a reader and would not pass a person. There was no field for any of it. That was not a complaint. It was simply true of the form and of every form. --- *Bittermouth* — she still called her that, out loud, and nobody had ever corrected it — sat in a cut in a rock nobody named, running short-haul on one and a half nacelles at about forty percent of what she'd once done. Six hundred klicks out and six hundred back, water and dry goods and pipe, to claims that didn't ask and couldn't afford anybody who did. The transponder was burned. Fen had done it himself in about nine minutes with a screwdriver and had not looked pleased about it, and had never once said anything about the eleven hundred she owed him, and she had stopped offering. They ate. That was the sum of it. Some months they ate well. Vega flew. Her right arm had come back most of the way and the left had never been any good since the water tank and now the shoulder on the right was bad from where the round had gone through, and she flew with the seat racked forward and her elbow braced on the coaming and she was still better than anybody who'd have taken this berth. She had never apologized and Hale had never forgiven her and both of those facts had gone quiet and become part of the furniture, the way things do on a small ship. They had crewed nine years before and they crewed now. Ottway's mouth had healed crooked. The socket had gone bad twice more and there was a dent along the jawline where the bone had gone, and he lisped a little on his *s* sounds and did not appear to have noticed. He still won at cards. Vega still wrote his score bigger than it needed to be. He would not wear the dead man's boots and they were still in Hoyt's bag in Hoyt's locker, which nobody had ever opened again and nobody had ever suggested opening. Fen had made no move toward Ceres. He called every ninety days for six minutes and came out of the compartment and said nothing and went back to his bench, and that was fourteen years and now fifteen. --- Pim came in while she was on the cargo line. He had grown another two centimeters and it had gone into his wrists. The palms had healed with a shine across them where the cable had gone through and he never mentioned that either, and she had watched him for three months learn how not to mention things, which was a thing she had taught him without meaning to and did not entirely feel good about. He got the coffee, found it empty, and put a fresh pot on, and Hale looked at the back of his head for a second and then went back to the form. "Captain." "Mm." "Do you think it lived." She finished the weight column. Nine hundred kilos, which was the truth, sitting in a document that was a lie from the master line down. "I don't know," she said. "You could say you think it did." "I could. It wouldn't be worth anything." She set the pencil down. "It had a leg it couldn't put down and it couldn't see in daylight and it had never been anywhere. And I don't know what it ate, and I don't know if there was anything out there for it to eat, and I don't know if anything on that pan was anything to do with it in the first place. Fen's paper said stock. It never said where from." Pim stood with his hand on the pot handle. "That's what we had," Hale said. "That's the whole of what we had. So: I don't know." "All right." "I'd like to say it lived." "All right," he said again, and got two cups down instead of one, which he had not done before, and put one in front of her. They sat there a while. The shortwave was on down the corridor because Ottway had it on, and it was the same three songs off the same relay, and after a while Ottway started humming the words he didn't know. "Twelve on the fourteenth," Pim said. "There was supposed to be a passenger at Perdition." "There was." "Did anybody ever—" "No," Hale said. Pim drank his coffee. He did not ask again, and Hale did not think about it, and whoever it had been stood in a fuel yard on the fourteenth with a bag and then did something else with the rest of their life. --- She signed the manifest *O. Marchand* and read it over once and it was in order. The ledger was on the table beside her in its plastic sleeve with the pencil shavings still in the gutter, and she opened it to file the form, and the bill was in there. Meg Cassity's yard, Perdition Wells, four hundred cubic water, half paid, balance eighty dollars, chalked and then written up properly on a slip in a fair round hand and mailed to a registry that no longer existed. It had come to Hollow Ford, and Hollow Ford had held it, and a man on the rock had brought it out with the rest of the mail four weeks ago. Eighty dollars. She had turned it over a few times when she first got it and she had never worked out what it was she was supposed to do with it. Paying it would mean writing to Perdition from a ship that did not exist. Not paying it did not appear to be a decision she was capable of making. So it sat in the ledger, folded once, against the second page, where the notice used to be before she took the notice out and burned it in the galley sink, which had been the only ceremony anybody aboard had got. She put the manifest in on top of it and squared the papers with two fingers and closed the ledger, and slid it back into the sleeve, and put it in the drawer under the table where it lived. Down the corridor Ottway hummed. Fen went past with his glasses up on his skull, looking for his glasses. "Nine hundred kilos to Bellum Deep," Hale said. "Tell Renata we lift at six."

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of writing that demonstrates genuine craft and restraint. Let me work through it carefully. The chapter opens with bureaucratic mundanity — a false manifest, eleven fields, none of which can hold what actually happened — and this structural conceit is earned rather than imposed. The form's inadequacy is stated plainly ("There was no field for any of it. That was not a complaint. It was simply true of the form and of every form.") without being over-explained or made to carry more symbolic weight than it can bear. This is the kind of restraint that separates competent writing from genuinely good writing. The status updates on each crew member are handled with economy and precision. Vega's arm, her continued presence, the mutual unforgiveness that has "gone quiet and become part of the furniture" — this is exactly the right register. The detail about Ottway's boots (the dead man's boots, still in Hoyt's bag, in Hoyt's locker, never opened) is devastating in its quietness. The plan called for Ottway's mouth healing crooked and the lisp, and both are delivered without fanfare. Fen's non-movement toward Ceres, the six-minute calls — these are the right details, chosen well. The Pim scene is the chapter's emotional center and it works. The exchange about whether the animal lived is genuinely moving because it refuses to be moving — Hale gives the honest answer, the uncertain answer, the answer that lists all the reasons for doubt, and then says "I'd like to say it lived," which is the most she can offer and the most the story can offer. Pim putting down two cups instead of one is a small gesture that lands because it's earned across eight chapters of characterization. The Perdition passenger callback is handled exactly as planned — mentioned, not explained, left alone. This is the right call and it's executed cleanly. The Meg Cassity bill is the chapter's closing image, and it's excellent. The eighty dollars, the impossibility of paying it or deciding not to pay it, the notice burned in the galley sink described as "the only ceremony anybody aboard had got" — this is the story's thesis delivered without being stated as a thesis. The final lines ("Nine hundred kilos to Bellum Deep. Tell Renata we lift at six.") are exactly right: life continues, the ship goes on, nothing is resolved, and that's the point. The Pim coffee detail — he finds the pot empty, puts a fresh pot on, and Hale watches him do it — is a beautiful callback to Hale's own habit described in the character profiles (making a fresh pot immediately so nobody finds it empty). This is the kind of detail that rewards close reading and suggests genuine authorial control. Dialogue is clipped, functional, and character-specific. "You could say you think it did." / "I could. It wouldn't be worth anything." — this is Hale's voice exactly. The dialogue never over-explains, never delivers thesis statements, never becomes clever at the expense of character. The prose is plain without being flat. There are occasional moments of slight over-construction ("the way things do on a small ship" is a touch explanatory), but these are minor. The writing avoids the purple prose trap entirely. Metaphors are sparse and when they appear they're grounded: "gone lean the way rope goes lean" (from the profiles) is the register this chapter maintains. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the false manifest, the crew status updates, Vega alive and unforgiven, Ottway's crooked mouth, Fen not going to Ceres, Pim's question about whether it lived, the Perdition passenger mentioned once and left alone, the Cassity bill in the ledger, the notice burned. The ending on something small is exactly what was planned. One minor criticism: the line "whoever it had been stood in a fuel yard on the fourteenth with a bag and then did something else with the rest of their life" is slightly too neat, slightly too composed — it risks becoming aphoristic in a way the rest of the chapter avoids. But this is a small complaint against a chapter that otherwise maintains its register throughout. The chapter is coherent, the characters are consistent with their profiles, the emotional beats are earned rather than manufactured, and the ending achieves genuine resonance through accumulation rather than declaration. This is the kind of writing that trusts its readers. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of space western fiction that demonstrates genuine literary craft throughout its eight chapters. Let me assess it comprehensively. STRENGTHS: The prose style is distinctive and controlled — a kind of stripped, laconic voice that owes something to Cormac McCarthy and early Ursula Le Guin but is genuinely its own thing. The sentence rhythms are carefully managed: short declarative statements punctuated by longer, more complex constructions that carry emotional weight. "She had the ledger open on her knee in the pilot seat, the plastic sleeve slid halfway off, pencil shavings in the gutter of the page" — this is economical world-building that also characterizes Hale immediately. The world-building is exceptional precisely because it's embedded rather than explained. The Belt, Combine tenders, cold-bonds, the reclamation notice — these accumulate into a coherent universe without any expository dumping. The social and economic texture (salvage law in two sentences, the finder's fee schedule, Cassity's yard) feels genuinely lived-in. Character work is strong across the board. Each crew member is individuated through specific behavioral tics rather than description: Ottway pressing two fingers under his jaw, Fen wiping his hands on the rag, Vega cleaning her nails with the multitool. The card score on the bulkhead is a masterful piece of characterization-through-detail. Pim's arc from naive moral absolutist to someone learning "how not to mention things" is handled with real subtlety. The central moral question — what is the creature, what do you owe it, what does economic desperation justify — is never resolved cleanly, which is exactly right. The vote scene in Chapter 6 is the emotional and thematic heart of the piece, and it's handled brilliantly: the vote happens "around" the tooth extraction, sideways, in pieces, which is how real decisions get made on small ships and in real lives. Fen's nine words about loading live for the Combine at nineteen are devastating in their compression. The Vega betrayal subplot is handled with unusual sophistication. She calls the Combine, Hoyt dies partly as a consequence, and yet the narrative refuses to make her simply villainous. Hale's recognition that the only difference between her and Vega was "forty meters of yard" is one of the finest moments in the piece — a genuine moral insight that doesn't let anyone off the hook. The creature itself is handled with admirable restraint. The disagreement about what it looks like (dog, spider, baby, shaved thing) is both realistic and thematically resonant — the crew can't agree on what it is because the question of what it is is precisely what the story is about. The final image of it going across the salt pan, getting smaller, becoming "a thing you had to decide you were still seeing," is genuinely moving. The ending is earned. The false manifest, the eighty-dollar bill from Cassity, the burned notice — these are the right details. The final exchange between Hale and Pim about whether the creature lived is perfectly calibrated: honest without being cruel, hopeful without being sentimental. WEAKNESSES: The piece occasionally tips into self-conscious stylistic mannerism. "The whole rest of the volume was wadded out with insulation batting, meters of it, gray and puffed, jammed floor to ceiling like packing in a jeweler's box" — the jeweler's box simile is used twice (once by Hale, once by Fen), which feels like either a deliberate echo or an oversight; it reads as the latter. Some of the sentence fragments, while generally effective, occasionally feel like affectation rather than necessity. The Perdition attack sequence in Chapter 4 is the weakest section — it moves very fast, which is appropriate for an ambush, but Hoyt's death feels slightly underweighted given how much the story subsequently leans on it. We don't know Hoyt well enough for his death to land with full force, though the detail of the coolant cans standing upright is excellent. The creature's nature is deliberately ambiguous, but the story occasionally wants to have it both ways — treating it as clearly sentient enough to warrant moral consideration while also maintaining plausible deniability. This is a feature more than a bug, but it means the moral stakes are slightly softer than they could be. The pacing in Chapter 3 (the document reading) is slightly slow, though the Vega/Pim argument about farm animals is sharp. The dialogue is generally excellent — naturalistic, character-specific, doing real work. "You can pack a hole. You can't pack a nerve" is the kind of line that feels found rather than written. The weakness is that occasionally the dialogue becomes slightly too aphoristic, too perfectly weighted, in a way that tips from literary to literary-feeling. Overall, this is a genuinely impressive piece of literary science fiction that takes its genre seriously and executes at a high level. The flaws are minor relative to the achievement. Initial Writing Prompt:
Possession Horror Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
