In through the nose on a count of four, hold two, out on six, and after a while it stops being a thing you're doing and starts being a thing that's happening, and you lie there in the dark listening to your own weather. The trick is not to swallow. You'd think it would be the eyes but it isn't, the eyes are easy, the eyes just stay shut. It's the swallow. Get it done before you settle and then you've got about eleven minutes before you want to again, and by then she's usually got bored, or bored enough, and you hear the chair. She sat there forty minutes. I'd say forty. There's no clock in the back room because the clock stopped and I put it in the wardrobe and never got another one, so I can't swear to forty, but it was long enough that my left arm went and I had to lie there with it dead under me and think about something else. What I thought about was the guttering. Then the chair — it's a wicker one, a bedroom chair, the sort nobody's ever sat in on purpose — and she got up and she came over and she did the blanket. She always does the blanket. Pulls it up over my shoulder and gives it a sort of pat. And then out, and the door left open four inches the way she likes it, and fourteen stairs, and the kitchen light going on and then off again, and then nothing. Which was fine. It wasn't fine, but I'd like to be clear that at that point it was mostly annoying. That's the thing I want to get across. It wasn't a horror. It was my sister coming into my room at night and standing about, and my whole feeling about it, lying there with my arm dead, was: *she's doing this so I'll know she's up.* Because she is up. She's up at all hours, she wants everybody to be aware of it, the light's on in the kitchen at three and Denise Halloran two doors down says to Ken, that light's on again. It's the same as the washing. She's been doing my washing since August without a word about it, my sheets, my socks, and it appears folded on the end of the bed like weather, and if I said thank you she'd say don't be daft, and if I said stop she'd say what am I supposed to do, leave it. There's a whole architecture in this house of things I've stopped saying. If you took one out I think the roof would come in. Anyway. The room. It's the back bedroom, which was mine and Bree's until she got the front one at thirteen, and it faces the fell and the wet side of everything. The back wall has damp in it. Not a patch — a district. It comes up from the skirting to about hip height and it's the colour of weak tea at the edges and darker in the middle and if you put your hand flat on it you can feel that it's colder than a wall should be, and it smells, and you get used to the smell in about a day and then you stop being able to smell it at all, which is worse. Bree's had two men look at it. The first one said guttering. The second one said guttering and also possibly the render, and quoted, and the quote is on the windowsill in the kitchen under the fruit bowl going soft. Fourteen pencil marks on the doorframe. Eight months. There's still a coat on the hook in the hall — her waterproof, the green one with the toggle gone — and there's a Boots receipt in the pocket from November and I know that because I went through the pockets in about my second week here, which I'm not proud of, and there was the receipt and a Fisherman's Friend gone soft in its wrapper and eighty pence. And then it was July and I was sitting in a flat I couldn't pay for with the curtains shut at two in the afternoon, and Bree rang about the headstone, and somewhere in that phone call, without either of us saying anything you could point at, it got decided. Two suitcases and a box of kitchen things. The box is still on the landing. It's got my good pan in it. She's got the front room, I've got the back, and it works, it does work, I want to be fair to her. She's easy to live with in the daytime. I should say how long. I've been trying to work it out and I can't, properly. It started in October — the clocks had gone back, I know that, because the first time it happened I thought the light in the hall was on and it wasn't, it was just that it was dark earlier than I'd got used to. So October. Which makes it what, three weeks? Five? I could count it if I sat down with a calendar and I've decided not to, and I'd rather not look at why I've decided that. And the other thing, and then I'll stop. I haven't been sleeping. Not since I got here. I don't mean badly. I mean I lie in that bed from about eleven till about six and I do the breathing and I go over things — the guttering, the meeting, the coat, the coat, the coat — and then the light comes and I get up and I'm fine. I'm actually fine. I make a cup of tea and I feel completely ordinary. I haven't mentioned it to her. Or to anyone. There isn't an anyone. Downstairs the kitchen light went on again. ## Three The summer I was fifteen the school kitchens had shut for the holidays and Mam was at home all day, which was its own weather, and it rained for eleven days and then it stopped and it was suddenly hot and stayed hot, and we were in the back room because it was the coolest room in the house, which it was then and isn't now. We played the staring game. I don't know where it came from. It's not a game anybody teaches you. You sit cross-legged on the floor facing each other with your knees touching — that was a rule, the knees had to be touching, it was no good if you were a foot apart — and you look at each other and you don't blink and you don't look away, and the first one to laugh loses. That's it. That's the whole thing. Except it wasn't, because we'd been doing it since I was about six and Bree was eleven, and by fifteen and twenty it had accumulated. There was a whole legislature. You couldn't talk, but you could make a noise. You couldn't touch, but knees didn't count as touching because knees were structural. You could pull a face, but only in the middle bit — there was a rule, and I couldn't tell you now how it was arrived at, that you couldn't pull a face in the first thirty seconds, because that was cheap. Blinking was allowed if it was involuntary and both of you agreed it was involuntary, which meant every game had at least one argument in it, and the argument didn't count as talking. She used to cheat. She cheated by being funny. She'd sit there absolutely straight-faced and then very slowly, over about a minute, she'd move one eyebrow. Just the one. And there is no defence against it. I'd go and she'd get up and do a lap of the room with her arms in the air like she'd scored. I won more than she did. I don't say that to be a certain way about it, it's just true, I've got a face that doesn't do much, everybody's told me so all my life. Teachers used to ask me what was the matter when nothing was the matter. Bree's got everything on her face at all times, always has, you could read her across a car park, and so the game was harder for her, and so she wanted it more, and so she cheated. The best one was 1996 or thereabouts. The eleven days of rain and then the heat. We'd been at it maybe twenty minutes, which is a very long time, and my eyes had gone past stinging into a sort of hot flat calm, and the room had done the thing it does, where the edges of the person go soft and start to move slightly, and their face isn't a face any more, it's a lot of parts that happen to be near each other. And she was winning. She was absolutely rock still, and I could see she'd got somewhere with it, she'd gone somewhere, and I was going to lose. And then she wet herself. Not much. Enough. Twenty years old and she laughed so hard she went, and she got up and did a sort of crouching run to the bathroom shouting *don't*, *don't*, *don't you dare*, and I lay flat on the floorboards and could not breathe. I've never in my life laughed like that. It hurt for two days. She came back with a towel and her jeans changed and she sat down on the bed and said, entirely reasonably, "Right, so I won that." We argued about it for eleven years. She maintained that she hadn't looked away and hadn't blinked and hadn't laughed *first*. She maintained the leaving of the room was not covered in the rules. Which it wasn't. That's the awful part. It wasn't covered. Mam came up. She'd have heard us through the floor, she always could, the house is nothing but floor. She stood in the doorway with one hand on the frame the way she did, and she looked at us on the floor with our knees together and our faces wrecked, and she didn't say what's going on or what's funny. She said: "Don't look at a thing straight. Look beside it." And then, "Pack that in, the pair of you. I can hear you through the floor." And went down. She said things like that. She said an enormous number of things and about three-quarters of them were sharp and unanswerable and had nothing to do with anything you'd said, and you learned young not to go after them, because if you asked her what she meant she'd look at you and say *well, you'd know, you always know*, and you'd have lost. I don't think it meant anything. I've never thought it meant anything. I think she'd come up the stairs to tell us to shut up and something about the two of us sitting on the floor like that got in under her, and that was what came out. Bree did an impression of her doing it, later, at the top of the stairs, one hand on the frame — *don't look at a thing straight* — and I laughed at that too. We didn't play it much after that summer. I went in the September, not to anywhere, just out, and after that when I came back there was less floor and more kitchen, and you don't sit down on the boards with your sister when you're home for four days. She's in the chair now. She came up at about half twelve and she's been there since and it's — I don't know. Late. There's a bird doing something outside that isn't a normal hour for a bird. I'm on my back with my hands folded, which Mam used to say was morbid, and I'm breathing on the four, and my eyes are shut, and I can hear the boiler dropping its spanner in the other house. ## Seven We started drinking at about four in the afternoon because there was nothing else to do with the day. There were two bottles of Mam's sherry in the sideboard, the cream one, with the dust in the shoulders, and Bree said "well, she's not going to want it," and that was Sunday. It didn't stay funny. I don't know who started it. That's true and it's also convenient. Somewhere round the bottom of the first bottle she said something about the box on the landing — my good pan, still in it, since August — and I said something about the quote under the fruit bowl, and after that it went the way these things go, which is sideways and downhill at once. She said I'd been sat in her house for four months like a lodger who doesn't pay. I said it wasn't her house. That was a bad one. I knew it while it was coming out. She went white round the mouth and said, "No. No, it's not. It's ours, and I lived in it for six years with her in it, and you've lived in it since August with the telly on." I said, "Immersion's on, is it," which I meant as — I don't know what I meant it as. A way of stopping. Some kind of white flag. She said, "Don't." And I said it again, because I'd got somewhere I couldn't get back from and the only direction left was further. "Immersion's on in August. Mam'd have your life." She looked at me for a second and then she laughed, one go, no tail on it, and said, "You're a horrible woman, you." Then we did the six years. Or she did. She did the six years standing up with a glass in her hand and I sat at the table and took it, and the substance of it was that she'd done everything and I'd done four days, and the substance of it was correct, and she knew I knew it was correct and it made her worse rather than better. "Four days," she said. "In December. She'd not known who I was since the October." "I know." "You don't know. That's the whole point. You don't know and now you never will and I've got to carry it about with me like a bag." She sat down heavily on the arm of the chair. "And I'd not have you know it for anything. That's the thing. I'd not have you know it." We were quiet a bit. And then she said, not looking at me, "You stand at the end of my bed." "What?" "You do. You come in the front room and you stand at the end of the bed." She was turning her glass. "I've woke up and you've been stood there. More than once. And I've said your name and you've gone out." I didn't say anything. "Don't," she said. "Don't look like that. I've not slept. I've told you I've not slept, and when you've not slept you get — Kath got it, after Ray. You get things. It's nothing. Forget I said it." And she got up and went and put the kettle on and stood in the kitchen with her back to me for about four minutes, and I sat there and did not defend myself. That's the part I keep coming back to. There was a whole answer available. *I don't. I haven't. Bree, I'm in that bed all night, I'm in that bed all night and you know I am because you're in the chair.* Two sentences and the whole thing would have been out on the table between us. I didn't say it because I couldn't have finished it. Because to say *you're in the chair* is to say *I'm awake*, and I have been sitting on that for four months like a woman sitting on a suitcase she can't shut. And because I didn't know if it was true. About the bed. I did not know. She came back through with the tea and neither of us drank it, and we opened the other bottle at about half seven, and somewhere in there it stopped being a row and turned into the other thing, the flat exhausted end of it where you're too tired to be enemies. She said, "What are we doing?" I said, "I don't know." And she said — and she was smiling when she said it, she said it as a joke, I want that written down — "Go on. I'll play you for it." So we got down on the floor of the back room. It took a bit of doing at forty-four and thirty-nine, with drink in us, and she made a noise going down that neither of us mentioned. Knees touching. Hands on our own knees. The light was the overhead one because the lamp bulb had gone, and it was that hard white that makes everything look like a corridor. "No faces for thirty seconds," she said. "No faces for thirty seconds." "And blinking's only if we both say." "Both say." "Right," she said. "Go on then." Her eyes are grey with a brown mark in the left one, low down, like something that's fallen in. I'd forgotten that. I'd have said I knew my sister's face better than my own and I'd forgotten a brown mark in her eye. The first bit is just difficult. Your eyes sting and water and you want to laugh at nothing, at the stupidity of two grown women. She did the eyebrow at about a minute and I nearly went and she made a small triumphant noise in her throat and I got it back. Then it goes past that, the way it does. Her face came apart. That's the only way I've ever been able to put it and it isn't right. The parts stop belonging to each other. There's an eye, and near it there's a nostril, and none of it is anybody, and the edges of her went soft and started to move very slightly, in and out, like something breathing that isn't the person. The tap in the bathroom went. It's gone for years. The floor was cold and got colder and I could feel it in the bone of my knee. And I was looking at her and in her eye, in the wet of it, there was me. Small and white and lit from above, the way you are. And I watched it, because there was nothing else to look at by then, and it was doing what I was doing. And then it wasn't. I don't want to say what I mean by that. I've tried three times. Somebody laughed. It went on a bit, the way hers does, that tail at the end. It went on longer than the joke. It was me. It was me that laughed.

[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of writing that executes its plan with remarkable precision and restraint. Let me work through the chapter systematically. The chapter opens with the sherry and the dead-mother joke, which lands exactly as planned — the "Immersion's on, is it" exchange is devastating in its specificity. The joke is used as a weapon, as the plan specified, and Nell's own commentary ("I meant it as — I don't know what I meant it as. A way of stopping. Some kind of white flag") is perfectly calibrated to her character: the self-aware coward who can't stop herself. The row itself is handled with exceptional skill. Bree's speech about the six years — "I'd not have you know it for anything. That's the thing. I'd not have you know it" — is one of the best lines in the chapter. It captures Bree's complexity exactly: the defensiveness that is also genuine love, the aggression that is also protection. This is not a character articulating a "true and beautiful thing about attention or love" — it's messier and more real than that. The pivot to Bree's accusation about the bed is the chapter's structural masterstroke. "You stand at the end of my bed" arrives without fanfare and is immediately walked back by Bree herself, which is more unsettling than if she'd insisted on it. Nell's non-defense — her sitting there and not saying the obvious thing — is the emotional core of the chapter, and the writing earns it: "I have been sitting on that for four months like a woman sitting on a suitcase she can't shut." This is a metaphor that actually lands, specific and physical and right. The staring game sequence is handled with great care. The plan called for it to be "not as a ritual, as a stupid thing to do," and that's exactly what it is — Bree says it as a joke, they get down on the floor with difficulty, there's the noise going down that neither mentions. The warmth and absurdity of it is real before it turns. The description of the game itself is where the prose reaches its highest level. "Her eyes are grey with a brown mark in the left one, low down, like something that's fallen in" — this is the kind of specific, strange detail that earns its strangeness. The face coming apart ("The parts stop belonging to each other") is described with appropriate restraint, not over-mystified. The ending — "Somebody laughed. It went on a bit, the way hers does, that tail at the end. It went on longer than the joke. It was me. It was me that laughed." — is exactly right. The repetition of "It was me" is the plan's "once too many," and it works. The reader is left with the ambiguity intact: did Nell laugh, or did something laugh through Nell, or is Nell lying to herself? The chapter declines to answer. The dialogue throughout is exceptional. It sounds like real people in a real row — the interruptions, the non-sequiturs used as weapons, the way Bree immediately walks back the accusation about the bed. "Bree Kearney, idiot of the parish" doesn't appear but the voice is consistent with the profile. The immersion heater joke lands as a weapon exactly as planned. Minor criticisms: The line "sideways and downhill at once" is slightly too neat, a touch of the writerly that the rest of the chapter avoids. The phrase "the flat exhausted end of it where you're too tired to be enemies" is good but perhaps the most conventionally "literary" moment in an otherwise unconventionally literary chapter. These are small complaints. The chapter follows its plan with extraordinary fidelity while never feeling mechanical. Every element specified — the row, the coat grievance surfacing wrong, Bree's accusation and retraction, the game on the floor, the ambiguous ending — is present and executed with skill. The characters are entirely consistent with their profiles. The horror is entirely situational and deniable. The prose is specific rather than atmospheric. The dialogue is the best in the story so far. ## Eight She's not in the house. Tuesday, that would be. I know it's Tuesday because the bins went, and the bins have been Tuesday since the council changed them, which Denise told me at the gate at some point, along with the knee. I went into the front room and the bed's made. She makes it the way Mam made it, with the corners done. Her phone's not on the side. The black thing from Kath's wedding is still on the back of the door. I looked in the kitchen and out the back. The back door was on the latch and I lifted it and looked and there's the shed and the wall and then it's just the fell going up, and the grass had that flattened look it gets after rain, and there wasn't anybody in it. That's two rooms and a garden. I want to be accurate about this. I did not go up to the reservoir. I did not walk down the top road. I did not ring her, and I did not ring Kath, and I did not go to the bungalow and ask Denise if she'd seen her, and there is no version of that afternoon in which any of those things were beyond me. I stood in the kitchen with my hand on the back of a chair for a while and then I filled the kettle. I'll say it plainly. I didn't want to find out. I emptied the dehumidifier. It was full to the line, which I've not known it do, and heavier than it should be, and I had to take it down the fourteen with both hands and my hip against the wall. It went into the sink and it went on and on, and it was clear. The coat's gone off the hook. Mam's green waterproof is there and the fleece is there and the grey wool one isn't, and there's a mark on the wall the shape of the shoulder where it's been rubbing the paint for four years. Good luck to her. I mean that in the way I mean things. On the windowsill by the tap there's the list. Towels, torch, bolt. And a fourth thing under them. *chair down* Her writing. She does a G like a number and there's a G in it and it's her G. I've looked at it a fair few times now. I don't know if it means take the chair downstairs, or the chair's to come down, or something else entirely, and I'm not going to know, and after a bit you stop turning a thing over and just leave it where it is. I put a bit of tea on and couldn't eat it. My mouth's all coins. I've moved into the front. It made sense. It's the dry side, it gets the morning, and there's a lamp in there that works. I brought my things through — there's not much, two suitcases' worth and it took one trip — and I got in her bed with the corners done and lay on my back with my hands folded. I left the box on the landing. My good pan. I'll get to it. It's a better room. You can hear the road from it, which I thought I'd mind and I don't. The dehumidifier's still out there by the airing cupboard and it clicks, and you can't get ahead of it, and I've decided I'd rather have it on. The light went at about four, the way it does now. I got the breathing going without meaning to. That's a thing I've noticed since. It starts on its own — swallow first, then four, hold, out on six — and after a while it stops being something you're doing and becomes the weather in the room, and you lie there and listen to it happening to you. I thought about the coat for a bit and then I let it go past. I thought about her going down the fourteen in the dark and lifting the back door on its handle, and the noise of the gutter coming in for a second, and then it going again. And then a while after that the door came off the latch downstairs, and the fourteen stairs went, in pairs at the bottom and then singly, and seven, which is the one that goes. The door here opens the other way to the back room. It came to about four inches. There's no chair in the front room. There was never a chair in the front room. The wicker one is where it's always been, in the back, at an angle to the bed, and I've not moved it and I'm not going to. I heard it take her weight. I've got good at this. That's the one thing I'd say for myself out of all of it. I'm thirty-nine and I've lost a husband and a job and a mother and I could not tell you what I've got in the bank, but I can lie on my back in the dark for six hours without moving my hands, and I can keep my face doing nothing while somebody four feet away looks at me, and there's nobody alive better at it. She sat forward with her forearms along the arms of it, because the back of that chair's no use to anybody. The grey cardigan with the pocket gone at the seam. Her fingers over the edge of the wicker. The dry patch on her jaw. My eyes are shut. They've been shut since four. She's not blinking. I can wait. I've nowhere to be and there's nothing coming, and in the morning I'll go down and put the grill on and burn a corner of it, and empty the jug, and that'll be Wednesday. She thinks I'm sleeping.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is an exceptional piece of writing that executes its plan with remarkable precision and restraint. Let me work through the chapter systematically. The opening is deliberately flat and functional: "She's not in the house." Three words, declarative, no drama. This is exactly what the plan called for — anticlimax and housework. The chapter earns its quietness because the preceding chapters (as described in the plan) have built the dread, and now the story refuses to pay off in any conventional sense. The absence of Bree is handled with a kind of willful incuriosity that is both psychologically precise and genuinely unsettling. The narrator's self-accounting — "I want to be accurate about this. I did not go up to the reservoir. I did not walk down the top road. I did not ring her" — is one of the finest passages in the chapter. The list of things she didn't do is more damning than any accusation. "I didn't want to find out" is delivered plainly, without self-pity or self-flagellation, and it lands with tremendous weight precisely because it isn't dressed up. This is the character's defining cowardice made explicit, and it works. The dehumidifier detail is perfect: "heavier than it should be," "it went on and on, and it was clear." The practical domestic object carrying uncanny weight without any authorial underlining. The plan specified "she empties the dehumidifier, which is very full" and the execution adds the detail of it being "clear" — water that should be murky or at least unremarkable, described in a way that makes you pause without explaining why. The coat's departure — "Good luck to her. I mean that in the way I mean things" — is a masterclass in compressed characterization. The qualification that undercuts itself, the bitterness that won't quite form into bitterness, the release that isn't release. This is Nell's voice at its most precise. The list with the fourth item, "chair down," is handled exactly as planned: Nell examines it, can't decode it, and "after a bit you stop turning a thing over and just leave it where it is." The refusal to interpret is itself interpretation. The impossible thing in the final section is executed with extraordinary control. Nell is in the front room, there is no chair in the front room, and yet: "I heard it take her weight." Then the description of Bree — the grey cardigan, the dry patch on her jaw, the fingers over the wicker — delivered while Nell tells us her eyes have been shut since four. This is the second impossible thing, handled exactly as planned: "not described mystically; she simply reports what's in the chair while telling us her eyes are closed, and moves on." The plan said "small and flat and unremarked" and the execution is precisely that. The final lines echo the prompt from the wrong side, as planned: "She thinks I'm sleeping." The inversion is there but it's not neat — it's not a closed loop, it's a continuation. Nell has become the watcher, or the watched has become the watcher, or nothing has changed at all and this is just what they do now. The ambiguity is total and earned. The voice is consistent throughout. The cheek-biting, the coin taste, the counting (fourteen stairs, seven being the one that goes), the qualifications that undercut themselves — all present and all organic. "I'm thirty-nine and I've lost a husband and a job and a mother and I could not tell you what I've got in the bank, but I can lie on my back in the dark for six hours without moving my hands" is a devastating sentence that earns its length. Minor criticisms: The chapter is almost flawless in execution, but "the weather in the room" as a metaphor for the breathing is slightly more poetic than the rest of the prose, a small departure from the register. The line "there's nothing coming" has a faint whiff of the thesis-ending the plan explicitly wanted to avoid, though it's saved by what follows. These are genuinely minor. The plan called for the chapter to be 400-500 words; this runs longer, perhaps 700-800 words. However, the additional length is entirely justified — the final section, with the impossible chair and the closing lines, requires the space it takes, and nothing feels padded. The chapter follows its plan with exceptional fidelity: Bree absent, Nell not looking properly, the dehumidifier emptied, the coat gone, the list with a fourth item, moving to the front room, the impossible chair, the final echo of the prompt. Every element lands. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of fiction. Let me work through its qualities and failings systematically. STRENGTHS: The voice is the piece's greatest achievement. The narrator's interiority is rendered with extraordinary precision — the counting of "anyways," the running inventory of her sister's physical changes, the architecture of things she's stopped saying. This is not a narrator telling us she's observant; she demonstrates it in every sentence. The voice is consistent across all eight chapters without becoming monotonous, which is a genuine technical achievement. The horror element is handled with remarkable restraint and intelligence. The piece refuses to resolve whether the supernatural is real or whether two grief-stricken, sleep-deprived women are haunting each other through mutual insomnia and guilt. The final chapter's ambiguity — is Bree back, or is something wearing Bree — is earned rather than cheap. The prompt ("I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping") is woven throughout and returns at the end with devastating effect. The domestic detail is superb. The wicker chair, the dehumidifier, the fourteen stairs with seven being the one that goes, the grill instead of the toaster, the coat — these accumulate into a fully realized world. The damp wall as a kind of presence is subtle and effective. The Boots receipt and the softened Fisherman's Friend in the dead mother's pocket is one of the finest details in the piece. The dialogue is exceptional. "She was a difficult woman" as a deflection rather than comfort. "You're a horrible woman, you." The sherry scene where the row turns into exhaustion. These feel completely real. The dialogue does enormous work without ever feeling expository. The staring game in Chapter 3 is a structural masterstroke — it establishes the sisters' history, their dynamic, their mother's strange oracular quality, and prefigures the final chapter's return to the game. The mother's line "Don't look at a thing straight. Look beside it" is the thematic key to the entire piece and is delivered with perfect casualness. Chapter 6 is the emotional and narrative peak. Bree finally speaking in the dark, the coat speech, "You never even asked for it back" — this is where the piece earns its horror. The horror is grief and guilt and the things sisters don't say to each other, and the supernatural is the pressure that forces the unsayable out. The ending is genuinely unsettling. The narrator has moved into the front room, taken Bree's bed, and something is in the wicker chair. The final line — "She thinks I'm sleeping" — reverses the opening and suggests the narrator has become the watcher, or that the roles have collapsed entirely. WEAKNESSES: The piece occasionally over-relies on its own technique. The "I'll say this quickly" and "I want to be accurate about this" constructions appear frequently enough to become a tic. The narrator's self-consciousness about her own narration is a strength but risks becoming a mannerism. Chapter 7's staring game scene, while structurally necessary, slightly over-explains its own uncanniness. "Somebody laughed. It went on a bit, the way hers does, that tail at the end. It went on longer than the joke. It was me. It was me that laughed." This is the one moment where the piece tells us to be disturbed rather than simply disturbing us. The dehumidifier as symbol (clear water, grief, the body's moisture) is effective but perhaps slightly too neat — it's the one element that feels consciously literary rather than organically observed. Chapter 8's resolution (or non-resolution) is powerful but the "I've nowhere to be and there's nothing coming" line edges toward the kind of portentous closing statement that slightly undercuts the piece's otherwise rigorous avoidance of easy profundity. The supernatural ambiguity is handled well overall, but the line "I heard it take her weight" in the final chapter is the one moment where the piece commits slightly too hard to the supernatural reading, potentially closing off the psychological interpretation prematurely. These are minor criticisms of a piece that is operating at a very high level. The writing is controlled, the characters are fully realized, the horror is genuinely unsettling, and the emotional core — two sisters failing to grieve together — is deeply felt and honestly rendered.
