# Brainstorming ## Reading the Prompt "They fucked with the wrong babysitter." — pulp revenge tale. The line is a boast, a tagline on a grindhouse poster. It implies: - A babysitter who is more than she appears (ex-military? ex-hitwoman? witness protection? a survivor with skills? something inhuman?) - Somebody who "fucked with" her — kidnapped the kid, hurt the kid, broke into the house, threatened her, underestimated her - Escalating violence, satisfying comeuppance, a body count, one-liners Pulp mode means: lean prose, hard verbs, chapter-end hooks, blood, a moral simplicity that's actually the point. Not literary ambiguity. But *good* pulp has texture — a specific voice, a specific city, weird little details, and characters who feel like people even while doing outrageous things. ## Character concepts for the babysitter 1. **Ex-cartel enforcer in hiding.** Fled north, changed her name, now sits for a suburban family. When the cartel's local franchise takes the kid to leverage her, she goes back to work. Classic, works, maybe too familiar. 2. **Retired mob "cleaner" / body disposal specialist.** Not a shooter — a woman who dissolved people for a living. Very pulpy, unusual skill set, means her revenge is *creative* rather than gun-fu. I like this a lot. She knows how to make people disappear, which is a much scarier threat than "I'll kill you." 3. **Former child soldier / trafficking survivor.** Darker, more thematically loaded — she was the kid once. Emotional engine is strong: she's protecting a child version of herself. Risk of misery-tourism. 4. **Nun with a past. / Ex-IRA. / Ex-Mossad.** Fun, maybe cartoonish. 5. **Sixteen-year-old babysitter who is just *very* mean and resourceful.** Home Alone as horror. Fun tonal swing, but limits the pulp violence unless we go full *Hardcore Henry*. 6. **She's not human.** Something old that takes work as a nanny because children are what it protects. Weird-fiction pulp. Tonally distinct but risks losing the visceral grounded satisfaction. 7. **Wet-work contractor on medical leave / burnout.** She's babysitting because it's the only job that doesn't trigger her. Good irony. 8. **Prison-yard shot-caller, newly paroled**, sits for her parole officer's sister's kids. Comedic-adjacent. The **body-disposal specialist** (option 2) is the most distinctive and most fun to write. Give her a name like **Marguerite "Margo" Vasquez**, or something plainer — **Dee**. Let's try **Wanda**? No. **Ruth.** Ruth is great: biblical, matronly, unassuming. Or **Delia**. Let's brainstorm: Ruth Salas. Ruth Zaragoza. "Miss Ruth" is what the kid calls her. Perfect — a name that sounds like a church lady. Age: 50s. That's better than a 30-year-old action babe — a heavy, tired, gray-rooted woman in orthopedic shoes with reading glasses on a chain. Nobody sees her coming. Pulp loves an underestimated protagonist. ## Who "they" are 1. **Home invaders who picked the wrong house.** Contained, tight, single-night siege story. Good for 8 chapters? Maybe too small — 8k words of one night can work but revenge needs a *hunt*. 2. **Local crew that snatches the kid for ransom** — dad's a crooked developer/lawyer/pharma exec who owes people. Kid taken on Ruth's watch. She goes hunting. Strong: gives her a quest, a chain of targets (escalating ladder: the driver → the fence → the middleman → the boss), which is perfect for episodic chapters. 3. **Traffickers running kids through a car wash / motel / church van.** Very pulpy, very dark. 4. **Cops.** The people who took the kid are or include cops. Adds a "no one will help you" pressure. 5. **The kid's own father** sold him — or the mother's new boyfriend. Domestic rot under the suburb. 6. **Her old outfit found her**, and hurting the kid was how they got her attention. Ties past and present. Best structure: **combine 2, 5, and 6.** The snatch looks like a professional job. It's actually messier — the kid's stepfather owes money, and the crew that came is connected to the very people Ruth used to clean up for. So her past isn't just backstory, it's the antagonist. And the final villain is someone she personally made disappear people for. ## The kid Needs to be specific and lovable fast. Options: - **Theo, 8**, obsessed with sharks / knows all the bones in the body / bad asthma. Asthma is a nice ticking clock: he has an inhaler and it's in the house. Clock = urgency. - A pair of kids: older sister hides, little brother taken. Sister becomes Ruth's reluctant sidekick. Adds dialogue partner. Risk: complicates. - **Nine-year-old girl, Birdie**, who is a liar and a thief and Ruth loves her for it. I like the **asthma inhaler clock** and a single kid, boy, ~7-8. Name: **Oscar**? **Theo**? **Gus**. "Gus" is warm and pulpy. Gus, 7, wears a plastic dinosaur mask. Loves the sanitation truck. Let's say Gus has one lung thing — the inhaler. Emotional core: Ruth has no children. Or worse — Ruth *had* a child, and the reason she got out of the business is connected. Maybe: she cleaned up after a job and one of the "packages" was a boy about Gus's age, and that broke her. That's a strong, ugly, motivating backstory — the sin she's atoning for. Her penance is watching other people's children safely, and now she's failed again. Good. ## Antagonist ladder (episodic chapter fuel) 1. **The driver / lookout** — a scared 20-year-old named Dustin. Gives her the first thread. Maybe she doesn't kill him; she uses him. 2. **The muscle** — two brothers, or a guy named Pigeon who works at a tow yard. 3. **The fixer / broker** — a woman named **Claudette**, runs a nail salon or a title loan office; she brokers "problems." 4. **The buyer / the boss** — the man Ruth used to work for. **Mr. Amado**? **Halloran**? Let's say **Emmett Boone**, or Greek/Armenian flavor: **Zervas**. Something ordinary and awful: **Mr. Fen**, **Uncle Sal**, **Pastor Dan**. Pulp loves a villain with a respectable front: a **funeral home owner** — beautiful thematic pairing with a body-disposal woman. The man who taught her the trade owns a crematorium/funeral home. YES. **Lyle Dupree, Dupree & Sons Funeral Home.** His retort ovens. Her final act could be putting him in his own oven. 5. Optional: a **dirty detective** who tells her to stand down. And the domestic villain: **Brett**, the stepdad, who owes $200k and offered the kid as collateral (or gave up the alarm code). He's the guy she deals with mid-story — a nasty, satisfying, non-final kill. ## Tone / voice options - **First person, past tense, Ruth's voice.** Dry, plainspoken, funny in a graveyard way. Great for pulp one-liners. "I have never liked the word 'closure.' In my experience things don't close. They get filled in." - **Third person close, present tense.** Punchier, more cinematic. - **First person is my instinct** — it lets her professional expertise become voice ("A man weighs less than you think, once you're organized about it"), which is the whole flavor of the piece. Chapter titles: short, punchy, like grindhouse cards. "1. The House on Verbena Court." Or single words. ## Possible 8-chapter structures **Structure A — Linear hunt** 1. Ordinary night, cozy, Gus. Invasion. Ruth wakes in blood. 2. Aftermath, she doesn't call police, reveals her past. Finds the first thread. 3. Squeezes Dustin the driver. 4. Stepdad Brett revelation; ugly scene. 5. The salon/broker, big set piece, she takes damage. 6. Learns the truth: her old boss. Flashback to the sin. 7. Assault on the funeral home. Gets Gus. 8. Final confrontation with Dupree; the oven; the aftermath / new normal. **Structure B — In medias res.** Open with her hauling a body, then flash back. Pulpier hook but linear is clearer at this length. **Structure C — Siege.** All one house. Too small. Structure A is right. Maybe start Chapter 1 with a cold open line that seeds the violence ("Two hours before they came, I made macaroni."). ## Set pieces to invent - Kitchen fight with a cast-iron skillet and a hot pot of water. She loses — gets tased/clubbed — that's how the kid gets taken. Important: she must *lose* first for revenge to matter. - A tow yard at night, dogs, an engine hoist. - Nail salon back room; she uses acetone and a lighter, or a UV lamp, drain cleaner. Her trade: lye, sodium hydroxide, drums. - She keeps a "kit" buried in a storage unit or a suitcase in a crawlspace: barrels, coveralls, a bone saw, a .38, a bolt gun. - A church van / bus with painted-over lettering. - Funeral home: coffin display room, embalming table, retort oven, a viewing with mourners while she works. - The inhaler as a talisman she carries and hands back at the end. ## Themes worth threading - Atonement vs. reversion. She thought she'd changed; she hadn't. Pulp answer: she's okay with it. Or bittersweet: she saves the kid but can't go back to babysitting. - The banality of the suburbs concealing the machinery of money. - Care work as combat: her competence with children mirrors her competence with corpses. Both are about *tending*. Nice. ## Lines / images to bank - "I used to make people not exist. It's a trade like any other." - Her purse: butterscotch candies, wet wipes, zip ties. - She wears gardening gloves. - "You're the babysitter." / "Yeah." - Ending image: mac and cheese on the stove, Gus asleep, sirens far away. - "There's no such thing as a clean job. Only a patient one." ## Ending options 1. She kills the boss, returns Gus to his mother, disappears. Bittersweet. 2. She takes Gus. Wrong/creepy — no. 3. She returns him, and the last scene is a new family hiring her, sweet and menacing. 4. She goes down with the villain — dies. Pulp sometimes likes that, but revenge tales usually want survival. 5. Ambiguous: the cops arrive and she is standing there with lye on her hands and the boy is fine, and the last line is her giving a statement that is entirely a lie. Option 3 or 5 — or combine: Gus safe with his mom, Ruth on a bus, a new town, a flyer on a laundromat corkboard: "Experienced sitter. References available." # Reflection The prompt is a tagline, so the piece has to *earn* the tagline rather than just illustrate it. The most common failure mode would be a generic ex-assassin-mom shooting her way through interchangeable thugs. What makes this idea live is **specificity of profession**. The body-disposal specialist is the strongest of my invented characters because it gives her a unique verb set. A shooter shoots; a cleaner *erases*. That produces horror instead of action-figure noise, and it produces dread in the villains, which is far more satisfying than mere gunplay. It also gives me a natural symbolic economy: she used to remove children's bodies; now she's retrieving a living child. And pairing her against a funeral director — the man who trained her, who has industrial ovens — makes the final act inevitable-feeling in the good way. That's the spine. I'm confident about it. Ruth being in her fifties, heavyset, unglamorous, with reading glasses and butterscotch candies, is the other strong choice. Pulp thrives on the reversal of underestimation, and "sweet church-lady sitter" hides more knives than "lithe leather-clad avenger." It also keeps the story from becoming a fantasy of physical prowess; her advantages must be patience, chemistry, anatomy, and nerve. That's more interesting to write in 8,000 words, and it constrains the set pieces usefully — she can't out-punch anyone, so every fight needs a device, an ambush, or a lie. That will keep the chapters varied. First person is the right call. Her voice — flat, procedural, deadpan, occasionally tender about the boy — is where the pulp pleasure lives, and it lets exposition arrive as trade knowledge rather than as flashback lumps. The risk with first person is that constant wisecracking becomes tiresome and the interiority slows the pace. I'd want the sentences short, the wit sparse and dry, maybe three or four real zingers total, placed to land. I should also be careful not to let her narrate too knowingly from the far future; keeping it close to the events preserves tension. The linear hunt structure (A) is the correct architecture for eight roughly-1000-word chapters, because each chapter can be one confrontation, and confrontations are self-contained units with clean hooks. Eight chapters is tight though — I need to be disciplined. The ladder of antagonists should probably be four rungs, not five: driver → stepdad → broker → boss. Adding a dirty cop is tempting for the "no help is coming" pressure, but it costs a chapter I don't have; better to fold that pressure into a single scene or a line of dialogue. Similarly, a sidekick child would eat words. Keep the cast small: Ruth, Gus, the mother, Brett, Dustin, Claudette, Dupree. Seven named people is plenty. The asthma inhaler clock is a good, cheap, effective device — it gives urgency without me needing to spell out worse threats, and it gives a physical object to end on. I should plant it hard in Chapter 1 so its return has weight. I also like her "kit" being buried — the moment she digs it up is a genre pleasure (the retrieval of the old self), and it should be underplayed rather than triumphant: she's sad about it, not thrilled. That keeps the character from being a cartoon. The backstory of the dead boy she once had to erase is the emotional load-bearing wall. My worry is tastelessness — a dead child as motivation fuel can be cheap. The fix is restraint: never render it in detail, let her refuse to describe it, one or two sentences, and let its meaning be about her hands rather than the child's suffering. If it's handled with reticence, it lands hard; if it's rendered lovingly, it's exploitative. Similarly, whatever they intend for Gus should stay mostly implicit — ransom leverage and a debt is enough. The story doesn't need trafficking; the debt-collateral angle is uglier in a mundane, believable way, and mundane is scarier. Where I'm less certain: how much to explain the villain's motive. Pulp doesn't need much, but a boss who orders a snatch just to be evil is flat. Making Brett's debt the cause, and Dupree recognizing Ruth's name in the process (or *not* recognizing it, which is even better — that she's a ghost to him, forgotten, is a good sting), keeps motives clean. Maybe the strongest version: they took the boy purely as collateral on Brett's debt, Ruth is incidental, and only midway does Dupree realize who the babysitter was — and *he's the one who should be afraid*. The reveal of her identity to the villains, rather than to the reader, is a better engine for the back half. Chapter 1 needs the cozy domesticity to be genuinely warm — mac and cheese, a dinosaur mask, a bad joke — because the invasion only lands if the reader liked the evening. And Ruth must lose that fight decisively and humiliatingly. Waking up in her own blood on the linoleum with the kid gone is the correct low point to start from. Titles as terse grindhouse cards will help the pulp texture. I'll keep the ending on the bittersweet side: boy returned, Ruth gone, a small menacing coda that suggests she'll do it again for someone else. That satisfies the tagline's swagger while leaving a residue.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **What I'm writing:** A pulp revenge tale in eight chapters, roughly 1000 words each, narrated in first person past tense by Ruth Salazar — fifty-six, heavyset, gray at the roots, reading glasses on a beaded chain — who for nineteen years made corpses stop existing for a man who owns a funeral home, and who has spent the last eleven years babysitting other people's children as penance. On a Tuesday night, four men come through the sliding door of a house on Verbena Court, put her on the linoleum, and take seven-year-old Gus Pilcher as collateral on his stepfather's debt. They leave her alive because she is nobody. That is their error. **Voice and style.** First person, past tense, close to the events — no wise retrospective framing from decades later. Flat, procedural, deadpan. Short sentences and hard verbs. Her expertise arrives as trade knowledge rather than flashback exposition: she tells you what lye does to a femur the way another woman would tell you how to get a stain out. Wit must be rationed — four or five genuine zingers in the whole piece, placed at chapter ends and kill-shots, or the deadpan curdles into quipping. Tenderness toward the boy is where the prose is allowed to soften, briefly, and nowhere else. No purple flourishes, no similes stacked three deep. Chapter titles as terse grindhouse cards. **What makes this work, and what I'm protecting:** Her profession, not her prowess. She cannot out-punch anyone and I will never let her. Every confrontation must be won with patience, chemistry, anatomy, a lie, or an ambush — which forces the eight set pieces to differ from one another. She takes real damage and it accumulates: a broken finger, a bitten cheek, a burn. Underestimation is the engine — nobody looks twice at a fat old sitter with butterscotch candies in her purse. **Plot spine:** Four rungs on the ladder — Dustin the driver (used, not killed), Brett the stepfather (killed, ugly, midpoint), Claudette the broker (killed, chemistry), Lyle Dupree the funeral director (killed, his own retort oven). Small cast: Ruth, Gus, Danielle the mother, Brett, Dustin, Claudette, Dupree. Motive stays mundane: a two-hundred-thousand-dollar debt and a child offered as security. No trafficking plot, no conspiracy. The mundanity is the horror. **Engine for the back half:** The reveal runs toward the villains, not the reader. Dupree does not remember Ruth's name. He forgot the woman who erased eleven of his problems. His discovery of who came for him is the story's real detonation. **The inhaler:** Gus's rescue inhaler, planted hard in Chapter 1, is the clock and the talisman. Ruth carries it through eight chapters and hands it back in the last one. **What I'm avoiding:** Generic gun-fu. Interchangeable thugs. A cool leather avenger. Slow-motion moral hand-wringing. Also — and this matters — I will not render the dead boy from her past in detail. Two sentences, refused rather than described, its meaning located in her hands. Whatever the men intend for Gus stays implicit. Reticence is the difference between hard and cheap. **Ending:** Gus goes home. Ruth does not. A short coda — a bus, another town, a flyer on a laundromat corkboard — swagger with a residue of grief. # Chapter Planning **1. Macaroni.** Tuesday. Ruth arrives at 6:40 on Verbena Court. Danielle's mascara is wrong; Brett won't meet her eyes; they leave for "dinner." Warm, specific domesticity: mac and cheese, the plastic triceratops mask Gus won't take off, his shark facts, the inhaler on the counter and the ritual of the two puffs at eight. Ruth's flat interior notes — she likes this house, she's good at this, she does not deserve it. At 9:50 the sliding door. Four men, unhurried, professional. She goes for the skillet and it isn't enough; the fight is short, brutal, humiliating, and she loses. Boot on her cheek. A voice says *she's nothing, leave her.* Black. **Hook:** she wakes on the linoleum in her own blood, alone, and the inhaler is still on the counter. **2. What I Used to Do.** Ruth doesn't call 911. Establishes why: the phone call, the cruiser, the nineteen hours of questions, the boy dead in fourteen. She reads the house instead — no forced entry, alarm disarmed with the code, Brett's overnight bag missing from the closet. She catalogs the men from memory: shoe sizes, a smoker's cough, a face with a jaw she'd know again, the plate of the van she saw at 7 p.m. and dismissed. Interleaved, spare, the reveal of her trade: nineteen years, eleven jobs, sodium hydroxide, blue plastic drums, the man who paid her. Danielle comes home at midnight, hysterical, and lies badly about where Brett is. Ruth drives to a storage unit in Coldwater and digs the kit out from under a false floor: coveralls, gloves, bone saw, a .38 she never liked, a bolt gun for cattle. **Hook:** "I put my reading glasses in the glove box. I wasn't going to be needing to read." **3. Dustin.** The van plate leads to a tow yard and a twenty-two-year-old lookout named Dustin who still lives with his mother. Ruth arrives at his mother's house with a casserole dish. Genuinely a casserole dish. The scene is horror-through-politeness: she sits in his kitchen, tells him precisely what she does for a living, describes the drum, and lets him understand she is not threatening him but *scheduling* him. He gives up two names — Pigeon at the tow yard and a woman called Claudette who "sets the price" — and the fact the boy is being held at a place with a chapel. Ruth doesn't kill him. She takes his phone and tells him to answer it when she calls, and he will, because he wants to live. **Hook:** the word *chapel*, and something turning over in her stomach that she doesn't name yet. **4. Overnight Bag.** Brett. She finds him at an extended-stay motel by the interstate with the missing bag and a woman who isn't Danielle. Ruth gets in as housekeeping. The confrontation: Brett's self-pity, the debt — two hundred grand, sports book, then worse people — and the deal he made, *it's temporary, they're not going to hurt him, it's collateral, Danielle doesn't understand business.* He says the thing that ends him: *he's not even my kid.* Ruth kills him with what's in the room — no gun, no flourish; the bolt gun, once, and then the practical, sickening competence of a woman who has done this eleven times and is very good at the after. She takes his phone, his laptop, and Claudette's address off a text thread. **Hook:** on his phone, a photo sent as proof of life — Gus in the dinosaur mask, sitting on a folding chair in front of a burgundy curtain Ruth recognizes. **5. The Nail Salon.** Claudette Reneau brokers other people's problems out of the back of a nail salon in a strip mall. Ruth walks in at closing and asks for a pedicure. Dialogue duel between two professional women of a certain age who understand each other perfectly; Claudette recognizes the type before she recognizes the woman. It goes wrong — Claudette is armed and has a nephew in the back, and Ruth takes her worst damage here: two fingers broken in a door, a scalp wound, a burn. She wins with acetone, a UV lamp, and drain cleaner, and it's the ugliest scene in the book. Before Claudette dies, she says the name: **Dupree.** And she laughs, because she thinks Ruth doesn't know what that means. **Hook:** Ruth sitting on the floor among the foot basins, taping her fingers together, saying the name out loud. **6. Eleven.** The short chapter. The one that hurts. Ruth in a parked car outside Dupree & Sons at four in the morning, and the ledger of what she was. How Lyle Dupree recruited her — a woman who cleaned houses and had no people — and taught her the chemistry, and paid in cash and Christmas hams. The eleventh job: a boy, and two sentences about it, refused rather than described, located entirely in her hands and what she did with the gloves afterward. Why she stopped. Why babysitting. Then the practical reversal: she knows this building. She built the disposal protocol for this building. She knows the retort's warm-up time is ninety minutes and the burgundy curtain in the photo hangs in Viewing Room B. She calls Dustin. **Hook:** "Mr. Dupree doesn't know my name. He signed nineteen years of my checks and he never once had to know my name." **7. Dupree & Sons.** The assault. Not a shootout — an infiltration by a woman in a black dress who looks exactly like a mourner, on the morning of a funeral, using the one door with no camera because she told him to put the camera elsewhere in 2009. Three men in the building. She takes them one at a time with drain cleaner in a spray bottle, a preparation-room scalpel, and the embalming table's own restraint straps; the fight in the casket showroom is close and terrible and she nearly loses. She gets Gus out of Viewing Room B: the mask, the bad lung, the wheeze already starting, the two puffs of the inhaler she's carried since Tuesday. Then Dupree comes down the stairs, sees a fat old woman covered in blood, and says, *Do I know you?* **Hook:** she tells him her name and he still doesn't know it. **8. Warm-Up Time.** Ruth walks Gus out to the loading bay and puts him in the car with Dustin and tells him to count sharks and not look. Then she goes back inside. Dupree in the retort room, offering money, offering the debt cleared, offering the eleven years he thinks she wants back. Ruth's monologue is short and not a monologue — she asks him to name the boy from job eleven. He can't. That's the verdict. The oven has been on for ninety minutes because she turned it on when she came in. Coda: the police tape on Verbena Court; Gus in his mother's arms and the inhaler pressed into Danielle's hand with instructions about the two puffs at eight; the paramedic asking Ruth what happened and Ruth's statement being a perfect, boring, unimpeachable lie. Then a Greyhound, forty miles of interstate, and a laundromat corkboard in a town she doesn't name: *Experienced sitter. Nights and weekends. References available.* Final line lands the tagline sideways.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a human would actually come at this A human writer given "they fucked with the wrong babysitter" would probably not start by building a symbolic architecture. They'd start with a *feeling*: the specific pleasure of watching someone underestimated do something appalling. Then they'd chase a voice until it caught. The structure would come third or fourth, and it would be lumpy — one chapter would run long because they got interested in a nail salon, another would be three pages because they were bored and wanted to get to the funeral home. More concretely, the human instincts I'd expect: - **They'd write for the reader's grin.** Pulp is a genre of pleasure. A human writing this wants you to laugh out loud once, wince twice, and read the last line of chapter four and immediately start chapter five. That's the whole job. Theme is a byproduct, not a design goal. - **They'd overcommit to one weird thing.** A real writer would fall in love with the lye, or with the butterscotch candies, or with the boy's shark facts, and let that thing spread through the book in ways that weren't planned. The obsession is what makes prose feel authored rather than generated. - **They'd let the protagonist be wrong.** Not morally ambiguous in a tasteful way — actually mistaken. Killing the wrong guy. Misreading a face. Getting a name confused. Losing a whole day. Humans write incompetence into competence porn because they know competence is only interesting under strain. - **They'd write dialogue that doesn't advance anything.** Two people talking about a coupon, a knee replacement, whether the salon takes Discover. The texture of American commerce and small talk is where pulp gets its grime. - **They'd leave stuff unexplained.** Who was the fourth man in the house? A human might simply never say. Not as mystery-box teasing — as a shrug. Life has extras in it. - **They'd resist the neat rhyme.** A human might notice that "she used to erase children's bodies, now she saves a child" is a bit too tidy and deliberately rough it up: maybe the boy from job eleven wasn't a boy, maybe it wasn't the eleventh, maybe her reason for quitting was mundane and physical — her back, her hands, a bad reaction to fumes — and the moral reason is one she invented later to live with. # Telltale LLM approaches, and why they'd hurt this piece specifically **1. Thematic over-tidiness.** The model's deepest reflex is to make everything mean something. Every object recurs, every wound pays off, the villain's job mirrors the heroine's trade, the last line echoes the first. In a literary story this reads as craft. In pulp it reads as *homework*. Pulp's authority comes from a feeling of reportage — this happened, in this order, and some of it was pointless. **2. Symmetry addiction.** Four rungs on a ladder. Eight chapters at 1000 words. One kill per chapter, escalating neatly. Real revenge stories are asymmetric: two guys die in the same paragraph, one target takes three chapters, one rung is skipped entirely because she gets lucky. **3. Explaining the subtext in the text.** The model will have Ruth say, or think, something like *I had spent eleven years trying to be someone who kept children safe.* That's the model annotating its own design. A human lets the reader do it. **4. Rationing wit "correctly."** My own intention says "four or five genuine zingers, placed at chapter ends and kill-shots." That is a spreadsheet, not a voice. Real deadpan comes out sideways and at bad moments — during grief, in the middle of gore, about nothing. **5. Terminal tastefulness.** "I will not render the dead boy in detail. Reticence is the difference between hard and cheap." This is a defensible artistic choice *and* it's the model protecting itself. Pulp is not a tasteful genre. There's a real risk the piece ends up gore-adjacent-but-never-committed: violence that's described with craft but no relish, no smell, no absurdity. The genre wants specificity that's uncomfortable. Not the child — but the adults, absolutely. If nothing in this story is genuinely ugly, the tagline is unearned. **6. Competence porn without cost.** LLMs love the calm expert. Every scene becomes Ruth being quietly better than everyone. That gets boring by chapter five. Also it makes her inhuman in the wrong way. **7. The graceful arc for every character.** Dustin will want to be redeemed. Danielle will want a moment of dignity. Claudette will want a mordant last line. The model will give them all one. Some of these people should just be dumb, or venal, or die mid-sentence. **8. Rhythmically uniform prose.** Short punchy sentences. All of them. Like this. It reads as style for two pages and as tic by page ten. Human hard-boiled writers vary wildly — Elmore Leonard runs long, comma-spliced, colloquial paragraphs and then drops a three-word line. **9. The reassuring coda.** My plan literally ends with a corkboard flyer and a "final line lands the tagline sideways." That's a bow with a bow on it. Extremely LLM: the closing image that reassures the reader the piece was designed. **10. Named-nobody syndrome.** Every character gets a first and last name, an age, a defining accessory. It signals thoroughness and reads as a character sheet. **11. Sanitized period/place detail.** LLMs write Anytown, USA. No brand names, no weather that inconveniences anyone, no smell. Pulp lives on Winn-Dixie parking lots, off-brand soda, humidity, a specific highway number. **12. The protagonist who never enjoys it.** The model will make Ruth grim and dutiful because enjoyment is morally uncomfortable. But the prompt says *fucked with the wrong babysitter* — that's a line spoken with relish. Somewhere in there, Ruth has to like this. That's the transgressive charge, and it's the thing an LLM will instinctively file down. # Deep dive: where my plan is already compromised **The funeral home.** A body-disposal specialist versus a funeral director with a retort oven, and she kills him in his own oven. This is the single most LLM thing in the document. It's *perfect*, which means it's schematic. The reader will see the oven coming from chapter two and the ending becomes an appointment rather than a surprise. Options: keep the funeral home as location but kill him with something stupid and small (a paperweight, a fall, her hands, a folding chair) — the oven is for the *after*, offhandedly, which is more horrifying and more in-character. Or: the oven is already occupied. Or: she can't get it to light. The gas is shut off because he's behind on the bill. That detail alone would do more for the piece than the whole thematic rhyme. **"He doesn't remember my name."** Strong beat, but I've now put it at the end of chapters 6 and 7 and again in 8, and framed it as "the story's real detonation." Repeating a reveal three times is how a model signals importance. Once. Underplayed. And there's a better version: he *does* remember her, warmly. Asks about her hip. Calls her Ruthie. Offers her a job. That's worse, and worse is better. **Nineteen years, eleven jobs, two hundred thousand dollars, ninety minutes' warm-up.** Numbers as texture is a real technique, but I've salted them everywhere and they all have thematic weight (eleven jobs → the eleventh was the boy). It's too neat. Real numbers are ugly: fourteen jobs, or she doesn't know, or she'd say nine and be lying. **The ladder.** Driver → stepdad → broker → boss, one per chapter, escalating, with the driver spared and the others killed in ascending order of intimacy. It's a videogame. Ideas to break it: Dustin dies pointlessly in chapter five because he came along; Claudette isn't a rung at all but a dead end who costs Ruth a day and a finger and gives her nothing; Ruth finds Gus's location in chapter four by accident, from the stepdad's phone, and the middle of the book becomes *she knows where he is and can't get to him yet* — which is far more tense than a scavenger hunt. **The casserole dish.** Ruth arriving to threaten a man while holding a casserole is a great image and also exactly the kind of "cozy menace" beat that circulates as a trope. It'd land better if it were unremarked, or if it were something worse than cozy: she brings the dish because she's genuinely planning to eat, hasn't eaten in a day, and eats it in front of him. **The inhaler.** Planted in ch1, carried for six chapters, returned in ch8. Textbook Chekhov. The problem isn't the object, it's the *tidiness of the loop*. Better: the inhaler's a real medical clock with real stakes and then she loses it. Or it's empty. Or the two puffs at eight is a lie Danielle tells sitters and the kid doesn't need it as often as she says, and Ruth doesn't know that. The object should stay useful and stop being a symbol. **Ruth's atonement structure.** "Babysitting as penance" is stated as the character's premise, which means the story will keep confirming it. Human alternative: she babysits because it pays cash, she's on nobody's books, and she is genuinely, uncomplicatedly good with children — she likes them, she always has, there's no trauma logic to it. Her past and her present don't explain each other. That's more human and more unsettling. **The refusal to describe job eleven.** I want to keep the restraint about the child, but the *way* I've planned it — "two sentences, refused rather than described, located in her hands" — is a self-congratulating move. The reader will feel the author being careful. Alternative: she describes something adjacent and banal in flat detail (the weight, the tarp, the brand of gloves, that she was worried about her car's suspension) and the horror arrives through her total absence of comment. That's colder and it doesn't announce its own tact. **Danielle.** Currently a hysterical mother who lies badly. She's furniture. Make her a problem: she blames Ruth. She calls the cops on Ruth. She knew about the debt. She's relieved Brett's gone. Give her one line that makes the reader hate her and then don't resolve it. **"Statement being a perfect, boring, unimpeachable lie."** Cute and very model-brained. Real version: nobody asks her anything, because she leaves before anyone comes, and the last we hear of the aftermath is a detail she has no access to. # Ideas for making it more human **Voice** - Let Ruth digress. One paragraph about why she won't buy the store-brand cheese. One about a bad knee. Let the digression land in the middle of violence. - Give her a private vocabulary from the trade — she calls bodies "the material," she calls the drums by a supplier's name, she says "warm work" and "cold work." Never define the terms. - Let her be funny about the wrong things and dead serious about small ones. She's unbothered by a corpse and furious about a scuffed floor. - Vary sentence length hard. One 60-word run-on when she's angry. **Texture** - Real weather. Ninety-four degrees and wet. Everyone's shirt sticks. The lye reacts faster in heat and she has opinions about that. - Real commerce: a Sonic, a Family Dollar, a title-loan place with a hand-painted sign, the Hampton Inn breakfast she eats twice. - One completely irrelevant good detail per chapter: a dog that follows her for a block, a wedding in the funeral home parking lot, a kid selling raffle tickets. **Plot roughness** - Ruth kills someone who didn't deserve it and doesn't dwell on it. One sentence, moving on. - She loses two days somewhere. Says so flatly. - One of the four men from the house is never accounted for. Mentioned once, in chapter eight, and dropped. - She gets caught by police mid-story and released because she's a fifty-six-year-old woman with a church bulletin in her purse. Underestimation as *plot mechanic*, not just characterization. **Ending** - Don't do the flyer. Options: end mid-action; end on a mundane physical task; end with her eating; end with a line of dialogue from Gus that has nothing to do with anything. The best pulp endings feel like the writer stopped because he was done, not because the shape closed. - Or: end on the tagline being spoken *by someone else*, wrongly, admiringly, in a way she'd find stupid. - Let one thread stay severed. She never learns who ordered it, or she does and it's boring. **The thing to protect above all** Somebody in this story has to be having a good time, and it should occasionally be Ruth, and it should occasionally be the reader in a way they feel slightly bad about. If I write eight chapters of tasteful, well-engineered, thematically resonant violence performed by a sad competent woman, I will have written the LLM version of this story, and it will be pretty good, and nobody will remember it.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The piece.** Eight chapters, ~1000 words each, first person past tense. Ruth Salazar, fifty-six, wide through the hips, gray at the roots, works cash-only as a sitter. For a long time before that she made bodies stop existing for a man who owns a funeral home. Four men come through a sliding door on a Tuesday, put her down, and take the seven-year-old she was watching as security on his stepfather's debt. She has a good time. So should the reader, in a way that makes them feel slightly bad. **Voice.** Flat, colloquial, digressive. Ruth talks the way a woman talks who has told this to nobody: she'll spend forty words on why she won't buy store-brand cheddar and eight words on a man dying. Sentence length varies hard — long comma-spliced runs when she's angry or bored, three-word lines when it matters. Trade vocabulary used and never explained: *the material*, *warm work*, *cold work*, *the blue drums*. Wit is not rationed or placed; it comes out sideways, in grief, mid-gore, about nothing. She is unbothered by corpses and furious about a scuffed floor. **Things I'm building the story on.** - *Underestimation as plot mechanic, not just flavor.* She gets stopped by police in Chapter 5 and walks because she is a fat old woman with a church bulletin in her purse. That's the thesis, dramatized. - *No atonement architecture.* She doesn't sit for kids as penance. She likes children, always has, and the money's off the books. Her past and her present do not explain each other. She'll say so. - *Asymmetry.* The middle of the book is not a scavenger hunt. She learns where the boy is at the end of Chapter 4 and then can't get to him, which is worse. Claudette is a dead end that costs her two fingers and a day and gives her almost nothing. Dustin dies pointlessly. One of the four men is never accounted for — mentioned once, dropped. - *Ugliness that commits.* The adults are rendered with specificity, smell, absurdity, no flinching. The one thing I hold back is the child from her old work — and I hold it back by describing the banal adjacent details in flat detail with no comment, not by announcing my own tact. - *Dupree remembers her.* Warmly. Calls her Ruthie, asks about her hip, offers her a job. That's worse than being forgotten. Said once, underplayed, never repeated. - *The oven does not kill him.* The gas is off — he's behind on the bill. He dies of something small and stupid. The retort is for afterward, mentioned in passing, which is more horrifying. **Prose rules.** Real weather (ninety-some degrees, wet, all week). Real commerce — Sonic, Family Dollar, a title-loan place with a hand-painted sign, a Hampton Inn breakfast eaten twice. One irrelevant good detail per chapter that pays off nothing. Numbers ugly and inexact; she doesn't know how many jobs, and the number she says is a lie. No thematic annotation — no line where Ruth explains what she represents. **Ending.** Gus goes home. No corkboard flyer, no bow. The last beat is Ruth doing something small with her hands and a piece of dialogue that isn't about anything. The tagline gets spoken — by somebody else, wrongly, admiringly, in a way she finds stupid. **What I refuse.** Gun-fu. A leather avenger. Grim dutiful sadness as the only permitted register. Every wound paying off. Every object recurring. A clean loop on the inhaler. The graceful arc for the minor characters. Any sentence where the story admires itself. # Chapter Planning **1. Tuesday, and What Was in the Freezer.** Verbena Court, 6:40, ninety-four degrees and wet. Danielle's mascara is wrong; Brett is friendly in the way men are when they've done something. Domesticity that earns its keep: Gus in a plastic triceratops mask he won't remove, shark facts delivered with total authority and partial accuracy, the box of macaroni Ruth won't use because Danielle buys the store brand — a whole digression on cheese. The inhaler on the counter, two puffs at eight, Danielle's fussy instructions. 9:50, the sliding door. Four men, unhurried. Ruth swings a skillet, connects once, and is on the linoleum in nine seconds with a boot on her cheek. Somebody says *she's nobody, leave her.* Somebody laughs. She goes out looking at the underside of a kitchen chair. Wakes at 11:20 alone, bleeding, and the first thing she notices is her own blood on the floor she mopped. **2. Cold Work.** No 911 — she explains why in two sentences of arithmetic about how long questions take. She reads the room instead: no forced entry, alarm off, code used, Brett's suitcase gone from the closet, the freezer door standing open because one of them wanted a popsicle. She catalogs the men flatly: a jaw she'd know, a smoker's cough, work boots too new. The van she saw parked at seven and dismissed. Her trade comes in sideways, as complaint — heat makes lye go fast, the blue drums cost more now. She says she did nine jobs. She's lying and doesn't say which way. Danielle comes home, and instead of dignity gives us venom: she blames Ruth, she says *what did you do*, she knew about the debt. Ruth drives to a storage unit in Coldwater. Digs the kit out from under the false floor. Ends on the humidity ruining the coveralls' plastic. **3. Dustin's Mother's Kitchen.** The van plate gets her a name. Twenty-two, lives at home, works the tow yard on Halsey. Ruth comes at eleven in the morning with a Corningware dish because she hasn't eaten in a day and a half, and she eats it in front of him while explaining, in the tone of a woman describing a recipe, what she does to material. Horror through household politeness. He gives her two things — a woman called Claudette who *sets the price*, and the fact that the boy is somewhere with a chapel. He also gives her something useless: there were five men, not four, and he doesn't know the fifth. She takes his phone, tells him to answer when she calls, and leaves the dish. A dog follows her car to the end of the street. **4. The Extended Stay.** Brett at a motel off the interstate with the suitcase and a woman named Sherri who is watching a home-renovation show. Ruth goes in as housekeeping and nobody looks at her. Brett's self-pity in full: the debt, the sports book, then worse people, *it's collateral, it's temporary, Danielle doesn't understand business.* He says *he's not even my kid* and that's the end of the conversation. It's small and short and there's no speech. Then the after — the practical, unhurried competence, the shower curtain, the towels, Sherri sitting very still on the bed and Ruth telling her to go home and Sherri asking, absurdly, if she should take the ice bucket. On Brett's phone: a proof-of-life photo. Gus in the mask on a folding chair in front of a burgundy curtain. Ruth knows that curtain. She hung that curtain's twin in 2011. She sits down on the end of the bed. **5. Two Fingers.** Claudette Reneau, nails and problems, back of a strip mall. Two professional women of an age talking about Discover cards and knee replacements while both know exactly what's happening. It goes wrong fast — Claudette's armed, there's a nephew in the back, and Ruth loses: two fingers broken in a door frame, a scalp split, acetone burn up her forearm. She wins ugly with a UV lamp and drain cleaner and a foot basin, and it takes too long, and it stinks. Claudette dies without a good line, mid-sentence, annoyed. And she gives Ruth almost nothing — a dead end. Driving away, Ruth gets pulled over doing forty in a thirty with blood in her hair, and the deputy sees a heavy old woman with a church bulletin on the passenger seat and lets her off with a warning about the heat. **6. Nine, or However Many.** Short chapter. Four a.m., parked across from Dupree & Sons. What Lyle Dupree was to her: found her cleaning houses, taught her the chemistry, paid cash and gave hams at Christmas, remembered her birthday. The one she won't talk about comes in as inventory — the weight, the tarp, the brand of the gloves, that she was worried about her car's suspension the whole drive, that she stopped at a Sonic afterward and ate. No comment on any of it. Then: why she quit — her hands went numb from the fumes, and her back. That's all. The moral reason she gives people came later and is decoration. Then the practical turn: she wrote the protocol for that building. She knows the door with no camera, because she told him to move it. Viewing Room B. She calls Dustin and tells him to bring the truck. **7. Dupree & Sons.** Morning funeral, a real one, mourners in the lot, and Ruth in a black dress with two fingers taped walks in the side door like family. Three men inside. She takes the first with drain cleaner in a spray bottle and the second with a scalpel from the prep room and the third nearly takes her — the fight in the casket showroom is close and stupid and she wins by falling on him. Dustin comes in to help, which nobody asked for, and is shot dead in the hallway by the third man before Ruth finishes him. Two sentences on it. She finds Gus in Viewing Room B: still masked, wheezing bad, and she gives him the inhaler she's carried since Tuesday and it's nearly empty and gives him one weak puff. Then Dupree on the stairs in a good suit: *Ruthie. My God. How's the hip?* And he offers her work. **8. The Gas Is Off.** Gus into the truck with instructions to count sharks and not look. Back inside. Dupree in the retort room, reasonable, generous, offering the debt cleared and a percentage and *you were always the best I had.* Ruth asks him to name the boy. He tries. He gets a letter wrong. She kills him with a folding chair and her hands and it takes longer than it should because of her fingers, and it is not dignified for either of them. She goes to fire the retort and the gas is off — he's ninety days behind — and she stands there for a second with the striker in her hand and then says something short and disgusted and leaves him where he is. Coda: Gus handed over in a Family Dollar parking lot; the inhaler pressed into Danielle's hand with instructions about the two puffs at eight, Danielle not saying thank you. On the news three days later a sheriff's deputy says the words *whoever did this messed with the wrong babysitter*, admiringly, and gets almost everything else wrong. Ruth is in a motel with her fingers in the ice bucket, and the last thing in the story is her rinsing out a coffee pot and something Gus said about hammerhead sharks that isn't about anything at all.

Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Ruth Salazar **Background.** Born in Bastrop, moved twice before she was ten, raised mostly by an aunt who ran a boarding house and taught her that a stain is a moral failing. Married at nineteen to a man named Cesar who drove a bread truck and drank; he left in '89 and she has no idea if he's alive. No children, and no story about why not — it didn't happen, she didn't chase it, she does not consider this a wound and gets short with people who assume it is. Cleaned houses and motel rooms for eleven years. In 1997 a funeral director named Lyle Dupree watched her get a rust ring out of a marble sill and offered her a different kind of work, and she took it because it paid four times as much and because she was curious, which is the part she doesn't say. She did that work for a long time — she says nine jobs, and that's a lie in a direction she keeps to herself. Quit around 2015 when her hands started going numb from the fumes and her lower back stopped forgiving her. Has sat for children ever since. Cash. No paperwork, no background check, and nobody has ever once asked for one, which she finds instructive. **Personality.** Practical to the point of rudeness. Enormous patience with children and almost none with adults. Not grim — she's actually pretty good company, in the way of a woman who's seen everything and finds most of it dull. Her humor is dry and comes out at wrong moments, usually when she's tired. She has a genuine, uncomplicated affection for kids: their logic, their negotiating, the way they lie badly. She does not think of herself as a bad person, and she doesn't think of herself as a good one either; she thinks in terms of whether a job was done properly. **Idiosyncrasies.** Will not buy store-brand cheese and has a whole argument prepared about the moisture content. Keeps butterscotch candies in her purse, the hard ones in the yellow wrappers, and eats four or five a day. Reading glasses on a beaded chain, one of the beads replaced with a different color because she lost the original. Mops floors in houses she's sitting in, unasked, because she can't sit still and because a clean floor is one of the few things in life that stays fixed for a while. Says "warm work" and "cold work" and has never explained either to a living soul. Hates a scuffed floor more than she hates most people. Eats standing up. Drives a 2004 Buick LeSabre, beige, with a coffee stain on the passenger seat shaped, she thinks, like Ohio. **Flaws.** Vain about her competence; being underestimated pleases her so much that she sometimes lets it happen when she shouldn't. Sentimental in ways she'd deny — she keeps a boy's inhaler in her purse for a week. Slow to anger and then not proportionate. Lies casually and constantly about small things, out of habit rather than need. Physically she's fifty-six and it costs her; she plans around her body the way you plan around bad weather, and she resents having to. **Physicality.** Five-four, heavy through the hips and upper arms, strong hands with short nails. Gray coming in at the roots in a stripe she doesn't dye anymore. Moves slowly, plants her feet, breathes through her nose. Wears cotton blouses with small prints, elastic-waist slacks, white sneakers. Sits down whenever there is a chair. Doesn't gesture much. When she's paying attention her face does nothing at all, which people read as slowness. **Motives and allegiances.** She wants the boy back. That's the whole of it and she'd be annoyed if you looked for more. Not guilt, not redemption — a boy was in her care, and men took him off her kitchen floor, and that is a thing that will not stand. Secondarily and privately, she wants Lyle Dupree to look at her. Allegiances: Gus. Nobody else. Not Danielle, whom she has never liked. Not Dustin, whom she uses. She has no friends and doesn't feel the absence. **Voice.** > "They left me because I was nothing. Fat old woman on a kitchen floor. I want to be clear that I'm not offended. It's a reasonable read. I've made a living off it." > "Danielle buys the store brand and then wonders why the sauce breaks. It's the moisture. There's more water in it and it doesn't melt, it *sweats*, and then you've got a pan of orange soup and a child who won't eat, and you've done all that work for nothing. I brought my own. I always bring my own." > "I did nine jobs for that man. That's what I say. Nine is a number people can hold." --- # Gus Pilcher **Background.** Seven. Second grade, going into third, at Ridgeview Elementary. Lives with his mother Danielle and his stepfather Brett in a three-bedroom on Verbena Court. His father is somewhere in Oklahoma and calls at Christmas. Mild asthma, worse in the heat, worse when he cries. Ruth has sat for him nineteen or twenty times over two years and he has never once said her name out loud to her face, though she's heard him say it to other people. **Personality.** Serious. Authoritative about a small number of subjects and completely uninterested in everything else. Sharks, mainly — he has a book, and he recites from it with total confidence and about seventy percent accuracy, and Ruth has never corrected him. Not a cuddly child. A negotiator. Will trade for anything. Cries silently, which is worse. **Idiosyncrasies.** Wears a plastic triceratops mask, from a Halloween he liked, indoors, for hours, and breathes wetly inside it. Won't eat anything orange, which makes macaroni a diplomatic problem they've solved by calling it yellow. Keeps a folded piece of paper in his sock with a list on it; won't say what the list is. Says "actually" at the start of most sentences. **Physicality.** Small for his age, thin wrists, a bowl of dark hair he hates having cut. Round belly. Breathes through his mouth. Sits on the floor rather than furniture. When he's scared he goes completely still and stops blinking. **Motives.** In the first chapter: to stay up past nine and to be believed about sharks. Later: to not be in the room he's in. He doesn't cry for his mother. He asks, twice, whether Ruth is coming, which is the detail that will do the most damage to a reader. **Voice.** > "Actually a hammerhead can't stop swimming or it dies. That's why they don't have them at the aquarium in Dallas. They died." > "You said eight o'clock but the microwave says eight-oh-one, so." --- # Danielle Pilcher **Background.** Thirty-four. Works front desk at a dental practice in a strip center by the highway. Married Brett three years ago after eight months; he had a truck and a manner and a plan involving flipping houses. She knew about the debt in April. She did not know it had been offered against her son, and she also did not ask very many questions, and both of those things are true at once. **Personality.** Anxious and self-dramatizing. Talks over people. Leaves instructions in three places for the same task. She is not a monster and she is not sympathetic; she is a woman who has been managing something she can't manage for a year and has run out of anything but blame. When she comes home to a broken door and no child, she does not fall to her knees — she turns on Ruth, immediately, with real hatred, because Ruth is standing there and available. **Idiosyncrasies.** Vapes strawberry. Buys store-brand everything and is proud of it. Keeps a laminated allergy card on the fridge for allergies Gus does not have. Says "I'm not being funny, but." Calls Ruth "Miss Ruth" in front of Gus and "the sitter" in front of everyone else. **Physicality.** Thin, tanned in a spray-on way, long acrylics that click. Wears her work polo to leave the house. Cries with her whole face and it goes away fast. Grips her phone in both hands like a hymnal. **Motives.** Wants her son back and wants none of this to be her fault, in roughly that order but not always. At the end she takes Gus and does not thank Ruth, and she will spend the rest of her life telling a version of this in which she did something. **Voice.** > "What did you *do*. I'm not being funny but you were here, you were *right here*, and you're telling me four men walked in and you what? You *fell down*?" > "He has two puffs at eight, I put it in a text, I put it on the fridge, I don't know how many ways I can put it." --- # Brett Kessler **Background.** Forty-one. Was a decent framer once, then got into buying at auction and selling at a loss and calling it a market correction. Went down two hundred and something thousand — sports book first, then a man who took over the sports book's debt and was less flexible. Offered what he had, and what he had was a house in his wife's name and a boy who wasn't his. Told himself it was a two-week thing. **Personality.** Affable, weak, and mean underneath in a lazy way. A man who talks about respect a great deal. Genuinely believes he's the one in a difficult position. Self-pity is his native language; he'll be explaining his own predicament while a woman stands in his motel room holding a bag. **Idiosyncrasies.** Wears sunglasses on the back of his head. Says "at the end of the day." Keeps his shoes very white. Chews the inside of his cheek. Has a Bible in the truck he has never opened, gifted at a men's breakfast. **Physicality.** Big-framed, gone soft, tan line at the bicep. Handshake like a demonstration. Won't hold eye contact with women he's wronged; talks to a spot near their collarbone. **Motives.** Wants to not be killed, wants to be understood, wants Sherri to see him handle this. Allegiance to himself, and after that to whoever he owes money to. **Voice.** > "You don't know what these people are like, Ruth. I did the only — at the end of the day I did the only thing there was. It's collateral. It's *paperwork*, is what it is." > "He's not even my kid." --- # Dustin Krebs **Background.** Twenty-two. Lives with his mother in a house that smells like carpet powder and cigarettes. Drives a wrecker for a yard on Halsey. Got pulled into this because a guy he plays basketball with needed a driver for a night and it paid six hundred dollars. Sat in the van the whole time and heard a skillet hit somebody and then everyone laughing. **Personality.** Not bright, not cruel, deeply agreeable. The kind of young man who says yes to things because saying no requires a follow-up sentence. Ashamed in a shapeless way. Wants very badly for someone to tell him it's fine. **Idiosyncrasies.** Vapes, apologizes for vaping. Keeps a Gatorade bottle of tobacco spit in the cupholder. Calls Ruth "ma'am" throughout, including while she is describing what a drum of lye does. Has a tattoo of his mother's initials done by a friend, slightly crooked. **Physicality.** Tall, no shoulders, sunburned neck. Hunches. Hands never still. Wears cutoff sleeves and a cap with the brim flat. **Motives.** Survival, then absolution. He comes into the funeral home in Chapter 7 without being asked because he's decided this is the thing that makes him not a bad person, and it gets him shot in a hallway, and Ruth gives it two sentences. **Voice.** > "I didn't go inside, ma'am. I want you to know that. I sat in the van the whole time. I had the radio off, even." > "Is that — is that so it goes faster? The heat?" --- # Claudette Reneau **Background.** Fifty-nine. Owns Claudette's Nails & Spa in a strip center between a vape shop and a closed Payless. Twenty-two years of legitimate pedicures and about fifteen of arranging things for people who can't arrange them themselves — she doesn't do anything, she *knows who does*, and she takes a percentage for the phone call. Her nephew Marcus sits in the back and does nothing useful. **Personality.** Warm, chatty, businesslike, entirely without conscience in a way she'd find rude to name. Talks to Ruth about her knee replacement and her sister in Beaumont while both of them know. Not afraid of much. Reads Ruth correctly as a professional and incorrectly as a professional who can be negotiated with. **Idiosyncrasies.** Wears reading glasses pushed up into her hair. Keeps a .380 in a drawer under the acetone. Takes Discover, and mentions it. Refers to every client, including Ruth, as "baby." **Physicality.** Bird-boned, immaculate, hair set weekly. Fast hands. One knee that clicks and a way of talking about it. **Motives.** Money and continuity. She'd give Ruth the name if the price were right; she gives her almost nothing because she doesn't get the chance, and she dies mid-sentence sounding annoyed. **Voice.** > "Baby, sit down, you're dripping on my floor. Now — do you want the deluxe? The deluxe has the paraffin." > "I don't *do* anything. I know a number. There's a difference, and the difference is what I charge for." --- # Lyle Dupree **Background.** Seventy-one. Dupree & Sons, third generation, no sons. Buried three-quarters of the county at some point. Found Ruth in 1997 and taught her the chemistry himself, patiently, over months, like a man teaching a niece to drive. Ninety days behind on the gas bill because the business has been dying for a decade and he has been solving that problem the way he solves problems. **Personality.** Courtly. Genuinely, awfully kind in manner. Remembers birthdays, sends cards, asks after your hip and means it. Has never once thought of himself as anything but a service provider to a community. Does not experience the two halves of his business as different. The horror of him is that he is not cold — he is fond of Ruth, delighted to see her, and offering her a job while standing in a room where a child was kept. **Idiosyncrasies.** Good suits, poorly pressed lately. Peppermints in a dish, and a bowl of them at the front desk, and he offers you one at bad times. Calls women of a certain age by diminutives — Ruthie, Dottie, Bev. Keeps a framed photo of a Little League team he sponsored in 1988. Hums hymns without knowing he's doing it. **Physicality.** Tall, stooped, liver spots on the backs of his hands, a tremor he covers by holding things. Moves at the speed of a man who has never had to hurry. Takes your elbow when he talks to you. **Motives.** Continuity of the business. Debt collection as a service line. Wants Ruth back on the payroll and cannot understand, right up to the folding chair, why the conversation isn't going well. He can't name the boy from the job she asks about. He tries. He gets a letter wrong. **Voice.** > "Ruthie. My *God*. Look at you. How's the hip — did you have it done? You said you were going to have it done." > "Have a peppermint. Now listen to me, because you're upset, and I understand. Sit down and let's talk about what you need. You always did good work for me. Careful work. There's nobody left who's careful."

# 1. Tuesday, and What Was in the Freezer Ninety-four degrees at twenty to seven and wet enough that the driveway steamed. I parked at the curb because Danielle doesn't like anybody in the drive but Brett, and I carried my own bag of groceries up the walk, which I do, because I've been in that kitchen and I know what's in it. Danielle opened the door with her mascara wrong. Not smeared. Wrong — one eye done and the other not, like she'd started and quit and then decided nobody would look. She had her work polo on to go to dinner. "Miss Ruth," she said. "Okay. So." Then the instructions. Danielle gives instructions like a woman leaving a child with a stranger for a year. Two puffs at eight, it's on the fridge, I put it in a text, the number's on the fridge too, there's a laminated card about his allergies and Gus has no allergies, I have never once seen that boy react to anything but the color orange. She said it all fast with her phone gripped in both hands and her thumbnails clicking on the case. Brett came out of the back hall with his sunglasses on the back of his head. He said, "Hey, Ruth," in that big warm way, and he shook my hand like he was showing somebody how it was done, and he looked at a spot about four inches under my chin the whole time. I've cleaned motel rooms. I know what a man looks like when he's already done the thing and is waiting on the consequence. I remember thinking: he's cheating on her. That's all I thought. I put it away and thought about the macaroni. They went out and the AC unit knocked and I had the house. Gus was on the living room floor in his mask. It's a triceratops, hard plastic, from a Halloween two years ago, and he wears it indoors for hours at a time and breathes wetly inside it and you can hear it from the next room. He didn't say hello. He has never said my name to my face, not once in two years, though I've heard him say it to his mother — *is Ruth coming* — which is worth more to me than hello. "Actually," he said, "a hammerhead can't stop swimming or it dies. That's why they don't have them at the aquarium in Dallas. They died." "They died." "All of them," he said, with real satisfaction. He has a book. He recites out of it with total authority and about seventy percent accuracy and I have never corrected him one time in his life. Correcting a child on sharks is a thing people do because they can't stand to be quiet. I made the macaroni. I brought my own because Danielle buys the store brand and I will not have it. It's the moisture. There's more water in the cheap block and it doesn't melt, it *sweats*, and you stand there stirring and what you get is a pan of orange soup and a child who won't eat it and you've done all that work for nothing. I bring a wedge of the sharp and I grate it myself. It takes four extra minutes. Four minutes. Orange is a problem in that house. Gus won't eat anything orange. So a long time ago we agreed the macaroni was yellow, and it is, if you don't put paprika in it, and I don't. He ate it at the coffee table with the mask pushed up on his forehead. He told me about a shark that lives four hundred years. He told me a great white has to be born already knowing how to hunt because its mother leaves. He said, "Actually that's sad but it's not sad because they don't know." At eight I said inhaler and he said the microwave says eight-oh-one, so, and I said so nothing, and he took his two puffs standing up with his eyes closed, holding it wrong the way he does, and I fixed his fingers on it the way I do, and he shook me off the way he does. Then he put it on the counter next to the paper towels, where it lives. I mopped the kitchen. I do that. Nobody asks me to and I don't tell them. I can't sit in a dirty room, and there's the other thing, which is that a clean floor is one of the very few things in this life that stays fixed for a while. Twenty minutes, and it was mine, and it shone. At nine he negotiated for nine-thirty and got nine-fifteen because he'd already gotten nine-fifteen the last two times and I like a child to learn the shape of a deal. He went down hard. Kids in this heat go down like something falling off a shelf. I got the freezer open at about nine-forty because I wanted the last of the ice cream sandwiches and I stood there in the cold with the door on my shoulder and I ate one over the sink. The sliding door came at ten of ten. Not fast. That's what I want you to understand about it. There was no crash. There was the sound of the track, which sticks and always has, and then a man's shoe on the tile, and then three more men, and none of them hurried. Four men walking into a lit kitchen at ten o'clock like they were coming to look at a water heater. I had the skillet in the dish rack. Cast iron, twelve inch, Danielle's mother's. It's a mild thing, Danielle makes a whole — she has a card on the refrigerator about allergies he doesn't have, you know this, you've seen the card." "Two puffs at eight." "He's fine." He was chewing the inside of his cheek. "You don't know what these people are like. You have no idea what I have been walking around with since April. "What?" "They put the code in. Nobody broke a window." He looked at the spot four inches below my chin, the way he does. You take the whole rod, you don't fool with the rings. I put the towels down first and then the curtain over him and I rolled him toward me and back, which is the whole trick of it, and I taped the ends and I taped the middle and I used the bedspread for the second layer because a bedspread from a place like that is essentially a tarp with a pattern on it. It took eighteen minutes. My back was ugly about it. I sat down on the end of the second bed to rest and I could hear the ice machine cycling out on the walkway. Sherri said, "Am I—" "Go home." She stood up and she picked up her purse and she got as far as the door and then she turned around and said, in a perfectly normal voice, the voice you'd use at a checkout, "Should I take the ice bucket? I filled it." I said, "Leave it." "Okay," she said, and left. His phone was on the nightstand, face down, and it wanted a code, and the code was Danielle's birthday, which I know because it's the same four numbers as the alarm. Nineteen messages from a number with no name. The last one was Tuesday at 11:52 p.m., which was thirty-two minutes after they had him, and it was a photograph. Gus on a folding chair. Dupree & Sons is a corner building on Hollis Avenue with a portico and a paved lot and a bay at the back where the coaches come in, and the front is glass, and there is a man in that building around the clock because that is the nature of the business — people die at three in the morning and somebody has to answer the phone. I had five rounds in a revolver with rust on it and a broken cheekbone and a back that had just quit on me over eighteen minutes of a shower curtain. You do not walk into a building you don't know at two in the morning. You go when there's a reason for you to be there, and in that trade there is one reason and it happens on a schedule, and the obituaries in the *Herald* said Duplessis, visitation Friday 9 a.m. So I had Thursday to spend, and I spent it on Claudette, because she sets the price and I wanted to know what the price was. Claudette's Nails & Spa sat in a strip center on Fondren between a vape shop and a Payless that had been closed so long the sign had ghosts on the brick. I went in at eight minutes to seven, which is closing, with my purse on my arm. Little bird of a woman, fifty-nine or sixty, immaculate, hair set. Reading glasses pushed up in it. "Baby, we're closing," she said, and then she looked up and got the whole of me — the cheek, the makeup two shades wrong over the cheek, the sneakers — and she did not stop wiping. "Well. "The deluxe has the paraffin. On you I'd say do the paraffin, your hands are—" she flicked two fingers at them. "You've had them in something." "Bleach." "Mm." There was a young man in the back. I could hear a phone game going, that little coin sound, over and over. "That's Marcus," she said. "He doesn't do anything. My sister's." "I'm here about the price on a boy on Verbena Court." The coin sound stopped. Claudette put the rag over the edge of the basin and squared it. Then she came and sat down in the technician's stool in front of me and crossed her ankles, and she had a face on her like a woman about to talk you out of a color that won't suit you. "I don't *do* anything," she said. "That's what people never get. I know a number. Somebody's got a problem, they call, and I say what it's worth, and I call a number. That's the whole enterprise. The difference between doing a thing and knowing a number is the difference, and the difference is what I charge for." "What was it worth." "Baby, I'm not going to—" "Fifteen? Twenty?" "Ten," she said, and then she was annoyed at herself for the first time, a little tightening around the mouth, because that was free and she doesn't give things free. "Ten to move him and hold him, and the holding was somebody else's building, so it was really eight." "Eight." "For a week. Do you know what my knee cost me? Do you have any idea what a knee is now? Sixty-one hundred out of pocket and they *gave* me the walker." She shifted, and the knee clicked, and she said, "There. You hear that? Twelve thousand dollars and it clicks." "I want the name of the building." "No." "Claudette." "No, baby." Very kind. Genuinely kind. "You seem like a person who's done real work. I can tell. And if I sold that, I wouldn't be able to sit in this chair, and I intend to sit in this chair another six years and then go to Beaumont, and my sister's got a room over the garage." Then she said, "Marcus," in a completely different voice, and stood up. I got out of the pedicure chair, which takes a second, which is the whole story of being fifty-six, and she went for the drawer under the acetone shelf and got it open, and she had a little pistol in it, and she had it in her hand before I was all the way up. Marcus came through the curtain and he was twenty-five and heavy and had a phone in his left hand still, and he got a fistful of my blouse and drove me back into the door frame between the front and the back, and my hand was on the jamb and he shouldered the door and the door took two of my fingers, the middle and the ring, and I heard them. I want to be plain. It hurt so much that I made a sound I have not made in my life. There was a bottle of acetone on the shelf at my shoulder, the gallon, and I got it with the good hand and I got the cap off with my teeth and put it in his face, all of it, and he let go of me and put his hands up to his eyes and started screaming. She didn't say anything good. That's what I remember. She got out, "Wait, no, listen, I can call—" and then it went into the throat and the rest of it wasn't words, and her leg kept going for a while against the base of the basin, and I sat down on the floor. Forty-one minutes I sat there. Foot basins on either side of me and the water in one of them still warm and the smell in that room was acetone and drain opener and burnt hair from where it got in the carpet, and it was so thick I had to put my face in my elbow. I taped my fingers together with the medical tape out of my purse, which I keep for other reasons. I did it wrong. They set crooked and they are crooked today. And she gave me nothing. Eight thousand dollars and a knee. I killed two people in a nail salon and I came out of it knowing one number I did not need. He came up on the passenger side and put his light on me, on the cheek and the tape on my fingers and the blood in my hair that I had not seen yet. "Ma'am, do you need medical assistance?" He tapped the roof twice and went back to his car, and I put my hands in my lap until they stopped, and then I drove to a Hampton Inn on the feeder and paid cash and sat on the end of the bed with a bucket of ice against my hand and said his name out loud into that room. Lyle. I hadn't said it in nine years.

Claudette is rendered with real specificity — the knee, the sister in Beaumont, the room over the garage, the genuine warmth that coexists with complete amorality. Two fingers broken in a door frame: check. Scalp split: the blood in her hair is there. Acetone burn: check. UV lamp: check. Drain cleaner: check. Claudette dying mid-sentence, annoyed: check. The deputy with the church bulletin: check. The Hampton Inn, the ice bucket, saying Lyle's name: check. The plan said "she gives Ruth almost nothing — a dead end" and the chapter delivers that with real bitterness: "I killed two people in a nail salon and I came out of it knowing one number I did not need." **Weaknesses** The chapter is not flawless.
