# How a human writer would actually come at this A person who got handed "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" wouldn't start by building a plot. They'd start because the line reminded them of somebody. The line has a specific rhythm — it's the kind of thing you say at a bar, half-laughing, about a man you're still not over. So the human writer's first move is *voice*, and the plot arrives late and grudgingly, mostly as an excuse to keep the two of them in rooms together. That has real consequences for the finished thing. A human-written version of this would probably be **lopsided**. Too much attention on one night that didn't advance anything, a fight remembered in obsessive detail, and then whole weeks of consequential plot dispatched in two sentences because the narrator doesn't want to talk about it. Memory is a bad archivist and a good stylist. It lingers where it shouldn't and skips where it should linger. A human would also let the narrator be **wrong about things**, and not correct him. He'd repeat himself. He'd have a phrase he over-uses because it's his tic, not because the author thought it was a nice motif. He'd contradict himself between chapter two and chapter six and never notice. He'd get petty. He'd say something ungenerous about Rafe's teeth or his laugh and then immediately soften it, which tells you more than any lyrical passage. And a human would probably be *funnier* and *cruder* than the plan suggests. Grief is vulgar. People make bad jokes about the worst things. Noir's whole tonal engine is a wisecrack over a corpse. # General LLM failure modes, and how they'd hurt this piece specifically **1. Thematic hygiene.** LLMs make every element earn its keep. Every object recurs, every motif closes, every character serves a function. The plan already has this disease: the borrowed light, the no-smoking rule, the returned key, the ledger, the lock metaphors — all load-bearing, all paying off. Real writing has junk in it. A detail that's just *there* because the world has stuff in it. The plan's tidiness will read as engineered. **2. The bow.** Even when an LLM writes a "sad ending," it's a *resolved* sad ending — the melancholy is administered in a controlled dose, and the final image tells you how to feel. Chapter 8's coda (Odile paid for and gone west, the ledger repurposed as neighborhood insurance, the key returned, the smell of smoke) is four separate resolutions stacked in about 400 words. It's the literary equivalent of a curtain call where everyone comes back out to bow. **3. Symmetry addiction.** Eight chapters, eight lock names, one motif per chapter, two reveals spaced exactly for maximum effect. Reveals in real narration don't get spaced for effect; they come out when the narrator can finally stand to say them, which is usually too early or way too late. **4. Writing impressively at the sentence level.** "Short declaratives; then one long sentence that gives everything away" is a *formula*, and formulas are audible. Read three chapters of it and you can hear the metronome. The plan's own craft notes describe a machine, not a voice. **5. Competence inflation.** LLM protagonists are good at their jobs and eloquent about their feelings. Emmett hears lies "the way he hears a lock." That's a superpower, and it's also a way of making him too knowing to be moving. A man who can hear the lie and picks it anyway is interesting; a man who genuinely can't tell, who fools himself with embarrassing ease, is human. **6. Emotional articulacy.** Everyone in LLM fiction can name what they feel and say it in a well-formed sentence. Odile "says it plain." Rafe delivers the "I don't know which came first" confession, which is a beautifully calibrated piece of ambiguity — and therefore reads as written. Real people evade, change the subject, get the wrong words out, or say something spiteful instead. **7. Political and moral safety.** The plan is careful — commendably — to avoid bury-your-gays and to locate the violence in the closet and the cops. But that care can become its own flatness: a story where the queer characters are victims of structure and never of each other, where nobody's cruelty is unmotivated, where the author's moral position is legible on every page. 1959 gay men were also petty, racist, classist, and mean to each other. Odile being wronged *only* by Cade is safer and less true than Odile also being wronged by Emmett in a small ugly way he doesn't fully own up to. **8. Uniform texture.** Every chapter the same length, same density, same weather. Rain the whole way is a decision that will feel like set dressing by chapter four. # Deep dive: where this specific plan is likely to go LLM-shaped ## The locksmith Genuinely the best idea in the plan, and also the most dangerous. It's *too* good — a metaphor so neat that even with "ration the metaphor" as a stated aim, the whole architecture is metaphor. The chapter titles are lock terms. The climactic crime is unlocking a door. The narrator's gift is *hearing* things open. There's no rationing possible; the scaffolding is the theme. A reader will feel the diagram. Ways out: make the locksmithing boring and specific most of the time — bad debts, a landlord who wants forty units rekeyed, a kid who broke a key off in a mailbox, Emmett's bursitis. Let the trade be a job before it's a symbol. And consider dropping the lock-term chapter titles entirely; they're the loudest signal that a clever person arranged this. ## Rafe The plan says he must be "lovable and indefensible at once," which is correct and is also the hardest thing in the piece. The risk is the standard LLM bad boy: charming, self-aware, poetically self-destructive, delivering aphorisms. "Tells true things carelessly and lies with total sincerity" is a *description of a character type*, not a person. What would make him human: give him something unglamorous and unromantic. He's cheap. He steals small amounts from Emmett and lies about it badly. He's boring on some subjects and won't shut up. He has a stupid opinion he'll defend for an hour. He's bad in bed in a specific way once. He's *afraid* in a way that isn't beautiful — whining, sweating, blaming. The love has to survive the un-photogenic version of him, or it isn't love, it's an aesthetic. Also: "never carries matches, always borrows a light" is a lovely observation and will die the moment it's used four times as a motif with a payoff. A human would notice it once and never mention it again. ## The betrayal "He came for your hands" is the plan's engine and it's a *construction*. It's the reveal that maximally complicates the romance, which is exactly why it smells designed. And Rafe's response — "I honestly don't know which came first" — is the most emotionally intelligent possible answer, which no cornered liar has ever given. Human alternative: Emmett has known, dimly, from the start. Chapter one already tells us he could read the wear on the key and cut it anyway. So the "betrayal" isn't information; it's *humiliation* — the moment it's said out loud in front of someone else, or the moment Emmett hears Rafe describing him to a third party in the past tense, as a resource. Overheard, not confessed. That's crueler and truer, and it doesn't require Rafe to become articulate about his own motives. ## Odile Highest tokenism risk in the plan. Sung-at-the-Verandah, knew-him-as-an-apprentice, tells-the-truth, gets-hurt, gets-paid-off-in-the-coda. That is a *function* with a name attached, and the coda where Emmett pays for her ticket west is the single most bow-tied moment in the outline — it's absolution purchased with plot. Better instincts: let her be wrong sometimes. Let her dislike Emmett for reasons that have nothing to do with Rafe — money he owes her, a time he didn't show up, the way he uses her bar as a place to be a version of himself he won't be anywhere else. Let her have her own plot that Emmett is barely paying attention to and that we only glimpse. And critically: don't resolve her. She can end angry, or gone without saying goodbye, or still there in six months with nothing changed. Not paid off. ## The dead mentor and the struck-through name This is identified in the brainstorm as the best idea, and it *is* strong — but it's also very tidy: the protagonist's respectability was secretly purchased, discovered at the exact moment it reframes his final choice. The timing is suspiciously perfect. And it makes the dead man's love legible and posthumously confirmed, which is the sentimental option. More human: Emmett finds the entry and it's *ambiguous*. Maybe Kell paid. Maybe Kell informed, and the strike-through is the reward. Emmett can't tell and never will, and he has to keep working in a shop with the man's name on the door. That's a much worse thing to live with, and it doesn't hand him a reframing on schedule. ## The ending "He leaves alive, which is its own kind of grave" is the right call and a well-worn one. Two tickets, one taken, on a dock — that's the ending of about forty films, and it's fine, but it's *the expected fresh alternative to death*, which is its own cliché now. The stack of codas is the bigger problem. Odile's ticket, the ledger-as-insurance, the returned key, the smoke in an empty room, the prompt line landing as elegy. Five closing gestures. A human writer, actually grieving on the page, would give you *one* and it would be the wrong one — something small and irrelevant. The last line of a real elegy is often anticlimactic on purpose because the speaker has run out of the ability to perform. Also "the ledger as the neighborhood's quiet insurance" gives Emmett dignity, agency, and a moral purpose in his final beat. That's the LLM instinct to leave the protagonist upgraded. What if he just keeps it in the safe and does nothing with it for years, and that's the honest ending — he had the whole city's throat in a drawer and he was too tired and too careful to squeeze? ## The dock scene Piers, ships, a departure — this is where noir goes to be beautiful. Consider whether the leaving should be far less cinematic. A bus. Rafe already gone when Emmett gets there. Or Emmett doesn't go at all, and we get the not-going instead, which is more like how people actually fail to say goodbye. ## Voice "Funny in a bleak register" is stated as an aim but nothing in the plan is actually funny, and there's no room reserved for comedy. If Emmett isn't genuinely funny — not wry-noir-funny, but *mean* and *petty* and occasionally *cheap* funny — the whole thing will be gorgeous and airless. ## Prose risk list - Fragments as emphasis. Constantly. - Tricolons: "the shop, the ledger, the rule about smoking near the brass." - "Not X but Y" constructions. - Body-part-as-subject sentences: "His hands knew before he did." - Weather doing emotional work on cue. - Every chapter ending on a resonant image or a line of dialogue with a click. - Perfectly balanced dialogue where each speaker gets equal, well-formed turns. - Sensory lists in threes (brass filings, graphite, wet wool — already in the plan). # Ideas to make it more human **Structural** - Vary chapter lengths hard: a 1,600-word chapter and a 400-word chapter. One chapter that's almost entirely a single conversation. One that's a list, or a bill of costs. - Let one chapter be about something else entirely — a job Emmett does for a stranger, in obsessive detail, while the plot happens offstage. Avoidance as structure. - Skip the heist's execution. Cut from the plan to the aftermath. The plan currently spends a chapter on the safe job because it's the exciting bit; a narrator who doesn't want to remember it would elide it. - Drop the lock-term titles. Or make them plain and dumb: "March," "The Verandah," "What I Did." **Character** - Give Emmett a small, unforgivable cruelty of his own, unexcused. - Give Rafe a genuinely annoying trait that never becomes charming. - Let Emmett be worse at his job than the plan implies. One failure. A safe he can't open. - Someone should be jealous in a small, undignified way. - Give Rafe a mundane want — a car, a suit, to be someone's favorite — rather than a tragic backstory. - Let Cade be *boring*. Menace that comes from tedium and paperwork rather than presence. He's a man with opinions about his lawn. **Voice** - Let Emmett address someone. Not the reader — a specific unnamed person, maybe a cop, maybe himself, maybe Rafe. It changes every sentence. - Let him lie to us once and get caught out by his own later account. - Repetition as tic, not motif: a phrase he can't stop using. - One paragraph where the prose gets bad because he's upset. Overwritten, or clipped to nothing. - Refuse to describe something. "I'm not going to write down what he said." **Content** - Let the sex be specific and awkward rather than lyrical. - Include a genuinely funny bad joke at the worst moment. - Money in exact amounts. Rent, a cylinder, a ticket, a payoff. - Someone should get a detail *wrong* — a name misremembered, a date Emmett isn't sure about. - Let there be a beat of pure boredom in the middle of the danger. **Ending** - One coda, not five. Pick the smallest. - Consider ending mid-scene, or on a line of dialogue that isn't a summation, or on a piece of trade business. - Leave one major thing unexplained and never come back to it. - Consider not landing the prompt line at the end at all. It's in chapter one; let it stay there.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention ## The core A locksmith remembering the man who used him and whom he loved anyway. The prompt line is a bar-story opening — rueful, half-laughing, not over it — so **voice comes first and plot is the excuse to keep them in rooms together.** The prompt line goes in the first paragraph of Chapter 1 and I will *not* bring it back at the end. Landing it again would be a bow. **Emmett Vance**, thirty-four, owns a lock shop on Water Street in a rainy port city, 1959. He is careful, petty, funny in a mean way, and *not* especially good at reading people — he mistakes wanting for knowing. Crucially: he understood from the first night that Rafe was working him. He cut the key anyway. So there is no "betrayal reveal." What arrives later is **humiliation** — Emmett overhears Rafe describing him to someone else in the past tense, as a resource. Overheard, not confessed. Rafe never explains himself, because cornered liars don't produce beautiful ambiguity. **Rafe Sandoval** is charming and cheap. He borrows money and lies about it badly. He has one long boring opinion about boxing he'll defend all night. He's a coward when it counts and it isn't pretty — sweating, blaming, whining. The love has to survive the unphotogenic version of him or it's just an aesthetic. **Detective Cade** is boring. He has opinions about his lawn and his son's grades. Menace by tedium and paperwork. He is never described as a shark or a wolf. **Odile** sings at the Verandah and does not like Emmett much, for reasons predating Rafe: eleven dollars he owes her, a night he didn't show up, and the way he uses her bar as the only place he'll be himself. She is not paid off, absolved, or resolved. She gets hurt because of this mess and she is still angry about it on the last page. **Sam Kell** is dead before page one, his name still on the door. In the ledger Emmett finds his own 1947 arrest struck through in Kell's handwriting with a figure beside it. **He will never know whether Kell paid to protect him or informed and got paid.** He works under that name for the rest of his life. No reframing on schedule. ## Plot, lightly Rafe wants a key copied that isn't his; the wear pattern tells Emmett so and he says so and cuts it anyway. Rafe needs Cade's safe in the vice annex opened. What's inside isn't money, it's a ledger of payoffs and names — everyone arrested in the bars and everyone who paid not to be. **I am skipping the heist.** Chapter 5 opens after it. A narrator avoiding a memory elides it; also the exciting bit is the least interesting bit. The price gets paid when Emmett unlocks a side door at a particular hour and doesn't ask what's coming through. Rafe leaves alive on a bus, not a ship, and Emmett isn't there to see it off — he gets the not-going instead. He keeps the ledger in his safe and does nothing with it. He had the city's throat in a drawer and was too tired and too careful to squeeze. ## Craft **Chapter titles:** plain and dumb. Months, places, flat statements. No lock terminology — that was the loudest signal of arrangement. **Lengths deliberately uneven.** Roughly: 1000 / 900 / 1200 / 1400 / 600 / 1000 / 1100 / 800. The 600 is the one that hurts. **Emmett tells this to a specific unnamed listener** — someone in a room with him, asking. Occasional "you asked about," "I'll get to it." Never resolved who. **Aiming for:** exact money amounts; the trade as tedium before symbol (bursitis, a landlord wanting forty units rekeyed, a kid with a key snapped off in a mailbox); one paragraph where the prose goes bad because he's upset; one refusal to describe; a phrase he over-uses as tic not motif ("which was fine with me"); a genuinely bad joke at the worst moment; sex that's specific and awkward; a date he gets wrong. **Avoiding:** fragments-for-emphasis, tricolons, "not X but Y," body-parts-as-subject, weather on cue, chapter endings that click shut, balanced dialogue, sensory lists in threes, one motif per chapter with a payoff. Rafe's no-matches habit gets noticed **once**, in Chapter 2, and never again. Rain is not constant; there's a dry stretch that's worse. **One coda, small.** One thing left unexplained forever. **Emmett's own cruelty:** he tells Cade something about Odile's savings to buy himself an afternoon. Small, deliberate, unexcused. He mentions it in passing and does not return to it. # Chapter Planning **1. The Key Wasn't His** (~1000w) Prompt line in the first paragraph, to the unnamed listener. The shop: rekey jobs, the smell, Kell's name on the door, the eleven dollars he owes Odile. Rafe comes in at closing wanting a duplicate; Emmett reads the wear and says *this isn't your key* and cuts it for forty cents. Ends on trade business, not resonance. **2. The Verandah** (~900w) Odile singing badly one night and well the next. She's cold with Emmett for old reasons. Rafe turns up, borrows a light off a stranger (noted once), talks about boxing for twenty minutes. Alley afterward, awkward and specific. Emmett already knows what this is. **3. Forty Units on Halloran Street** (~1200w) Mostly a rekeying job in obsessive detail — the landlord, the cylinders, Emmett's shoulder — while Rafe makes the pitch in pieces across three visits. Cade appears at the Verandah collecting, and he's tedious about his son's report card. Emmett says no. The no doesn't hold and he doesn't pretend otherwise. **4. March, or April** (~1400w) The good weeks. Dry weather, which he says was worse. Rafe in the shop after hours, learning to listen to a lock and being bad at it. Money missing from the register, twice, and the lie about it. Emmett gives him a key. Somewhere in here, the eleven dollars still unpaid, and the afternoon he buys from Cade with Odile's business. He mentions it and moves on. **5. After** (~600w) Post-heist. The ledger on the workbench, unread. What he ate. What Rafe wouldn't stop saying. Flat, short, refuses to describe the annex at all. **6. What I Heard Through a Door** (~1000w) Overhears Rafe pitching a third party, describing Emmett past-tense as the man with the hands. No confrontation scene; Emmett walks. Odile's room turned over, her savings gone, her wrist broken. She blames him accurately and won't take his money. **7. Kell's Handwriting** (~1100w) He finally reads the ledger. His own name, 1947, struck through, a figure, Kell's hand. Both readings available; neither closed. Rafe surfaces cowardly and sweating, out of moves, asking. The prose goes bad here for a paragraph. Emmett agrees to the side door and doesn't ask. **8. Water Street** (~800w) The door, told at a distance and briefly. He doesn't go to the bus. What he did instead. The bad joke, to nobody. Coda months later: one small object, one unexplained thing, the ledger in the safe untouched, Odile still angry. No return to the prompt line. Ends mid-thought on something trivial.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Emmett Vance **Background.** Born 1925 in this city, in the flats below the reservoir. His father drove a delivery truck for a bakery and died of a heart attack at forty-six while parked, which Emmett considers a very Vance way to go. His mother remarried a man named Hollis and moved to Spokane in 1950; they exchange Christmas cards with almost nothing written in them. Emmett went into the Navy in '43, spent the war in San Diego doing supply inventory, and came back with the useful knowledge that he could live a long time on very little conversation. He apprenticed with Sam Kell in 1946 because the shop was hiring and it was indoors. He turned out to have hands for it. In 1947 he was arrested outside a bar called the Bantam with eleven other men, held two nights, and released without charges. Nobody at the shop ever mentioned it. Kell died in 1956 of something in his stomach, and left Emmett the business, the tools, and a debt of $1,900 to a man named Tomich that Emmett paid off over nineteen months. **Personality.** Careful in a way that has curdled slightly. He balances his books every Friday and enjoys it. He is not the noble reticent type — he's *stingy*, and he knows it, and he makes jokes about it to get ahead of other people making them. He owes Odile eleven dollars from November and has had the eleven dollars in his pocket on four separate occasions. His real flaw isn't repression, it's that he mistakes wanting something for understanding it. He believes he's a good reader of people because he's a good reader of locks, and those are not the same skill, and it takes him the whole story to notice. He knew Rafe was working him from the first ten minutes. He mistook knowing for control. He is funny, but meanly — his humor is mostly at other people's expense and occasionally at his own, and it's a defense he deploys about four seconds too early. **Idiosyncrasies.** He says "which was fine with me" constantly, including about things that were not fine with him. He won't let anyone smoke within six feet of the brass stock, then smoked next to it himself the night Rafe first came in and hasn't mentioned that to anyone. He eats the same lunch — a fried egg sandwich from Krebs' counter, thirty cents — five days a week and can tell you when they changed suppliers. His left shoulder aches when he works overhead; he calls it bursitis, a doctor has never called it anything. He keeps a jar of failed keys, about sixty of them, and he can tell you what each one was for. He is bad at one thing professionally and mentions it once: he has never gotten the hang of certain German import safes, and he refers jobs on them out to a man in Tacoma and charges a finder's fee. It embarrasses him. **Physicality.** Five-nine, thickening through the middle, dark hair going back at the temples. Hands stained at the fingertips with graphite that doesn't come out; a permanent nick in his left thumbnail. He stands very still when he's frightened, which reads to most people as composure. He wears a grey cardigan in the shop with two pens in the pocket and a good brown suit that's five years old and he keeps it good by not wearing it. His voice is quiet enough that people lean in, which he learned to use. **Motives.** He wants, more than anything and unglamorously, to not be found out — not for moral reasons but because he has a business with his name on it and a mortgage of $58 a month. Underneath that he wants somebody in the shop after hours. He would not have phrased it that way. **Allegiances.** To Kell's memory, complicatedly. To the Verandah as a place, not to the people in it, which is his sin. To Rafe, entirely and stupidly, and then afterward still. **Voice.** > "He asked did I ever get lonely, sitting in here with the door locked. I told him I get about the right amount." > "You want to know what I thought when I saw the wear on that key. I thought: this man is going to cost me money. I want that on the record. I wasn't fooled for one minute, and I've had eleven years to be proud of that, and it hasn't done a thing for me." --- # Rafe Sandoval **Background.** Twenty-nine, from somewhere down the coast he's vague about — he's said Eureka and he's said Vallejo. Middle of five children, and the only detail he ever gave that Emmett believed completely was that his mother made him take a scholarship exam for a Catholic school and he deliberately failed it, and she didn't speak to him for a month, and he thought that was funny. He came north in '54. He's been a bellman, a driver for a florist, and a collector for a man who lent money out of a barber shop on Grand. He got into blackmail sideways: he was fetching for the barber-shop man, saw how the vice-squad money moved, and decided he was smarter than the people doing it. He isn't. He's currently working for, and afraid of, a man he never names, and he owes that man something like $600. **Personality.** Charming and cheap. Those aren't in tension for him. He'll buy a round for six people with money he took out of Emmett's register and won't understand why that's two separate facts. He lies constantly and *badly* — not elaborate fabrications, just small immediate lies to get past the next thirty seconds, and he'll contradict himself in the same evening and be genuinely irritated when it's pointed out. He has one long boring passion: boxing, specifically the argument that Marciano only looked good because of who he was matched against, which he will defend for an hour and a half with the same four examples. It is not charming. People leave the table. His flaw isn't self-destruction; it's that he's a coward and hasn't accepted it. He thinks of himself as a man who takes risks, and he does, right up until something goes wrong, at which point he sweats through his shirt and starts assigning blame out loud. Emmett has seen this twice and loved him both times. **Idiosyncrasies.** He never carries matches — always borrows a light, off strangers, and makes it a small event. He calls everyone "chief," including women. He can't sit still in a chair; he sits sideways, one leg over the arm, and Emmett has two chairs with loosened joints because of it. He whistles two bars of something and stops. He's fastidious about his shoes — polishes them nightly, owns two pairs and one of them cost more than his coat. **Physicality.** Tall and thin in a way that looks fed on cigarettes and nerve. Very black hair he keeps too long for the year. A nose broken and set badly, which he tells people happened in a fight and which happened when he was nine. He touches people constantly while talking — forearm, shoulder, back of the neck — a habit that is not sexual and reads that way, and he knows it does. He laughs with his head back and his mouth open, no sound for the first second. **Motives.** He wants a car. Specifically a used '56 Chrysler he saw in a lot on Fenner, and he brings it up maybe nine times. He wants to be somebody's favorite. He wants to stop being afraid of the man he owes, and he has confused that want with a plan. **Allegiances.** To himself, but not competently. To Emmett, actually, in a way he can't manage — he did come for the hands, and it did stop being only that, and he wouldn't be able to tell you when, and he never once tries to explain it, because he doesn't have the equipment. **Voice.** > "Chief, you're going to like this, because it's easy, and I know you don't like anything unless it's easy." > "I never said Tuesday. Why would I say Tuesday. Somebody told you Tuesday, that's on them." > "You've got the only pair of hands in this town that can do it and you're standing there telling me about your shoulder." --- # Odile Grange **Background.** Forty-one. Sings at the Verandah Wednesday through Sunday and has since 1951, and books the acts, and does the ordering, and is not the owner, which is a sentence she has said in exactly that order many times. Born in Vancouver, Washington. Married at nineteen to a bandleader named Arthur who was a good man and left her the way good men do — slowly and while apologizing. She has $1,340 saved in a Chase & Sanborn coffee tin behind a loose board, toward a room in San Francisco and a season of work she's been promised by someone she doesn't fully trust. **Personality.** Practical to the point of unkindness. She has no patience for men who use the Verandah as a place to be themselves for four hours and then walk out onto Water Street as somebody's respectable neighbor — and Emmett is exactly that man, and she has told him so, once, in 1957, and neither of them has forgotten it. She's not the wise mouthpiece; she's frequently wrong, she holds petty grudges, and she thinks Rafe is a bore, which she is right about. She sings badly when she's tired or angry and doesn't apologize for it. She sings genuinely well maybe two nights out of five. **Idiosyncrasies.** Keeps a running tab of small money owed to her by about nine people and mentions the amounts by way of greeting. Reads the racing form and does not bet. Calls Emmett "Vance," never Emmett. Has a chipped front tooth she got from a microphone stand and refuses to have fixed on the grounds that it cost her nothing. **Physicality.** Tall, broad-shouldered, carries herself like the room owes her something. Wears the same three dresses in rotation and one very good coat. Smokes while singing between numbers. After Chapter 6 her left wrist is in a cast and she does the ordering one-handed and won't be helped with it. **Motives.** San Francisco. That's it and it's enough. She wants the money and the season and to be somewhere the police collect on a different schedule. **Allegiances.** To the room. To two of her regulars. To Emmett, thinly and against her better judgment, until he gives her a reason not to be. **Voice.** > "Eleven dollars, Vance. You know what's funny is I don't need it. I just want to see what you look like when you hand it over." > "Don't. Don't stand there working out what to say. You went and got yourself something to want and you brought it in here and let it look around." --- # Detective Sergeant Wendell Cade **Background.** Forty-eight. Vice squad eleven years. Lives out past the fairgrounds with a wife, a daughter, and a son, Dennis, who is failing algebra, a topic Cade will raise with anyone. He collects from the bars on a schedule and has never in his life described it to himself as extortion; it's an arrangement, and he'd tell you the bars prefer it, and in a narrow sense he's right. **Personality.** Tedious. That's the whole horror of him. He's not cruel for pleasure, he's cruel the way weather is, and he'd rather talk about crabgrass. He's *pleasant*. He remembers Emmett's father's bakery route. He asks after the shoulder. His one real appetite is the paperwork — the ledger is his and he keeps it beautifully, in a small tight hand, because it's the only thing he's ever made that's complete. **Idiosyncrasies.** Eats hard candy constantly, peppermint, and the cellophane is his signature sound. Says "well, now" before delivering anything bad. Has a photograph of his lawn. Actually has it, in his wallet, and shows it. **Physicality.** Heavy, soft-faced, sweats in every weather. Sits down without being asked. Wears his hat indoors. His hands are small and clean. **Motives.** To retire with the pension and the house paid. To have Dennis pass algebra. To have things stay arranged. **Voice.** > "Well, now. Your father did the Halloran route, didn't he. Six days. That's a man who worked." *(unwraps candy)* "Your friend has something of mine." > "Nobody's getting hurt here, Mr. Vance. That's not how I do business and you can ask anyone on this street." --- # Sam Kell (dead, 1956) Never appears. Present as a name on the door, a jar of failed keys, and eight words of handwriting in a ledger: *Vance, E. — 4/47 — paid, S.K. — $300.* He was seventy-one when he died, a widower, tidy, and he taught by standing behind Emmett and saying nothing until Emmett got it right. He never once acknowledged the two nights Emmett spent in a cell in April of 1947, and Emmett took that silence for kindness for twelve years. The three hundred dollars can be read two ways. Emmett will never know which. He will keep the name on the door, because taking it down would mean deciding.

The shop was Vance & Kell, Lock and Safe, 1114 Water Street, between a printer's and a place that sold surgical supply. Kell died in '56 and I left his name up because you don't change a sign for nineteen dollars when the sign is doing its job. That's what I said at the time. I've thought about it since. It was February and the rain was doing what it does here, which is not fall so much as hang around. I'd spent that whole week on a rekey job — a widow on Beacon whose son-in-law had a key she wanted him not to have, and she wanted the old cylinders back in a bag so she could look at them. People are like that. She paid $4.50 and gave me a slice of cake, and I ate it standing in her hallway because she wanted me to eat it in front of her. I say all this because you want the man in the smoke and I want you to know what he walked into. A Friday. I'd balanced the books, which takes me forty minutes and which I enjoy, and don't let anybody tell you that's a sad thing to enjoy. Krebs' counter down the block does a fried egg sandwich for thirty cents and I'd had one at noon. My left shoulder was going, the way it does when I've been working overhead, and I'd taken two aspirin with coffee and was sitting on the stool behind the counter waiting for six o'clock so I could go up the stairs to my rooms and be tired in private. The bell over the door went at ten to. "You closing, chief?" "Ten minutes." "I only need two." He came in wet and didn't apologize for dripping, and he went to the radiator like he'd been in the room before, and he put his hands on it and made a noise. He had a cigarette going and he was holding it in the corner of his mouth while his hands were busy, which I hate. There's a sign. Sixty years of brass stock behind that counter and I've got a sign about it. "There's no smoking near the brass." "Where's the brass." "Behind me." "Then I'm not near it," he said, and he grinned at me. Later I'd learn he did that with everything. He'd answer the letter of it. It was maddening about the small things and it turned out to be the whole architecture of him. He was tall and too thin, black hair longer than men wore it that year, and a nose that had been broken and set by somebody in a hurry. Good shoes. That was the thing I noticed and kept noticing about him for as long as I knew him — the shoes were always better than the coat. There was a story in that and it took me a while to work out what it was. He came over and put a key on the counter. "One copy," he said. "How fast." I picked it up. I want to be clear about this part because it's the part people get wrong when I tell it. I want to be clear that I knew. It was a five-pin, common as dirt, and it had come off a ring with something heavy, you could see where the bow had rubbed. But the wear on the cuts was wrong. A man's own key wears even because he uses it the same way ten thousand times, same angle, same hand. This one was bright at the tip and hardly touched further in, which is what you get from a key that's been in a lock a handful of times, quick, by somebody who wasn't sure of the door. I turned it over twice, and I looked up, and I said, "This isn't your key." He didn't flinch. He took the cigarette out of his mouth and he looked at it like it had said something. "No," he said. That was all. He didn't build me a story. If he'd built me a story about his brother's cabin I'd have known that too, and I might have thrown him out for the insult of it. He just said no, and stood there, and let me hold the thing. "You want me to cut a copy of a key that isn't yours." "I want two." He put a dollar on the counter. "You said one, I'm saying two." The machine was already off and covered. I could have said the machine's off. It's a duplicator, it takes ninety seconds, and forty cents apiece is forty cents apiece, and the widow on Beacon had been the whole week and I was $58 a month into a mortgage. None of that is the reason. I took the cover off the machine and I cut him two keys, and while the wheel was going he stood close enough that I could smell the wet wool and the tobacco off him, and he didn't say anything, and I want it on the record that I was not fooled for a single minute. I've had a long time to be proud of that. It hasn't done one thing for me. I brushed the burr off and put both keys in his hand. "Eighty cents." He looked at the dollar on the counter like it was somebody else's. "You've got change," he said. I gave him twenty cents out of the drawer. He put the keys in his coat and the change in his trouser pocket, separate, and he went to the door and turned around with his hand on it. "Rafe," he said. "That's fine with me." He laughed at that. Head back, mouth open, no sound at all for about a second, and then the sound. The bell went and the door shut and I locked it and pulled the shade, and then I stood there in the smell of him for a while like a man who's forgotten what he came into the room for. The argument was that Marciano was a made record, that they'd fed him old men and hard-luck cases, and he had four examples and he used all four twice, and when I said Walcott he told me what Walcott was in '52 and I said yes but he was still Walcott and Rafe said that's exactly my point, chief, which it was not. He got warm about it. He got his forearm on the table and his ash on the floor. Two men came over to say hello to him and both of them left again. I sat there and let it go over me and I thought, this is the most boring man in this room. It didn't matter what the answer was. He was finding out whether I'd give him one. Around one I said I was going, and he said he'd walk out with me. Up the stairs and out and it was raining in the way where you don't notice starting to be wet. There's an alley beside the Verandah with a tin awning over the back door of the printer's and you can stand under it if you don't mind the noise, and the noise is considerable, and that's the point of it. He got hold of my coat and I got hold of his and it was awkward for a while. My hat came off. He was taller than me by four inches and neither of us worked that out until we'd tried three or four ways, and at one point he laughed into my collar and I said, don't, because I could hear Purdy's radio through the wall and I couldn't tell how far off it was. He tasted like gin and tobacco and something sweet underneath, and his hands were cold, and he put one of them flat on my chest and held it there like he was taking a reading. "You're not surprised," he said. "No." "You want to be? I can do surprised." "No." He looked at me under the awning with the water coming off both ends of it and he said, "I've got something you're going to like, because it's easy, and you don't like anything that isn't easy." # 3. Forty Units on Halloran Street The Halloran job came in the third week of February and it was the biggest thing I'd had since Kell died. A man named Ostrand had bought two buildings, four floors each, twenty units to a building, and he wanted the whole works rekeyed on a master system because the previous owner had been handing out keys for eleven years like a man throwing bread at ducks. Forty units, forty cylinders, plus two street doors, two basements, a boiler room, and a laundry. Ostrand wanted a master that did everything and a submaster per building and he wanted it done inside two weeks, and he wanted a price before he'd let me measure anything, which is how you know a man's going to be trouble on the invoice. I quoted $310 including hardware. He said $260. We settled at $285 and I made $71 on it in the end, which sounds like nothing now and was rent for five months. I tell you this because it's what I was actually doing. People want the other business to have been the whole of it and it wasn't. It was three days a week on Halloran Street with a bag on my shoulder, pinning cylinders on a stair landing in the cold with a fifteen-watt bulb over me, and my shoulder going by two in the afternoon every day. Here's how it goes, if you want to know. You take the cylinder out. You get the plug out, you dump the pins, and you pin it fresh off your chart — bottom pins to your change key, master pins on top of those, drivers on top of that. Forty cylinders means two hundred pins and one wrong one means a tenant standing in a hallway at seven in the morning with a key that turns halfway. You do it with tweezers on a felt cloth and you don't talk to anybody. By the fourth day the tenants had worked out who I was and had opinions. A woman on the second floor of the north building wanted to know why she should have to have a new key when she'd never lost the old one. A man on four wanted three copies for people I doubt existed. A kid, eleven or twelve, had snapped a key off in the mailbox bank downstairs and stood next to me for forty minutes while I pulled the stub out with an extractor, telling me the whole time that it wasn't him, and when I got it out I gave it to him and said, then this belongs to nobody, and he took it and ran. That was the best conversation I had that week. Rafe came to me three times about it and he did it in pieces, which I've thought about since, because doing it in pieces isn't accident. It's a man who knows the whole thing at once would get him thrown out. First time, the shop, Tuesday. He sat sideways in the chair by the counter with his leg over the arm, and I told him about the pins because he asked, and he listened to about ninety seconds of it and then said, "What's the hardest thing in this town. Professionally." "Import safes. There's a German make I've never got on with. I send those to a fellow in Tacoma and take ten percent." "You do not." "I do." He was delighted. That's the word. He put his head back and did the silent laugh and then said, "So there's a thing you can't do," and I said there's a lot of things, and he said, no, but there's a *thing*, and he was pleased with me for about ten minutes after that. Second time, Thursday, in Krebs' at noon, which he shouldn't have done and did. He ate half my sandwich. He asked what a five-lever cabinet safe was worth to get into if it was in an office in a building with a night man, and I said it depends on the safe and it depends on whether you like prison, and he said suppose it's a Diebold from about 1930 and suppose the night man's a fixture, and I put my coffee down and said, whose is it. "It's nobody's." "Whose." He looked at me with the mouth going and said, "There's money in it that's already stolen, chief. It's already stolen. Somebody took it off working people and put it in a box and I know where the box is." Which was, I want you to notice, true. Every word of that was true, and it was not the truth, and I've never met anybody else who could do that. I said no. I said it flat and I said it twice. Third time was the following Tuesday and by then I'd met Cade. Cade came into the Verandah on the Sunday at about ten, and the room got quiet in a way that wasn't quiet — the volume was the same, everything just got careful. He took his hat off nobody, he had his coat over his arm, and he sat down at Odile's end of the bar without being asked and put a bag of hard candy on the wood. Peppermints. He unwrapped one while he waited and the cellophane went on and on. Purdy brought him an envelope and he put it inside his coat without looking at it, and then he stayed. That's the part I hadn't understood before. He stayed forty minutes. He talked to Odile about the acts and about the ordering, and then he saw me down the bar and he came over with his candy and said, "Vance, isn't it. Water Street." "That's right." "Your father did the Halloran route. For Bregman's, the bakery. Six days a week." He said it like he was awarding me something. "That's a man who worked. You've got the shoulder, don't you, I've seen you carry that bag on the one side." I stood very still. People take that for composure and I let them. He told me about his son Dennis for eleven or twelve minutes. Algebra. Dennis was going to fail algebra unless something happened, and Cade had a theory that the trouble was the teacher's handwriting on the board. He asked me if I'd been good at school. He showed me a photograph out of his wallet and I looked at it and it was his lawn. Just the lawn, taken from the porch, with the hose coiled up at the edge of the frame. "Kentucky bluegrass," he said. "You have to feed it in the fall, that's what people get wrong." Then he put the wallet away and said, "Well, now," and looked at me pleasantly and said nothing else at all, and put his hat on, and left. Tuesday, Rafe came to the shop and sat sideways in the chair and didn't say anything for a while, and I said, whose safe is it. He told me. I said no. I want that in. I said no, and I meant it, and I went upstairs that night and lay there working out how you'd do it.

I've tried to fix it by the Halloran invoice, which I have, and the invoice says the 6th of March, and that doesn't help because I don't know how long after. The weather turned dry, which people here talk about like a holiday. Ten days of it. High cloud, cold, no rain, and the whole city smelling of what the rain had been keeping down. I've heard men say that was a fine spell. It was the worst part of my life and I didn't know it yet, and I've never been able to like dry weather since, which is an inconvenient thing to carry in this town. He came to the shop after hours. That started the same week as the dry and I don't think that's a coincidence, because a wet man at your door has a reason and a dry man doesn't. I taught him to listen to a lock. He wanted to be taught and I wanted to be the one teaching, and neither of those is a good reason for anything. I put a cutaway padlock in the vise, the kind an apprentice starts on where the case is milled away so you can see the pins move, and I gave him a hook and a wrench and told him to feel for the one that binds. He was terrible. He had no patience in his hands. He'd get a pin set and then he'd get excited and put weight on the wrench and drop the whole stack, and he did that eleven or twelve times, and the twelfth time he threw the hook down the counter and said the lock was defective. I told him it wasn't. He said everything in here is fifty years old, chief, including you, and then he laughed at his own thing for a while. But he'd sit there. That's what I want down. He'd sit on the stool with his shoulders hunched over a two-dollar padlock at eleven at night with his tongue between his teeth, and get nowhere, and stay. He was never once bored in that shop, and he was bored everywhere else, and I have thought about that more than I've thought about almost anything. The first night we went upstairs it was not good. I'll say that because everything else you get told about these things is a lie of omission. He got a cufflink caught in my cardigan and we spent a full minute on it, and he wouldn't let me get the lamp, and I said I need the lamp for the cufflink and he said leave it, and I left it, and we broke the cufflink. The second night was better. The fourth night was the one I'd take back if they let you take one. There were brass filings in the bed for a month. They get on your hands and then they get everywhere and you can't see them, you find them because they catch the light at the wrong angle at seven in the morning. He said something about that, the first time, something about sleeping in a machine shop, and I don't remember what it was and I've tried. He talked about a car. There was a '56 Chrysler on a lot on Fenner, blue over white, and it was $1,340, and he brought it up — I counted, later, which tells you something about me — he brought it up nine times. He'd describe the dash. He had no license that I ever saw. Twice he took money out of my register. First time was four dollars and I thought I'd made an error, and I balance my books on Friday and I don't make errors, and I sat with it for two days. Second time was seven and he was in the shop when I counted, and I said there's seven dollars out of here, and he said when, and I said tonight, and he said, chief, I've been sitting right here. He never gave the eleven dollars back either, though he didn't take that. That was mine to owe. I gave him a key to the shop on a Wednesday. I cut it myself, obviously, and I did it badly on purpose — I let the machine leave a burr on the bow so it would feel like something in the pocket. There's no reason for that. I stood there with it in my hand for a while and then I said, here, this is for the alley door, don't use the front because Meecham next door notices the front. He put it on his ring, on the ring with the heavy thing on it that had rubbed the bow of the first key I ever cut for him, and he didn't say thank you, and I've decided he didn't know how to and that's why. He whistled about two bars of something and stopped. I had eleven days off from the Halloran job in there because Ostrand's hardware order came in short and we waited on cylinders. Eleven days with a key out in the world in a man's pocket. I have never in my life been that easy to find. Now here's the other thing and then I'm going to move on. Cade came into the shop on a Thursday in that dry stretch, alone, and sat down without being asked, and unwrapped a peppermint, and talked to me about Dennis's algebra for a while. Then he said he'd heard the Verandah was doing all right. Then he said he'd heard Odile Grange was leaving for California, and wasn't that a shame for the room. And I said she'd been saying that for two years and she'd never save the money, and he said, well, now, and looked at me. And I said she had it. I said it because he was sitting in my shop with his hat on and I wanted him out of my shop, and because if he had Odile to think about for a week he wasn't thinking about me, and I got that week. # 5. After I'm not going to describe the annex. You've got the reports. You've got Rafe's version if he ever gave one, and I doubt it. You want the room, the hour, the drill, what the night man was doing, and I've decided I'm not going to. It happened. It took less time than the Halloran job took in one afternoon, and every part of it that was difficult was difficult in a way nobody would find interesting, and the part that was easy was the part I'd said couldn't be done. Put down that it was done and move on. We came back down the alley to the shop door at about a quarter to four and he had it in his coat, and I got the door open on the second try because my hands were bad. There was no money. I want to be fair, because I've been unfair about him in a lot of ways since. He hadn't promised money. He'd said *there's money in there that's already stolen*, which was true about the world in general and about that box in particular at some point in its history, and he'd said it in my face over half my sandwich. But I'd built a number out of it. I'd built about four hundred dollars out of it in my own head across three weeks, without him putting the figure there, and when the coat came open on the counter and it was a ledger and a bundle of envelopes and no cash at all, I stood there feeling like a man who's been lied to and had to admit privately that he'd done it to himself. It was a black book. Cloth boards, about the size of a hymnal, and the corners were soft from handling. He put it on the workbench between the vise and the felt cloth and he wiped his hands down his front twice, which he did when he was pleased and also when he wasn't. "There it is," he said. "There's no money in that." "There's more than money in that." Then he said it again about ten minutes later and then he said it again, and by six in the morning he'd said *there's more than money in that* five or six times, and every time he said it, it was less true, because he was saying it to get himself to believe it. I know the difference now. I didn't then. Then I just wanted him to stop. He wouldn't sit down. He walked the shop, which is nineteen feet, and he went up and down it with his hat still on and told me what we had. Names. Payments. Every bar on Colfax and two on Grand and the one out by the fairgrounds, dates, figures, initials. And the other column, which was men — men who'd been picked up in the bars and let go, and what it had cost them, and men who hadn't been let go, and what had happened to those. I didn't open it. He opened it and put his finger on things and read parts out and I looked at the wall over his shoulder. I have never been able to explain that. It was on my own bench and it was the only interesting object that has ever been in my shop and I did not put a hand on it for eleven days. I made eggs. Four eggs in a pan with butter, at some point past six, and I ate three of them standing at the sink upstairs and he ate one and left the yolk. He wouldn't sit down for that either. He wanted to burn the envelopes and I said no, because you don't burn paper in a building with a printer next door and a fire marshal who'd been in that week. He said that was a coward's reason. I said it was a landlord's reason. He said what's the difference, and I didn't have anything for that, and I still don't. Then he stopped in the middle of the floor and said, "Chief, we are going to be rich or we are going to be dead," and he laughed the way he did, head back, nothing for a second, and then the noise. I laughed too. I want that in. I stood in my own shop at half past six in the morning next to a book that had my life in it, and I laughed until my eyes ran, and I have thought since that if you'd asked me at that exact moment whether I was happy I'd have said yes without stopping to check. I put the book and the envelopes in the floor safe under the bench, which is a Mosler I got out of a bankrupt jeweller in '52, and I set the day book on top of the bench, and I opened the shade at eight and turned the sign, because it was a Wednesday and I had a lockout on Beacon at half past nine, and that's what I did that day. A woman had put her keys in the mailbox with the letters. It took four minutes and I charged her three dollars and she wanted to tell me about her sister. He went out the alley door at about ten past seven. He said he'd be back that night. He came back that night and the next and then he didn't, for two days, and when he came back after that he had a new hat and I didn't ask what he'd sold and he didn't say. That's what after was like. I've heard people talk about the quiet before a thing. This was the quiet after a thing, which nobody warns you about, and it was six eggs and a lockout and a woman's sister and a man walking nineteen feet up and down my shop saying the same sentence, and I would go back into that week and live in it.

# 6. What I Heard Through a Door The Verandah has a door at the end of the back passage that's the old coal chute door and it doesn't fit its frame anymore. Odile keeps the stock in there — cases, the tins, a broken cabinet where she puts the sheet music. Purdy calls it the cellar and it isn't one. I was in the passage on the Saturday because I'd gone to the water closet and the water closet is past it, and I heard Rafe's voice through the door, and I stopped, and I'm not going to pretend it was an accident that I stayed. He was talking to a man whose voice I didn't know, and I still don't, and I have never found out who it was. That's one thing in this whole business I never got to the bottom of and I've made my peace with it. He was pitching. He had the whole thing going. He was doing the same three-week job on this man that he'd done on me, and I could hear the shape of it, the way you can hear your own tune played on somebody else's instrument. And he said, and I've had this for eleven years, he said: "— it's already in hand. That end's done. I had a man on Water Street, best pair of hands in this city, he had it open in under an hour." *I had a man.* Past tense. Not *I've got*. And *a man*, which is what you call a supplier. And *on Water Street*, which is not a person, it's a location, it's where you go for a thing, the way you'd say there's a fellow on Grand who does upholstery. Then he said something I didn't catch and the other man said something, and then Rafe said, "He'll do it again if I need him to," and the other man laughed and said something like, what's it cost you, and Rafe said — and this is the part, this is the only part I'd take out of my head if they gave me the tool — Rafe said: "Nothing. It doesn't cost me anything." And he laughed. Head back. I couldn't see it. I know exactly what it looked like. I want to be clear that none of it was news. I'd known from the first ten minutes, from the wear on that key, and I'd said so out loud in my own shop with him standing there, and he'd said no and I'd cut it anyway. So there was nothing in that room I hadn't already had in my hands. I've told myself that a great many times, most often at about four in the morning. But knowing a thing and hearing a man say it to a stranger for free are not the same, and I've decided the difference is that one of them is private. As long as it's between the two of you it's a bargain, and the moment he's describing you to somebody else you find out you were never in the bargain, you were in the inventory. I didn't go in. There was no scene. I've read that people do that and I don't know who they are. I went back up the passage and through the room and up the stairs past Purdy, and Purdy said something about the weather and I said something back, and I walked home in the rain, which had come back that week, and it was the first thing about that week I was grateful for. He came to the shop Tuesday and I let him in the alley door and I didn't say a word about it. Not then, not ever. He never knew. He's alive somewhere right now, probably, and he doesn't know I heard it, and out of everything I have that's the only thing I've got that's mine. Wednesday morning Odile's building was gone through. They did it in the afternoon while she was at the Verandah doing the ordering, which is how you know it wasn't kids. Her rooms were turned over properly — mattress off, drawers out, the picture off the wall — and they found the loose board first go, because there's not that many places, and they took the coffee tin with the $1,340 in it, and they took a wristwatch that had been her husband Arthur's and left her mother's ring, which she said was the most insulting part of it. She came back and interrupted them. That's not in any report. There were two of them and she got hold of one, and he put her arm behind the door and shut the door on it, and that's how the wrist went. Two bones. She had it in a cast up past the elbow by Thursday and she was doing the ordering one-handed on the Friday and she took the pencil out of my hand when I picked it up. I went to see her Friday afternoon before the room opened. She was at a table with the invoices and she didn't look up when I came down the stairs, and she said, "Don't." I said I was going to say I was sorry. "Don't stand there working out what to say." She put the pencil down. "You went and got yourself something to want and you brought it in here and let it look around. Two years I've been putting that money in a tin. Two years. And it took you six weeks." I said I had money and I could get more. "You've got eleven dollars," she said. "You've had eleven dollars in your pocket since November and you couldn't hand it over because then it'd be done between us, and you like it not done, because a man who owes you eleven dollars is a man who has to come back." I don't know if that's true. I've never worked out if that's true. I put sixty dollars on the table anyway, which was everything I had that wasn't the mortgage, and she looked at it and left it lying there and picked the pencil back up with her good hand. "Take it off the eleven," she said. It was still on the table when I left. I don't know what she did with it. She never said and I never asked, and she never said thank you, and she was right not to. Rafe didn't come Wednesday. He didn't come Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday. I went to two places I knew he sometimes was and he'd been at neither of them for a week, and the barber shop on Grand had a different man behind the chair who didn't know anything and wanted me to know he didn't. Nine days. And in those nine days I finally opened the book.

# 7. Kell's Handwriting I'd like to say I put it off out of principle. It was ten dollars. There's a page toward the back where the names run in a column with dates and figures beside them, and it isn't the payoff side, it's the other side, the men. And on the ninth page of that section, in a small tight hand that I'd learn was Cade's for the recent years and somebody else's for before, there's an entry from April of 1947. There were twelve of us picked up outside the Bantam on the 19th. I was twenty-two. They held me two nights in a cell with a man from the gas company who cried the whole first night and apologized for it, and then they let me out on the Monday morning with my belt and my shoelaces in a paper bag and nobody said anything to me. No charge. Nothing in the paper. I walked to the shop and Kell had the machine running and he looked up and said the Ferris job needs doing and I said yes and I did the Ferris job. Twelve names on that page from the 19th of April. Nine of them have a figure and a set of initials next to them and three of them have a notation I'd rather not put down. Mine reads: *Vance, E. — 4/47 — paid, S.K. — $300.* I want to tell you what that's like and I can't do it properly so I'm going to do it badly. Three hundred dollars in 1947 was four months of the shop's whole take. I have looked at the day books from 1947, all of them, I got them out of the crate under the stair that night and I went through them with a lamp until half past four in the morning, and there is nothing. There is no gap and no adjustment and no cash out of the ordinary in April, May, June, or July of 1947. Nothing. Either it never went through the books, which means he had three hundred dollars somewhere I never knew about, or it went the other way, or there's a third thing I haven't thought of, and I have had years and I haven't thought of it. Because *paid* has two doors on it. He paid them. That's one. Sam Kell went down to that building and put three hundred dollars of his own money on a desk and had my name struck through and never told me and never once, not in nine years, in the shop, in a car, at a counter, drunk at Christmas, in the hospital at the end with a tube in him, not once mentioned it. And that would be the largest thing anybody has ever done for me and he would have done it in a way that made it impossible for me to know, which would be exactly like him, because that man taught me by standing behind me and saying nothing until I got it right. Or they paid him. That's the other. A man's apprentice comes up on a list, and somebody at that desk says, we can take the name off, and what have you got for us, and you tell us who else comes in your shop and what for, and here's three hundred dollars for your trouble, and you go back and say the Ferris job needs doing. I don't know. I have run it both ways for eleven years and both ways fit every single thing about him, and that is the part nobody understands when I try to tell them. It isn't that I lean one way. It's that the man I knew is the man in both versions. The silence works for either. The kindness works for either. The three hundred dollars works for either. His name is still on my door. I've had two chances to change the sign — once when the plate cracked in '61 and once when I moved the shop — and both times I had the money and both times I stood there with the sign man waiting and I put the same name back up, because taking it down is a decision and putting it up is a decision, and leaving it there is the only thing I can do that isn't one. That was the night the writing goes bad. I know it does. I read it back and it's a man talking too fast about pin stacks and day books and Ferris and a paper bag with his shoelaces in it because he can't stand still long enough to say the other thing. So put down that I sat on the floor of my own shop next to an open safe at four in the morning with a cloth-bound book in my lap and I couldn't breathe right and I couldn't stop, either, and I went through those day books twice more the following week looking for three hundred dollars, and I still get them out. I got them out last year. Rafe came on the tenth day, at about one in the morning, and he used the alley key. He was in a bad state and it wasn't a beautiful one. He'd been sleeping somewhere with his coat on. He came in fast and shut the door and stood with his back against it and he was wet through the shirt at the chest and under the arms, in March, and it wasn't warm. He said the man he owed had had a conversation with Cade. Or Cade with him. Both, either. He said it four different ways in about two minutes and the versions didn't agree and I didn't ask him to reconcile them because I could see he couldn't. And then he started in on whose fault it was. Purdy's, for talking. Mine, for keeping the book in the shop instead of moving it. The man in the cellar whose name he still didn't give me. He got to Odile — he got to Odile, and said she'd have talked to Cade about California because she talked to everybody, and that's what put them on the flat, and I stood there and let him say it, and I said nothing, and if you want the worst thing I've done it's not the sixty dollars on the table, it's that. Then he sat down on the stool and put his head in his hands and said, "Chief, I can't be here Thursday." There was a way out and he had most of it. There was a bus, and there was a hundred and forty dollars he needed which I had upstairs in a tobacco tin, and there was a thing that had to happen at the annex on Thursday night so that the book stopped mattering, which meant a door on the Fenner side that's locked at nine and that I could have open at eleven. He didn't tell me what was coming through it. That was the arrangement, that he wouldn't, and it was my arrangement, I made it, I said don't tell me and he said fine and looked relieved. I knew. I want that written plainly because everything else I've said has had a wall around it. Nobody told me and I knew, the way you know the weight of a thing before you pick it up, and I said eleven o'clock, and I went and got the tin.

# 8. Water Street I opened it at ten past eleven and I was home by twenty to twelve. It's a service door on the Fenner side with a Corbin mortise in it that was old when it went in, and I had it open in under a minute and I left the bolt thrown back and the latch taped, which is a thing kids do, and that was the point. I put the tape on flat with my thumb the way you'd smooth down a stamp. Then I walked to the end of Fenner and turned left instead of right, because right is shorter and passes the annex, and I went home the long way past the surgical supply, and I let myself in the front for once because I didn't want the alley. The fire was at about half past one. I heard the engines from the bed. Two men were in the building and one of them was the night man, whose name was Ellery Boyce, and he got out, and the other one didn't, and the one who didn't was not Cade, and I'll come to that. Cade was at home in bed out past the fairgrounds with his wife and his daughter and his son Dennis. I have never been sure whether the intention was for him to be at the annex and it went wrong, or whether the intention was only ever the room and the files and it went exactly right except for a man being in it. Rafe wouldn't have known. Rafe wasn't the one making that decision by then and I doubt he was told either. So there were two of us that night who didn't ask. The man who died was a clerk named Wallace Doerr, thirty-one, who had put in to be transferred and had come in at night to finish the paperwork for it. That was in the paper on the Friday, four inches, and it said the cause was undetermined and it said the department's records were a total loss, and it said Doerr was survived by his mother in Aberdeen. I have his name written on the inside cover of my 1959 day book. That's the only place I've ever written it down and I don't know why I did it there, because that's a book I look at. Cade retired in the November. Not because of any of it — he'd have gone anyway, he had the years. There was no investigation that came near me and no one ever asked me a question about a door. He came into my shop one last time in October and unwrapped a peppermint and told me Dennis had passed algebra with a C-minus and was going to the community college, and he said, well, now, and left. I didn't say anything the whole time. He never mentioned the annex and I've decided he'd have mentioned it if he'd cared, and that's what I mean about him. It was arranged and then it wasn't and he went and did his lawn. The bus was Thursday morning, ten forty, from the depot on Second. I didn't go. I had the hundred and forty in a tin on Wednesday night and he took it and he said the bus and the time twice, and he stood in the shop with his hat on and waited a minute for me to say I'd be there and I didn't say it, and he didn't ask, and then he said, "Well, chief," and went out the alley door. Thursday I opened at eight. There was a lockout at nine on Beacon and a woman with a stuck sash lock at eleven who wanted it oiled and I told her it needed replacing and she said oil it, so I oiled it and charged her a dollar and it was working badly again by summer. At twenty to eleven I was on my knees in a hallway on Beacon with a bag on my shoulder and my left shoulder going, and that is where I was, and I have never dressed that up. I could have gone. That's not a story about a man kept away by circumstance. The Beacon job was mine to move and the sash lock could have waited a week. I've had a long time with it and the best I can say is that going would have meant standing on a platform being a man saying goodbye to another man, in public, at ten forty in the morning, in this city, in 1959, and I couldn't. I would like to tell you it was something better than that. I did tell one joke that day. There was nobody there. I was putting the cover on the duplicator at six and I said out loud, to the shop, "Well, that's eighty cents I'll never see again." That's the whole joke. I laughed at it for a while, and then I stopped, and it was quiet in there. — Odile went in September, with the arm out of the cast and set slightly wrong so she couldn't get her hand flat, and she did not tell me she was going. I found out from Purdy on a Saturday. She sends a card at Christmas with her name on it and nothing else written, which is a thing my mother does too, and I've noticed that and I don't like to look at it. She was right about the eleven dollars, or she was right about something, and I have never been able to get the sentence out of my head, and the eleven dollars is still not paid, because now there's nowhere to send it that would mean it. The book is in the Mosler under the bench. It's been there eleven years. I've had it out four times, and three of those were the day books and 1947. I never used it for anything. There were nights early on when I thought about what a man could do with it — protect the room, protect the street, put a bad cop in a corner — and I want to be honest with you that I thought about that mostly because it sounded like a thing a better man would think about. I was thirty-four and then I was thirty-five and I had a mortgage of fifty-eight dollars a month and a shoulder, and I had the whole city's throat in a drawer under my bench, and I was too tired and too careful, and that's all there is to that. The key came back in the post in the spring of '61, no note, no return address, postmarked Denver, which is a place he never once mentioned. He'd never taken it off the ring; there's still a mark on the bow from the heavy thing. Nobody smokes in the shop now. Nobody has since. I put the sign back up when I moved and it's still there, six feet from the brass, and about twice a year, usually in the dry weather, I'll come down the stairs in the morning and get it in the doorway for a second before it goes. I've got the burr key in the jar with the others. Sixty-odd keys in there and I can tell you what every one of them was for, and I'm not going to be the man who takes that jar out and looks in it, so it sits on the shelf over the bench with a bit of a rag on it, next to the graphite and the extractors and the tin I keep the small springs in, which needs sorting.
