The trouble with a chained woman was that everything took two hands and you only had two hands. Water first. He climbed up into the bed with the skin and knelt where he could reach her, and she tipped her head back and opened her mouth, and he poured, and half of it went down her chin and into the neck of her dress, which was the fifth time in six days he'd done that. "You're bad at this," she said, when he'd stopped. "You could hold still." "I'm holding perfectly still. You're pouring like a man watering a plant he doesn't like." She worked her jaw. "There's a way. Thumb under the lip, tilt with the other hand. That's how they do it in the hulks." "You've been in the hulks." "I've been told about the hulks." She said it flatly, without ornament, and he had no idea whether that was the truth or a better lie than usual. He tried it. Thumb under her lower lip, the pad of it against the wet inside, and the other hand tilting the skin, and it worked — she drank half a pint without losing a drop and shut her eyes doing it, and he was suddenly, sharply aware of his own hand and of the fact that it was warm in there, and he took it back and dried his thumb on his coat. "See," she said. Bread next. He tore it and gave it to her a piece at a time, and she had to lean forward and take it off his fingers with her teeth, because there was no other way to do it and hadn't been on any of the nine before her either. Nine, and it had never once occurred to him to be embarrassed. He was now. "Fat on the outside," she said, chewing. "That's tallow. You've been keeping it against a hot plate." "I keep it in the wax cloth." "It's tallow, Marrick. You've had it near a candle." She swallowed and opened her mouth again, and he put another piece in it. "When I'm out of this I'm going to eat an egg. Two eggs, in butter, with the yolk soft, and pepper on them, and a heel of black bread to take up what's left in the pan. That's the whole of my ambition. You can keep your nine acres." "You're not getting out of that." "Then let me have the eggs in my head and don't interrupt." Then there was the other thing, and there was no way to do the other thing that wasn't what it was. He unhooked her right wrist and left the left one on, and ran the long rope from the loose cuff back through the ring bolt at the tail of the wagon, and had it round his fist before he'd let her stand. She'd gone through the whole business four times now and it hadn't got quicker. "You could look at the sky," she said, out on the salt with her back to him and the rope going slack and taut, slack and taut. "I am looking at the sky." "You're looking at the sky like a man being made to look at the sky." "Be quicker." "It's *cold*." Something in her voice had thinned. "It's cold, and my hands don't work — do you know they don't work? Six days up over my head. I can't feel the third finger on either one and I can't get my own skirt up, and you're stood there twelve feet away with the rope round your fist and looking at the *sky*." He looked at the sky. There was nothing in it. After a while she managed, and came back, and put her wrist up into the cuff herself without being told, which she had not done before. He hooked her. He oiled the iron where it had taken the skin off the heel of her hand. She let him. "Marrick." "Don't." "I haven't said anything." "You're going to." "I was going to say that your mother must have had a great deal of practice with a rasp, to get you as smooth as—" He had the gag out of his coat and round her head before he'd made any decision he could later find. It was a strap and a wooden bit, standard, in the kit of every hauler who worked long roads, and he had used it perhaps six times in a decade and never twice on the same cargo. She didn't fight it. That was the thing. She turned her face away and let him buckle it at the back of her head under the hair, and when it was done she went entirely still — not slack, *still*, the way the salt flats were still — and looked at nothing, and her tail, which had been moving all day, lay down along the boards and stopped. He got down out of the wagon and stood there with the strap-end still in his hand. "You don't talk about my mother," he said. She did not look at him. He built the fire out of dung and two fence rails he'd been carrying since the ford, and he ate, and the silence came in off the flats and sat down with him. Twelve feet away in the dark under the canvas she made no sound at all. Not one. He had wanted quiet for six days and now he had it and it was like a hand on his chest. At the second hour he went up and took it off her. She worked her jaw and spat, and said nothing, and he waited a while for her to start again and she didn't, and he went back to the fire. Later — a long way from the wagon, out at the fence post he'd measured by eye and thought was far enough — he sat down on the salt with his back to the fire and unrolled the oilcloth. Rasp, whetstone, candle-end. He lit the candle in the lee of his hat and put his hat down over it, and knelt over the little light, and did the two hard places under his hair where the winter's growth had come up. It was not a loud sound. It was a small dry sound, like a mouse in a wall, three or four strokes and a pause, three or four and a pause. It carried further than he had ever bothered to work out. He was a man who counted miles and coins and days and had never in thirty-one years counted this. He rolled the cloth up, put out the candle with his thumb, and came back in. She was awake. He could tell by the eyes, which had no whites and caught the fire. She said nothing. He lay down with his hat over his face and listened to her not saying anything, and did not sleep for a long time.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably controlled piece of writing that demonstrates genuine craft in nearly every dimension. Let me work through it carefully. The opening line — "The trouble with a chained woman was that everything took two hands and you only had two hands" — is an excellent entry point. It's practical, slightly comic, and immediately establishes Marrick's mode of thinking: logistics first, everything else second. It doesn't strain for effect; it earns its place. The water-feeding scene is handled with precision. The detail about the thumb under the lip, the warmth of her mouth, and Marrick drying his thumb on his coat afterward — this is showing at its best. The physical intimacy of the act is rendered without being underlined, and the reader feels the discomfort without being told to feel it. The bread-feeding scene similarly works: the tallow detail is characterful (she notices things, she catalogs), and the egg speech is perfectly calibrated — funny, humanizing, and quietly devastating in context. The toilet scene is the chapter's bravest passage. The writing plan called for "the genuinely awkward logistics of unhooking a chained woman so she can piss," and the chapter delivers this without flinching or making it grotesque. Her line about her fingers not working, about not being able to get her own skirt up — this is the moment where the chapter earns its emotional weight. It's not played for pathos; it's stated flatly, which makes it land harder. His response (looking at the sky "like a man being made to look at the sky") is a perfect character beat. The gag scene is the chapter's dramatic center, and it's handled with real skill. The plan specified that "he gags her on Night One and she never forgives it," and the execution honors this: her stillness, the tail going down along the boards, the absence of fight — these are more damning than any struggle would be. The tail detail is particularly good; it's been established in the character profile as an honest tell, and its sudden stillness here is genuinely chilling. His line "You don't talk about my mother" — said to someone who cannot respond — is a small, ugly moment of cowardice dressed as authority, exactly as the character profile demands. The rasp scene is the chapter's quietest triumph. The plan called for him to use the rasp at night, for her to hear it, and for the chapter to end on "him lying awake, listening to her not saying anything." The execution is faithful and then some. "It was not a loud sound. It was a small dry sound, like a mouse in a wall" — this is the chapter's best simile, and it earns its place because it's precise and unexpected without being showy. The observation that "He was a man who counted miles and coins and days and had never in thirty-one years counted this" is a genuinely good line — it uses his established characterization to reveal something new about him without explaining it. The ending — her eyes catching the fire, her silence, him unable to sleep — is exactly right. The plan called for ending "on nothing: him lying awake, listening to her not saying anything," and the chapter delivers this without embellishment. Dialogue is consistently strong. Both characters sound like themselves. Her voice has the right mixture of wit, exhaustion, and precision. His responses are appropriately terse and occasionally self-betraying. The exchange about the sky is particularly good — it's funny and sad simultaneously, and neither character is made to look foolish at the other's expense. Are there weaknesses? A few minor ones. "The silence came in off the flats and sat down with him" is the chapter's one moment of slightly strained personification — it's not bad, but it's the most "literary" gesture in an otherwise unliterary chapter, and it sits slightly awkwardly. The line "like a hand on his chest" following it compounds this slightly. These are small complaints against an otherwise disciplined piece. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the logistics, the gag, the rasp, the ending on silence. It honors the character profiles — Marrick's compulsive counting, his cowardice dressed as pragmatism, his need for the rasp; her tail as honest tell, her relentlessness, the moment she goes still. The darkness is well-earned throughout; nothing is cheap. This is writing that trusts its reader, which is the rarest thing. She kept it up all the next day. He hadn't known a person could. She took water when he offered it and said *thank you*, which was worse than spitting, and she ate the bread off his fingers without one word about tallow, and when he unhooked her at midday she went out on the rope and came back and put her wrist up and that was all. No sky. No eggs. By noon he had stopped being pleased about it. By the middle of the afternoon he was going up the road at a mare's walk with his shoulders round his ears, and every quarter hour he found himself listening — actually listening, head cocked, the way you listen for a wheel that's begun to complain. The flats gave out around three and the country came up in low grey folds with gorse in them, and he could smell rain coming from the west, hours off. "You're not going to say anything," he said. Nothing. "Fine." He got two miles further before it came out of him. He hadn't been building it. That was the part he'd think about afterwards — he'd have sworn he had nothing in there at all. "I feed you twice. I water you when you ask, which is more than the writ requires, and I've oiled that iron every night since Sennet and there's not a hauler between here and the coast would do it. There's men on this road would have had you in the box." She could not see his face and he could not see hers, and he kept his eyes on the mare's ears and went on. "There's a box, on some of the wagons. Four foot by two. You go in it at dawn and you come out at dark and you don't talk to anybody because you can't get the air for it. I've never owned one. I've never wanted one. And I've never — not once, not with any of them — touched what I was hauling, and you can ask up and down this road, they'll tell you Marrick Fen brings it in the way he took it up. "I didn't make the writ. I didn't make Irongate. Irongate was there before my mother's mother and it'll be there when I'm in the ground, and the price they pay is the price they pay whether it's my wagon or Corry Bant's or some Sennet boy who'd have you in the box on the first day. That's not an excuse, it's arithmetic. Somebody hauls. If it's me, you get water when you ask. "And I'll tell you what else. Nine. Nine before you, and I can give you the name of every one of them, which is nine more than the man who signs the receipt can do. Patience out of Hask. Corvel. There was a boy at Weir Bridge called Ansel who couldn't have been sixteen and I gave him my own coat and he had it off me by the time we made the gate and I let him keep it, and I stood outside and I heard the bell go and I counted it and I know which stroke was his." He wiped his mouth. "So don't sit there being *polite* at me. I know what I am. I've known longer than you've been alive. I'm going to have nine acres and a spring and I'm not going to speak to another living soul, and when I'm dead there'll be a hole in the ground and no one'll put anything over it, and that's the whole of the account, and it balances." The gorse went by. The mare's ears went round and forward again. "Marrick," she said. "When you hand me over. Does the writ open the inner gate, or only the yard?" He had his mouth open for the next of it and nothing came. "What?" "The inner gate. There's a yard, and a ledger, and then there's a door behind the ledger. Does the writ take a man through that door, or do you stand in the yard with your hat in your hands and wait for them to bring the money out?" "You want to know how far in you're going." "I want to know how far in *you're* going." "They take you through," he said slowly. "Hauler comes to the table, the clerk weighs — there's a weighing, they take a cut off the finger and they weigh what comes out of it, that's how the price is set — and then two of theirs take you through and the hauler waits at the table for the count. Some of them let you come in as far as the second bench. Depends who's on." "Mm," she said. And then, after a while, in a different voice altogether: "It's Sorrow, by the way." "What is?" "My name. It was Temperance yesterday. I've thought about it and it's Sorrow." The rain came in an hour before dark, and it came in sideways. He got the canvas down and the mare in the lee of the wagon and himself under the tail-board with the fire going out in front of him like something drowning, and after twenty minutes of that he climbed up into the bed and found her soaked to the skin on the weather side. The canvas was old. It let water at the seam and the seam ran directly over her, and she was sitting under it with her arms up in the iron and her teeth going. "Right," he said. He got the knife out. She watched him come with it and said nothing at all, and he took the shoulder of the dress and cut, and cut down, and pulled the wet cloth off her in two pieces and dropped them out the back into the mud, and she was shaking too hard to make anything of it. He had the horse blanket and his own, and he dried her with his coat lining because it was what was dry, roughly, the way you rub down a beast, and got the blankets over her and round her and under her where he could, and there was no way to do it with her wrists up in the iron so he took the left cuff off and re-hooked it through the blanket and back into the iron, which was against every instinct he had. "You'd be no use to me with a chill," he said. "Eleven hundred crowns," she said, through her teeth. "That's right." Later, when she'd stopped shaking, he did her wrists. There was a raw ring on each and the right one had gone shiny and hot at the edge. He worked the salve in with his thumb, one wrist and then the other, in small circles, the way you'd do it to a girth gall — the heel of the hand, the little bones, the soft place under. It took a long time. She had her head turned away and her breath came slow and level and audible. Neither of them said anything for the whole of it. Rain on the canvas. He worked the salve in.

The toll-house at Coldwater was a stone box with a chimney and a bar across the road, and the man in it had a ledger, and Marrick's stomach turned over the moment he saw the ledger come out. "Writ." He handed it down. The clerk was young and clean and had ink on the side of his hand, and he read it the way clerks read, with his lips moving on the numbers and not on the words. "Sennet issue." "That's right." "Sennet's a nine-day writ." "It's a fourteen-day writ." "Sennet went to nine in the spring." The clerk turned the paper over as though the back of it might argue. "Countersign's Halloway. Halloway's not on the list any more." Somewhere behind Marrick's breastbone something cold came up through him, and it was worse than any of it — worse than the two men at the Weirs, worse than the dog at Hask. He had eleven hundred crowns in the back of that wagon under a horse blanket and a boy with clean hands was going to void it over a countersign. "He was on it in Sennet six days ago." "He may have been." "There's nothing wrong with that writ." "There may be nothing wrong with it." The boy put it down on the desk and squared its edges with two fingers, which Marrick would remember longer than he remembered the fight. "I'd have to hold the stock here and send to Irongate for a confirmation. Eight days, I should think. Ten. There's a pen out back." Marrick stood in the road with his hat in his hand and did arithmetic he did not want to do. Ten days of feed. Ten days of that boy's pen, and what came out of a pen at a toll-house after ten days would weigh light at the table, and the weighing was the price. "What's the toll," he said. "Wagon and beast, four pence." "What's the toll," Marrick said again, "with the stock." The boy looked at him for a moment with an expression of purely professional interest, and said, "Sixty." He paid sixty. It was two months of nails and salt and tobacco and it hurt him in a place further down than money usually reached, and he counted it out into the boy's clean palm and got his writ back with a fresh stamp on the corner, and the bar went up. She had heard the whole of it through the canvas. He knew she had. She said nothing until they were half a mile on and then she said, "Sixty." "Shut up." "I wasn't going to—" "Sixty," he said. "For a stamp." The two men came up on them at the ford below the wayhouse, and it took less than a minute and there was nothing in it he could be proud of. They were both younger and one had a mail shirt on under his coat, which Marrick found out with his knife. They wanted to buy her and he said no, and they said a price, and he said no again, and then the one in the mail took hold of the canvas and it stopped being a conversation. He got the first one across the forearm and put his shoulder into him and went down with him in the shallows, and he had eleven years of the Ninth Levy in his hands and none of it helped, because the other one came round the tail-board and got him low on the ribs with something short, and he felt the cold of it going in and the heat coming after, and then he was on one knee in eight inches of water with his hand pressed into his side and his knife two yards off in the gravel, and it was over. Then she started talking. He never got the whole of it. He had his head down and there was water going over his boots and a high thin note in his left ear, and above him her voice came flat through the collar, steady, unhurried, saying something about Halloway, and about a nine-day writ, and about how a stamped writ with a hauler's mark on it went into the Irongate ledger the same hour it came through the gate, and how the two of them might care to think about which of the three of them the Reckoners would send men out after, and whether either of them fancied being on a road with sixty pence of Coldwater stamp against their names. She said it the way a woman reads out a list of prices. Somewhere in it she started calling one of them *son*. By the time Marrick got up out of the ford they were on their horses, and one of them was saying something about no harm meant, and she was telling him, mildly, that there was harm meant and they both knew it, and he should get on. They got on. He stood in the water and bled and looked up at her. She was hanging forward in the iron with her hair in her eyes and her wrists taking her whole weight because she'd been leaning out to see, and she was breathing hard, and her tail was absolutely still. "You want to sit down," she said. He sat down on the tail-board and did the wound with his own hands because there was no one else to do it — it had gone in over the hip and out again through a fold of coat and it was long and shallow and full of ford-water, and he packed it with tow and salve and strapped it and it hurt more than the sixty pence. It came to him while he was pulling the strap tight. She had been six feet from open road for the whole of it. Both of them off the wagon. Him on his knees in the water. Twelve, fifteen seconds where nobody on that ford was looking at the back of a prison cart, and she had a chipped horn and no boots and she'd have got two miles at most, and she'd have got them. She'd leaned *out*. Towards it. He looked at the iron on her wrists and did not say anything, and she watched him not say it, and something went across her face that he could not read at all, and she turned her head away. Pilgrim was lame by the top of the rise. The splint on the off fore had come up hot and the mare was going short and dipping her head at every stride, and Marrick got down and felt it and swore twice, quietly, and then took the bridle in his hand and walked. Eleven miles and a bit to go, and a lame horse, and a hole in his side, and sixty pence gone. He walked at the mare's head with the reins over his arm and she talked at him from the wagon, and he answered, and neither of them used the horse's name again.

She waited until the afternoon had gone soft and yellow and there was nothing on the road ahead of them but road. "Marrick." "Mm." "I'm going to tell you something and you're going to keep walking." "I'm walking." "If my hands worked," she said, "the first thing I'd do is put them on the back of your neck. Not the front. You'd want the front, you'd expect it, you'd have your chin up ready for it. The back — up under the hair, both hands, thumbs in the hollow at the base of the skull. That's where you carry it. Six days I've watched you carry it there." He kept walking. "And I wouldn't say anything, and I wouldn't let you say anything either, because you'd start explaining. You'd tell me about the writ. So I'd put my thumb across your mouth and hold it there until you stopped." The mare went short-short-long on the off fore. Gorse, and the road, and a hawk sitting on a post doing nothing. "Then I'd get that coat off you, which will take some doing, because you sleep in it. Then the shirt. And then I'd stand you there and look at you for a while, and you'd hate it, you'd want to get your hands over yourself like a girl — no, don't make a noise, I'm not finished — and I wouldn't let you, and after about a minute of it something would happen to your breathing and you'd stop being able to hear the road." "Stop." "I'd start at the collarbone." Flat. Unhurried. The collar took the ring off her voice and left it lying against his ear like a hand. "Not with my mouth, with the flat of two fingers, and I'd go down slow enough that by the time I got anywhere near where you wanted me you'd have forgotten how to ask. And then I'd take my time. I've got nothing else to spend and I'd spend all of it. You've been six days in front of me, Marrick — I know how long you can stand a thing before you break. It's about forty minutes. It's about forty minutes and then you'd tell me anything I asked." He walked. His ears were going and his hand had come off the reins and gone flat against his chest, which was a thing he'd done as a boy when he was caught out in something. "Look at me," she said. He didn't. "That's what I thought." She went on for another mile and a quarter. He could not have repeated a sentence of it. When they came off the rise into the beech scrub he stopped and staked the mare and got the fire going with his hands not working properly, and he did not look into the back of the wagon once. He gave her the bread. He held it out and she took it off his fingers, and he was still not looking at her, and she said, "Say it." "Stop doing that." "Doing what?" "You know what." "Say what you want and I'll stop." "I want you to stop." "No," she said. "That's what you want me to *do*. What do you want?" And he stood there in the beech scrub with the fire going behind him and found there was nothing in him at all — no word, no shape, thirty-one years of not looking at a thing and now here it was and he had no name for it. He opened his mouth and shut it. His tongue found the bad molar and pressed. "I don't know," he said. "No," she said, quite gently. "I know you don't. Come here and I'll tell you." He came. She had him kneel up on the boards where she could reach him, which was not far, four foot of chain a wrist and her arms up over her head, and she could not use her hands at all and never once tried. Everything went through her mouth. *Slower. There. No — flat, all of it, the whole hand.* When his hands were clumsy she told him, and when they weren't she told him that too. He had the blanket back off her and she had nothing on and could not cover herself and did not appear to want to, and the iron was there above her wrists the whole time and he could not stop seeing it and she watched him not stop seeing it. "You can," she said. "You've been thinking about my wrists since Sennet. Go on." He put his hands round them, over the salve and the raw rings, and held. She made a sound then that was not for him at all — it went somewhere off past his shoulder — and her tail came up off the boards and went round his forearm, twice, and tightened. She told him what to do with his mouth, and he did it, and she was not gentle about the instruction and it did not last forty minutes and she did not seem to mind. She got a heel into the small of his back at the end and her wrists went hard against the iron above her, and after, she hung there in it breathing with her eyes shut, and the wagon creaked twice as it settled, and that was all. Then she said, "You've not — " and stopped, and said, "Come here, then." He did not know what he'd expected. It was fast and it was undignified and he had one hand braced on the wagon rib beside her head and his forehead down against the iron above her wrist and she talked the whole way through it, low, unhurried, into his ear, and when it went through him it went through him like the cold of the knife had, in first and hot after, and he heard himself make a noise he'd never heard from himself before. He sat back on his heels on the boards. And out of nowhere, unbidden, complete: *eleven hundred, less sixty at Coldwater, less two for the toll and the feed, that's a thousand and thirty-eight, eight hundred for the freehold, forty for the mule—* He stopped. He looked at the iron. He looked at the raw ring on the wrist nearest him, and the salve gone tacky, and the four feet of chain, and did the sum again from the top without meaning to, and found he could not stop doing it. "Marrick." He got the blanket over her. "Marrick." "What." "Bread," she said. "If you've got it. I'd rather bread than the rest of the conversation." He got the bread.

He found it in the morning, oiling the iron. It was in her right palm, held in the fold at the base of the fingers where a coin goes when a man doesn't want you to see him take it. A nail. Four inches, square-cut, wagon-stock, and bent — bent properly, in two places, a hook and a shoulder, the way a man bends one who has done it before. He took it out of her hand. She let him. He sat back against the ribs with it between his finger and thumb and turned it in the light. The oil was still on his hands. "Where." "The ford. It was in the boards by the wheel-box. You had your head under the water at the time." "It's bent." "Yes." "It's bent right." "It's bent right," she said. He said nothing for a long time. There was a wren going in and out of the gorse beside the road and he watched it and did not see it. "Six days," he said, "I've had that iron on you, and you've told me — you said to me on the salt that you couldn't feel your third finger. You said you couldn't get your own skirt up." "That was true." "And this?" "That's true as well." "You could have gone at the ford. There was nobody looking at that wagon for fifteen seconds. You had a bent nail in your hand and you leaned *out*—" "I leaned out to see if they'd kill you," she said. "It seemed material." He put the nail down on the boards between them, very carefully, the way you put down something that has gone off in your hand once already. "Why are you still here." She looked at him with those gold eyes with no white in them, and she did not answer, and he understood after a moment that she was not going to — not stalling, not building to it, simply not going to, and that if he sat there until the sun came round she would still be there and the answer would not. "You want to go in," he said. "Yes." "To Irongate." "Yes." "They'll bleed you at the table and take you through that door and you'll not come out of it. Nine, I told you. Nine and I've never had one come out." "I know what's through the door." "Then—" "No," she said. "There's something in there." "There's something in there." "What." "No." He got up. He got down out of the wagon, and stood in the road, and got back up into it, because there was nowhere to go and the whole of it was in there with her. "A person." "I'm not going to talk about it, Marrick. I've thought about whether to and I'm not. If you want to put the gag back on you can, it won't make any difference either way, it's the same silence." She said it without heat. "You'd only worry it. You'd worry it all the way down the switchbacks and by the gate you'd have talked yourself into something, and I need you to walk me up to that table and say what haulers say and take the money and not be doing anything else. That's all I need out of you. It's less than you've been doing all week." He stood there with his hands hanging. "You picked me," he said. It had come to him in the night and he'd put it away and here it was again. "At the crossroads at Sennet. There was four of us in that yard and you stood in the open and let me take you." "Yes." "Why me. Because I'm soft." "You're not soft. You paid sixty pence to a boy with clean hands rather than see me put in a pen for ten days, and you'd tell yourself that was the weighing." She let that sit. "No. I picked you because you smell like the underside of a forge, same as I do, and because you keep everything on you short except your hair." The wren came out of the gorse and went in again. "I heard you the first night," she said. "The little dry sound out by the fence post. I'd worked it out before you'd got the candle lit. Three or four strokes and a rest — you do it like a man planing a door he's ashamed of." He had his hand up at the side of his head before he knew it, and took it down. "You've been at that thirty years," she said, "so that when a man looks at you he doesn't see it, and every time you sit down at a table in this country they hand you a paper that says your blood's clean and you put it in your coat and you thank them. And then you haul us in. Nine of us. And you'll tell me it's arithmetic, and it *is* arithmetic, that's the horror of the thing, it balances beautifully—" "It was a sergeant," he said. She stopped. "At Bellow Ford. I was fifteen. I stood in the line and he came down it and he got to me and he said *not with those, son*, and went on down the line." Marrick was looking at the boards. "And there was a girl in Alder Cross called Ennet Vale who laughed. Not — she wasn't cruel with it. That's the thing you'd want to know. She laughed like you'd laugh at a dog in a hat. And I went home and my mother had a wood rasp in the drawer and had had it there since I was nine, and she got it out and she never said one word about it, then or after." The wren. The road. The mare shifting her weight off the bad leg. "So it's not what you said," he said. "You've made it big. It's a sergeant and a girl, and thirty-one years, and the paper's just the paper, they hand it to you and you put it in your coat because that's where paper goes." She had nothing to say to that, and did not pretend otherwise. He walked the mare the rest of that day and she said almost nothing, and by the afternoon he understood that this was not the polite silence of the second day and was not doing anything to him on purpose. She had folded herself down against the wagon rib with her cheek on the iron and her arms up in it and she was simply finished — grey around the mouth, breathing shallow, six days of shoulders and one night in her and nothing left over for him at all. He said, "Do you want water," and she said, "No," and that was the whole of the conversation between noon and dark. He found he could not bear it. He got two miles on and found he could not bear it, and went on being unable to bear it, and hated the sound of his own feet. The wind turned in the evening and came up out of the valley and brought the bell with it, very small and far off, striking somewhere down there under the smoke. He counted it. He couldn't help it. Nineteen.

He got the fire going in the beeches above the switchbacks and then he climbed up into the wagon with the key. She lifted her head off the rib. "What are you doing." "Nothing." He got the first cuff off. Her arm came down and she made a sound through her teeth like a man taking a splinter out. "Hold still." "Marrick—" "Hold still." The second one came off and both her arms were down and she couldn't do anything with either of them. He'd known that would happen. He'd seen it at Weir Bridge with the boy. He got her hands into his own and worked the fingers one at a time, and then the wrists, and then up the forearm with his thumbs, and she sat there with her head back against the ribs and swore steadily at the canvas in a language he didn't know. "Six days," he said. "I'm aware of how long it's been." "You could have said." "I did say. On the salt. You looked at the sky." He kept working. When the blood came back into her hands properly she pulled them away from him and looked at them, turning them over, and then she reached up and got hold of her own hair and pushed it back off her face with both hands, which was apparently the thing she'd been wanting for six days, because she shut her eyes doing it. "Why," she said. "Because I'm not going to be the man who didn't." "That's not a reason." "It's the reason I've got." She looked at him for a while. Then she put her hand flat on his chest and pushed, and he went back against the opposite rib with the tow packing pulling in his side, and she came after him. It was nothing like the night before. She had hands now and she was bad at it — greedy and out of practice and shaking with it, and she got his coat open and then couldn't get it off his shoulders and had to be helped, which she resented, and she said so. She got his shirt up and put her palms flat on him and stopped there a moment with her forehead against his breastbone, breathing, and he had his hands round the back of her ribs and could feel every one of them. Then her calf cramped. She went rigid and swore and half fell off him, and he had to take hold of her foot and put his thumb up into the arch and lean on it, and she lay on her back on the boards with her heel in his hand going *ah — ah — there — there* until it let go. "Sixty pence," she said, to the canvas. "For a stamp." He started to laugh and then couldn't stop, and it pulled the wound and he had to hold his side, and she began to laugh too and it was worse for her because she hadn't the breath. It went on for a while. Neither of them was any use for anything for a while. Afterwards she got herself up over him again, slower, and it was better slow, and she was still bad at it and it did not matter at all. She put her mouth on his throat and he felt her teeth there and she did not do anything with them. Then she got both hands up into his hair. He had it away from her before he'd made a decision — one hand round her wrist, hard, the way he'd taken the nail off her. She didn't fight him. She hung there on her other arm above him and waited, and he could hear himself breathing, and after a moment he let go of her wrist. She put her hands back up. Fingers in under the hair, both sides, and found the two hard places. Nobody had touched them since his mother. Her thumb went over the left one, and round it, and the ridge of scar where the file had gone too deep once when he was nineteen and drunk, and she did not say a word about any of it, and he found that his eyes had gone and his face was screwed up like a child's and there was nothing at all he could do about it. She kept her hands there. She kept them there through the whole of the rest of it, and he could feel his own pulse coming up into her palms. Later they lay on the boards under both blankets with the fire dying out through the gap in the canvas. "You're still not going to tell me," he said. "No." "There's a name in there. Something in the ledger." "Marrick." "I'd help. That's what I'm saying to you. Whatever it is—" "You'd help me right up to the moment it cost you eight hundred crowns," she said, "and then we'd both find out something we'd rather not know. So no." He thought about that for a while, and could not honestly say she was wrong, and did not say she was. "I'll walk you up to the table," he said. "Say what haulers say." "Say what haulers say. Take the money." "And not be doing anything else." "And not be doing anything else." "Then that's all of it." She turned over. "The chains go back on at dawn." "I know." "Not because you're making me. Because they'll be looking, and there's a Reckoner on the gate who's been doing it twenty years and he'll know a loose hauler at forty feet." She got her arm out from under and shook it. "Have you got the salve left?" He had. He did her wrists, one and then the other, and she let him, and then she said, into the dark: "I'm going to say this once and then never again, and you're not going to answer it." "Go on." "The gag," she said. "On the salt. Six days I've had it on you and I've not said it because I wanted you soft, and I'll want you soft in the morning too, so this is the only time it gets said." Her voice hadn't changed at all. "You put a bit in my mouth because I mentioned your mother. Everything you've done for me since — every bit of it, the oil and the sixty pence and the blanket and your hands, all of it — you were paying for that. And it isn't paid. It's not going to be paid. Not tonight and not at the table and not on your nine acres, and when you're old and there's nobody to talk to, that's the thing you'll still be doing sums about." He lay there. "That's all," she said. "Go to sleep." He did not sleep for a long time, and neither, by her breathing, did she, and neither of them said anything else.

Model Output:
She put her wrists up herself at dawn, before he'd got the key out. The switchbacks took two hours with a lame horse, and the valley came up out of the smoke a piece at a time: the wall first, then the roofs, then the four chimneys of the forge-house standing over everything with their heads in the weather. The gate itself was open. It was always open. He'd been coming here eleven years and had never once seen it shut, and had never before found that worth thinking about. There was a queue. That was the thing that got him, and it got him every time and it got him worse today. Two carters with pig iron. A woman with a barrow of cabbages arguing about her tally. Then him. The Reckoner on the gate was the same one — sixty, grey, a scar through one eyebrow — and he came down the line with a slate and looked at the mare's leg and said, "That'll not do another road." "No." "Fen, isn't it." "That's right." "Yard's on the left, past the weighbridge. Mind the cabbages." The yard was flagged and swept and there was a drain down the middle of it, and along the far side a long bench and a table and behind the table a door. Ordinary door. Oak, iron studs, a hatch at eye height with a plate over it. There were pot plants on the sill of the office window. Somebody watered them. He unhooked her and brought her down out of the wagon and she stood in the sun in her bare feet with her wrists in front of her and looked at the drain, and then at the door, and then she stopped looking at anything and just stood. The clerk was a woman of about fifty with spectacles on a cord. She had a ledger, and beside the ledger a tray with a small knife in it, and a brass cup, and a set of jeweller's scales. "Writ." He gave it her. "Sennet. That's a nine-day." The cold came up through him again exactly as it had at Coldwater, and he heard his own voice say, "There's a Coldwater stamp on the corner," and the clerk turned it and looked and said, "So there is. Sixty, was it? They've gone up." She wrote in the ledger. "Hauler's mark here. And here." He made his mark twice. "Right hand, please," the clerk said to her, not unkindly, the way you'd say it to someone at a cobbler's. She held out her right hand and the clerk took the third finger and pricked it below the nail and held it over the brass cup, and it came out black in the daylight and ran, and the clerk milked the finger twice with a professional thumb and then gave her a square of lint for it. The scales took a long time. The clerk moved little brass weights with a pair of tweezers and wrote a number and moved one back and wrote it again. "Eleven-forty," she said. "Writ says eleven hundred." "Writ says *not less than*. She's eleven-forty. Do you want it in the ledger as eleven hundred?" "No," Marrick said. "No," the clerk agreed, and wrote it, and turned the ledger round to him and put her finger under a line. "Name as taken, if you have it. Or description." He looked at where her finger was and saw that the line was already filled in, in a clerk's hand, three days ago, in the column headed *entered on advice*. *Aureth Vane. Warrens-born, 3rd quarter. Female, red, one horn.* He read it twice. He looked up at her and she was looking at the door, and she had known, and had known for six days, and had let him call her Temperance and then Sorrow all the way down the road, and he understood then that it had never been a game she was playing with him; it was simply a thing she was not prepared to hand over, and she had gone on not handing it over right up to the point where a woman with spectacles on a cord handed it to him for nothing. "That's correct," he said. Two of theirs came out from the office. Not brutes. Two men in aprons, one of them chewing something. They took her by the elbows, not hard, and one of them said, "Steps," because there were two steps up to the door. She turned her head. "Marrick." He had his hat in his hands. "Say what haulers say," she said. He said it. "Stock delivered whole and warm, one body, no debts against it." "That's it," she said. "That's the whole of it." They went up the two steps and the man in the apron worked the latch with his thumb and the door opened, and there was a corridor behind it with a lamp in a bracket and the floor sloping away, and it was not hell, it was a corridor. She did not look back. He had thought she would and she did not, and afterwards he was never sure whether that was for his sake or because there was nothing behind her worth turning round for. The door shut. It made a very small sound. "Count with me," said the clerk. It took a while. She did it in stacks of twenty on a felt cloth, sovereigns and half-sovereigns and the last of it in shillings because the tin was short, and she counted each stack twice and made him count the last one back, and put it in a canvas bag with a lead seal on the neck and wrote a receipt and stamped the receipt, and pushed it across. Eleven hundred and forty crowns. "Sign for the writ's discharge. Here." She capped her ink. "There's a farrier at the bottom of Wick Lane who'll give you something for the mare. She's not worth taking out again." He said thank you. He put the bag inside his coat and buttoned it, and it hung there against his ribs with a weight he hadn't been expecting, and he went out past the cabbages and the weighbridge and under the gate that was always open, and got the mare's head and walked. It took him better than two hours to make four miles, because she was going short and dipping and he wouldn't put her to the trot. The road came up out of the valley and there was a place at the top of the second switchback where the wind got round and you could see the whole of it below — the wall, the roofs, the four chimneys. He stopped there to let the mare blow. He stood in the road with the reins over his arm and the bag against his ribs and worked it through: eleven hundred and forty, less sixty at Coldwater, less the farrier's, and eight hundred for the widow, and forty for the mule, and sixty for the roof, and twelve for the share off Corry Bant, and a hundred and eighty put by against a bad year. Nine acres. A spring, with the sand jumping in the bottom of it. The mare stopped blowing and put her head down and began to eat the grass at the edge of the road. He did the sum again from the top. Behind him, down in the valley, the bell started. He stood there.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkable piece of writing that executes its plan with unusual discipline and intelligence. Let me work through it carefully. The chapter opens with a single sentence of devastating economy: "She put her wrists up herself at dawn, before he'd got the key out." This is the whole of her character in one gesture — the decision made, the performance of compliance that is also a kind of ownership. It follows the plan precisely and earns its placement. The bureaucratic texture is handled with genuine skill. The queue, the cabbages, the pot plants on the sill, the clerk with spectacles on a cord — these details are not decorative. They do the work the plan called for: Irongate is polite, ordinary, and that ordinariness is the horror. The blood-testing scene (the pricking, the black blood, the jeweller's scales, the professional thumb) is clinical and quietly devastating. The clerk's "not unkindly, the way you'd say it to someone at a cobbler's" is exactly the right register. The ledger revelation — *Aureth Vane. Warrens-born, 3rd quarter. Female, red, one horn* — lands with the weight the plan promised. The prose around it is restrained and precise: "he understood then that it had never been a game she was playing with him; it was simply a thing she was not prepared to hand over." This is not over-explained. It's given once and trusted. The farewell exchange is the chapter's emotional peak and it's handled with admirable restraint. "Say what haulers say" is a perfect line — she's asking him to perform the ritual that makes this real, and he does it, and it's the most intimate thing in the chapter. The plan called for her not looking back, and the prose earns that: "He had thought she would and she did not, and afterwards he was never sure whether that was for his sake or because there was nothing behind her worth turning round for." This is genuinely good — it holds two possibilities without resolving them, which is the right move. The ending is exactly what the plan promised: him doing the arithmetic again, the bell starting, him standing there. The plan said "end on him not moving" and that's what we get. The arithmetic is his prayer, his defense mechanism, his whole interior life — and the bell interrupts it, and he doesn't move. The story doesn't tell us what the bell means. It doesn't need to. The dialogue is sparse and functional throughout, which is correct for this chapter. "That'll not do another road." "Sixty, was it? They've gone up." These are the right voices for bureaucratic Irongate. The clerk's lines are particularly good — professional, not cruel, which is worse. Where the chapter is slightly less than perfect: the corridor description ("it was not hell, it was a corridor") is a good line but perhaps the one moment where the prose reaches for effect in a way that's slightly more visible than the rest. It works, but it's the one place where you can see the writer's hand. Also, the mare eating grass at the road's edge is a fine detail but the transition from the arithmetic to the bell could be one beat tighter. The chapter is consistent with both character profiles throughout. Marrick's compulsive arithmetic, his hat in his hands, his "thank you" to the clerk — all of it is him. Her putting her wrists up first, her final instruction to him, her not looking back — all of it is her. The plan called for "mostly paperwork" and the chapter delivers that without making it dull. The plan called for her true name arriving from a clerk's ledger, not from her mouth — executed perfectly. The plan called for him stopping on the road and not moving — executed. The plan called for no callback last line — honored; the bell is not a callback, it's an intrusion. This is disciplined, intelligent, emotionally precise writing. It does not overreach. Its metaphors are earned. Its silences are load-bearing. The darkness is well-earned because the whole story has been building to this ordinary door and this ordinary corridor and this very small sound. [Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of fantasy erotica that transcends its genre constraints to become something genuinely literary. Let me assess it carefully across all dimensions. **Craft and Execution** The prose style is distinctive and controlled: short declarative sentences, precise physical detail, a refusal to over-explain emotional states. The writer trusts the reader to infer. The recurring motif of arithmetic — Marrick doing his sums about the nine acres — is brilliantly deployed as both character revelation and structural spine. It never becomes a tic; it earns its repetitions because each iteration carries new weight. The dialogue is exceptional. It does multiple things simultaneously: reveals character, advances plot, creates tension, and contains genuine wit. "Her name's Bishop now. Sorry. It's done." is perfect. The exchange about the inner gate in Chapter 3 is a masterclass in subtext — she pivots from his emotional outpouring to a tactical question, and the pivot itself tells us everything about her. The collar detail — that it flattens her voice, takes the ring off it — is a beautiful piece of world-building that also functions as metaphor without being forced. **Character** Marrick is one of the more interesting morally compromised protagonists in this genre. The revelation about his own nature (the rasp, the sergeant at Bellow Ford) is handled with restraint and lands with genuine force. It recontextualizes everything — his nine-before-her, his arithmetic, his careful maintenance of the cargo. He is not a villain and not a hero; he is a man who has found a way to live with himself that is slowly being dismantled. Sorrow/Temperance/Aureth is equally well-drawn. Her tactical intelligence is consistent throughout — she is always working, always calculating — but the writer avoids making her purely instrumental. The moment she leans out toward the fight rather than away from it is the story's pivot, and it's earned. The final revelation of her name in the ledger is devastating precisely because it's so quiet. **The Erotic Content** The intimate scenes are handled with unusual skill. They are explicit without being pornographic in the degrading sense; they are embedded in the power dynamic and the emotional reality of the characters. The detail of her not being able to use her hands, the cramped calf interrupting the second encounter, the laughter — these are humanizing without being deflating. The moment with his hair is the emotional climax of the story, not the physical one, and the writer knows this. **Pacing** The pacing is excellent. Each chapter advances both the external journey and the internal one. The story knows when to slow down (the salt flats, the rain) and when to compress (the ford fight, which is deliberately rushed because Marrick is barely conscious for it). The final chapter is perfectly calibrated — the bureaucratic mundanity of the transaction, the pot plants on the windowsill, the clerk counting stacks of twenty on felt cloth. The door making "a very small sound" is exactly right. **Potential Weaknesses** The story occasionally risks preciousness — the "small and hot, like a seed in a tooth" simile is slightly overwrought, and there are a handful of moments where the prose reaches for effect a beat too hard. The "going through him like the cold of the knife had, in first and hot after" construction is the most egregious example of this. But these are minor. The transformation in Marrick is rapid but not unearned — six days is a long time on a road, and the writer has been careful to show the accumulation. The final image of him standing on the switchback doing his sums while the bell rings is perfect: he is unchanged and changed simultaneously, and the story refuses to resolve which. The world-building is economical and effective. Irongate, the Reckoners, the writ system, the weighing — all of it is conveyed through action and dialogue rather than exposition. The tiefling biology (tail, gold eyes, the blood that runs black) is integrated naturally. **Faithfulness to Prompt** The prompt is followed precisely and imaginatively. The three days, the king's ransom, the talking-into-an-early-grave — all present, all transformed into something more interesting than the prompt suggested. This is genuinely impressive work. Its flaws are minor and the ambition is largely realized.
