Small, careful, upright, ballpoint — the same hand, I'd bet money, that wrote the dates on the pantry doorframe. And they were recipes. That's what I need you to understand. They were ordinary competent recipes, written by somebody who cooked. One was for pancakes and it used the milled cap in place of half the flour and it said *don't bother with sugar, it's plenty sweet.* One was for a hash with potato. One was a stock, and it was a good stock, and the method was better than mine — she'd worked out that if you take the outer skin, the tarp part I'd been throwing away, and roast it hard first, you get something with real body in it, and I've used her way ever since and it's in this book on page fourteen with her name on it, except that I don't know her name. And the last one was the steaks, more or less as I do them, dry pan, don't crowd, and at the bottom in the same neat hand it said: *good with a little vinegar if you have it.* That's all. That's the whole of it. No warning anywhere on any of those cards. No line about the pamphlets. Nothing crossed out, no shake in it, no *God forgive us*, no note for whoever came next. # Fresh I came down at three in the morning on the second of January because I'd heard the kitchen door. It was open about a foot. There was snow on the boards inside it in a fan shape and the cold coming in off it like a hand, and there was one of them standing between the table and the stove. It filled that space. I'd never had one under a roof before and you don't understand the size of them until there's a ceiling above it — the top of it was maybe eight inches off my beams, pale in the dark, that close ridged grain, and the whole thing had a bloom on it like a plum. It was steaming faintly at the top where the warm air off the stove came up past it. It smelled of cut potato and, underneath, of the good smell, faint, the way an oven smells the morning after. I stood on the bottom stair. I want to put down what I did and not what it meant, because I've had eleven weeks to decide what it meant and I haven't got anywhere. I didn't scream. I didn't go back up for Teo. I went past it — within a foot of it, my hip brushed the table getting round — and I took the lid off the braise pot on the cool end of the stove, and I put a ladle of it in a bowl, and I set the bowl down on the table on the side nearest to it. Then I stood there with my hands on the back of a chair. It didn't take it. It hadn't got anything to take it with. I knew that. There's no mouth on the old ones, there hasn't been for years, and I have taken twenty of them apart with my own hands and I know exactly what is and isn't there. I did it anyway, is the point. Some part of me that has been doing this for fifty years looked at a thing standing in my kitchen and put food in front of it, and I have thought about that a great deal and I can't get it to mean anything except that habit goes down further than sense does. It stood there about four minutes. I counted, or I thought I was counting. Then it went out the way it came, sideways, careful of the frame, and it did not knock into one thing on the way, and I have wondered since about that too, in a house where Teo can't cross a room without catching the dresser. I shut the door and bolted it and mopped the snow up and washed the bowl and went back to bed and slept until eight. I didn't tell them for two days. Then I did tell them, at breakfast, flatly, and Teo said "*In* the house?" about six times and went and looked at the door, and Susannah said, "Well," and Wren wanted to know which one it was, whether it was Gary. Teo brought the fresh one in on the sixth. He'd gone down to the yellow house for the last of Susannah's kerosene and he was gone longer than he should have been, and he came up the lane pulling the sled with the tarp over it and I knew from the shape of it under the tarp before he'd got to the gate. The old ones don't lie like that. They haven't got the joints for it. He came into the kitchen and he was shaking. Not cold-shaking. He stood there with the rope still in his hand. "It was on the road," he said. "By the culvert. It was just — it was down already, Margit, it was down when I got there, I didn't do anything, it was already down in the ditch and it wasn't — " I said, "All right." "I didn't. It was already — " "Teo. All right." And he said, "Okay," and put the rope down, and went and sat on the floor by the stove and hummed for a while, those four notes, and then stopped. Nobody said anything. Susannah was at the window with the sock and she did not turn round and she did not put the sock down. Wren was under the table and stayed under it. There was no conversation. There had never been a conversation, that was the whole arrangement, and this was the other end of the same silence we'd started in October, and it turned out to be a very short piece of rope from one end to the other. I did it in the shed with the doors shut. It's different. That's all I'll put in the practical part of this book and I'd want whoever's reading it to take it as practical: it is different work and it takes longer and it doesn't come apart along seams, it comes apart along joints, because they're still there. There is more waste. There is a great deal more waste. I was two hours in that shed and I came out and washed to the elbow twice in water I'd carried and heated myself. And then I cooked it, and I'm going to say the thing I've been walking around for six chapters. It was the best thing I have ever cooked in my life. I've had thirty-two years. I have cooked for four hundred people in a night. I have cooked one dish eleven thousand times and got it right eleven thousand times and been proud of it. And I stood at that stove on the sixth of January and put a piece of it in my mouth off the tip of the knife and it was the best thing that has ever come off any range I have worked, and I say that as a professional, and I don't expect it to be forgiven and I'm not asking. It didn't taste of my mother's paprika. It didn't taste of anything I could name at all. It was just further along. Everything else had been in that direction and this was further along it. They all ate. Every one of us. Susannah had two helpings and said nothing about the salt, and that was worse than if she'd said something. Wren's tooth came out at breakfast on the ninth. She was eating and she stopped and put her fingers in and came out with it and held it up, delighted, because she's eleven and that's the correct response. "That's four," she said. It was a molar, and it was clean, and there was no blood in the socket at all. There was something soft in there instead. White, and fine, and not much of it, like the first fur on a jar of jam. I said, "Let me see." She tipped her head back and opened her mouth and let me, and I looked at it in the window light for a good while, and Susannah came and looked too and stood up straight afterwards and went back to her chair. And Wren said, "Do I still put it under the pillow?" I said she did. "Because there's no — I know there's no. But does it still *work?*" And I said we'd find out, and she put it under the pillow, and I put a sugar packet under there in the night out of the stash she thinks I don't know about, and in the morning she was pleased and made a great deal of it and asked whether it would work again for the next one. There were two other chimneys going in the valley that January, Kessler's and the one down past the bridge that I never knew who had, and I could see them both from the top window, morning and evening, every day.

This is exactly the voice promised — practical, self-aware about its own limits, refusing to philosophize while philosophizing anyway. The cook's professional pride in the declaration about the best thing she's ever cooked is devastating precisely because it's delivered in the register of a performance review. **The Three-A.M. Scene** The standing one in the kitchen is handled with extraordinary restraint. The detail of the bloom like a plum, the steam at the top where warm air rises, the smell of cut potato — these are specific and strange without being overwrought. His repetition — "It was down already, Margit, it was down when I got there, I didn't do anything" — is exactly right for his character: narrating himself, trying to establish a version of events, needing absolution without asking for it. Margit's "All right" twice is perfect. The humming of the four notes, then stopping, is the right amount of detail. The rope image — "a very short piece of rope from one end to the other" — is one of the few metaphors in the chapter and it lands cleanly. **The Butchery Paragraph** The plan called for "one paragraph of genuine unpleasantness" and the chapter delivers it with appropriate restraint: "it doesn't come apart along seams, it comes apart along joints, because they're still there. This is not gross-out; it's professional assessment, which is its own horror. **The Best Thing She Ever Cooked** The declaration is earned. The chapter has been building to it. "I say that as a professional, and I don't expect it to be forgiven and I'm not asking" — this is the chapter's moral center, delivered without drama. Susannah having two helpings and saying nothing about the salt is a perfect character beat: the plan called for it to be "worse than if she'd said something," and the execution makes that implicit without stating it. **Wren's Tooth** This is the chapter's most unsettling moment and it's handled with exactly the right flatness. "Something soft in there instead. White, and fine, and not much of it, like the first fur on a jar of jam." The simile is specific and domestic and wrong in the right way — it's not a horror-movie image, it's a kitchen image, which is worse. Wren's response ("Do I still put it under the pillow?") is perfect for her character: not creepy, just practical, just eleven. The sugar packet Margit puts under the pillow in the night is the chapter's most quietly devastating moment — the same habit that put a bowl in front of the creature in the kitchen, the same fifty years of feeding and caring, now applied to a child who is becoming something else, and Margit does it anyway. **The Final Line** "There were two other chimneys going in the valley that January, Kessler's and the one down past the bridge that I never knew who had, and I could see them both from the top window, morning and evening, every day." This is exactly right. It implies everything and states nothing. The plan called for "two other chimneys smoking. One line." The execution gives it slightly more — the specificity of Kessler's, the unnamed one, the morning and evening rhythm — and it's better for it. **Weaknesses** There are very few. The chapter is almost uniformly excellent. One small issue: "it was the best thing that has ever come off any range I have worked" — "range" feels slightly off for Margit's voice; she'd more likely say "stove" or "line." Minor. The transition from the three-a.m. scene to Teo's return is handled with a simple "Teo brought the fresh one in on the sixth" which is appropriately flat but could be accused of being slightly abrupt even by this story's standards. These are genuinely minor complaints. **Adherence to Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely and improves on it in several places. The three-a.m. scene, Teo's return, the butchery, the declaration, Wren's tooth, the two chimneys — all present and executed. The plan's note that "nobody says a word" when Teo returns is honored. The plan's note about Wren being "unbothered" is honored. The sugar packet detail is not in the plan and is the chapter's best addition. **Overall** This is exceptional work. The horror and the coziness are genuinely the same substance here. The chapter does what the best horror does: it makes you feel the warmth of the fire and the wrongness of the warmth simultaneously, without ever separating them into alternating beats. The voice is sustained, the characters are consistent, the restraint is almost total, and the moments that land do so because of that restraint. # How to Bank the Stove Susannah does the cooking now. She does it badly. I want that on the record along with everything else. She boils what wants roasting and she puts the pot on the hot end and walks away from it and she has never once in her life let a pan get properly hot before she puts anything in it, and I sit in the chair by the window and watch her do it, and I say so, and she says, "Well, get up then," and I don't get up, and we go on. My hands stopped being any use in the last week of January. It isn't pain. I want to be accurate because I've read what people wrote about this in the spring, in the pamphlets and on the boards at the crossroads, and they all had it as agony, and mine isn't. My fingers have gone thick at the joints and they don't close the whole way and they don't come apart the whole way either, and there's a stiffness through the wrist and up, and it's the feeling of a sleeve that's dried in a shape. That's all. I can hold a pencil against the side of my hand and write, which is what I'm doing, and I can hold a cup, and I cannot hold a knife by the spine and rock it, which is the thing I could do better than most people alive and which I did for thirty-two years, and I've had to stop going in the kitchen when she's cooking because I can't watch it. I never could. The flue's smoking. It's been smoking since December and it wants sweeping and none of us is going to sweep it, and every evening at about six the good room fills up grey at ceiling height and Susannah says the thing about the flue and I say I'll see to it and everybody knows I won't. That's this evening. That's tonight, the twenty-eighth of February, which I've had to ask about twice. Wren's reading. She got hold of the fat one about the sailing ship in November and she's been at it since, and she reads aloud in the evenings and skips any word she doesn't like the shape of, so we've had four months of a story with holes in it and none of us has ever asked her to go back. Teo's asleep on the floor by the stove with his coat over him. He goes down at about seven now, sitting up first and then over sideways, and he sleeps twelve, thirteen hours, and wakes up cheerful. Susannah's in the chair with the sock. She has been mending that sock since August. There is more of Susannah's thread in it than there is of sock. I have offered her another sock. She has one of mine in her basket and won't start it. I'll put the last of the practical things down while it's quiet, because that's the assignment and I've made a poor job of sticking to it. There's about sixty pounds on the racks and two pillowcases of the meal in the cold pantry, which is more than we'll need. The starter's in the crock and it wants feeding twice a week and Wren does it and does it properly. Roast the outer skin before you make the stock — that's not mine, that's the woman with the four cards, and her way is better than my way, and her cards are in the pocket at the back of this book where I found them, and I've left them there. Don't crowd the pan. That's the whole of the steaks and it's the only thing anybody ever gets wrong. The one I'd want you to have, if you got this book off the table and you're standing in my kitchen and you don't know what you've walked into: **How to bank the stove so it holds till morning.** Let it burn down to a bed of coals about two inches deep and no flame — you'll be tempted to do it too early, don't, wait for the flame to go. Rake the coals level to the front where the air comes in, not to the back. Then lay one big piece on. One. Not three small ones, they'll burn out by two in the morning and you'll be up in the cold splitting kindling with your hands like mine. You want the biggest ugliest round you've got, the one you've been leaving in the pile all winter because it wouldn't split — that's the one. Green's fine. Green's better. Lay it on top of the coals, don't bury it. Then shut the ash door most of the way and close the damper to about a thumb's width and leave it alone. Don't check it. That's the last part and it's the part everybody fails. You'll want to open it at midnight and look, and if you open it you'll lose it. Leave it shut. It'll be there in the morning under the ash, orange, about the size of your two fists, and all you have to do is rake it forward and put the kettle on. If you get that right you never have to start a fire again all winter. You start one fire in October and you tend it. That's the whole thing. That's all of it. Wren's put the book down to say the word she just skipped was on purpose because it was a stupid word, and I've agreed with her, and she's carrying on. She's got a pale patch in the crook of her left arm, at the elbow. About the size of a thumbnail. It's soft. It's been there since the middle of the month and it doesn't bother her and she scratches at it the way you'd scratch a scab. Teo's hairline is going back at the temples in two clean curves and he's decided it's a wolf thing and he's pleased about it. Susannah's wrists have filled out so she doesn't look at them any more. Mine's under the tongue, and I'm not going to write about it. They're out at the fence. Five of them along the west side and one at the gatepost, which is Gary, and Wren says Big Gary's got more snow on him than he had, and the snow doesn't come off them, and they've stood there since November without moving. I keep thinking I ought to put something here at the end. Something for whoever's got this. I've started it four times tonight and taken it out four times because every version of it came out either sorry, which I'm not, or sensible, which is a thing I've got no business being at this hour. So I'll say only that it's warm in this room. The flue's smoking and there's a girl reading a book wrong and a boy asleep on the floor and a woman who has told me my hand is heavy at every meal she has ever eaten under my mother's roof, and we are all four of us full, and we have been full since October, and I would do the whole of it again tomorrow morning without being asked twice. The bread's on the fifth page. One big round, coals to the front, damper a thumb's width, and don't open it.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkable piece of writing that executes its plan with almost surgical precision. Let me work through it carefully. **Voice and Frame** The voice is the chapter's greatest achievement. Margit sounds exactly like the character profile describes: practical, slightly contemptuous of sentiment, proprietary about her craft, and incapable of the literary gesture she keeps reaching for and pulling back from. "I've started it four times tonight and taken it out four times because every version of it came out either sorry, which I'm not, or sensible, which is a thing I've got no business being at this hour" — this is exactly right. It's a character refusing to perform emotion while performing it anyway, and the refusal is the emotion. The voice never slips into self-consciousness or authorial intrusion. The frame device — a practical document contaminated by memory — is executed beautifully. The stove-banking instructions are genuinely useful and technically specific, and they're also the most emotionally resonant thing in the chapter, because they're about tending something through the night without checking on it, which is what Margit has done with these people. That's not a heavy-handed metaphor; it emerges from the material naturally. **Character Consistency** Every character is exactly where they should be. Susannah mending the same sock, refusing to start a new one. Teo asleep on the floor, going down at seven, waking cheerful. Wren reading aloud and skipping words. Susannah still cutting about the cooking. These are not gestures toward character; they're the characters themselves, rendered in behavior. The detail about Susannah's wrists filling out and her not looking at them anymore is devastating and earns its place. The horror details are dropped with exactly the flatness the plan called for: Wren's pale patch in the crook of her arm, scratched at like a scab. Teo's hairline receding in "two clean curves" and him deciding it's "a wolf thing" and being pleased. The thing under Margit's tongue that she won't write about. These are not announced. They are not italicized. They are placed between domestic observations and left there. **The Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely. The smoking flue, Susannah cooking badly, Wren reading aloud and skipping words, Teo asleep, the flat unremarked horror details, the stove-banking instructions as the final practical entry, the ending that refuses a bow. The "pale bloom in the crook of Wren's arm" is there. Teo's hairline is there. The last entry is the stove instructions. The invitation is left incomplete. The one element from the plan that's handled slightly differently: the plan mentions "Margit finishes the practical part of the book because that's the useful part" and the chapter does this, but it also includes Margit's four failed attempts at a closing statement, which is a small addition that works better than the plan's version would have. It's an improvement on the plan, not a deviation from it. **What Doesn't Work** Very little. The line "mine's under the tongue, and I'm not going to write about it" is perhaps the one moment where the horror is slightly too pointed — the refusal to write about it is itself a kind of writing about it that draws more attention than the other dropped details. The other horror details work because they're embedded in observation; this one is a direct statement of withholding, which is a slightly different and slightly lesser technique. But it's a minor complaint. The phrase "about the size of your two fists" in the stove instructions is a small tonal wobble — the sudden second-person "you" in an otherwise first-person document. It's defensible as a recipe convention, and the plan does mention recipe fragments, but it's a slight seam. **The Ending** "The bread's on the fifth page" — this callback to the opening of the whole document is exactly right. It's not a beautiful line. It's a practical redirect. And it lands harder than any beautiful line would. The repetition of the stove instructions as the final words is the correct choice: the reader is left with a practical task, and the dread is entirely supplied by what they've just read. The penultimate paragraph — "it's warm in this room... and we are all four of us full, and we have been full since October, and I would do the whole of it again tomorrow morning without being asked twice" — is the chapter's emotional center, and it earns it. The horror and the coziness are the same substance, as the plan promised. Margit is not sorry. She would do it again. And the reader believes her, and is warm, and is horrified. **Overall** This is a chapter that does what it sets out to do at a very high level. The voice is consistent and specific. The horror is real and unannounced. The characters are themselves. The practical frame earns its emotional weight. The ending refuses sentimentality without refusing feeling. It is not perfect — the "mine's under the tongue" line is slightly too pointed, and there's a minor second-person wobble — but these are small complaints against a chapter that is, in its way, a small masterpiece of the form it's working in. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptional piece of post-apocalyptic fiction that operates almost entirely against genre conventions. Rather than delivering action, horror, or dramatic confrontation, it delivers something far more difficult: the texture of survival as domestic routine, the way catastrophe becomes ordinary, and the slow, quiet horror of transformation that nobody names aloud. The narrative voice is the piece's greatest achievement. Margit's voice is utterly consistent across all eight chapters — dry, precise, self-aware without being self-congratulatory, and possessed of a dark humor that never tips into irony for its own sake. The cookbook framing device is not merely clever; it's structurally load-bearing. The recipes interrupt and anchor the narrative, and the tension between the practical (don't crowd the pan) and the existential (what exactly are we eating, what are we becoming) is maintained with remarkable discipline throughout. The characters are genuinely nuanced. Susannah's arc — from refusing to eat, to being broken by the smell of bread, to eventually cooking herself — is handled with extraordinary restraint. The moment where she eats the bread crying, furious, "the way you'd cry at a machine that wouldn't work," is one of the finest character moments in the piece. Teo's bee theory, his cartoon dog tattoo, his habit of getting in front of the joke — these are specific, lived-in details that make him real. Wren's unsentimental adaptation (eating the forbidden food four times in one morning and never mentioning it again) is genuinely chilling and true to how children process the unprocessable. The horror elements are handled with masterful restraint. The spore mutants are never over-explained. The piece trusts the reader to feel the wrongness accumulating: the pencil marks on the doorframe, the reading glasses in the mud, the four recipe cards from an unknown woman, Wren's tooth with something soft in the socket, the changes in Teo's hairline, Margit's hands, the thing under her tongue she won't write about. These details land because they're embedded in the domestic texture rather than spotlit. The horror is cozy in the most genuinely unsettling sense — it's happening inside warmth, inside routine, inside care. The dialogue is excellent. It's specific, character-revealing, and often funny without being written-for-laughs. The exchange about Gary and Big Gary, the argument about whether cake counts as dinner, Susannah's "You've oversalted the crust" after eating the bread while crying — these are all perfectly calibrated. The dialogue never explains itself. The pacing is deliberate and controlled. Some readers might find it slow, but the slowness is the point — it mirrors the experience of a long winter with nothing to do but tend the fire and count the days. The structure of moving from chapter to chapter through the winter, each anchored by a recipe or practical concern, gives the piece a satisfying architecture. The world-building is accomplished almost entirely through implication. We never get an infodump about what happened. We get the county pamphlets, the radio crackling once, the two other chimneys visible from the top window, Sparks being gone by May. This is exactly right. The piece's central conceit — that the spore mutants are delicious, and that eating them causes transformation — is handled with extraordinary subtlety. The transformation is never announced. It accumulates: the shared dreams of standing in warm fields, each person tasting a different beloved meal from the same pot, the physical changes in the final chapter. The piece earns its darkness completely. The final chapter's inventory of changes — Wren's pale patch, Teo's receding hairline, Susannah's filled-out wrists, Margit's thing under the tongue — is devastating precisely because it's delivered in the same flat, practical voice as the recipe for banking the stove. The piece ends on warmth and fullness and the implicit horror of what that warmth and fullness is costing them, and it refuses to editorialize. Weaknesses are minor. Occasionally the voice risks becoming too self-consciously literary — the observation about habit going "down further than sense does" is slightly too neat. The Loretta digression in Chapter 5, while characterful, slightly disrupts the momentum. The piece is long, and a few of the November passages could be tightened. But these are small complaints against a genuinely accomplished work. The piece is faithful to the prompt, creative in its execution, coherent across its considerable length, and emotionally devastating in a way that earns every moment of it. # Brainstorming **Unpacking the prompt.** "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows." The voice is wry, retrospective, faintly boastful — a first-person narrator with practiced criminality or practiced trespass. "One quickly learns" implies necessity and repetition. Who enters manors through upper windows? A cat burglar. A jewel thief. A spy. A resurrectionist. A lady's illegitimate son gathering proof of parentage. A doctor smuggled in to attend a lady whose illness must not be known. A woman disguised as a man. A young widow visiting her lover. A chimney sweep grown up into second-storey work. A private inquiry agent. A poacher's daughter. A cracksman's apprentice. An escaped asylum patient returning home. **Romance angles:** 1. *Thief and the master of the house.* Classic and satisfying. She burgles the same manor twice; the second time he's waiting, and instead of the constable he offers her a bargain. Slow build of mutual recognition — two people who both live behind facades. 2. *Thief and the imprisoned heiress.* She climbs in to steal and finds a woman locked in the east wing — not mad, merely inconvenient. The romance is between the two women, or between thief and heiress's brother. 3. *Two thieves.* She climbs in through the window and finds someone else already at the safe. Rivals, then partners, then lovers. Fun banter, heist plot. 4. *Physician and patient.* A woman doctor (unlicensed, or a licensed apothecary/midwife) smuggled up a ladder to attend the lady of the house, whose condition is scandalous. The romance: the lady's brother? The lady herself? Or the man who holds the ladder every night. 5. *Reverse gender.* Male narrator — a young man, disgraced, who climbs to a young woman's window nightly. But the prompt's wry practicality suits a woman narrator better; it subverts expectations more pleasingly. Actually: a male narrator who is a *thief* and falls for the lady of the house whose jewels he's stealing — also good, and a nice inversion of the "gentleman burglar" trope if he's decidedly *not* a gentleman. 6. *Governess/tutor secretly educating herself.* Someone climbing into a library at night to read books she's forbidden. Sweet, quiet, but low stakes. 7. *Spy/political.* Fenian dynamite plot, Crimean-era letters, blackmail of a cabinet minister. Adds thriller texture but may crowd out romance in 8000 words. 8. *Letter-thief.* She's employed to retrieve compromising letters — a specialist in "recovering" indiscretions for wealthy families. This gives her a professional identity, a reason to enter many manors, and moral ambiguity. She retrieves letters for a fee; then she's hired to retrieve letters *from* a man she comes to love, or hired against a woman she pities. 9. *The house itself as the mystery.* She burgles a manor and finds the master has been drugged/held by his own steward or fiancée. She becomes his only access to the outside world, climbing nightly. 10. *Debt and inheritance.* Her family's house was sold out from under them; she enters her *own former home* through the upper windows to retrieve what was hers. The new owner catches her. Delicious — the intimacy of her knowing every creak of a house that is no longer hers, and his slow realization that she knows the place better than he does. **Idea 10 feels strong and fresh.** Combine with 1 and 8: A young woman, Rosalind/Verity/Constance, whose father died in debt (or in disgrace — a bank failure, a fraud accusation). The estate sold. She now works as a "recovery agent" for a discreet London firm — retrieving letters, jewels, indiscretions — because she learned to climb out of her own nursery window as a child and never lost the knack. Her final commission brings her back to her childhood home, now owned by a new man — a manufacturer? a barrister? a man who bought the house with new money and is despised by the county. She's hired by a third party to steal something from him. She finds instead evidence of her father's innocence — or evidence of his guilt, which is worse. **Characters:** - **Narrator: Miss Theodosia "Thea" Marchmont?** Hmm, too grand. Try **Juliet Rook** — a bird name, apt for climbing. Or **Verity Fane**. Or **Cordelia "Delia" Vance**. Let's consider **Miss Rosamund Wilde**... Settle later. Something with a slightly common surname beneath a genteel Christian name signals fallen gentility: **Isabel Crane**? Crane is good — long-legged, climbing. **Isabel Crane**, aged 26, sharp, unsentimental voice, gloves worn at the fingertips, an inventory of the manors of England catalogued by drainpipe. - **The man: Mr. Gideon Hale**, 34, ironmaster/engineer from Manchester or a colliery owner's son, bought the Hall three years ago. Or better: he's a *surveyor/engineer* who bought it cheap and is doing something odd with it — draining, rebuilding, tearing out the panelling. Which enrages her: he's dismantling her memories. But he's dismantling them because he's searching for something too. Oh — that's a lovely convergence: they are both searching the same house for the same hidden thing. He bought the house *because* of what might be in it. - Why? His father was ruined by hers — or his father was the clerk who took the blame for her father's fraud and hanged himself/transported. So Gideon believes her father guilty and has bought the house to prove it and clear his father's name. She believes her father innocent. They both want the same papers, for opposite reasons. Excellent engine. - **Third party antagonist:** the man who hired her. **Sir Lucian Bellhaven** / **Mr. Prothero**, a solicitor or the co-director who actually committed the fraud and now wants the evidence destroyed. He hired Isabel precisely because she knows the house — cruel irony; he thinks her a tool. Reveal: he ruined her father, and he has been employing her for years, keeping her close and starving, enjoying it. Good. - **Supporting:** a housekeeper who recognises her — **Mrs. Purefoy** / **Mrs. Sowerby** — kept on by the new owner. Her old nurse? That's a nice emotional hinge: the one person who knew her as a child, now bound to a new master, who must choose. Also a boy, a bootboy/apprentice, who spots her and keeps mum for sixpence. And a **dog**, which is a good practical obstacle and a good emotional one when it remembers her. **Tone.** Wry, precise, sensuous about texture — lead flashing, ivy, wet slate, hot wax, the smell of a house. First person, retrospective, slightly arch, with sudden drops into feeling. Think Sarah Waters' *Fingersmith* narration crossed with Georgette Heyer's lightness; some Wilkie Collins plotting. Period markers: 1867–1874ish. Railways, telegraph, joint-stock banking crashes (Overend & Gurney, 1866 — perfect: a real bank collapse to hang the ruin on). Set present action 1873. Father's ruin 1866. She was 19 then, 26 now. **Structural options for 8 chapters (~1000 words each = 8000 words total — tight!).** Version A (chronological, single house): 1. The art of entering (voice-establishing burglary at a different house; commission received). 2. Return to Ashcombe/Thrushcross; up the ivy; the house is wrong inside. 3. Caught — but by the housekeeper, or by the dog. Encounter with Gideon in the dark, unrecognised. 4. She returns as a guest/employee under a false name? (Risky — may overcrowd.) 5. Discovery of his purpose; joint search. 6. The papers found; the truth is double-edged (father partly guilty). 7. Prothero arrives; confrontation; fire or flood or fall. 8. Resolution: the window, reversed — she lets him in, or she leaves openly by the front door. Version B (frame narrative): She narrates from years later, married, in the same house, teaching her daughter to climb. Opening and closing frame. Charming, gives the wry voice its justification. Version C (dual timeline): alternate chapters between 1866 and 1873. Elegant but expensive in 8000 words. Version A + light frame from B seems right. **Set pieces to include:** - The mechanics of climbing: sash windows, putty, a knife, a length of picture wire to lift the catch; the leaded valley between roofs; the nursery window whose catch never held. That detail is the story's heart: *she can only get in because of a fault her own child self discovered.* - The smell of a house you grew up in. - Panelling torn out; her mother's mural under the wallpaper; the schoolroom used as a store. - A first meeting in absolute darkness where they speak but do not see. - A second meeting by daylight where he doesn't know she's the burglar — no, better: he *does* know, immediately, and says nothing, which unsettles her more. - A shared, silent search behind the chimney breast. - Rain on the roof; the two of them on the leads at dawn. - Kiss on a window ledge (romance requires a physical climax of some sort; a ledge kiss is irresistible and thematically apt). - The villain's arrival with a constable/thief-taker. - Final image: a front door, open. Or the reverse: he climbs to *her* window at the end, having learned the art. **The hidden thing.** Options: a ledger; a codicil; letters between her father and Prothero; a bearer bond; a false set of accounts. Best: her father's own confession-and-accusation, written before his death, hidden where only a child would look — inside the nursery window seat / behind the loose brick in the nursery chimney / in the hollow newel post. Even better: it's hidden in the *dolls' house* — a scale model of the manor itself, which her father made, and which contains a folded paper in its own miniature nursery. That's a beautiful object: a manor entered from above, a lid lifted off. And it explains the roofline knowledge. The dolls' house was sold at auction and Gideon bought it back / it's in the attic. Yes. Use the dolls' house. Wait, refine: the paper is in the dolls' house's nursery chimney. She knows because as a child she hid things there. Father knew she hid things there. He left it for her, believing she'd come home. She never did — she thought the house lost forever. Devastating and good. **Complication of moral texture.** The document should not simply exonerate. Let it say: her father signed what he knew to be false, out of cowardice and hope, and Prothero directed it, and Gideon's father (Hale senior, a clerk) was made to sign too and then blamed. So: both fathers guilty-and-victim. That gives the lovers equal footing and makes the ending about choosing each other over vindication. Prothero must be undone by his own signature on the accompanying letters. **Ending options.** (a) Prothero prosecuted; they marry; frame closes with her teaching her daughter to climb. (b) Prothero escapes but is ruined socially; they burn part of the papers to protect both fathers' memories and keep only what condemns Prothero. (c) She leaves; a year later he climbs to her window in a Camden lodging house, badly, and falls into her room. Very charming ending line: he has learned the art, poorly. I like (b) + (c) combined, then frame. **Possible titles:** "The Art of Upper Windows," "A Fault in the Sash," "The Nursery Window," "Ashcombe." House name candidates: Ashcombe Hall, Thrushmere, Hollybourne, Marlcote, Wrenfield, **Caldicott Hall**, **Larkspur**... Let's use **Hollow Ash** or **Ashcott Hall**. Pick **Ashcott Hall** — plain, northern-Midlands feel. Or since he's a Manchester ironmaster, set it in Cheshire/Derbyshire border. **Ashcott Hall, Derbyshire.** Good — gritstone, ivy, cold rain. **Chapter-by-chapter drafts (Version A refined):** Ch1: Frame line + the art itself. A demonstration burglary at Lady Somebody's house in London to establish voice, skill, employer (Prothero's agency), her history in compressed strokes. Ends: Prothero gives her the Ashcott commission and she recognises the name. Ch2: Journey, reconnaissance, the climb, the nursery window's fault, entry, the wrongness of the house (panelling stripped, mural exposed), and the first encounter — a voice in the dark, a lamp, and she escapes with a torn sleeve, leaving a glove. Ch3: She can't leave; she takes a room at the village inn; the housekeeper (her old nurse) recognises her in the churchyard; exposition of Gideon's arrival and purpose; the returned glove delivered to the inn with a note inviting her to dine. Nervy. Ch4: Dinner at the Hall by the front door. Fencing conversation; he knows; he shows her the drawing room, the stripped walls, tells her what he wants and who his father was. She denies her father's guilt. Antagonism with heat under it. He offers a truce/alliance: search together. Ch5: The search. Chimney breasts, cellars, the attic. Intimacy of labour. The dolls' house discovered under a dust sheet — but empty; the miniature nursery chimney bricked/soldered? Or the dolls' house is missing its roof/attic and she realises the real hiding place is the *real* nursery, and vice versa. Let's keep it: they find the dolls' house, she opens it, the paper is gone. Someone has been there first. Dread. Ch6: Who took it — the nurse/housekeeper, who has been paid by Prothero for years to watch and to send word if anyone came. She took it in 1866 and never handed it over out of love/fear; she gives it up now. Reading it: both fathers dirty, Prothero the architect. The kiss on the leads at dawn. Then: Prothero's telegram/arrival. Ch7: Confrontation. Prothero with a police inspector and a warrant for her arrest (a genuine one — she is a thief, and he has evidence). Gideon must choose; she must choose which papers to produce. Fire? Chase over the roof? Let's have: she goes up and out onto the roof with the papers; Prothero follows (badly); the roof, the rain; he falls or is left clinging; she saves him or doesn't; the inspector reads the letters. Ch8: Aftermath: Prothero's trial or flight; her arrest brief and dismissed / she must leave England for a time? Better: she is charged with lesser thefts, Gideon and the nurse testify, she serves nothing or a short sentence — hmm, too legalistic for 1000 words. Simpler: Prothero, to save himself from the letters, withdraws the charge; he is ruined; she goes anyway, out of pride, to earn honest money. Then the coda: months later, at her Camden window, a clumsy man on a ladder. Final frame: the two of them at Ashcott, the daughter, the window catch left unmended on purpose. **Pacing check.** 8 chapters × ~1000 = 8000 words. Ch1 exposition-heavy; Ch4 dialogue-heavy; keep Ch7 lean and physical; Ch8 short and warm. Need to resist subplot bloat: no siblings, no rival suitors, no elaborate heist crew. Cast: Isabel, Gideon, Prothero, Mrs. Sowerby (nurse/housekeeper), plus a boy and a dog as texture. That's it. **Alternative lighter version** (in case the fraud plot is too heavy): pure caper romance — she steals a diamond, he catches her, they fall in love, she returns the diamond and steals him instead. Sparkling, less substantial. Or the "imprisoned wife" gothic. But the fraud/dolls'-house version has emotional depth and a natural romance-through-alliance structure. **Voice sample lines to aim for:** - "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows. The lower ones are for guests." - "A house will always tell you where it is weakest, if you are patient and willing to be rained on." - "I had been in and out of forty-one houses. Ashcott was the forty-second, and the only one I had ever been born in." - Endings of chapters as small turns rather than cliffhangers, mostly. # Reflection The prompt's real gift is its *voice*: "one quickly learns" promises a narrator who is wry, competent, experienced, and slightly performing for us. Any plan that doesn't foreground first-person retrospective narration wastes that. So: first person, past tense, arch and tactile, with a light frame if it can be done in a few lines rather than a whole apparatus. Of the concepts, the pure caper (thief vs. master of the house) is reliable but thin — over 8000 words it risks being all banter and no ache. The gothic imprisoned-woman version is atmospheric but tends to make the romance secondary to the rescue, and the "mad wife in the east wing" is very well-trodden. The doctor-up-a-ladder idea is charming but doesn't sustain eight chapters of tension. What excites me most is the convergence in idea 10: the burglar entering her *own* childhood home. It makes the prompt's practical boast into something bruising — she knows the drainpipes because she used to climb *out* of them as a girl, which means every professional skill she has is a monument to what she lost. That's a real engine, and it turns the burglary set-pieces into emotional set-pieces automatically. Panelling torn out, a mural uncovered, the schoolroom used for storing seed potatoes: these details do double work as description and grief. Pairing her with a man who bought the house for the same buried secret, from the opposing moral position, gives the romance a structure rather than mere attraction: enemies → forced allies → confidants → lovers. The mirrored fathers (fraudster and scapegoat, both coerced, both weak) prevents a tidy vindication and forces the lovers to choose each other over being *right*, which is a much better climax than a courtroom. I'm wary that "both our fathers were partly guilty" could read as fudging; it needs to be specific — a signature knowingly given, a letter that names the real architect — so the moral picture is precise rather than mushy. The dolls' house is the best single object I've generated. A miniature manor whose roof lifts off; a paper hidden in its toy chimney by a father who assumed his daughter would come home. It rhymes exactly with the prompt (entering from above), it's period-plausible, it's visual, and it converts the search from ledger-hunting into something intimate and childlike. The twist that it's already empty gives me a mid-story reversal at exactly the right place (Ch5/6) and pivots attention to the housekeeper — who should be the old nurse, so the betrayal has warmth in it and can be forgiven. I should be careful that Mrs. Sowerby's long silence is motivated plausibly: fear, a small pension, and a genuine belief she was protecting the child from a father's shame. That's enough, if I dramatise it rather than explain it. Prothero worries me slightly. A villain who has employed the heroine for years without her suspecting is a lovely irony, but if he's too obviously sinister in Chapter 1 the reveal loses force; if he's too bland he's forgettable. The solution is to make him charming and *useful* — the man who fed her when no one else would, whose patronage she is genuinely grateful for. Her gratitude is the trap. Then his exposure costs her something. I'll also keep him offstage through the middle so he doesn't compete for space; a telegram or two, then arrival in Ch7. Pacing is the real risk. Eight thousand words is not much for a ruined-bank backstory, a house, a romance, a mystery, a betrayal, a confrontation and a coda. Ruthless economy required: the 1866 collapse conveyed in a paragraph, not a chapter; no second suitors; no elaborate legal aftermath. The dinner chapter (Ch4) can carry most of the exposition through dialogue, which is more efficient and more charged than narration. Chapter 7 should be short, wet, and physical — roof, rain, rope, a hand offered — and Chapter 8 shorter still, mostly warmth and the reversal of the prompt: *he* climbs to *her* window, badly. That reversal is the payoff the prompt is practically begging for, and it makes the title's boast into a love token. Two further things to hold onto. First, the recurring motif of window catches, sashes, putty, and faults — she should read houses the way others read faces, and I should let one specific fault (the nursery sash whose catch she loosened at eleven years old) be the hinge of the whole plot, discovered in Ch2 and remembered in Ch8. Second, the sensory register: rain on gritstone, ivy dust, tallow, cold lead, the particular smell of one's own childhood staircase. Period authenticity can live mostly in objects and money and manners rather than in explanatory prose. The one thing I want to guard against is the narrator becoming merely quippy. The wryness must be armour, and it should crack — once in Chapter 2 (the mural), once in Chapter 6 (the letter), once in Chapter 8 (the ladder). If those three cracks land, the story will be more than a caper. Setting: Derbyshire, 1873, with the ruin in 1866 (Overend & Gurney gives it real historical footing without requiring much explanation). Names: Isabel Crane, Gideon Hale, Mr. Prothero, Mrs. Sowerby, Ashcott Hall. Frame: two or three sentences at the start of Ch1 and the last paragraphs of Ch8, no more. # Reflection on Chapter Plan Given all the above, the eight-chapter shape I'd commit to is: (1) the art, the trade, the commission; (2) the climb home and the wrongness within, plus a voice in the dark; (3) the village, the nurse, the returned glove, the invitation; (4) dinner and the truce, both histories laid bare; (5) the search and the empty dolls' house; (6) the nurse's confession, the letter read, the kiss on the leads; (7) Prothero, the warrant, the roof in the rain; (8) the withdrawal, the parting, the ladder at her Camden window, and the catch left unmended. Each chapter ends on a turn rather than a stunt, and each contains at least one piece of practical climbing lore so the title-promise keeps its currency to the last page.
