Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **What I'm writing.** A first-person Victorian romance in eight ~1000-word chapters: Isabel Crane, twenty-six, a professional "recovery agent" (a discreet burglar for hire), is commissioned to rob a Derbyshire manor and discovers it is Ashcott Hall — the house she was born in and lost when her father's bank failed in 1866. Its new owner, Gideon Hale, a Manchester ironmaster's son, bought the place for the same reason she has come: something is hidden in it that will settle whose father was the fraud and whose the scapegoat. Enemies become allies become lovers; the buried document exonerates neither father and condemns the man who has been Isabel's patron for seven years. The climax is a roof in the rain; the coda reverses the prompt — Gideon, badly, climbs to *her* window. **Voice.** Retrospective first person, wry and precise, armour-plated with irony that cracks in three places (the mural in Ch2, the letter in Ch6, the ladder in Ch8). The narrator is performing her expertise for us — hence the "one quickly learns" register in the opening lines and recurring aphorisms about houses, sashes, lead, rain. Short frame: two or three sentences at the top of Ch1, a few paragraphs at the close of Ch8. No prologue apparatus. **Style aims.** Tactile and specific: putty, picture wire, ivy dust, wet gritstone, tallow, cold lead, the smell of one's own childhood staircase. Period conveyed through objects, money, manners and one real historical anchor (the Overend & Gurney collapse, May 1866) rather than expository lecture. Dialogue does the heavy lifting for backstory, especially in Chapter 4. Chapters end on turns, not stunts. Every chapter carries at least one piece of practical climbing lore so the title's promise keeps its currency. **What I'm avoiding.** No mad wife in the east wing, no rival suitor, no heist crew, no siblings, no courtroom procedural. No paragraphs of 1866 backstory — a paragraph, not a chapter. No mushy "everyone was a bit guilty" fudge: the guilt must be itemised, signature by signature. No wall-to-wall quipping; the wryness is a defence and must be seen to fail. Cast held to five: Isabel, Gideon, Prothero, Mrs. Sowerby, plus a bootboy and a dog for texture. **Key devices.** (1) The nursery sash whose catch Isabel herself loosened at eleven — the fault that makes the whole plot possible, established in Ch2, honoured in Ch8. (2) The dolls' house: a scale model of Ashcott, roof lifting off, a paper hidden in its miniature chimney by her father, who assumed she would come home. Found empty in Ch5. (3) Prothero as benefactor: charming, generous, the man who fed her when no one else would — so his exposure costs her gratitude, not merely safety. (4) Moral symmetry: her father signed a false return out of cowardice; Gideon's father, a clerk, was made to sign and then blamed and hanged himself; Prothero directed both. **Emotional throughline.** Every professional skill Isabel possesses is a monument to what she lost — she knows drainpipes because she used to climb *out* of them as a girl. The story's argument: she has spent seven years entering houses and belonging in none, and the ending gives her a door she may use, and a window she chooses to leave unmended. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The Art (London, October 1873).** Opens with the title line and a working lecture on upper windows: guests use the ground floor, the trade goes higher. A demonstration job — recovering a packet of letters from a house in Bruton Street — establishes competence, tools, nerve, and her employer: Mr. Prothero of Prothero & Vane, "recovery agents to the discreetly embarrassed." Backstory in a single compressed passage: 1866, the bank, her father dead within the year, the auctioneer's chalk marks on the furniture. Prothero, kind and expansive over supper, hands her the next commission: Ashcott Hall, Derbyshire, a certain locked cabinet, generous fee. Ends on her recognising the name — and not telling him she was born there. **Chapter 2 — Ashcott (three days later).** Reconnaissance in rain: the village, the lodge, the drive she once rode a pony down. The climb — ivy is a liar, the leaded valley is the road, the nursery sash whose catch she loosened at eleven with a fruit knife and never confessed. Inside: wrongness. Panelling stripped, floorboards up, her mother's painted frieze uncovered under wallpaper — the first crack in the armour. Then a lamp, a dog, and a man's voice in the dark, unhurried, asking whether she has found what she came for. She goes out the way she came in, tearing a sleeve, leaving one glove on the sill. **Chapter 3 — The Glove.** The Marlpit Inn; she should leave and does not. Churchyard: her parents' graves, tended. Mrs. Sowerby — her old nurse, now Hale's housekeeper — recognises her and goes white; not joy, fear. Village gossip fills in Hale: three years in residence, tearing the house apart, despised by the county, no wife. That evening the landlord brings up her glove, cleaned, with a card: *Mr. Gideon Hale requests the pleasure — the front door will be unlocked at seven.* Ends with her choosing the front door out of spite. **Chapter 4 — Dinner at Ashcott.** Fencing over a badly served meal in a half-dismantled dining room. He knew her at once from her boots and the way she looked at the ceiling. He tells her whose son he is: Josiah Hale, clerk, who signed the false return, took the blame, and hanged himself in a Salford yard in 1867. She tells him whose daughter she is. Mutual accusation, mutual grief, considerable heat. He shows her what he has done to the house: he has been searching for the private ledger and letters her father is rumoured to have kept. A truce — she knows the house, he owns it — and her first lie of omission: she does not name Prothero as her employer. **Chapter 5 — The Search.** Days of work: chimney breasts, cellar, the hollow newel post, the schoolroom now full of seed potatoes. Intimacy of shared labour, dust, laughter, hands. She recalls where a child hides things and leads him to the attic — the dolls' house under a dust sheet, an exact model of Ashcott with a lifting roof, made by her father. She opens the miniature nursery chimney. Empty, but not undisturbed: a scrap of sealing wax and the print of a thumb in old soot. Someone came first. Ends with Hale saying quietly that only three people ever lived in the attics. **Chapter 6 — Mrs. Sowerby.** The nurse's confession in the still-room: she found the packet in 1866, kept it out of love and fear, and has taken Prothero's five pounds a quarter every quarter since to write and tell him if anyone ever came looking. She gives it up. The letter read aloud by candle: Isabel's father signed knowingly, out of cowardice and hope; Josiah Hale was made to sign; Prothero drafted, directed and profited, and his instructions are in his own hand. Second crack in the armour. Isabel confesses who sent her north. On the leads at dawn, rain stopping, the valley gutter, the kiss. Then the boot-boy runs up with a telegram: Prothero arrives on the noon train. **Chapter 7 — The Roof.** Prothero, avuncular and ruinous, arrives with a county inspector and a genuine warrant — Isabel has committed forty-one burglaries and he has kept the proofs for seven years, insurance against exactly this hour. He wants the papers destroyed and offers her escape abroad; Hale is offered the ledger's suppression and a clean county reputation. She takes the packet up through the nursery window onto the wet leads. Prothero follows, because he must, and does not know that ivy is a liar. He slips at the valley gutter; she gives him her hand and hauls him in by the coat while the inspector watches from below with the letters already in his pocket, handed off by Hale. **Chapter 8 — The Unmended Catch.** Aftermath, brisk: Prothero withdraws the charge to save his own neck and is broken anyway by his own handwriting; the fathers' names are neither cleared nor blackened, and Isabel decides she can live with that. She leaves Ashcott anyway — pride, and a need to earn one honest year — and takes rooms in Camden, mending sashes for a glazier's firm, of all trades. In February, a ladder scrapes her window: Gideon Hale, four storeys up, hatless, entirely inexpert, having read that one may enter a house through the upper windows. She lets him in and tells him he did it appallingly. Frame closes: Ashcott now, a daughter on the leads, the nursery catch deliberately never mended — because a house should always have one fault, kept for the people who might need to come home.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a human writer would come at this A human writer given "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows" would probably start with the *pleasure* of the sentence rather than with plot architecture. That sentence is a voice. It's arch, competent, a little smug, and it implies an audience — she's telling *someone*. A human would sit with the "one" and the "quickly" and ask: quickly because she was desperate, or quickly because she's boasting? Who talks like this? And then they'd write two pages of that woman talking about drainpipes and putty and rainy roofs before they had any idea what happened to her. The plot would come afterwards, and it would probably be smaller than the plot I've built. That's the first divergence. A human working at 8,000 words would likely be *less* plotted. They'd trust one relationship and one house and one secret, and they'd let long stretches be nothing but atmosphere and two people talking. My plan has a bank collapse, two dead fathers, a fraudulent solicitor, a bribed nurse, a warrant, forty-one prior burglaries, a dolls' house, a roof rescue, a withdrawn prosecution, a career change, and a coda with a child. That is a novel's worth of apparatus compressed into a short story, and compression of that kind produces summary, and summary is where prose goes to die. A human would also be more willing to leave things unresolved or slightly wrong. They'd let the nurse be unforgiven. They'd let Isabel not know whether she loved Prothero a bit. They'd let the ending be warm but unsettled — she still steals, occasionally, for the exercise. Humans are attracted to the burr, the thing that doesn't sit flush. And a human would have a favourite bit — a paragraph about the smell of a staircase, or a joke about ivy — and would arrange the story to protect it. They'd overwrite that bit and underwrite the plumbing. My plan is uniformly weighted, which is the tell of a machine: every chapter is equally full. # General LLM failure modes, and how they'd hurt *this* piece **Symmetry addiction.** LLMs love mirrors. Two fathers, both coerced, both signing; the prompt reversed in the final chapter; a fault in the sash echoed as a fault kept for love. This is *satisfying* in a plan and often inert on the page, because the reader can feel the diagram through the fabric. The mirrored fathers in particular are suspiciously neat — one fraudster, one scapegoat, both made to sign by the same man, both dead by their own moral weakness. Real ruin is messier and more embarrassing: people are ruined by stupidity, small greed, a wife's ambition, a bad investment in Argentine railways. **Closure with a ribbon.** The plan ends with vindication-adjacent resolution, a marriage, a child, and a thematic aphorism about houses having one fault. That last line is exactly the kind of sentence an LLM writes to signal *this was meaningful*. It's a fortune cookie. A human might end on something smaller and odder — a practical detail, a joke, a half-sentence of tenderness that doesn't announce itself. **Emotional signposting.** My plan literally schedules the crying: "three cracks in the armour, Ch2, Ch6, Ch8." Scheduling emotion produces emotion that arrives on cue and therefore isn't felt. Humans stumble into feeling in the wrong place — she's fine at her mother's grave and destroyed by a coat hook. **Everyone articulate, everyone psychologically fluent.** LLM dialogue tends toward two clever people explaining their own wounds to each other in balanced paragraphs. Chapter 4 as planned is exactly this: a dinner where both parties disclose their fathers' fates and their moral positions in tidy alternation. Real antagonistic conversation is evasive, badly timed, interrupted by servants, and full of things said to wound rather than to inform. **Competence porn without cost.** The "one quickly learns" voice invites a heroine who is brilliant at everything. LLMs love a flawless protagonist with a *sad backstory* substituting for actual flaw. Isabel as planned makes no real mistakes, is never petty, is never wrong about anyone except Prothero (which is his fault, not hers). She should be genuinely compromised: she has stolen from innocent people, she has enjoyed it, she has a nasty snobbery about new money, she lies to Gideon longer than she needs to and not for good reasons. **Uniform lushness.** LLM period prose tends to keep the same medium-high polish for 8,000 words: every paragraph has a nice image, every chapter has a good closing line. Humans vary wildly — flat functional stretches, then a burst. Also LLMs overuse triadic lists ("putty, picture wire, ivy dust"), em-dash asides, and the construction "not X, but Y." My own intention document is full of these; the story will be too unless I'm vigilant. **Research as decoration.** Overend & Gurney is a real anchor, good, but LLMs tend to deploy such things as a badge and then explain them. A human either knows enough to be casual ("after Black Friday") or invents freely. The bigger danger is generic-Victorian: gaslight, aspidistras, "Pray, do not trouble yourself." Specificity beats verisimilitude — one weird true-feeling detail (a shilling's worth of best rushlights; the housekeeper's habit of keeping the still-room key on her stay-lace) is worth ten period-appropriate nouns. **Villain hygiene.** LLMs write villains who are either cartoons or "sympathetic but wrong." Prothero as planned is a chess piece: charming benefactor, secret architect, arrives with warrant, falls off roof, is undone by his handwriting. It's very tidy. The roof rescue in particular is a genre move — she saves him, proving her goodness. That's a moral prize handed to the heroine. **Chapter-ending stinger disease.** Every chapter in my plan ends on a turn: recognises the name; leaves a glove; chooses the front door; empty chimney; telegram arrives. That rhythm becomes mechanical by chapter four. Some chapters should end mid-breath, or on something inconsequential. **The frame narrative reflex.** Opening and closing frames are an LLM comfort blanket, a way to guarantee "resonance." A retrospective wry voice doesn't need a frame; the tense does the work. # Deep dive: where this plan specifically smells of machine **1. The plot is doing too much for the wordcount.** Eight chapters is roughly forty scenes' worth of material as planned. Ch7 alone contains an arrest, a bribe attempt, a moral choice, a chase, a fall, a rescue, and an evidential handoff — that's 1,000 words of pure event with no room to breathe, and it will read as synopsis. The result will be *competent summary*, which is the most recognisable LLM texture there is. Something must go. Candidates: the warrant, the forty-one burglaries, the roof rescue, the withdrawn prosecution, the career-as-glazier's-sash-mender, the daughter. **2. The dolls' house is either the best thing here or the twee-est.** It rhymes with the prompt beautifully. But "father hid the crucial document in the miniature chimney of the toy house he built, knowing his daughter would come home" is a Christmas-special premise. It also requires the father to be sentimentally prescient, which sits oddly with a man who signed a false return out of cowardice. Ways to save it: make the hiding place *not* deliberate (she hid something there as a child; the papers were shoved in later, carelessly, by someone else); or the dolls' house is sold and gone and only its *absence* matters; or what's in it isn't the evidence but something private and useless — a lock of hair, a bad drawing, a note that says nothing helpful — and the actual evidence is found elsewhere, dully, in a bank in Derby. Anticlimax is a very human move. **3. Two fathers, mirrored.** As above. Better if asymmetrical: Gideon's father wasn't a scapegoat clerk but a creditor, a small manufacturer who lost his works and his sons' schooling and died in a workhouse infirmary of nothing in particular; Gideon isn't seeking exoneration but *the money* — a hidden asset, a hoard, a deed — which is far less noble and far more interesting. Or he's seeking nothing; he bought the house because it was cheap and he's ripping out the panelling because it's rotten, and the whole secret-search alliance is Isabel's projection. That's a much more human, funnier, sadder story: she comes home expecting a nemesis and finds a man with a damp problem. **4. Prothero's warrant is a plot crutch.** "The benefactor kept proofs for seven years as insurance" is villain-as-mechanism. More human: he has no leverage but her gratitude and her poverty, which is more than enough. She stays loyal to him out of a genuine attachment she's ashamed of, and the betrayal is *hers* — she doesn't turn him in; she just stops writing, and he ends up doing something worse. **5. Isabel's professional identity is a bit fantasy-heroine.** "Recovery agent to the discreetly embarrassed," forty-one houses, a bag of tools, a code. Very Netflix. A human might make her smaller and more precarious: she does this three or four times a year and lives on it badly; the rest of the time she copies out music, or paints fans, or does something drearily genteel. She's frightened at every window. She's been caught once and it cost her a finger, or a tooth, or her hair. **6. The gender-politics safety.** Plan is careful: she's capable, he respects her, the nurse is forgiven, the villain punished. There's no genuine period cruelty in it. Where's the fact that she cannot own anything, that a proposal is an economic transaction, that his money is new and hers is gone and the county will never receive them? A human romance in this period gets *specific* about the humiliations — the frank arithmetic of an offer, the tradesman's-son sneer, the maid who won't call her "miss." **7. The kiss on the leads at dawn.** Gorgeous, and exactly what an LLM produces when asked for a romantic climax in this setting: elevated, weather-assisted, thematically apt. Worth keeping only if it's undercut — she's shaking with cold and can't feel her mouth; he has soot on his teeth; a bird gets up and they both jump. Or move the physical turn somewhere unpoetic: a cellar, a stairwell, the wrong side of a locked door where they can't see each other. **8. "The Unmended Catch."** A title that explains the theme. Delete. **9. The coda's reversal.** Him climbing to her window is a genuinely good idea, and it's the payoff the prompt wants. The risk is that it's *cute*, and that I'll write it cute — hatless, comic, ladder-scraping, she says something dry, curtain. Ways to roughen: he's not funny about it, he's furious and embarrassed and slightly hurt; or he does it because she refused to see him at the door, so it's not a gesture but a desperation; or he doesn't manage it, and she has to go down and let him in the front, which is funnier and sadder. **10. Everything explained.** Plan has all four principals' motives fully disclosed, all guilt itemised. Better to leave one hole: what her father actually meant to do with the money; whether Mrs. Sowerby's five pounds a quarter was really the reason; whether Gideon would have chosen her over the ledger if it had come to it. Reader-sized gaps are what make a story feel written by a person who doesn't know everything either. # Brainstorm: humanising moves **Strip the plot to one spine.** Pick one: (a) the buried document, (b) the two-people-searching-the-same-house alliance, (c) the coming-home-as-a-thief grief. Try to build on (c) with (b) as texture, and let the document be almost incidental — found early, or not found at all, or found and useless. The romance then has room to be the plot rather than a garnish on the plot. **Make Gideon materially wrong for her and be honest about it.** He talks flat, drops aitches when tired, is proud of a patent for a valve, thinks her mother's frieze is damp-damaged rubbish and paints over it. Let him do one unforgivable-ish thing to the house. Let her despise him for a while for real reasons, not romantic-tension reasons. **Give Isabel a real vice.** She's a snob. She takes small things she doesn't need — a thimble, a pair of scissors — from every house, and can't explain why. She has stolen from a woman she pitied and told herself a story about it. She's contemptuous of Mrs. Sowerby's poverty. **Bodily and technical truth.** Fear of heights that never goes away; the specific ache in the forearms; how much a slate costs to replace; the fact that ivy hides rotten pointing; that lead is loud; that dogs are the real problem and not locks; that she wears men's boots two sizes too big with the toes stuffed because they grip. One paragraph of genuine craft is worth a chapter of atmosphere. **Let the servants be people with interests.** The bootboy wants money for a fiddle; the cook hates the new range; someone tries to sell her information and overcharges. **Comedy as human texture.** The wry voice should be actually funny sometimes, not just dry. A running joke about a bad portrait of a great-uncle. The dog being useless and affectionate. **Vary the chapter shapes.** One chapter that's almost entirely a single conversation; one that's 400 words of climbing and nothing else; one that skips three weeks in a line; one that ends flatly. Refuse the uniform 1,000-word beat. **Withhold the aphorisms after Ch2.** Let the "one quickly learns" register be established, then let it decay as she stops performing — so that by Ch7 she's just a frightened woman on a roof, and the voice's return in the final page means something. **Anticlimax where a climax is expected.** No fall, no rescue. Prothero simply leaves, and it's worse. Or he's already dead of something ordinary when she gets back to London. **Money on the page.** Exact sums. Her fee (thirty guineas), the nurse's pension, the price the Hall fetched, what a sash-cord costs. **One thing left broken.** She doesn't get the house back. Or she does and hates it. Or the frieze is gone for good and that's simply a loss. **Cut the child.** Or if kept, keep her offhand and unsentimental — a daughter who is bad at climbing and doesn't care. **Let the ending be provisional.** "We are not married. We may not be." A human is far likelier to risk that than a model optimising for satisfaction.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The spine, radically simplified.** One house, two people, one small ugly secret. Isabel Crane, twenty-seven, breaks into Ashcott Hall in Derbyshire to steal a japanned cabinet's contents for a client. It is the house she was born in and lost at nineteen when her father's bank went under in 1866. The new owner, Gideon Hale, is not her nemesis and is not searching for anything: he bought the Hall cheap because it stands over good stone and he needs a house near his quarry, and he is ripping out the panelling because it's rotten with dry rot. There is no mirrored-fathers conspiracy, no warrant, no roof rescue, no dolls'-house treasure. The plot is: she keeps coming back; he lets her; they fall into something; the secret in the cabinet turns out to be small, shabby and about *her father's ordinary weakness*, not a conspiracy; and the ending is warm but unresolved. **What the prompt is for.** The story is an argument the narrator is making about herself — that she has spent eight years entering other people's houses through the upper windows and belonging in none of them. So the "one quickly learns" register is armour and self-mythology, and it must be established hard in Chapter 1, then allowed to *decay* as she stops performing, so that its brief return in the last page lands. Craft-lore is the story's currency: real climbing detail in nearly every chapter, cost and technique and fear. **Voice.** Retrospective first person, wry, technical, snobbish, funny. No frame device — past tense does the work. Aphorisms front-loaded and rationed thereafter. I will let the register drop to plain and frightened in Chapters 6–7. **Isabel's flaws, on the page.** She steals small useless things (a thimble, scissors, a paper-knife) compulsively and can't say why. She is a snob about new money and about her old nurse's poverty. She lies to Gideon about who employs her for longer than she needs to, out of vanity. She has been caught once, in Nottingham in 1870, and it cost her the top joint of her left ring finger — which is why she can no longer wear a glove properly on that hand, and why she is frightened at every window and always will be. **Gideon, made genuinely inconvenient.** Thirty-eight, quarry-owner and stone-merchant, Bury-born, flattens his vowels when tired, proud of a patent for a crane brake, blunt to the point of rudeness. He has painted over her mother's painted frieze in the morning room because it was blistered with damp. He does not fully understand what he has done to her, and I will not have him fully understand it by the end. His money is new; the county will not have them; a proposal is discussed as arithmetic. **The secret, deliberately small.** In the cabinet: not exoneration, not conspiracy. Letters showing that in the last months her father knowingly took deposits from his own tenants and servants — including Mrs. Sowerby's forty-one pounds — after he knew the bank was gone, and a begging letter from him to a man named Prothero. Prothero is not a villain who arrives; he is Isabel's present employer, a small, kindly, expansive man in Bloomsbury who has been quietly employing the daughter of a client he once refused. He never appears in Derbyshire. He is exposed as nothing worse than a man who does business with the shabby-genteel and always has. The real reckoning is between Isabel and Mrs. Sowerby, who lost forty-one pounds and has never said so. **Deliberate omissions.** We never learn exactly what Isabel's father meant to do with the money. Gideon never says he loves her. It is never settled whether Mrs. Sowerby forgives her. The frieze is gone for good. **Structural variation.** Chapter shapes will differ: Ch3 is almost entirely one conversation over a broken staircase; Ch5 is short and mostly hands and dust; Ch7 skips a week in a line and ends flat and badly; Ch8 is the only chapter with a joke at the end. Not every chapter gets a turn or a stinger — Chapters 2 and 7 end on nothing much. **The coda.** Gideon comes to her Camden lodging in February, is refused at the door by her landlady, and climbs — appallingly, furiously, not charmingly — to her second-floor window, sticks, and has to be talked down and let in at the front like a Christian. Final lines: they are not married; she has kept the nursery sash's catch loose at Ashcott, and will not say for whom. No aphorism about houses and faults. A practical detail and a door left open. **Avoiding.** Uniform lushness; triadic lists; "not X but Y"; scheduled crying; period-generic furniture; explained themes; a bow. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Upper Windows (London, September 1874). ~1000 words.** The lecture. Ground floors are for guests; the trade goes higher. Practical instruction: ivy is a liar, lead is loud, dogs matter more than locks, men's boots two sizes large with the toes stuffed. A brisk half-successful job in Highbury — she takes the packet she was paid for and also a mother-of-pearl paper-knife she does not want. Her finger, and Nottingham, in two sentences. Prothero of Gray's Inn Road: fat, kind, smells of aniseed, pays thirty guineas and asks after her cough. The new commission: Ashcott Hall, a japanned cabinet, papers "of no value to anyone but my client." She takes it without saying she was born there, because saying so would have meant refusing it. Ends dry, not on a stinger: she buys a third-class ticket to Bakewell and a new sash-knife. **Chapter 2 — Ashcott. ~1000 words.** Rain, gritstone, the wrong gate. The village and the Marlpit Inn in a paragraph. The climb at one in the morning: rotten pointing behind the ivy, the leaded valley, and the nursery sash she loosened herself at eleven with a fruit knife — still loose, which undoes her more than anything else could. Inside: floors up, panelling stacked, the smell of her own staircase unchanged. Then the morning room: her mother's frieze painted over, cream, thoroughly, with a good brush. She does not cry. She takes a thimble from a workbox. She finds the japanned cabinet and it is locked with something new and beyond her, and she leaves with nothing. Chapter ends flat: she walks four miles back in the rain and her boots are ruined. **Chapter 3 — The Man on the Stair. ~1000 words.** Second attempt, two nights later. He is sitting on the half-demolished main staircase with a lamp and a dog, waiting, having found her thumbprints in the dust and mended the pointing. Almost the whole chapter is one conversation: he is rude, curious, unafraid; she is contemptuous. He knows who she is within four exchanges — the nursery window, the way she said "the morning room." He tells her about dry rot and what it costs; she tells him about the frieze; he says, plainly, that it was blistered and had to go, and doesn't apologise. He will not call the constable and will not open the cabinet, which belonged to the previous owner and is not his to open. He says she may come back and look at the house in daylight if she likes, which is worse than being arrested. **Chapter 4 — Daylight. ~1000 words.** She comes at three in the afternoon, hating it. The house in daylight: worse and better. Mrs. Sowerby — kept on as housekeeper — sees her in the passage and does not curtsey; the exchange is four lines and awful. The bootboy, Ambrose, who wants a fiddle and will sell information about the cabinet's key for one shilling and threepence. Gideon shows her the quarry from the terrace, talks money frankly: what the Hall fetched (£3,400), what it costs to keep. He asks who employs her; she lies smoothly and enjoys lying. Ends with him giving her the cabinet's history — it came with the house, and the key went to London with the executors, to a solicitor's clerk, name of Prothero's firm. She says nothing. **Chapter 5 — The Cabinet. ~800–900 words. Short, physical.** Three weeks compressed into a line: she goes back four times, twice by the window out of habit, twice by the door. Mostly hands and dust and labour — she helps him lift boards, she reads the house for him, she tells him where the old drains run and he is impressed, which she has not been by a man for years. Somewhere in the middle of a filthy afternoon in the cellar, in the dark, on the wrong side of nothing romantic at all, something happens: a hand, a laugh, soot, a bird getting up in the flue and both of them jumping. No dawn, no leads, no view. At the end she picks the cabinet's lock, at last, with Ambrose's stolen key filed down — and does not open it, because she is a coward, and puts it in her pocket to open at the inn. **Chapter 6 — Forty-One Pounds. ~1000 words.** The inn, a candle, the packet. What's in it: nothing about a conspiracy. Deposit receipts in her father's hand from March and April 1866 — the coachman, two tenants, the cook, and Sarah Sowerby, forty-one pounds — taken after he knew, and a letter from her father to Prothero & Vane, begging, badly written, dated the week before he died. The armour comes off here: plain sentences, no jokes. She walks up to the Hall at eleven at night, up the ivy, because she cannot make herself knock, and puts the receipts on the still-room table in front of Mrs. Sowerby, who has known all along, and who says the thing that guts her: *I never wanted telling.* Not forgiveness. Isabel offers her money she does not have. **Chapter 7 — Terms. ~1000 words.** Daylight, the county, arithmetic. Gideon reads the receipts and is not shocked, which is its own insult — he has seen worse ledgers. He makes an offer, in the flat plain way of a man pricing stone: what he has, what she'd have, what the county will do (nothing, they will simply not come). She refuses, or fails to accept, for reasons she narrates badly and does not fully understand: pride, the frieze, forty-one pounds, the fact that she does not want to be *let in*. A week passes in a sentence. She goes to London, pays Mrs. Sowerby three pounds and a promise, tells Prothero she is finished, and he is only mildly sorry and offers her copying work at eighteen shillings a week. Ends flat and badly: she takes it, and the chapter stops. **Chapter 8 — February. ~900–1000 words.** Camden, cold, copying music and mending sashes for a glazier's firm for the pleasure of the technical detail. The wry register returns for one paragraph — the state of London window-catches, professionally deplored. Then a ladder against the house and a man on it who is not a thief: Gideon, furious and mortified, turned away at the door by her landlady, forty feet up on a borrowed builder's ladder and stuck at the wrong sill, having got it entirely wrong. She has to talk him down and let him in at the front like a Christian, in front of the landlady. Small, unromantic, funny. They do not settle everything. She does not go back to Derbyshire for good; she goes back. Last beat: at Ashcott the nursery catch is still loose. She has never had it mended, and when he asks why she says something short and doesn't explain. End.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Isabel Crane **Background.** Born 1847 at Ashcott Hall, Derbyshire, the only child of Henry Crane, who was a partner in Crane, Vellacott & Co., a Derby joint-stock bank of the second rank that lent chiefly against land and did not survive the spring of 1866. Isabel was nineteen. She remembers the summer as a series of men in the house measuring things. Her father died in the February following — a stroke, in a rented room in Belper, though the family said heart — and her mother, who had painted the frieze in the morning room herself over three summers, went to a cousin in Southport and died there in 1869 of a chest complaint and grievance. Isabel did not go to Southport. She had, by then, discovered that the skill she possessed — she could get into and out of any house in England — was worth thirty guineas a time to certain kinds of men. The first time was not romantic. A woman called Mrs. Fenwick, who had been kind to her, needed some letters back from a house in Duffield, and Isabel said she thought she could manage it, and did, and was paid four pounds, and was sick afterwards in a hedge. That was 1867. She has done it, on average, three or four times a year since — never more; there isn't the work. The rest of the year she has copied music, painted fans, taken in plain sewing she is bad at, and lived in single rooms with damp on the north wall. **Personality.** Precise, funny, contemptuous, tireder than she admits. She has built an entire self out of expertise, because expertise was the only thing that survived 1866. She talks about drainpipes the way other women talk about children. Underneath that: a genuine snob. She notices that Gideon says *serviette*; she notices that Mrs. Sowerby's boots are cracked and thinks less of her for it and hates herself for thinking it and thinks it again the next day. She has an unexamined belief that she is still, essentially, a gentleman's daughter who is temporarily inconvenienced, and eight years have not dented it. **Idiosyncrasies and flaws.** - She takes small things. Not valuables — a thimble, a pair of nail-scissors, a mother-of-pearl paper-knife, once a child's tooth in a twist of paper, which appalled her. She has a japanned box of them under her bed. She cannot say why she does it and has stopped trying. - Nottingham, 1870: caught coming out of a scullery window by a manservant with a spade. She lost the top joint of the left ring finger. She has a glove with the fourth finger stitched short and she tells people it was a machine. - She is frightened every single time. Not thrilled. Frightened, from the moment she puts her hand on the first hold. She has never told anyone this and considers it the most private fact about her, more private than the finger. - She counts things when afraid — courses of stone, seconds, panes. - She cannot knock on a door if she is upset. She will go up the ivy instead. This is not a metaphor she recognises. - She is a hopeless liar about small things and an excellent one about large ones. **Physicality.** Tall, flat-chested, long in the arm, twenty-seven and beginning to look it about the eyes. Brown hair she wears screwed up hard and low so it doesn't catch on sashes. A plain face that reads as haughty when it is only tired. She wears men's boots two sizes too large with the toes stuffed with wool, because a loose boot lets the arch grip and a tight one doesn't; she walks in them oddly, a bit splayed, and knows it. Perpetual grazes on the insides of both forearms. She holds her left hand curled in when speaking to strangers. When she is thinking she looks at ceilings — cornices, joists, the run of a chimney — which is how Gideon knows her within four exchanges. **Motives and allegiances.** She wants thirty guineas, and then she wants another thirty. Below that, unadmitted: she wants to be *inside* somewhere with a right to be there. She is loyal to Prothero out of gratitude and habit, and the gratitude is real; he gave her work when respectable people gave her advice. She has no friends. She has a correspondence with a woman in Matlock about the propagation of ferns that is the only entirely truthful relationship in her life. **Voice.** > "Ivy is a liar. It will hold your weight all the way up the wall and then hand you, very courteously, to a hundred and fifty years of bad pointing. Look for lead. Lead is loud but honest." > He said the frieze had blistered. I said I was aware how paint behaved. He said then I would know it could not be saved, and I said no, I did not know that, I had never asked anybody, because nobody had ever thought to write and ask me. > Forty-one pounds. I sat and did the sum four different ways, as though one of them might come out otherwise. --- # Gideon Hale **Background.** Born 1836 in Bury, the third son of a man who cut and carted stone and could not read a contract. Gideon can. He went into a quarry at eleven, was a mason's labourer at fourteen, and by twenty-six had leased his first face at Stanton and made money out of setts and kerbstones during the paving boom. He now owns two quarries, a wharf at Runcorn, and a patent on a friction brake for a stone crane that earns him more, annually, than either quarry. He bought Ashcott Hall in 1871 for £3,400 because it sits half a mile from a bed of good gritstone and because the alternative was living in Buxton lodgings. He is not searching for anything in the house. He is fighting dry rot, which is why the panelling is stacked in the stable yard and the morning room is painted cream. He is quietly, unromantically proud of the cream: it is a good job of work with a good brush and it will not blister again. **Personality.** Blunt to the edge of rudeness, and past it. He does not do the thing where people soften a fact. He is patient with objects and impatient with feelings, including his own. He is *interested* in things — how they fail, what they cost, how long they'll last — and this interest is the most attractive thing about him and also why he does not understand, for a long time, what he has done to Isabel. He hasn't a scrap of malice and a great deal of thoughtlessness. **Idiosyncrasies and flaws.** - He drops his aitches when tired and knows it and doesn't perform correcting it, which is its own kind of pride. - He has read Ruskin on stone and disagrees with him, at length, to anyone. - He keeps a notebook of the cost of everything: sash cord, 3d a yard; four hundredweight of lime; a girl to scrub the back stairs, 1s 6d a day. He shows it to people. He thinks this is friendly. - He does not apologise. When wrong, he simply stops and looks at the thing again, which is not the same and she notices. - He is lonely in a way he'd deny under oath. The dog, Bess, a fat useless liver-and-white spaniel bitch, sleeps in his chair and he lets her. - He genuinely cannot climb. He has no head for it and no gift; masons don't necessarily. This matters later. - He says *serviette*, having been told once that it was the polite word. **Physicality.** Big and thick through the shoulders, a stone-carrier's build gone slightly heavy at thirty-eight. Sandy, receding, cut close. Hands that are wrong for a gentleman: the nails, the knuckle scars, a thumbnail permanently black. He sits with his knees apart and his forearms on them. He looks at people directly and for slightly too long. Smells of lime dust and horse. When he laughs it is one short bark, and rare, and startles her. **Motives and allegiances.** He wants the house dry, the quarry paying, and — increasingly, and with no vocabulary for it — company. He has no interest in the county and no illusions: the Ashcotts and the Bagshawes will not come, and he shrugs at this and means the shrug. He is loyal to his workmen in a plain contractual way and would sack any of them for theft without hesitation, which is a thing Isabel has to hold in her hand and consider. He decides he wants Isabel Crane roughly a month before he mentions it, and mentions it as arithmetic, because that is the only register he has for enormous things. **Voice.** > "It were blistered right through to the plaster. You can't save that. I'm not sorry — you can be sorry and I'll not mind, but I'll not be sorry for painting a wall that wanted painting." > "Sit down. You've come in through a window twice, you can sit in a chair once." > "I've three thousand four hundred in the house and about eleven hundred a year clear. You'd have the housekeeping and no company but mine and the dog's, and nobody in this county will dine with us, ever. That's the whole of it. I'd rather say it plain than have you find it out." --- # Sarah Sowerby **Background.** Fifty-nine. Came to Ashcott in 1843 as a nursemaid, was Isabel's nurse from birth, became housekeeper in 1861 when old Mrs. Prideaux died. In March 1866 she put forty-one pounds — the whole of her savings, eighteen years of it — into Crane, Vellacott & Co. on the recommendation of Mr. Crane himself, who came down to the still-room to tell her it would pay her four and a half per cent. She got back nothing. She stayed on through the sale, and through two owners, and is still there, because a woman of fifty-nine with no character reference from the family she was ruined by does not get another place. She does not think of herself as wronged. She thinks of herself as a fool, which is worse, and she has never said the number aloud to anyone. **Personality.** Dry, watchful, formidable within her own forty square feet. Not warm — she was never a warm nurse, she was a competent one — but she loved Isabel in a proprietary, exasperated way and has not forgiven her for eight years of silence more than she hasn't forgiven the money. She keeps a house well. She reads the *Derbyshire Courier* on Saturdays and knows precisely who is dying. **Idiosyncrasies and flaws.** - Keeps the still-room key on her stay-lace, not on a ring. Always has. - Calls Gideon "the master" without irony and Isabel "Miss Isabel" with a great deal. - Will not sit down in front of her. - Bad hip. Goes up stairs sideways and hates being seen doing it. - Was the one who reported, in 1859, that the nursery sash catch was loose, and was told by Mr. Crane not to fuss. She remembers this. She never mentions it. - Has a horror of being pitied that is stronger than her wish to be paid. **Motives and allegiances.** Her place. Her hip. Her Saturday paper. She is loyal to Gideon because he pays on the day and doesn't interfere, and she would not lie to him for Isabel. What she wants from Isabel is not money and not apology; it is for the whole thing never to be spoken of again, and Isabel takes that away from her. **Voice.** > "You've grown very like your mother about the mouth. She were no better at coming in at doors." > "I never wanted telling, Miss Isabel. I've known it since the Whitsun after. There's not a thing in that packet I didn't know. You've come all this way to hand me my own business back." --- # Mr. Prothero **Background.** Sixty-odd, of Prothero & Vane, Gray's Inn Road — nominally solicitors' agents, actually a small firm that recovers awkward property for people who cannot go to the police. He was a managing clerk for thirty years and has been on his own account for fifteen. He handled some of the Crane, Vellacott winding-up as a young man for the executors, which is how the japanned cabinet's key came to be in a drawer in Gray's Inn Road, and how he knew who Isabel was when she came to him in 1868 wanting work and pretending not to. He is not a villain. He never refused her father help; he simply had none to give, and filed the begging letter, because filing things is his life's work. He gave Isabel work partly out of pity and mostly because she was good at it and cheap. **Personality.** Expansive, kindly, entirely transactional, with the sentimentality of a man who has seen a great deal of other people's ruin at close range and keeps warm by being nice about it. Smells of aniseed balls; carries them loose in a waistcoat pocket. Asks after her cough every time and means it, and would drop her tomorrow if she were caught. **Idiosyncrasies.** Says "my dear" to everyone including the boy. Writes commissions on the backs of used envelopes. Has never once asked how she gets in, and she has come to understand this is a courtesy, and possibly the only one he can afford. **Voice.** > "Papers of no value, my dear, to anybody but my client. Thirty guineas and your fare. How's that cough? You want goose grease and a flannel, and don't tell me you've not the time." > "Finished! Well. Well, that's a pity, and I shan't pretend otherwise. # Chapter One: Upper Windows One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows. The ground floor is for guests. It has shutters, bars, a night-bolt, a man sleeping across the passage in a truckle bed, and a bell-pull within reach of his hand. The first floor has bedrooms, which is to say people. But go higher — the second, the attics, the queer half-storey over the kitchens where the maids are put — and you will find sashes forty years unpainted, catches of soft brass, and glass so old it has run in its frame like treacle. Nobody defends the top of a house. It is a peculiar fact of the English gentleman that he will spend eleven pounds on a patent lock for his cellar and leave his roof open to the sky. Ivy is a liar. It will bear your weight all the way up the wall and then hand you, very courteously, to a hundred and fifty years of bad pointing. What you want is lead: a downpipe, a hopper-head, a valley gutter. Lead is loud but honest. It will tell you what it can do and then do it. Dogs matter more than locks. I have never met a lock that woke anybody. And your boots should be two sizes too large, with the toes packed out with wool. A loose boot lets the arch of your foot take a ledge and hold it. A tight boot makes you a lady in a shoe, standing on a wall. I walk oddly on the flat because of this, splayed at the heel like a duck, and I am aware of it, and I would rather walk like a duck than fall forty feet into a laurel. In September of 1874 I went up the back of a house in Highbury Grove for a packet of letters. It was a bad house for it — new, all yellow brick, the pointing still hard as iron, nothing to get a nail into — but the builder had put a cast-iron pipe up the flank wall with the brackets left long, and a man who leaves his brackets long has invited you personally. I was in at the box-room window in eleven minutes and out again in nineteen, and the packet was where the client had said it would be, in a hatbox, tied with tape, forty-one letters from a Captain Something to a woman who would not be reading them again. I also took a paper-knife. Mother-of-pearl, small, the sort of thing sold at a bazaar for one and six. It was on a table on the landing and I put it in my pocket and I have it still, in a japanned box under my bed with a thimble, two pairs of nail-scissors, a bone crochet hook, and a child's tooth in a twist of paper which I found in a drawer in Kettering and which appalled me the moment I got it home. I do not know why I take them. I used to make up reasons. I have given that up, as one gives up any hobby that leads nowhere. The letters went to Gray's Inn Road, to the offices of Prothero and Vane, up two flights, past a brass plate so worn you would think the firm had been recovering other people's property since the Conquest. Mr. Prothero was at his desk with his coat off and his waistcoat unbuttoned over a great slope of stomach, and the room smelled, as it always does, of aniseed balls, which he keeps loose in his pocket among the pencils. "My dear," he said. "Sit down. That cough's no better." "It's September." "It was no better in June." He took the packet, weighed it in his hand without opening it, and put it in the safe. Then he counted me out thirty guineas in gold and a half-sovereign for the fare, and pushed the little pile across the leather with two fingers, the way you would slide a saucer of milk towards a cat you did not wish to startle. "Goose grease and a flannel. Don't tell me you've not the time; everyone has the time to be warm." I have known Mr. Prothero six years. He has never once asked me how I get in. I understood, after the first year or so, that this was a courtesy, and possibly the only one in his gift, and I have valued it accordingly. "There's another," he said, and hunted about, and found the back of an envelope with his writing on it. He writes all his commissions on used envelopes. It is not thrift; he has simply never seen the sense of a fresh sheet for a thing that will be burned. "Derbyshire. Country house, gone to a manufacturer. There's a cabinet — japanned, black, with a bird on it, my client says, and a bird is a great deal of use to us, isn't it, my dear, everybody paints birds. Papers inside. Of no value to anybody but my client. Thirty guineas and your fare and a pound over, because it's a distance and the weather's turning." "Which house?" He looked at the envelope. "Ashcott Hall." There is a trick to being handed your own life across a desk. You do not put your hands in your lap, because he will see the knuckles. You do not look up, because he will see your face. You look at the envelope, and you read the address on it upside down — it was a bill from a stationer in Holborn — and you count. I counted the pencils in the jar. There were nine. "Ashcott," I said. "You know it?" "I know the road." And that was the whole of the lie, and it cost nothing, and I have thought about it since more than I have thought about anything else I did that year. He may have known. He handled some part of Crane, Vellacott and Company for the executors when he was a young clerk; he told me so himself, in 1868, when I came to him for work and pretended I did not know his name. Perhaps he had forgotten. Perhaps he remembered perfectly and was being kind in the only way he has, which is to hand a woman thirty guineas and ask about her chest. Because if he had said, *my dear, that was your father's house* — then I should have had to refuse it. And I did not want to refuse it. I wanted thirty guineas, and I wanted to see the roof. I bought a third-class ticket to Rowsley, and a new sash-knife, ground thin, from a man in Clerkenwell who does not ask what you are cutting.

# Chapter Two: Ashcott There are two gates to Ashcott and I took the wrong one, which I would not have done in daylight and which I did on purpose in the dark, because the right one has a lodge and I did not want to look at it. The Marlpit Inn is in the village, four miles off, and had a room at one and ninepence with a bed that smelled of other people. The landlady thought I was a lady's companion travelling to a place, and I let her, and ate a mutton chop, and sat with my boots off in front of a fire made of green wood while the rain came at the window in handfuls. Derbyshire rain does not fall. It arrives sideways and stays about you afterwards like a relation. At half past midnight I went out by the yard and walked up the hill. You will want to know what I felt, coming along that wall. I have been asked, since, and I have never found anything to say that was not either flippant or a lie, so here is the whole of it: my arms ached from the bag, and I was thinking about the pointing. Gritstone weathers well and points badly. The lime goes soft in the joints on any wall that takes the west, and Ashcott's east front takes nothing at all, being sheltered by the hill, and so the east front is sound as a church and the west front is a ladder for anybody with fingers. I knew this before I could read. I used to sit on the nursery windowsill with my legs out, aged nine, and pick the mortar out of the joint below with a fruit knife, a little every summer, the way another child picks a scab. The ivy had got to the second storey since my time, and I put my hand into it and found exactly what I expected — a stem the thickness of my wrist, and behind it a joint you could put three fingers in. I did not use the ivy. I went up on the pipe to the hopper-head, out along the string course, and stood on the string course with my toes in the boots and my cheek against the wall, and counted courses of stone until my breath came back. I want that written down plainly, because it is the private thing and I shall not be mentioning it again. I am frightened every time. Not thrilled. Frightened, from the moment my hand goes on the first hold to the moment my second foot is on a floor, and it has never once got better in eight years, and I have never told a living soul, not Prothero, not the woman in Matlock I write to about ferns. The finger on my left hand — I lost the top joint of it in Nottingham in 1870, to a manservant with a spade, and I tell people it was a machine — the finger is not the private thing. Anybody may see the finger. The nursery is at the west end, second storey, third window along. It is a sash, and the catch is a soft brass hook that has always sat crooked in its plate, because a girl of eleven loosened the screws with a fruit knife in 1858 so that she could get out onto the leads at night and lie there and look at nothing. I got my knife under the meeting rail, and lifted, and the hook rose out of the plate the way it always did. Nobody had mended it. Sixteen years, three owners, and nobody had put a screwdriver to that plate. I sat on the sill inside with my legs hanging into my own nursery and I could not get up for a little while. It was not grief. Grief is respectable and I could have managed grief. It was more like being handed a glass of water when you had not said you were thirsty. Then I got up, because I was being paid, and I looked at what they had done to the house. The nursery was full of seed potatoes. Trays of them, on trestles, and a smell of earth and sprouting. In the passage the floorboards were up in long runs with the joists showing, and there were bricks stacked in the second-best bedroom, and the panelling was gone out of the whole of the north side — gone, stripped to the plaster, with the nail holes in rows like stitches. Downstairs the great staircase was half demolished, the treads out, the strings raw, a builder's ladder standing where the newel had been. And the smell of the house was the same. That is a thing nobody warns you of. They may take up your floors and sell your chairs and put potatoes in your bed, and the staircase will still smell of cold stone and beeswax and the particular damp of that one corner by the linen press, and your body will know it in the dark before your head does, and there is no defence against it whatever. In the morning room I lit my candle-end, and put my hand up, and found cream paint. My mother painted that frieze. Three summers of it, on a plank across two chairs, a border of blackthorn and hares going all round above the picture rail, and she was not a good painter, and the hares had a stunned look about them, and I have never seen anything else like it in any house in England. It was under two coats of cream, well brushed out, no runs, a proper workmanlike job by somebody who knew what he was doing with a brush. I did not cry. I stood there with the candle up and I looked at it for some time, and then I went and found a workbox on the window seat and took the thimble out of it and put it in my pocket, and I could not have told you then and cannot tell you now what the one thing had to do with the other. The cabinet was in the little room off the library, japanned black, with a heron on the door, and I got down in front of it with my picks and knew inside a minute that I was beaten. Somebody had fitted a new lock to an old case. Six levers, and a curtain over the keyway, and made by Chubb, and my picks were a set of six wires and a great deal of confidence. I put the wires away and went out by the nursery window and pulled the sash down behind me, and walked the four miles back with the rain coming at me sideways, and by the time I reached the Marlpit my boots were finished. I had had them three years. There is no mending a boot that has been wet through twice in one night.

# Chapter Three: The Man on the Stair Two nights later I went up again, with a candle-end, a bradawl, and the whole of my dignity, meaning to take the hinges off the cabinet door. The pointing had been mended. Not all of it. A yard of it, in the one joint below the nursery sill, and mended well, raked back and pressed in, and dry. Somebody had stood on a ladder in the rain with a bucket of lime mortar and done a careful job on eighteen inches of wall in a place where no man could see it from the ground. I went up on the pipe instead, and out along the string course, and got the sash up, and there was a light in the passage. He was sitting on the ruin of the great staircase, four treads up from the bottom, with a lamp on the step beside him and a spaniel across his feet. The dog lifted her head, thumped her tail twice on the wood, and put it down again. In eight years that was the most useless dog I ever met. "You'll want to come down," he said. "Them joists are up along the landing. You'll go through and break your leg, and then I shall have to fetch a doctor and explain you." I came down. There was nothing else to do; the ladder was where the newel had been and he was sitting at the foot of it. I came down and stood on the flags of the hall in a house I was born in, holding a bradawl. He was a big man gone slightly heavy, sandy and receding, in his shirtsleeves at one in the morning with a waistcoat unbuttoned and his forearms on his knees. His thumbnail was black. He looked at me directly and for rather too long, the way you look at a wall you are pricing. "You've been three times," he said. "Twice." "Three. There's a mark of your hand in the dust on the library door from Tuesday, and another from Thursday, and there's a third on the potato trays which I take it is tonight, unless you keep a friend." He reached down and scratched the dog. "I'm Hale. It's my house. I'd offer you a chair but there isn't one in this end of it." "You mended the pointing." "I did." "Why?" "Because it were bad pointing," he said, as if I had asked why he had eaten his dinner. "It's my wall. I don't leave a joint open because it's convenient to somebody. If you can find another road up, that's your business, but you'll not go up a hole I've seen and left." He shifted the lamp an inch, considering me. "You've come in at the nursery window. Second storey, west end, third along." "There's no proving that." "There's your boots. That sill's leaded and the lead's soft and there's two marks on it the size of a horse's foot." He looked at my boots with real interest. "What d'you take, four sizes too big?" "Two. Stuffed." "Ah," he said, and I saw him file it. "That'd hold better. I'd not thought of that." We stood and sat in the dark of my father's hall and I understood, with a kind of cold slither, that he was not going to shout for anybody, and that he was enjoying himself. "The morning room," he said. "You said the morning room, Tuesday night, out loud, to yourself. Bess heard you and went to look and I called her back. Nobody's called that room the morning room in three year. Sowerby calls it the green room and my men call it the room with the fireplace." He put his chin up. "You're Crane's daughter." I did not answer him. It was not a question that wanted an answer and he did not wait for one. "You painted out the frieze," I said. "I did." "My mother painted that." "Then I'm sorry it were your mother's," he said. "It were blistered through to the plaster. There's a gutter over that corner been running down inside the wall since before I come, and the render behind that picture rail were wet as a sponge. You can't save paint off wet plaster. You can wash it and you can size it and it'll come away in your hand in a twelvemonth." He said it flatly, the way a man reads out a figure. "I'm not sorry for painting it. You can be sorry and I'll not mind you being sorry. I'll not be sorry for painting a wall that wanted painting." "You might have written." "To who?" And there it was, and I had no answer to that either. To who. To Miss Crane, of somewhere; of a room in Camden with damp on the north wall; of nowhere, care of a fat man in Gray's Inn Road. "There were hares on it," I said. "She wasn't any good. They looked stunned." He barked once — one short laugh, out of nowhere, and it made me jump, and the dog got up and turned round twice and lay down again. "Sit on the step," he said. "Go on. You've come in at a window twice, you can sit in a chair once, and there being no chair, sit on the step." I sat on the step. Three treads below him, in my ruined boots. "Now then," he said. "The cabinet." "I've no idea what you mean." "You've been at it with wires. There's scratches on the escutcheon like a cat's been at it." He let that stand a moment, kindly, the way you leave a man his coat. "You'll not open it. It's a six-lever and a curtain and it cost thirty-two shillings, which I'll thank you to consider, and it were fitted by me the month I come." "Why would a man put a Chubb lock on a cabinet that isn't his?" "Because it isn't mine," he said. "It come with the house, and the house come with a deal of rubbish nobody claimed, and I'll not have it said the man from Bury went through the drawers. So it's locked and it stops locked, and if the party as owns it wants it they can write to me and I'll cart it to the station myself." He picked up the lamp. "The key went to London with the executors, to a firm of agents. Ten year gone. Now — are you fed?" "What?" "Are you fed. It's a plain question." "I had a chop at eight." "Then come at three tomorrow," said Mr. Hale, "and look at the house in the daylight, if you've a mind to. Front door. It's not locked till nine; there's nowt in it worth taking." I would have preferred the constable.

# Chapter Four: Daylight I went at three the next day, and I hated it, and I went. The drive is a quarter of a mile of lime trees, and I had ridden a pony down it, and now I walked up it in a mended jacket with my hair screwed low, past a heap of panelling stacked in the stable yard under a tarpaulin. Oak, that. Jacobean in the dining room and 1780 in the rest, and it was stacked like deals with the nail holes weeping rust. There must have been eighty pounds' worth of it going soft in the wet. The front door was on the latch, as he had said. Ashcott in daylight is worse and better than Ashcott at one in the morning. Worse, because you can see the plaster down in patches and the marks on the wall in the long gallery where the pictures were, twelve rectangles, cleaner than the rest, so that the house has the look of a mouth with the teeth out. Better, because the light comes in off the hill in the afternoon through the west windows in a way I had entirely stopped remembering, and it was doing it, and it did not care who owned the place. Mrs. Sowerby came out of the passage by the still-room with a basin in her hands. She was fifty-nine and I had last seen her at forty-nine and the difference was in her hip. She stopped, and looked, and did not put the basin down, and did not curtsey. "Miss Isabel," she said. "Mrs. Sowerby." "You'll be stopping to tea, then." Flat as a slate. "Mr. Hale asked me to come and see the house." "Aye," she said. "He would." And she stood there with the basin and looked at me for as long as it takes to count four, and there was a thing behind her face that I did not read then and have thought about every week since. Then she said, "You've grown very like your mother about the mouth," and went past me up the stairs, sideways, one hand on the rail, taking each step with the good leg first, and she knew I was watching her do it and she went slower on purpose. I stood in the hall of my father's house and thought: *her boots are cracked across the toe*, and thought less of her for it. I want that written down too. I have said what I am frightened of; I may as well say what I am. The bootboy sold me the key for one and threepence. He was fourteen or so, small, chapped, one ear standing further out than the other, and he found me in the long gallery and put it to me directly, as one tradesman to another, that he knew what I was after and that the price was a shilling and threepence and he'd want it now, not after. "You've a very good opinion of yourself," I said. "I've priced a fiddle at Bakewell at nine shilling," said Ambrose Peel. "I've four and tuppence. Do you want it or don't you?" I gave him the money. He told me that the key to the japanned cabinet was not in the house at all, but that there was a *drawing* of it — the master had had one made when he fitted the lock, on a card, with the levers set out, and it was in the estate room in the bureau with the drainage plans, second drawer, not locked. Also that Mrs. Sowerby knew perfectly well I had been in the house at night and had not said so to the master; and that if I meant to stop I should keep off the back stairs, because she was up and down them at all hours with her hip. "She knows?" "She's known since Tuesday," he said. "There's soot off the nursery sill on the passage floor and nobody in this house cleans it but her." And he whistled his way off down the gallery, badly, the same four notes over and over, and I stood there with a shilling and threepence gone and the whole of my professional standing in ruins. Hale showed me the quarry from the terrace at four o'clock. It is half a mile off, over the shoulder of the hill, and you cannot see the face from the house, only the spoil and the sheds and a thread of smoke and, when the wind sits north, hear the ring of it. He talked about it for eleven minutes without stopping. Setts and kerb, chiefly; the Manchester paving contracts; how a bed will run good for thirty feet and then take a fault and be fit for nothing but rubble. He was pleased with a brake he had patented for a crane, a friction thing, and made a shape with his two hands to show me how the shoe closed, and looked at me to see if I had followed it, and I had, and he was pleased about that too. Then he took out a notebook and told me what the house cost. "Three thousand four hundred, the freehold and forty-one acre. Roof, eight hundred and thirty, and that's not finished. Lime, forty ton. Sash cord, threepence a yard and I've used near a mile of it." He turned a page. "A girl to scrub the back stairs, one and six a day, three days a week. Sowerby, thirty pound a year and her keep, which is over the odds and I know it and I'll not haggle with a woman of her age." He shut the book. "Nobody ever tells you the small ones. Everybody'll tell you what a house cost. Nobody'll tell you the sash cord." He thinks that showing you his notebook is friendly. It took me a long while to understand that he is right, and that it is. "Who is it employs you?" he said. "A private party." "In London." "In Manchester," I said. "A woman. Her husband's people bought a quantity of furniture at the sale here in 'sixty-six, and there were papers in it that were hers, and she'd rather not go to law about it." It came out of me smooth as cream. I am a hopeless liar about small things — I cannot tell a landlady I have paid when I have not — and a very good one about large ones, and I enjoyed it, and I want that written down as well. "Ah," said Hale. He looked out at the smoke over the hill. "Because the executors' agents had the key, and I'd wondered if it were them. Prothero and Vane, of Gray's Inn Road. Ten year and never a word. There's a firm as does that class of work, I daresay." The light came off the hill and I said nothing at all.

# Chapter Five: The Cabinet I meant to be four days about it. I was three weeks. I went back seven times. Twice by the nursery window, out of habit and because I would not give it up all at once, and five times by the front door at three in the afternoon like a caller, and after the third time Mrs. Sowerby set a cup out for me without being asked and without looking at me, which was a form of speech. I earned it, mostly. Hale had eleven men on the roof and in the cellars and not one of them knew where the old drains ran, and I did. I remembered a summer when the kitchen court flooded and my father had the flags up and I sat on the wall and watched, and the run went under the yew and out to a soakaway in the paddock, not down the hill as every plan in the estate room said. I told him so. He went and dug where I said, on my word, in front of two men who thought me mad, and found a stone culvert eighteen inches wide, choked with roots, and stood in the hole up to his knees looking at it with his hat off. "Fifty year that's been backing up under my kitchen," he said. "Fifty year." "Sixty," I said. "There was a Rowsley man dug it. He'd a beard down to here." "You'd not remember that." "No. My mother did." It was a great deal easier to talk to him at the bottom of a hole than anywhere else. That is most of what those three weeks were: hands, and dust, and boards up, and lime in the seams of my fingers. I helped lift joists. I held a chalked line. I learned that plaster dust gets into the eye and stays a week, and that Hale sings under his breath when he is measuring, tunelessly, one bar of something over and over, and that when a man's shirt is wet through at the shoulders the shape of him is not a thing you can politely stop noticing. And on a Thursday afternoon we were down in the west cellar looking for the head of that culvert, with one lamp between us on a stone, and he had his arm in a flue up to the shoulder feeling for a brick that ought to have been a lintel, and I put my hand up beside his to take the weight of a slab, and he took my hand instead — not for anything, only to move it clear — and did not let go of it. Neither of us said a word. His thumb went over the short finger, the fourth on the left hand, where the joint isn't, and stopped, and then went on again, and I did not take my hand away. Then a jackdaw came down the flue. I have never in my life heard such a noise in a small stone room. It came out of the dark in a black rag with its wings going like slapped hands and hit the lamp and put it out, and Hale said a word I shall not write, and I went backwards into a stack of slates, and for perhaps ten seconds we were both of us shouting in absolute blackness at a bird that was shouting back, and then it found the doorway and was gone up the stair. He got the lamp lit. I was sitting on the slates. There was soot down the whole of one side of him, and soot on his teeth when he laughed, and I laughed until I had to hold my ribs, in a cellar, with my hair down and a bruise coming on my elbow, and it was the first time I had laughed like that since some date I could not tell you. "Well," he said at last, wiping his face and making it worse. "There's your lintel." There was, too. The bird had knocked it down. So that was that, and I shall not make more of it than it was, which was a hand held for perhaps four seconds and a great deal of noise. The card was where Ambrose said, in the bureau in the estate room, second drawer, with the drainage plans. A pasteboard card with the levers of the Chubb set out in ink, and the depths marked, and *fitted 14 Apl 1871* in Hale's own hand at the corner. He had had it made because he is a man who has a drawing made of everything; he had put it in a drawer that does not lock because there is nothing in this house worth taking; and he had told me himself, on the stair, that the cabinet was not his to open. I took the card up to Bakewell on the Tuesday, to a locksmith who asked no questions for two shillings, and had a blank filed from it, and came back with it in my glove. It went in sweet and turned at the second try. I remember the sound of it — a soft double click, like a knuckle — and the little heron on the door coming towards me as it swung. Inside there was one japanned tray, and on the tray a packet perhaps two inches thick, tied with pink tape gone brown, and no dust on the tray at all, because it had been shut up eight years. I did not open it. I want to be exact about this, because I have told it wrong before, to make myself better company. I did not open it because I was afraid to, in that room, with the light going and Hale's men whistling somewhere over my head and Mrs. Sowerby's step on the flags of the passage. I put the packet inside my jacket and I locked the cabinet again and I put the key in my pocket, and I walked out of the front door and down the lime avenue and four miles into the village with it against my ribs, and I told myself the whole way that a professional does not read what she is paid to carry. Which is true, as it happens. It was not why.
