# Chapter Six: Forty-One Pounds The candle at the Marlpit was tallow and guttered on one side. I cut the tape with the sash-knife. There were no ledgers. There was nothing that a court would have wanted, and nothing that a newspaper would have printed. There was a bundle of receipts and two letters, and the receipts were in my father's hand. He wrote a beautiful hand. I had forgotten how beautiful. Small, upright, the loops shallow, the sort of hand that makes a grocery list look like a treaty. *Received of Thomas Barber, coachman, the sum of Twelve Pounds, to be placed on deposit at four and one half per centum. 8 March 1866.* *Received of Mrs. Ellen Wass, cook, Twenty-Two Pounds. 14 March 1866.* *Received of John Fearn, of Ashcott Grange, One Hundred and Six Pounds. 2 April 1866.* *Received of Wm. Fearn, his son, Thirty Pounds. 2 April 1866.* *Received of Sarah Sowerby, housekeeper, the sum of Forty-One Pounds. 19 March 1866.* There were nine of them. They ran from the eighth of March to the eleventh of May. I sat and did the sum four different ways, as though one of them might come out otherwise. Overend and Gurney went down on the tenth of May, and the town of Derby knew what was coming by the middle of March, because the second letter in the packet said so. The second letter was from my father to Prothero and Vane, of Gray's Inn Road, dated the fourth of February 1867, three weeks before he died. It is not a letter I shall copy out. It was four pages and it began by reminding Mr. Prothero of an acquaintance in 1859, and it went on to a great deal about the state of his health and the unkindness of certain persons in Derby, and it asked for a loan of two hundred pounds, and then for one hundred, and then, on the fourth page, in that same beautiful hand gone slightly wide, for whatever Mr. Prothero could see his way to. There was a postscript about me. It said that he had a daughter of nineteen who played very prettily and that he did not know what was to become of her. The first letter was from a man in Derby, a Mr. Vellacott, in March of 1866, and it said in eleven lines that the position was hopeless, that Halliday would not renew, and that Henry must for God's sake take nothing further in over the counter. March the twelfth. He took Sarah Sowerby's forty-one pounds on the nineteenth. I had it all wrong, you see. Not the facts — I had never had any facts, that was rather the point — but the shape of it. For eight years I had carried about a thing with a villain in it. There had been men in the house measuring the furniture and a chalk cross on my mother's writing desk, and somewhere behind all that, I had assumed, there was a wickedness of the ordinary sort: sharp men, a conspiracy, my father unlucky or hard-used or made a fool of by his partners. I had never asked. There had been nobody to ask and it had been comfortable not to. And it was not that. It was a frightened man in a room, who could add, being nice to his housekeeper in the still-room about four and a half per cent. I know exactly what it looked like. He would have gone down himself, with his hat in his hand. He was charming with servants; everybody said so; it was the thing they praised him for. I do not know what he meant to do with it. I have gone at that from every side for years and I cannot get in. Perhaps he thought Halliday would renew after all. Perhaps he meant to put it in the Post Office in her name and never got to it. Perhaps he was simply not thinking at all by then, the way a man in deep water is not thinking, only reaching. I have wanted very much to believe that last one and I do not trust myself on it. It was eleven at night. I put my boots back on. I could have gone up in the morning and knocked at the door at three o'clock with the packet in my hand and a cup of tea set out for me. I went up the hill in the dark and up the pipe and in at the nursery window instead, over the potato trays, and down the back stairs with the packet in my jacket, and I have never been able to tell anybody why, and Hale asked me once and I said something flippant. She was in the still-room with a rushlight and the tea things, in her cap, with the key on her stay-lace. She did not scream. She looked at the state of me — soot on both cuffs, hair down — and then at the packet when I put it on the table, and she wiped her hands on her apron before she touched it, which is what did for me finally, and turned the receipts over one at a time with two fingers. She read the top one. Then she put the whole bundle down and squared it with the side of her hand. "Forty-one pound," I said. "The nineteenth of March. He knew on the twelfth. There's a letter here from Mr. Vellacott—" "I know when he knew." "You—" "I've known since the Whitsun after," said Mrs. Sowerby. "Barber's brother were clerk in that bank till the Easter, and he told Barber, and Barber told me at the sale, stood by the gig. There's not one thing in that packet, Miss Isabel, as I've not known these eight year." She put her hand flat on it. "I never wanted telling." "I thought—" "You've come four mile in the wet and in at a window at eleven at night," she said, "to hand me my own business back." I have been hit in the face. It is nothing to it. She would not sit down in front of me. I stood there and offered her money I have not got — three pounds then and something quarterly, I heard myself say it — and she looked at the wall over my shoulder while I said it, the way you let a child finish. "And what would I tell the master," she said, "when a woman as comes in at windows starts paying me a pension?" Then she took the rushlight and went up the back stairs, sideways, with the good leg first.

# Chapter Seven: Terms I gave the receipts to Hale in the estate room the next morning, at nine, having sat up all night not deciding to. He read them standing at the window with the light over his shoulder, going through the bundle in order, and then he read the Vellacott letter twice, and he did not say anything for a while. I had prepared myself for various things. Shock was one of them. "Nine of 'em," he said. "Two hundred and forty-odd, all told." "Two hundred and forty-three." "Aye." He squared the papers off on the sill and set them down. "Fearn's boy'd be William Fearn as farms Blackwell now. He'd have been twenty. That'd be every penny he had." He said it the way you would say a bed of stone ran ten foot and then took a fault. "I've seen worse ledgers than that, Miss Crane. I bought a wharf off a man in 'sixty-nine as had two sets of books and a wife in each of 'em." "He was my father." "I know whose he was." He looked at me then, straight on and too long, as he does. "What d'you want me to say? That he were a blackguard? He were a frightened man with a good hand of writing. There's ten thousand of him. I'll not stand here and pull a face for you, if that's what you've come for." It was, in fact, precisely what I had come for. I had wanted somebody to be appalled, so that I might have something to argue with. "Sowerby's forty-one pound," he said. "That I'll see to. Not as a pension — she'd not have it and she'd be right. There's a cottage at the Green wants a tenant and she can have it at nothing when her hip's done with stairs, and I'll put it in writing so it stands if I'm dead." "You'd have done that anyway." "I'd not thought of it till this minute," he said, "which is a different thing." And he put the papers in the bureau drawer, the one without a lock. Then he asked me to marry him, and did it as follows. "Now then. I've three thousand four hundred in this house and there's eleven hundred a year clear off the quarries and the brake, more some years. There's no settlement to speak of on my side beyond what a lawyer'd draw and I'll have it drawn generous, and there's no family to please. You'd have the housekeeping and the keys, such as they are, and Sowerby to fight, and I'd not interfere with you." He had got the notebook out. I do not think he knew he had. "The county will not come. Not the Bagshawes, not old Ashcott at Stancliffe, not the parson's people. They've not come for me in three year and they'll not come for a bank's daughter as married a Bury quarryman. There'll be nobody at your table but me and the dog and whoever we can get from Manchester on a Saturday. That's the whole of it, and I'd rather say it plain than have you find it out in a twelvemonth." There was a wasp on the inside of the window. I watched it walk up the glass. "And the frieze?" I said. He did not follow, for a moment, and then he did. "It's painted," he said. "It'll stop painted. I'll not have wet plaster in my house because a thing were sad." Which was the honest answer, and he could have lied to me in about four words and I would have known it was a lie and I would probably have accepted him. I said no. Or rather I did not say no; I said that I could not, and that he was very good, and one or two other things that were true and which I have not repeated to him since, and he stood there with his notebook open and let me get to the end of it. I have had eight months to make out why, and here is the best I can do. It was not the frieze; he was right about the plaster. It was not the county; I have never had a table anybody came to. It was partly my father, sitting in a rented room in Belper with a postscript about his daughter who played very prettily — because a woman who takes what is offered at nine o'clock in the morning by a kind man with money is a woman who has been *provided for*, and I had watched what came of being provided for. But mostly it was this, and it is not creditable. I did not want to be let in. Being let in is a thing done to you by somebody who could as easily not. I had spent eight years going up the outsides of houses precisely because up the outside of a house you are the only party with a vote. "Right," said Hale, when I had finished. He shut the notebook. "Well. You'll want the key back off that cabinet before you go, for I'll not have you keep it." I gave him the key. A week went by in the way that weeks do. I finished at Ashcott — I gave him three days on the drains and the roof valleys and wrote out what I remembered of the wells, eleven pages, and he paid me two pounds for it and made me take it. Ambrose Peel got his fiddle and played four notes on it at me in the stable yard, badly. Mrs. Sowerby put out a cup for me on the last afternoon and stood on the other side of the table while I drank it and told me about a woman in the village who was dying, at length, and then said, at the door, "You'd best write. To me, I mean. Not to him." Which I do, on the first Sunday of the month, and she answers on the third. In London I took the packet — the receipts, the two letters, all of it — to Gray's Inn Road, and Prothero opened it in front of me, and read the lot, and put an aniseed ball in his cheek. "Well," he said. "My client will be disappointed. He was after a conveyance." "You knew whose house it was." "My dear," he said, kindly, "of course I did." And that was all he said about it, then or ever. I told him I was finished. He was mildly sorry and said so, and observed that everybody was, and offered me copying at eighteen shillings a week, dull as ditchwater, and said I should be back by Michaelmas; they generally were. I took the copying.

# Chapter Eight: February The room in Camden was on the second floor at the back, eight shillings a week with coals extra, and I copied part-songs for a publisher in Hatton Garden at threepence the page and did not go back by Michaelmas. In November the glazier round the corner — Sowden, two men and a boy — put a card in his window for a hand at putty-work, and I went in and told him I could ease a sash and reglaze a Georgian bar and hang a cord single-handed, and he laughed at me until I did it, and then he gave me eleven shillings a week and the use of a bench. I liked it better than the copying. It was the same knowledge and nobody had to be frightened of me. And I will say this, since I began by saying the other. The state of the upper windows of the borough of St Pancras is a disgrace. There is not a house in three where the top sash will move at all; the cords are rotten in a quarter of them and painted solid in the rest; I have taken out catches so soft you could bend them on your thumb, and in one house in Mornington Crescent a hook screwed into bare plaster, and nothing behind it, and four people sleeping under it. I told the man so. He said his wife liked a window that stayed shut. I said his window would stay shut for a shilling and open for four and six, and he took the shilling. I do not steal now. I would like to be able to write that I have no thimble, and I have. It sits in the japanned box with the paper-knife and the child's tooth and I have never quite been able to get rid of the box, though I have carried it as far as the ash-pit twice. Then, on the eleventh of February, at about four in the afternoon, a ladder went up against the back of the house. I heard it before I saw it — that particular grind of a builder's ladder finding a windowsill, which is a noise I know the way a mother knows a cough. I got up from the bench. There was a man on it, coming up in a good coat, hatless, forty feet of London brick below him and his hands wrong on the stiles. He had gone one bay too far to his left, which put him at the sill of the water-closet window, which is eighteen inches wide and does not open. He had got both hands on it. He could not go up and he was not going to be able to go down, and the ladder foot was on cobbles with nobody standing on it. I put the window up. "Mr. Hale," I said. "You are at the wrong window." He turned his head about four inches, which was the most he had in him, and looked at me along the wall. "I'm aware," he said. "There is a door." "I've been at the door." His hands did not move. "There's a woman at the door in a cap as says there's no Miss Crane in the house and there's no gentlemen above the ground floor, and she said it twice, and then she shut it. So I've hired a ladder off a man in Bayham Street for one and six, which is robbery, and I've come up. It says in the papers it's the coming thing." "You cannot get in there. That window is eighteen inches and it does not open." "No," said Hale. "I have worked that out." So we stayed as we were for a moment, he on the ladder, I leaning out of my own window three yards to his right, and I discovered that I had my hand pressed flat on my chest like a woman in a magazine, and took it off. "Listen to me," I said. "You are going to put your right foot down two rungs. Not three. Feel for it, do not look for it, if you look down you will let go with one hand and you must not. Then the left. Then stop." "Aye." "Do not hurry, and do not be brave. Being brave on a ladder is how men die." He came down like that, two rungs at a time, with me talking, for the whole thirty-eight feet of it, and when he had six left he simply came off it in a heap onto the cobbles and stood up and brushed at his knees. I got downstairs faster than I have gone down any stairs in my life and out through the scullery, and my landlady came into the passage behind me with her mouth open, and I said, in front of her, that this was Mr. Hale of Ashcott Hall in Derbyshire and that he had come in at the front like a Christian and would be taking tea in the parlour, and she gave me the parlour for tenpence. His hands shook for about a quarter of an hour. He was furious — not with me; with the ladder, and the man in Bayham Street, and himself, and mortified past speaking of it, and he would not sit down until his hands had stopped, and then he sat and looked at the fire. "I can't do it," he said at last. "I'd not thought there were anything to it. It's only a ladder." "There is a great deal to it." "Aye. Well." He turned his hat over. "I'll not do that again." "No," I said. "Don't." We did not settle it that afternoon. We have not settled it now. I went up to Derbyshire in the April, and again in June for three weeks, and I have a room at the Marlpit and my own key to it, and there is talk of a licence in the autumn and there has been talk of a licence for two autumns. Sowden keeps my bench. I am nearly thirty and I have a trade and eleven shillings a week of my own money and I find I am not in a hurry to be provided for. He does not press me. He prices it up occasionally, out loud, and I let him. The frieze is still painted out. The culvert runs clear. And the catch on the nursery sash at Ashcott, second storey, west end, third window along, has never been mended, and will not be while I have anything to do with it. He asked me once, last summer, standing under it with a screwdriver in his hand, whether he should see to it while he had the ladder up. I said I would rather he left it. He looked at the window for a while, and then he put the screwdriver in his pocket, and we went in to our tea.

Good for melancholy-romantic atmosphere; good for the "why on earth are you here" question. - **Blaenau Ffestiniog / slate country** — grey, dramatic, rain-slicked, mountains of waste slate. Very cinematic. Could be a film shoot location: a big-budget fantasy or a gritty drama filming in the quarries. That gives the actor a *reason* to be in town, which is better than coincidence. - **Combination**: fictional town, "Porthgwyn" or "Llanfarian" or "Aberdaron"-adjacent, on the Llŷn Peninsula, with a film unit up at the old quarry/castle nearby. Or English name because the previous owner was English and she never changed the sign: **"Trellis Books"** — inherited from her father, or from an old Englishwoman. I like the detail of a sign that doesn't match the shop. ## The Actor Needs: rogue, fragile ego, charm as a survival mechanism, needs to be liked by *everyone*, including the postman, including the dog. Thoroughly charming. Derailed by indifference. Names: something with a bit of matinee gloss. Options: - Callum Vane - Dashiell "Dash" Kerrigan - Rafe Sutherland - Nico Hale - Ruairi Blaine - **Cal Ransome** — good. - **Jonah Vale** - **Teddy Marchetti** - **Kit Marlowe** — no, too literary-joke. - **Alec Sable** - I like **Cal Ransome** or **Rafe Dunmore**. Or something faintly absurd that he chose himself, and his real name is duller: born **Colin Prosser** in Swindon, professionally **Cal Ransome**. That's a good reveal — a mid-story vulnerability. Maybe even Welsh origins he's buried: born in Newport, accent sanded off by drama school. That's *very* good for the romance: the bookshop owner catches a vowel. Yes. Let's hold that: **Cal Ransome, né Callum Prosser of Cwmbran/Newport**, RP now, a "Welsh actor" only when it's awards-convenient, otherwise mid-Atlantic. - Career: was in a huge franchise ("the *Ferrymen* films," "the *Redcrown* saga"), now doing a prestige BBC/A24-ish drama shot in Wales to rehabilitate his image after a scandal. Scandal options: (a) leaked video of him shouting at a runner; (b) a very public break-up with a co-star; (c) punched a photographer; (d) an ill-advised interview where he insulted a beloved actress; (e) he walked out of a play mid-run. The most fitting for "fragile ego needing to be liked": **he was filmed berating a young crew member and the internet turned on him.** His whole crisis is that people don't like him, which is the only thing he's ever been able to guarantee. Excellent engine. - Or something milder: he's just relentlessly hounded because of a break-up with a pop star. Less thematic. I prefer the crew-member incident but softened — maybe it's more ambiguous, edited footage, but the ugly truth is that the unedited version is worse in a different way (he was cruel, then charming, and the charm was the worse part). ## The Bookshop Owner Options: woman, man, either. Prompt is gender-neutral ("bookstore owner"), "themselves." I'll make her a woman for a straightforward romance, though a male owner is interesting. Let's go with a woman — or reconsider: a queer romance with a male bookseller would also work and is fresh. But the "immune to charm" dynamic reads richest with clear class/culture friction. I'll go with a woman: strong voice, Welsh, dry, not impressed. Names: Nerys, Mared, Alaw, Bethan, Eira, Ffion, Gwenllian, Nia, Siân, Rhiannon, Carys, Elin, Heledd, Mair. - **Nerys** is great for dryness but risks sitcom associations. - **Mared** — lovely, less familiar to English readers, distinct. - **Heledd** — beautiful, mournful (Canu Heledd), maybe too obscure. - **Elin Vaughan**, **Mared Pritchard**, **Nia Llewelyn**, **Carys Bowen**. - I like **Mared** — I'll shortlist Mared Pritchard / Mared Owen. Or **Bethan** for warmth. Let's tentatively go **Mared**. Backstory options: - Inherited the shop from her father; stayed when she meant to leave; a half-finished PhD on someone unfashionable (Dorothy Edwards? Margiad Evans? Lynette Roberts — a real Welsh modernist poet, lovely deep cut). Actually **Lynette Roberts** or **Dorothy Edwards** or **Brenda Chamberlain** (painter-writer of Bardsey Island) — Brenda Chamberlain is a *gorgeous* thread for a Llŷn setting since she lived on Ynys Enlli/Bardsey. Yes: Mared abandoned a PhD on Brenda Chamberlain; the shop has a shelf of her. - Recently divorced, or widowed, or never married and tired of being asked. - Better than tragedy: something quietly humiliating. Her ex ran off with... no. Let's make it: she came back to nurse her father, he died, she stayed, and now the shop is failing and she's been offered money to sell to a holiday-let developer. That gives PLOT: money. And it gives Cal a way to be both useful and insulting (he can throw money at it; she refuses; later he does something better/worse). - Her immunity: not performed coldness but genuine preoccupation — she's doing stock-take, the roof leaks, the VAT is due, and a film star's face means nothing next to that. She also, crucially, doesn't watch his films. Or she has seen one and thought he was the least interesting thing in it. That line could be devastating and delicious. - She should NOT be a shrew. Her rebuffs should be funny, accurate, and a little kind by accident. - Inner life: flustered. We can access this via close third on her in some chapters, or keep POV with Cal and let her fluster leak through physical business (dropping a stapler, misfiling, saying "yes" to something she meant to say no to). The prompt says "inwardly more than a little charmed" — so I probably want at least some chapters in her POV. Alternating POV by chapter is clean. ## Supporting Cast - **Gwil / Gwilym** — 80-year-old regular who does the crossword in the shop and never buys anything; recognises Cal immediately and is deeply unimpressed / or is a superfan, which is funnier. - **Osian** — teenage part-timer, TikTok-fluent, who is the leak (he posts a photo) — good plot device for the midpoint betrayal. - **Del** — the dog. A three-legged lurcher who loves Cal instantly, which Cal takes as vindication. - **Ffion** — Mared's sister, in Cardiff, on the phone, telling her to sell. - **Marguerite / Suzy** — Cal's publicist, phone voice, brisk, terrifying. - **Toby** — the young runner Cal shouted at. Could appear in person late, which would be a strong beat: Cal has to apologise for real, off-camera, with nothing to gain. - **Rhys** — local farmer/lifeboat crew, mild romantic-rival red herring? Maybe unnecessary in 8k words. Could be a two-line presence, better as texture than triangle. - The **paparazzi**: two of them, one weary and almost sympathetic (**Lenny**), one feral. Making one of them human is good — Cal's relationship to being photographed is the theme. ## Plot Shapes (8 chapters, ~1000 words each = ~8,000 words total) **Shape A — The Week (linear, small, warm):** 1. He hides in the shop. The conversation. (Mostly dialogue, per prompt.) 2. He comes back next day with a pretext. Sparring. She puts him to work. 3. He works the shop, is seen by the town, charm offensive on Aberllwyd; a real moment with Mared over Brenda Chamberlain / her father's marginalia. 4. Night: the leak. A photo online. "Cal Ransome's mystery bookshop girl." 5. Fallout: press descends on the shop, Mared is exposed and humiliated; Cal handles it badly by trying to make it *nice* (spins it, uses it, boosts the shop's sales) — this is the betrayal: he made her a story. 6. The rupture. Her speech. He goes back to set. 7. He does the un-photographed thing: apologises to Toby; or turns down the redemption interview; or refuses to use the shop in the press narrative and takes the hit. Meanwhile Mared makes her choice about the shop. 8. Return. Rain. A reconciliation in the mode of the first chapter — dialogue, sparring, but with the armour off. Ambiguous-but-hopeful ending: he asks for a job application; she hands him a duster. **Shape B — Frame with time jump:** Chapters 1–5 the week; ch 6 six months later, he's at a premiere; ch 7 she comes to Cardiff / or he returns for the festival; ch 8 the shop. Slightly more sprawling; risks losing intimacy. **Shape C — Two-hander, near-real-time over one long day and night:** Storm strands him in the town, all eight chapters in ~24 hours, the shop, the flat above, the harbour at 4am, the paparazzi outside like a siege. Very charged, very unified, very dialogue-driven. Risk: too little plot, and the "fragile ego needs everyone to like him" theme needs a town to work on. **Shape D — He buys the shop.** Grand gesture; she is insulted. Could be a late complication in Shape A rather than the whole plot. Good ch 5–6 material: he offers to buy the building to save it and she experiences it as a purchase of her. Yes — keep. I like **Shape A with the storm-night compressed into chapters 2–3** and the money/ownership complication in 5–6. ## Beat-by-beat possibilities for the crucial Chapter 1 - Opening line options: from her POV, "The bell over the door went at ten past four, which was wrong..." Or from his: dialogue-first, "Is there a back door?" / "There is." / "Does it lock?" / "It's a door." - The comedy of her not recognising him — but careful: her not recognising him at all is a cliché, and slightly implausible for a world-famous actor. Better: **she recognises him perfectly well and simply doesn't consider it relevant.** That's funnier and sharper. "I know who you are." "Ah." "You were in that thing with the horses." "The— yes. Broadly." - She keeps working through the conversation: pricing, unpacking a box, dealing with a customer, the leak in the ceiling with a bucket. - Physical comedy: he hides in the Welsh Interest section / behind the curtain of the stockroom / under the desk; Gwil is doing the crossword throughout and offers a clue. - The charm offensive escalates: he uses her name too soon, uses the "I never do this" line, offers to buy the most expensive book in the shop, tries to make her laugh, tries self-deprecation, tries confession. Each fails or half-fails. - The turn: she says something true and unflattering and *not cruel*, and he goes quiet, and the quiet is the first real thing. Then he ruins it by being charming again out of panic, and she notices the ruin, and *that's* the hook. - End of ch 1: she sells him a book he didn't ask for and won't read (or will). He asks if she'll be here tomorrow. "I'm always here. That's rather the tragedy of it." Or he leaves out the back into the rain and the paparazzi get him anyway, and she watches him become a photograph. ## Themes / motifs - **Being looked at vs being seen.** Photograph vs portrait. Brenda Chamberlain painted people on an island. - **Second-hand books**: previous owners' names in flyleaves; being one in a series of hands. Cal has never owned anything second-hand. - **Language**: Welsh as a room he can't enter; his buried Welsh vowels; the shame of the sanded accent. "Dŵr" pronunciation joke. He can do any accent but not his own. - **Repair**: the roof, the shop, the man. A leak you can't fix, only re-route. - **Weather**: rain as constant, and one absurd clear evening. - **Reading vs performing**: she reads; he memorises. "I don't read books, I read scripts. It's a different organ." - Cal's trick: he asks everyone one good question, remembers the answer, and everyone thinks he's wonderful. Mared clocks the technique in ch 1. Later, he asks her a question and doesn't have a follow-up ready, and that's love. ## Voice notes - Cal: fluent, rhythmic, deflects with jokes, litters speech with endearments and "darling"/"love" (careful — could be off-putting), self-mythologising, quotes himself, name-drops, then abruptly plain when wounded. Long sentences. He performs shame charmingly, which is the tell. - Mared: short sentences, flat declaratives, literal answers to rhetorical questions (great comic device), Welsh idiom syntax ("There's a lovely thing," "Are you not going to...", "Now then"), occasional Welsh words, deadpan. Her flusterment shown in stage business, not confession — mostly. In her POV chapters we can go inward briefly and lyrically. - Keep dialogue-dominant. Minimal but precise stage directions. Avoid dialect spelling; get rhythm instead. ## Risks / clichés to dodge - *Notting Hill.* It's unavoidable as a shadow; lean into inversion instead of pretending. Maybe even hang a lampshade once, briefly, and then don't do it again. Actually — better if *he* makes the Notting Hill joke and she hasn't seen it. - The "you've made me a better man" speech. Avoid. His change should be small, verifiable, and undramatic (one unwitnessed act). - Her being magically un-materialistic. She should want money. The shop needs money. Her refusal of his money is not saintly, it's about not being a plot in his life. - Wales as quaint backdrop with sheep and rain and choirs. Need specificity: slate, VAT returns, second-home crisis, Welsh-language school, the lifeboat, Cadwyn shops, Trip Advisor. - Too-quick capitulation. She should stay prickly to the end; the ending's warmth comes from her *choosing* to be warm once, briefly, not from softening generally. - Endings: don't marry them. Best ending is provisional — a next thing, small: he's staying two weeks; she's letting him; the sign's being repainted wrong. ## Possible strong lines/moments to seed - "You're not going to ask for a photograph." / "I know what you look like. I'm looking at you now." - "Everyone likes me." / "That must be exhausting for everyone." - Her father's marginalia in a book; Cal reads it aloud and does it well, and she has to leave the room. - He does an accent for her; she asks him to do his own; he can't. - The three-legged dog loving him: "See? Dogs know." / "That dog loves the postman and hates my sister. That dog is an idiot." - The photograph that leaks isn't of them kissing — it's of him laughing at something she said, and the caption is about him. She's a blur in the corner, "unidentified local woman." That's the wound: not exposure, erasure. **That's very good — keep.** - Late: he gives an interview and says her name correctly and nothing else, or refuses to say it at all. Better: he's asked about the "mystery bookshop girl" and he says, "There's a bookshop in Aberllwyd. It has a leaking roof. That's all." Or he says nothing and the silence costs him a headline. - Very end: he's shelving. Someone comes in and asks if he's Cal Ransome. He says, "No." First time he's ever said it. That last beat feels like the ending. Strong. # Reflection The prompt's engine is very specific and I shouldn't let plot machinery crowd it out: a man whose entire self is built on being liked meets a woman who won't do the liking, and the failure of his technique is the first honest experience he's had in years. Everything in the eight chapters should be tested against that. Chapter 1 in particular must be almost pure dialogue, and the chemistry has to come from *misfires* — his lines landing wrong, her literalism puncturing his rhetoric, and both of them noticing the punctures with interest. **Setting.** Hay-on-Wye is tempting but wrong: a bookshop there is unremarkable, and the town is already saturated with literary celebrity, so no friction. A small, wind-scoured coastal town on the Llŷn with a film unit up the road gives me everything: a plausible reason for him to be nearby, a bookshop whose existence is an act of stubbornness, Welsh as a living language that excludes him, and the second-home/holiday-let economy as a real-world pressure on the shop. Inventing the town (Aberllwyd, or something close) frees me from geography-policing while letting me be specific about slate, salt, lifeboats and VAT. The Brenda Chamberlain thread — Bardsey, painting, an artist who chose an island — is a genuinely lovely deep-cut for the setting and gives Mared an intellectual life that isn't "bookish woman likes books." I should use it lightly, two or three touches, or it becomes a lecture. **Him.** "Cal Ransome, formerly Callum Prosser of Newport" is the right build. The buried Welsh accent is almost too neat, but it earns its place because it dramatises the theme physically: he can do every voice but his own. I must resist over-explaining it. The disgrace should be the crew-member incident rather than a break-up, because it makes his need to be liked a live emergency rather than a character quirk — he's in Wales doing a prestige drama specifically to be liked again. The subtlety I want: the leaked clip is bad, but what he's actually ashamed of is that he charmed his way out of it afterwards and the boy forgave him. That's a more interesting confession than "I lost my temper," and it lets the late redemption beat (a real, unwitnessed apology) land without a speech. **Her.** The biggest risk is that she becomes merely acerbic — a wall of comebacks. She needs to be funny by accident as much as by design, and her deflections should be *literal* rather than cutting: answering rhetorical questions straight, treating a famous face as a mildly inconvenient object. And she needs wants of her own that predate him: money, the roof, a decision about selling, an abandoned thesis, a father recently dead whose handwriting is in the stock. Her flusterment must be shown, not stated — misfiled books, saying yes when she meant no, rereading the same invoice line four times. If I give her one or two POV chapters, I can dip inward briefly, but I should be sparing; the delight of the prompt is inference. **Structure.** Shape A (the week, linear) beats the alternatives. The storm-night two-hander (Shape C) is atmospheric but starves the "everyone must like him" theme, which needs a town to charm. The time-jump frame (Shape B) risks diluting the intimacy in only 8,000 words. So: hide-and-meet, return-with-pretext, the town charmed and the first real intimacy, the leak, the fallout, the rupture, the private act, the return. Eight chapters maps onto that cleanly with roughly one movement each and no chapter doing double duty. The two structural details I'm most confident about: first, the leaked photograph should be an *erasure* rather than an exposure — he's laughing at something she said and she's "an unidentified local woman," cropped to a blur. That converts the standard fame-intrusion beat into something specific to these two people and to the theme of being looked at versus being seen. Second, his grand gesture should be the *wrong* one — offering to buy the building — so that his real change is measured by what he does afterwards with no camera present. The money question also keeps her refusal from being sanctimonious: she wants the money, badly; she just won't be a line item in his rehabilitation. **Ending.** Anything approaching a declaration will kill it. The strongest option I found in brainstorming is small and behavioural: a stranger asks if he's Cal Ransome and he says no. That's the whole arc in one syllable, and it leaves the romance provisional — he's staying a fortnight, she's letting him, the roof still leaks. I want the final chapter to rhyme with the first: same shop, same bell, same bucket, similar sparring, but with the technique gone. The last note should be warm and unresolved rather than triumphant. **Craft cautions.** *Notting Hill* is the ghost in the room; one glancing joke from him — and her not having seen it — inoculates me, and then I never touch it again.
