# Brainstorming ## The Asimov Register What makes something feel like Asimov rather than just "old sci-fi"? A few load-bearing elements: - **Dialogue as the engine.** People sit in rooms and talk, and the talking *is* the action. Reversals happen mid-sentence. A character says one thing, then reveals he meant another. Asimov's characters explain things to each other constantly, and the explanations are the plot. - **The small lever moving the large mass.** One man, one document, one clause in a contract, one fact of physics — and empires shift. Hari Seldon with a psychohistorical equation; Salvor Hardin with a bluff; Elijah Baley with a deduction. - **Bureaucracy and law as terrain.** Asimov loved jurisdiction, precedent, charters, protocol. Guns are less interesting than mineral rights. - **Retrofuturism:** brass fittings, pneumatic tubes, punch tape, "calculators," slide rules, viewplates, ashtrays in spaceships, cigars, decanters of sherry. Radio, not internet. Hard copy. Men in waistcoats aboard nuclear vessels. - **No graphic violence, low sexuality, wry humour, moral seriousness.** Violence happens offstage or is threatened and averted. - **The "puzzle-box ending."** The protagonist wins by seeing an implication nobody else saw. Often the reader is told everything and still doesn't see it. - **Big-and-small.** A page on the economics of interstellar shipping, then a page on a man worrying about his sister. ## The Substance: Azra Azra accelerates radioactive decay. Let me think hard about implications, because Asimov would. Physical/technical consequences: - **Drives:** a pinch of Azra makes a tonne of low-grade ore behave like weapons-grade material. Fission/fusion drives become cheap and small. Any nation can go interstellar. - **Weapons:** you don't need enrichment. You need dirt and Azra. The whole non-proliferation architecture of humanity collapses. *Any* actor with Azra and uranium tailings is a nuclear power. - **Waste disposal:** the *civilian* miracle — a century of nuclear waste can be aged into inertness in a week. This is a beautiful, underused angle. Earth has vast waste stockpiles. Whoever controls Azra controls whether Earth's poisoned zones ever become habitable again. - **Medicine:** targeted isotope therapy, sterilisation. - **The catch:** Azra doesn't discriminate well. Near a large enough concentration, *everything* decays faster — including potassium-40 in your bones. Miners get sick. Also, an Azra field can pre-detonate or fizzle a warhead — so it's simultaneously the ultimate weapon and the ultimate shield. That duality is very Asimovian: the same fact serves both, so the *interpretation* is what matters. - **Scaling law:** perhaps effect scales with mass in a nonlinear way — a small sample is a curiosity, a vein is a strategic asset, and a *sufficiently large contiguous mass* is... something else. A civilisation-ender or a civilisation-maker. Arthur's vein might be the first known deposit large enough to test the nonlinearity. - **Where did it come from?** A neutron-star collision remnant? Mars was struck by a fragment of an r-process ejecta cloud? Or — spooky option — it's manufactured, a relic. Asimov would probably keep it natural and geological but let a character *speculate* wildly, then have another character deflate them. Better: leave the origin as a genuine open scientific question with a beautiful mundane answer (Mars's missing magnetic field, a deep impact, isotopic dating suggesting the vein is *younger* than the planet). Economic consequences: - Azra collapses the value of enriched fissiles. Old uranium cartels ruined overnight. Someone loses a fortune — and that someone has fleets. - Indenture economics: Mars labour is cheap because Mars is worthless without a product. Azra makes Mars the centre of the human economy. The indentured are suddenly standing on the most valuable real estate ever. ## The Political Board Asimov-style: three or four named powers with clear, cynical interests, each convinced of its own necessity. 1. **The Antares Combine** (via its "Diplomatic Corps"). Off-world commercial dynasty. Old money from the outer shipping lanes. Nominally a chartered trading company with quasi-sovereign powers — the East India Company in space. They want Azra to *keep it scarce*, because they own the existing fissile trade. Or — more interesting inversion — they want to *give it away* to break Earth's monopoly on force. 2. **Earth / the Terrestrial Directorate.** Old, bureaucratic, still holds legal sovereignty over Mars leases. Wants Azra suppressed or nationalised. Terrified of proliferation — legitimately so. Represented by an aging, decent, exhausted commissioner. 3. **The Mining Consortia on Mars** (e.g., Kessel-Rhone, Tharsis Extractive). Brutal, local, immediate. They hold the indenture contracts. They want Arthur's plot and will get it by law, fraud or accident. 4. **The Indentured themselves** — the Free Labour Compact / "the Ledger" — a nascent movement. Arthur's own people. His father was one. 5. Possibly a **Spacer/outer-system** faction, or a scientific institute (the Rossum Institute? the Cavor Foundation) which is the only party interested in Azra as *knowledge*. Asimov would give us a scene where these interests are laid out in conversation, with the punchline that all of them are rational and all of them lead to war. ## Arthur Neegan - First-generation settler, born on Mars? Or born on Earth and came as a child? "First generation settler" — let's say his father was indentured, worked off his term, died of dust-lung, left Arthur a scrap of freehold and a debt. Arthur bought his own certification, became a survey engineer for a consortium, quit or was let go. - Character: competent, literal-minded, unromantic, stubborn. Not a hero. His weapon is that he reads the fine print — he's an engineer, and a lease is just another kind of load-bearing structure. This gives him an Asimovian toolkit: he wins by *technicality* and by *insight*, not by shooting. - Flaw: he's naive about people. He assumes documents mean what they say. His arc: learning that documents mean what people can be made to *enforce*, and then learning to weaponise that. - Personal stake: needs a small human anchor. A sister? A neighbour? Options: - **Delia**, his late wife — too maudlin maybe. - **A younger sister, Mireille**, still indentured to Kessel-Rhone because Arthur couldn't buy out both their bonds. Guilt engine. Excellent — makes the indenture system personal and gives the climax stakes beyond politics. - **Old Halvard**, a neighbour and former driller, comic-relief cynic, who becomes the voice of the labouring class. Could die to raise stakes, but Asimov rarely kills sympathetic characters. Maybe he just gets bought off, which is sadder and more interesting. ## The Antagonist/Patron: The Unknown Party Options for who's waiting at the end of the transfer: - **A Duchess/Director figure**: "Vashti Ono-Serrat, Plenipotentiary of the Antares Combine." Elegant, candid, terrifyingly reasonable. Offers Arthur a fortune, a title, and a cage. - **A machine/computer**: too late-Asimov, but a "Multivac" cameo is tempting. - **An old man who turns out to be a figurehead for a committee** — the reveal that the person offering is himself a hostage of his own institution. - Best: a **charming, elderly plenipotentiary named Sir Ewart Coyne / Alexei Vondt / Elias Marat** with a decanter and an ashtray, plus a silent aide who is the real power. Asimov loved the pairing: the talker and the watcher. Let me try: **Consul-General Isolde Varr** — no. **Plenipotentiary Deverell Achill**? I like something faintly baroque and corporate. **"Mr. Chandrasekhar Reyes, Plenipotentiary Extraordinary of the Antares Combine"** — hmm. Let's go with **Vasquez? Odaal?** I'll settle in reflection. Something like **Sable Antioch**, **Lady Serris Vane**, **Consul Emeric Vaal**. The offer itself should be *good*. Asimov's best scenes have the villain's proposal be genuinely attractive and mostly honest. Suggestions: - "We'll buy the plot for more money than exists on Mars." (Too crude.) - "We won't buy it. We want you to *keep* it. We want you to be its owner, publicly, loudly, and we will make you the most famous man alive — because a private owner is a legal firewall Earth cannot cross without breaking its own charter." — This is *excellent*. Arthur as a legal instrument, a human shield. Very Asimov: the value of a man as a jurisdictional fact. - The hook: they want him to sign a *development compact* rather than a sale, which makes them his agent — and quietly makes him liable/controllable. - The threat, delivered politely: "If you decline, we shall of course escort you home. We cannot guarantee the interest of others will be as gentle as ours." ## Plot Shapes (8 chapters, ~8000 words) **Shape A — The Legal Gambit.** 1. Aboard the transfer, retrograde retrospective of the retinue's arrival. 2. The meeting/offer aboard a station or ship. 3. Return to Mars; the counter-offers pile up; the consortium's coercion. 4. The scientist explains what Azra really is; the true stakes. 5. Betrayal — his sister's bond used as leverage; assassination attempt. 6. Arthur constructs a gambit involving the charter/lease law. 7. The confrontation: all parties in a room; Arthur plays his card. 8. Coda: consequences, cost, the wider historical frame. **Shape B — The Physics Gambit.** Arthur discovers the vein is not what anyone thinks — it's already been triggered, or it's a natural reactor, or its mass is above a threshold such that it can never be mined safely, only *managed*. He reveals this to make it worthless as a prize and valuable as a commons. Weakness: might feel like a cop-out deus ex machina. Strength: very Asimov ("the only winning move is a fact"). **Shape C — The Human Gambit.** Arthur uses the indentured labour force: 200,000 bonded workers whose contracts contain a clause. Freeing them makes the vein unminable. He becomes a labour Moses. Strength: emotional. Risk: sentimental, and a bit too politically on-the-nose for the register. **Best: braid A + B + C.** The legal instrument (A) is the mechanism, the physical fact (B) is the leverage that makes the legal instrument bite, and the indentured (C) are the beneficiaries and the cost. That's a proper Asimov three-layer solution. Concretely, a candidate gambit: Under the Mars Development Charter (Earth law, drafted a century ago to encourage settlement), *freehold* mineral rights are absolute — but they vest in the *registered occupier*, and cannot be alienated to a chartered body without ratification by the Directorate, which takes years and requires publication. Meanwhile Azra's decay-acceleration means the vein, once opened, sterilises the region and cannot be worked by indentured labour without violating the Directorate's own radiological covenants — the same covenants Earth uses to justify sovereignty. So: Arthur *publishes*. He gives the assay data away — to everyone, simultaneously, on open beam. Scarcity destroyed. But that's not quite enough of a personal win. Alternative, sharper gambit: Arthur discovers that Azra's effect is *not* a property of the metal alone but of its *geometry/isotopic matrix* — that the vein is a natural artefact that, if mined piecemeal, becomes inert. Only intact does it work. Therefore the prize can only be held, not divided; and a thing that can only be held whole is a thing that must be *governed*, not owned. He turns himself into the trustee. He signs a trust deed in which the beneficiaries are the indentured of Mars, with Earth as guarantor and Antares as contractor — making every power a stakeholder in restraint. Deliciously Asimovian: he builds a balance of power out of a legal document, exactly like the Foundation's Seldon-esque political engineering. I like this a lot. And the personal cost: he has to give up ownership, wealth, and his home; and Mireille's freedom comes at the price of his own permanent captivity as the trust's living signature — he becomes a state, and a prisoner of it. Bittersweet, cool-eyed, Asimov. ## Set Pieces & Scenes - **The retinue arriving**: eight men in Antares dove-grey, sidearms holstered, a polite lieutenant with a printed card. Arthur's dust-tarped rover, the greenhouse, the smell of onions. Retro detail: they present a *paper* warrant with a wax-and-foil seal. - **The transfer vessel**: cramped, hot, brass gimbals, acceleration couches with buckled straps, a viewport with Mars shrinking. A steward with a tray. Chapter 1 opens here — Arthur, in a borrowed jacket, watching Mars go small, replaying the past eleven hours. - **The meeting room**: a converted observation blister aboard the *Sagittarius Regnant* or on a station at Deimos-synch. Real wood panelling shipped from Earth as an obscenity of wealth. A globe of Mars in brass. Ashtray. Sherry. The plenipotentiary in a high collar. - **The assay**: Arthur's own instruments; a scintillation counter that shrieks; his father's old drill log. - **The Directorate commissioner** in a shabby office on Deimos with an actual paper filing system and a portrait of a dead president. - **The indenture hall**: workers queuing to have their bond-chits stamped; a wall of names. - **The climax room**: a hearing. Everyone present. Arthur reads a document aloud. Asimov would absolutely do this. - **Coda**: a historical-encyclopaedia excerpt? Asimov's Foundation used the Encyclopedia Galactica. Tempting to open or close with a dry encyclopaedia entry on Azra or on Neegan. That's a strong flavour move. Maybe use it once, at the very end, for the long view — or as chapter epigraphs. Epigraphs on all 8 might be too cute at 1000 words/chapter; using it twice (start of Ch1 and end of Ch8) could bookend nicely. Or just once at the end for the punch. ## Titles for chapters "The Courteous Arrest", "An Offer in Brass and Sherry", "The Value of a Man", "Sixty Grams of Certainty", "The Fine Print", "The Weight of a Vein", "The Hearing", "Trustee". Something like that. ## Tone & Voice Third-person limited, past tense, dry and clean. Long dialogue exchanges with minimal beats. Occasional authorial aside about historical context. No purple prose but vivid concrete detail: the taste of recycled water, the ochre light, the way Martian dust gets into a wristwatch. Avoid modern idiom. Use "calculator", "beam", "screen-plate", "spool", "chits". ## Risks to manage - 8000 words is *tight* for this much politics. Must not introduce more than ~6 named characters. - Must keep chapter 2 primarily dialogue as instructed, and make it sing. - Need to seed the physics fact early enough that the ending isn't a cheat. Seed it in Ch1 (Arthur's own anomalous readings) and Ch4 (the scientist), pay off in Ch7. - Avoid the story becoming a lecture. Keep Mireille and Halvard present as human ballast. - The ending must feel earned and slightly cold, not triumphant. --- # Reflection **What the prompt actually demands.** Three non-negotiables: (1) Chapter 1 opens aboard the transfer vessel with Arthur in retrospective bewilderment, and the Antares retinue's arrival is rendered (naturally, as flashback within that chapter). (2) The meeting with the unknown party is mostly dialogue, vividly staged, seeding larger intrigue. (3) Asimov's register — big-and-small worldbuilding, retrofuturism, political tug-of-war, a competent civilian protagonist. Everything else is mine to choose. So chapters 1 and 2 are effectively spec'd; chapters 3–8 need a spine strong enough to carry the promised intrigue to a real conclusion. **On the ending, which is the real design problem.** Shape A (pure legal thriller) risks being dry and, worse, arbitrary — legal cleverness with invented statutes can feel like the author moving goalposts. Shape B (pure physics revelation) risks deus ex machina; if the vein "turns out" to be harmless or unminable, the reader feels the stakes were fake. Shape C (labour liberation) is emotionally satisfying but tonally a poor fit; Asimov was not a barricades writer, and a triumphant uprising in 8000 words would be glib. The braid is clearly right, and the ordering matters: the *physical fact* must be discovered and verified in the middle of the story, not produced at the end. If Arthur learns in Chapter 4 that the vein is only potent while intact — that it cannot be divided without being destroyed — then Chapters 5–7 become the far more interesting question of *what a man does with a fact like that*, and the ending is a choice rather than a revelation. That's the Asimovian sweet spot: the reader has all the pieces, and the pleasure is watching a mind assemble them. The trust-deed climax appeals to me strongly because it does the thing Asimov does best: it converts a physical constraint into a political structure. "A thing that can only be held whole must be governed, not owned" is a sentence a Foundation character would say, and it gives me a climactic hearing scene where the solution is a document read aloud, with each great power discovering, one clause at a time, that it has been made a hostage of the others. That's dialogue-as-action, which is also the mode the prompt asks for in Chapter 2, giving the story pleasing symmetry — it opens with an offer made *to* Arthur and closes with an offer made *by* him. **On the cost.** A wholly triumphant Arthur would be false to the register. Asimov's winners usually pay in freedom, obscurity, or loneliness — Seldon dies in a wheelchair, Hardin becomes a legend and a prisoner of his own precedent. So: Arthur wins the vein for Mars and loses the vein for himself. He becomes the trust's living signature, which means he can never leave, never sell, never be private again. His plot is gone under a works complex; the greenhouse with the onions is bulldozed. And the sister's freedom is purchased, but she doesn't entirely forgive him for the manner of it — that human sourness is worth more than a hug. I want the last note to be Arthur alone with a document and a view, and then a cool historical frame pulling back a century. That's the correct Asimov exhale. **On the encyclopaedia device.** Epigraphs on every chapter would eat 400–600 of my ~8000 words and start to feel like a gimmick. But *one* use — as the final beat of Chapter 8 — pulls the camera back to the long historical view in exactly the way the prompt's "big-and-small-picture worldbuilding" wants, and it lets me state the stakes (proliferation, the century that followed) without a character lecturing. Perhaps a very short one at the head of Chapter 1 as well, to establish the frame and license the later payoff. Two total. Restrained. **On character economy.** My instinct to cap the named cast at six is right and I should hold to it, because at 1000 words a chapter every new name costs a scene. The essential set: - **Arthur Neegan** — engineer, literalist, quietly stubborn. - **The Antares plenipotentiary** — the Chapter 2 voice. Needs to be charming, candid, and genuinely persuasive; the scene fails if his offer isn't tempting. His silent aide can be an unnamed presence rather than a character, which is cheaper and creepier. I favour a name with a slightly baroque colonial-mercantile ring — something like *Consul Emeric Vaal* or *Plenipotentiary Sable Antioch*. Vaal is crisper and more Asimovian in its bluntness. - **Mireille Neegan** — the sister, still bonded. The human cost made specific. Must appear in person at least twice or she's a prop. - **Halvard** — old driller, neighbour, chorus of the labouring class, dry comedy. His being *bought off* rather than killed is the more interesting and more honest choice, and it teaches Arthur something about what money does to good men. - **A Directorate commissioner** — Earth's tired, decent, dangerous face. Someone like *Commissioner Iyov Rand* or *Auberon Quill*. Should be sympathetic and still willing to bury Arthur "for the species." - **A scientist** — the one party who wants Azra as knowledge; delivers the physics in Ch4. Could be a woman with an Institute affiliation and no patience for any of the powers. She's also the natural verifier of Arthur's ending, and a potential co-conspirator so Arthur isn't solving everything alone. That's six, with the consortium represented institutionally (through a manager who need not be deeply drawn, or better, through the commissioner and Vaal referring to them) — good discipline. **On the physics, and honesty.** I need the "intact vein" property to feel like real speculative physics rather than a convenient magic rule. The way to do it: introduce it as an *anomaly Arthur himself noticed* in Chapter 1 — his own field samples read hot at the drill face and cold in the assay tray, which he initially assumed was instrument fault or a bad standard. That plants the fact as observation, not decree. Then the scientist in Chapter 4 supplies the mechanism (coherence across the lattice; the effect is collective, scaling with contiguous mass; fragment it and you have expensive grey metal). Then everyone's strategic position inverts: Antares can't smuggle it out, Earth can't seize it piecemeal, the consortium can't strip-mine it, and the only usable form of the asset is a single object under single control — which is precisely a *government*, not a commodity. That inversion is the engine of Acts 2 and 3 and it arises from a seeded observation. Good. Honest. There's a nice secondary irony available: because the effect requires intactness, the vein is simultaneously the ultimate weapon-enabler and the ultimate deterrent, since anyone who bombards it destroys the prize. Mutual assured *nothing*. Arthur can name that in the hearing. **On pacing.** The tight risk is Act 2 sprawl. Mapping: Ch1 abduction/transfer, Ch2 the offer, Ch3 return to a changed Mars and the counter-bidders converging (Earth's commissioner + the consortium's squeeze on Mireille's bond), Ch4 the scientist and the physics turn,

Model Output:
# Intention **What I'm making.** A tight, cool-blooded Asimov pastiche in eight ~1000-word chapters: a legal-political-scientific puzzle in which one stubborn engineer converts a fact of physics into a constitutional arrangement. The pleasure on offer is watching intelligent people talk in rooms while the map of human power quietly redraws itself under them. **Plot spine.** Arthur Neegan's freehold sits on the largest known Azra vein. Chapter 1: he is politely abducted by the Antares Combine's "Diplomatic Corps," and we get the retinue's arrival as flashback aboard the transfer. Chapter 2: Consul Emeric Vaal makes an offer that is genuinely, dangerously good — he doesn't want to *buy* the plot; he wants Arthur to keep it, loudly, as a jurisdictional firewall against Earth. Chapters 3–4: Arthur returns to a Mars swarming with bidders; Earth's Commissioner Auberon Quill offers protection-as-burial; the consortium squeezes his indentured sister Mireille's bond; and Dr. Sofiya Ambrose supplies the physical fact — Azra's decay-acceleration is a *collective* property of a contiguous lattice. Fragment the vein and you have expensive grey metal. Chapters 5–6: the fact inverts everyone's position (nobody can smuggle, seize, strip-mine, or bomb it), Halvard is bought off, an attempt on Arthur's life proves the courtesy has expired, and Arthur drafts his gambit with Ambrose. Chapter 7: a hearing in which Arthur reads a trust deed aloud and each power discovers, clause by clause, that it has been made hostage to the others. Chapter 8: the cost — Arthur owns nothing, cannot leave, cannot be private again; Mireille is free and does not entirely forgive him — closing with a dry encyclopaedia excerpt pulling back a century. **The central idea I'm committing to:** *a thing that can only be held whole must be governed, not owned.* The physics constrains the politics; the politics is the climax. Crucially, the physical fact is **seeded as Arthur's own anomalous field observation in Chapter 1** (hot at the drill face, cold in the assay tray, dismissed as instrument fault), explained in Chapter 4, and weaponised in Chapter 7 — so the ending is a *choice*, not a revelation. **Voice and style.** Third person limited, past tense, clean and dry. Dialogue-forward; talk is the action. Reversals mid-sentence. Minimal interiority, conveyed through what Arthur notices — an engineer's eye for load paths, tolerances, and fine print. Retrofuturist furniture used concretely, not decoratively: paper warrants with wax-and-foil seals, spooled tape, scintillation counters, brass gimbals, calculators, ashtrays and decanters aboard nuclear vessels, hard copy that must be physically carried. Occasional short authorial pull-back for the big picture (proliferation economics, waste remediation on Earth, indenture as the price of a worthless planet), always in service of the immediate scene. **What I'm avoiding.** Purple prose; modern idiom; action set-pieces; graphic violence (the assassination attempt is brief, offstage-adjacent, and its aftermath is a conversation); a triumphant fist-pump ending; a labour-uprising climax; more than six named characters; epigraphs on every chapter (exactly one, at the very end); and any legal cleverness that isn't grounded in a stated charter provision the reader has already met. **Costs I will honour.** Arthur wins Mars's future and loses his own. His greenhouse goes under a works complex. Halvard takes the money, because good men do. Mireille gets her freedom and resents the manner of it. The last image is one man, a document, and a view. # Chapter Planning **1. The Courteous Arrest** (~1000w) Aboard the transfer *Ossuary-class* cutter, Mars shrinking in a brass-rimmed viewport, Arthur in a borrowed jacket he didn't choose. He replays the last eleven hours: eight men in dove-grey, sidearms holstered, a lieutenant with a printed card and a paper warrant sealed in wax and foil; the onions in his greenhouse; his father's drill logs bundled under his arm because nobody told him not to. Establish Mars, indenture, Azra's gold rush in compressed authorial strokes. Seed the anomaly: his samples read violently hot at the face and nearly inert in the assay tray — he'd filed it as a bad standard. Seed Mireille: eleven years left on her bond. End on the steward saying the Consul will see him. **2. An Offer in Brass and Sherry** (~1000w, near-total dialogue) An observation blister aboard a station at Deimos-synch: wood panelling shipped from Earth as an obscenity of wealth, a brass globe of Mars, an ashtray, a decanter. Consul Emeric Vaal, high-collared, candid, charming; a silent unnamed aide. Vaal explains Azra's real stakes — the end of enrichment, therefore the end of nuclear monopoly, therefore the end of Earth's authority; also the redemption of Earth's poisoned zones. The offer: *keep* your freehold. Be famous. Be a private citizen whose title Earth cannot void without voiding its own Charter. Antares will be his contractor, his counsel, his shield. The polite threat: "We shall of course escort you home. I cannot promise the next callers will knock." Arthur asks what happens to the indentured; Vaal's answer is honest and appalling. Arthur asks for time. Vaal grants seventy days, precisely, which tells Arthur something. **3. A Market in One Man** (~1000w) Return to a transformed Mars: claim-jumpers, surveyors, three offers on his door. Halvard's dry commentary. Commissioner Auberon Quill of the Terrestrial Directorate — shabby office, paper files, a portrait of a dead president — offers protection: nationalisation, a pension, a quiet residence on Earth. He is decent, exhausted, and perfectly willing to bury Arthur "for the species." Then Kessel-Rhone's move: Mireille's bond has been reassigned to a deep-face crew at the very vein — leverage with a human face. Arthur visits her at the indenture hall; she is not grateful for his interest. **4. Sixty Grams of Certainty** (~1000w) Dr. Sofiya Ambrose, Cavor Institute, no patience for any power, meets Arthur over his father's logs and his anomalous assays. The physics: acceleration is a collective lattice effect, scaling nonlinearly with contiguous mass; below a threshold, Azra is grey metal worth its shipping. His vein is the first mass ever measured above the knee of the curve. Implications land like dominoes: no smuggling, no piecemeal seizure, no strip-mining, and no bombing — destroy it and you destroy the prize. Also: nobody can work the face with human crews and honour Earth's own radiological covenants. Arthur, an engineer, sees a load path. **5. What Money Does to Good Men** (~1000w) Arthur begins quietly assembling: Ambrose's assay data duplicated to hard copy in three places; a reading of the Mars Development Charter's freehold and ratification clauses (planted, cited, quotable). Halvard has sold his adjoining strip and his testimony — apologetic, unashamed, wrenching. A survey rover is sabotaged; a man dies who isn't Arthur. Vaal's courtesy audibly cools by beam; Quill warns him he has run out of parties willing to lose. Arthur understands he is not a bidder but a commodity, and decides to become an instrument instead. **6. The Instrument** (~1000w) Arthur and Ambrose draft. The logic stated plainly: an indivisible asset cannot be property; the only usable form of it is a single object under single administration — which is a government, not a commodity. The trust deed: beneficial interest vested in the bonded and freeholders of Mars; Antares as sole contractor with a revocable licence; Earth as guarantor of the radiological covenants and holder of a veto on export; the Institute as auditor; Arthur as trustee — irrevocable, unsalable, and personally bound. He gets Mireille's bond bought out as his precondition, and she takes it badly. He sends seventy-day notice to all parties: a hearing, hard copy, with witnesses. **7. The Hearing** (~1000w) Deimos, the Directorate's chamber. Vaal, Quill, a consortium counsel, Ambrose, spectators. Arthur reads the deed aloud. Each clause detonates: Antares gets the work but not the ore; Earth gets the veto but not the title; the consortium gets indemnity but loses its bonds. The counter-arguments come and are answered with the physics and the Charter. Quill's crucial realisation: refusal means proliferation, acceptance means restraint, and no party can improve its position by defection. Vaal, admiring and cold, signs — and warns Arthur what he has just made of himself. Ambrose's audit clause is the hinge nobody thought to fight. **8. Trustee** (~1000w) Aftermath, quiet. The plot is gone under a works complex; the greenhouse bulldozed; the onions replanted in a tray on a windowsill Arthur no longer owns. Mireille, free, working for wages, angry at having been an instrument, honest about it. Vaal's parting courtesy. Quill's grudging respect and a caution about the next century. Arthur cannot sell, cannot leave, cannot be unwatched — he is a signature that must go on breathing. Final beat: a short dry excerpt from an encyclopaedia article on the Neegan Trust and the Azra century, pulling the camera back a hundred years to the wars that didn't happen, and the one line about the man himself.

# How a human writer would come at this A human writing an Asimov pastiche about a man who owns the most valuable dirt in the solar system would probably not start from a thesis. They'd start from an itch: *what does it actually feel like to be the guy whose land is suddenly worth a war?* And they'd chase the small, absurd, humiliating particulars of that — the fact that he has to borrow a jacket, that the men who abduct him are unfailingly polite and slightly bored, that he keeps thinking about whether he shut the greenhouse valve. Asimov himself worked this way: he was interested in ideas, but the ideas got into the story through people being petty, tired, vain, and clever at cross purposes. A human would also almost certainly let the story go somewhere they didn't plan. They'd write chapter three and discover Halvard was funnier or sadder than intended and give him more room; they'd find that Mireille refused to say the line they'd assigned her. The plan above is *very* well-behaved. Every beat has a function. Nothing is there because the writer liked it. Crucially, a human writing in a strong pastiche register would be having fun with the register. Asimov is *pleasurable* to imitate — the crotchety old men, the sherry, the person who says "Nonsense" and then explains why for two paragraphs, the way nobody ever describes what anyone looks like but everybody has a distinctive way of being irritating. A human would lean into that texture and let the plot creak a bit in service of it. The plan as it stands is more Asimov-shaped than Asimov-flavoured. # General LLM failure modes, and how they'd bite this piece **1. Thematic over-determination.** LLMs decide what a story is About and then make every element serve it. Here: *"a thing that can only be held whole must be governed, not owned."* That's a good line and a real idea — but the plan has the physics, the law, the sister, the neighbour, and the ending all pointing at it like a laser. Real stories have organs that don't do anything. The onions in the greenhouse are currently a *symbol* (they recur in Ch1 and Ch8 as bookend); a human might just have onions because Mars settlers grow onions, and never mention them again, and instead have Arthur worry about something stupid like a library book. **2. Everything pays off.** The plan is a closed circuit: the anomaly in Ch1 is explained in Ch4 and weaponised in Ch7; the Charter clause is planted in Ch5 and fired in Ch7; the seventy days is noted as significant and presumably resolves. This is *craftsmanlike* and also the tell. Chekhov's gun is a rule of thumb, not a law of nature, and when every gun fires the world feels like a set. Asimov, for all his tidiness, was constantly mentioning things that just existed — trade routes, minor officials, planetary quirks — because the universe was bigger than the plot. **3. The competence fantasy.** Arthur "sees a load path" and drafts an instrument that boxes in three great powers, and it *works*, and the only cost is a melancholy loneliness. This is the LLM's favourite protagonist: quietly brilliant, morally clean, vindicated. Asimov's cleverness-heroes usually win by *luck plus nerve plus being right about one thing*, and they're frequently pompous, wrong about adjacent matters, and rescued by circumstance. Salvor Hardin's coup works partly because his enemies are idiots. Arthur should be less competent and more lucky, and should be wrong about something important. **4. The bittersweet bow.** "He wins the vein and loses his own future; his sister is free and resents him; the last image is a man, a document, and a view." This is a *bow*. It's a tasteful, muted, tied-with-grey-ribbon bow, which is the most LLM kind. The story announces its own maturity. A human ending might be flatter, or funnier, or leave a genuine loose thread — or, most Asimovian of all, end on a *joke* or a piece of dry irony rather than an elegy. **5. Symmetry addiction.** "The story opens with an offer made *to* Arthur and closes with an offer made *by* him." The plan literally congratulates itself on this. Symmetry is pleasant but when it's this visible it flattens surprise. **6. Everyone is articulate and reasonable.** Every named character in the plan is *smart and candid*: Vaal is "charming, candid, genuinely persuasive," Quill is "decent, exhausted," Ambrose has "no patience for any power," Halvard is "apologetic, unashamed." Nobody is a fool. Nobody misunderstands. Nobody has a hobbyhorse they won't shut up about. Real committee rooms are full of people who are stupid in specialised ways. **7. The encyclopaedia coda as safety net.** Ending on a dry archival excerpt is a real Asimov move — but it's also a way of *telling the reader what the story meant* and how big it was, from outside. It's the literary equivalent of a title card saying "the wars that didn't happen." It converts ambiguity into scale, which is comforting. If used, it should be *unhelpful* — pedantic, mildly wrong, missing the point — rather than summarising. **8. Named-thing inflation.** Cavor Institute, Kessel-Rhone, Terrestrial Directorate, Antares Combine, Mars Development Charter, Ossuary-class cutter. The plan has good discipline on *characters* but the proper nouns are proliferating, and LLMs use capitalised nouns as a substitute for texture. Asimov used fewer names and more *specifics* — a number, a distance, a price, a temperature. **9. Prose that's already slightly proud of itself.** "Cool-blooded," "detonates," "the map of human power quietly redraws itself." The plan's register suggests prose that will reach for the impressive phrase. Asimov's actual sentences are plain to the point of homeliness, and the effect is dry authority. The danger is writing *literary* prose in an Asimov costume. # Deep dive: specific weak points in the plan **Chapter 2's offer is too clean.** "Keep your freehold, be famous, be a jurisdictional firewall" is a genuinely clever offer — maybe *too* clever. It's the kind of offer that makes Vaal an author-surrogate explaining the plot's mechanism. A human might make Vaal's offer cruder and let the *firewall* idea be Arthur's later reinterpretation of it. Or have Vaal make three offers in descending order of dignity, getting progressively more honest and less flattering as Arthur declines, ending somewhere quite ugly. Or — better — have Vaal spend half the scene talking about something else entirely (his own career, a grievance about a rival, the difficulty of getting decent tobacco past customs) because that's how powerful people actually conduct meetings. **The physics rule is load-bearing and slightly convenient.** "Collective lattice effect, nonlinear with contiguous mass, fragment it and it's grey metal" solves *all four* of Arthur's problems at once: no smuggling, no seizure, no strip-mining, no bombing. That's a rule designed backwards from the ending. It's not implausible, but it's suspiciously tidy. Ideas: make the rule *partially* true, or contested, or make it true with an ugly exception (you *can* fragment it usefully, but only at a scale of loss that no accountant will accept — which is a business fact, not a physical law, and therefore fragile). Or: the rule is true but *nobody believes Arthur*, and half the story is the humiliation of being right and unpersuasive. **Ambrose is a plot-delivery mechanism.** She arrives in Ch4 to explain, and in Ch6 to co-draft, and in Ch7 to be the audit clause. She has no interests of her own that cut against Arthur's. Asimov's scientists are usually monomaniacal and inconvenient — they want the *sample*, they don't care who dies, they'll leak the data to a journal because publication matters more than politics. A version where Ambrose betrays Arthur *for good reasons* (science must be open) or nearly wrecks him by publishing early would be much livelier. **Halvard's arc is a moral lesson with a bow.** "He takes the money, because good men do" is a nicely unsentimental idea, but the plan positions it as *teaching Arthur something*. Better if it's just a thing that happens and hurts and Arthur never quite processes it — or if Halvard's betrayal turns out to be *useful*, or if he takes the money and then does something loyal anyway for reasons he can't articulate. **Mireille risks being the Sister-Shaped Stake.** Her function is: exist as leverage, be visited, be freed, resent it. That's an arc with no agency. She should want something Arthur doesn't want. Options: she doesn't want out — she's got seniority, a crew, a position in the bond hall's informal hierarchy, and Arthur buying her freedom *demotes* her socially and strands her. Or she's already politically active and thinks Arthur's trust is a sell-out that entrenches Antares. Or she's simply not very nice and finds him embarrassing. **The hearing climax is a courtroom-drama shape with clauses instead of testimony.** Reading a document aloud while powers realise they're trapped is satisfying on paper but risks being a lecture with reaction shots. Asimov would probably keep the hearing *short* and put the real action in a corridor conversation before or after it — the deal done between two men over a cigar while the formal proceeding is theatre. Also: the plan has the powers *understand and accept* Arthur's logic. More human: one of them agrees for a completely wrong reason, one agrees out of spite toward another, and one never agrees at all and simply loses. **"Seventy days, precisely, which tells Arthur something."** This is a coy withholding — the narrator knowing more than the reader for effect. It's a tic. Either tell us or don't flag it. **The costs are all elegiac and none are stupid or ironic.** Losing your home, being watched forever, a sister's resentment — these are dignified costs. Human costs are often undignified: Arthur becomes a minor celebrity and hates it; he has to sit through ceremonial dinners; he gains forty pounds; people write to him asking for money; he develops a reputation as a bore; he's outlived by the trust and misquoted in it. Asimov would find the *comedy* in becoming an institution. # Ideas to make it more human **On structure and shape** - Let one chapter be an apparent detour: a chapter where nothing plot-critical happens but we learn how Mars works — a bond-hall queue, a water tariff argument, a funeral. Resist making it thematically resonant. - Break the symmetry: don't close with Arthur making an offer. Close with him being asked something small and answering badly. - Consider ending a chapter mid-argument rather than on a beat of realisation. - Let a chapter open in the middle of a conversation whose beginning we never get. **On Arthur** - Give him a specific, non-heroic incompetence: he's bad at names, or he's a pedant about units and corrects people at terrible moments, or he cannot stop talking about drainage. - Let him be wrong. He should misjudge one party badly — trust Vaal too long, or dismiss Quill as a nobody and be nearly destroyed by it. - Give him a bodily fact: bad teeth, dust-scarred lungs like his father, a tremor. Asimov's characters are rarely physical, but a first-gen Martian engineer would have specific ailments. - Let him want something petty and get it: a decent chair, credit for his father's survey, his name spelled right. **On the antagonists** - Give Vaal a hobbyhorse: he's obsessed with a legal precedent from two centuries ago and quotes it constantly. Or he's a snob about Earth vintages and mildly ridiculous. - Make Quill's decency partly performance and partly genuine, and never resolve which. - Introduce one genuinely stupid, dangerous person — a consortium manager who understands none of it and is therefore unpredictable. The most human threat in the story. - Let one power simply not show up when expected. Absence as menace. **On the physics and the idea** - Let the science be *argued about* by two people who both know more than Arthur, and let Arthur back the wrong horse briefly. - Include one wrong theory that's beautiful and gets a paragraph and is never mentioned again. - Have someone propose the horrifying application nobody wants stated: Azra as a way to make anyone's bones fail from orbit. Let it hang, unresolved. **On texture and register** - Numbers. Prices. Tonnages. Distances in kilometres and days. Asimov loves an actual figure. - Petty bureaucratic obstruction as comedy: a form filed in the wrong colour; a witness who must be physically present because the Charter predates beam-attested signature. - One long, slightly boring, entirely convincing paragraph of exposition delivered by a man who enjoys the sound of his own voice. - Avoid metaphor almost entirely. Let description be measurement. **On the ending** - Make the encyclopaedia excerpt *wrong* in a small way the reader can catch — misattributing the key insight to Ambrose or Vaal, or getting Arthur's initial wrong. - Or drop the excerpt and end on dialogue. Asimov ended plenty of stories on a punchline. - Leave the proliferation question genuinely open. The trust might not hold. Somebody should say so, and be right. - Let Arthur's last line be about drainage, or onions, or nothing at all.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The piece.** Eight chapters, ~1000 words each, in the plainest Asimov register I can manage: dialogue-forward, argument-as-action, numbers and prices and tonnages instead of metaphors, powerful people conducting business badly in comfortable rooms. Retrofuturism used as furniture, not decoration — paper warrants, spooled tape, scintillation counters, ashtrays aboard nuclear ships, signatures that must be made in person because the Charter predates beam-attestation. **Plot, plainly.** Arthur Neegan's freehold sits on an Azra vein of unprecedented mass. The Antares Combine's Diplomatic Corps collects him politely; Consul Emeric Vaal makes him three offers in descending order of dignity. Back on Mars, Arthur is bid for by Earth's Directorate (Commissioner Auberon Quill), squeezed by the Kessel-Rhone consortium through his indentured sister Mireille, and told by a physicist, Sofiya Ambrose, that Azra's effect is a *collective* property — fragment the vein and its potency collapses, not to zero but to unprofitability. That is a business fact, not a law of nature, and it is *contested*: Ambrose's own colleague disputes it, and nobody in power much believes her. So Arthur spends the middle of the book being right and unpersuasive, which is a humiliation rather than a triumph. His solution is not brilliance but exhaustion and a pedant's instinct: an asset that cannot profitably be divided cannot usefully be *owned*, only administered. He converts himself into an instrument — a trust with the bonded and freeholders of Mars as beneficiaries, Antares as revocable contractor, Earth as veto-holder on export, the Institute as auditor, and Arthur as irrevocably bound trustee. It works, but not because everyone sees the logic. Vaal signs out of a two-hundred-year-old legal grudge. Quill signs because a stupid, dangerous consortium manager has made the alternative frightening. One party never agrees at all and simply loses. Ambrose nearly wrecks everything by trying to publish. **Deliberate anti-tidiness.** Chapter 3 is largely a detour — a bond hall, a water tariff, a funeral — that is not thematically resonant and does not advance the plot much. Arthur is badly wrong about Quill, whom he dismisses as a clerk. The seventy-day deadline is explained flatly the moment it appears. Halvard sells his adjoining strip and his testimony and is never redeemed and never punished. Mireille does not want to be rescued: she has seniority in the bond hall and Arthur's purchase demotes her. The hearing is short and half-theatre; the actual deal is done in a corridor over tobacco. One horrifying application of Azra is named aloud and left hanging. One beautiful wrong theory gets a paragraph and is dropped. **Voice.** Third-person limited on Arthur, past tense, short declaratives, almost no metaphor. Description as measurement: 0.4 gravities, 11 degrees, 60 grams, 9,400 credits. Arthur's specific tic — he corrects units and cites clause numbers at socially catastrophic moments — carries characterisation without interiority. Comedy is dry and comes from vanity, procedure, and men not listening. **Ending.** No elegy, no bow. Arthur becomes a minor institution and finds it tedious: ceremonial dinners, begging letters, a plaque with his initial wrong. Mireille is free, employed, and unimpressed. Quill says plainly that the trust probably will not hold a century, and he may be right. The final beat is a short encyclopaedia excerpt that is *pedantic and slightly wrong* — it credits Ambrose with Arthur's insight and misspells his name — followed by one flat line of Arthur's about drainage. The proliferation question stays open. **Avoiding:** purple prose, thematic laser-pointing, symbol bookends, everyone being articulate and reasonable, courtroom triumph, competence fantasy, tasteful melancholy, proper-noun inflation, coy narratorial withholding. # Chapter Planning **1. The Courteous Arrest** — Aboard the Antares cutter *Bellona*, 0.3g, Mars shrinking in a brass-rimmed port. Arthur in a borrowed jacket, worrying whether he shut the greenhouse valve. Flashback: eight men in dove-grey, a bored lieutenant, a paper warrant with a wax-and-foil seal, the request that is not a request. Compressed authorial exposition on Mars, indenture, and Azra's eighteen-month gold rush. Seed the anomaly flatly: his face samples read 40× standard at the drill, 3× in the assay tray; he filed a fault report on his own counter. Mireille: eleven years on her bond. Ends with a steward saying the Consul is free now, and Arthur asking whether he may keep the jacket. **2. Three Offers** — (near-total dialogue) Observation blister at Deimos-synch; Earth-shipped walnut panelling, brass Mars globe, ashtray, decanter, silent aide. Vaal talks for two minutes about customs difficulties with tobacco before mentioning Azra at all. Offer one: purchase — 4 million, insultingly generous, refused out of confusion. Offer two: Arthur keeps title, Antares develops, Arthur is made famous as a legal firewall against Earth. Offer three, when Arthur hesitates: honesty. What Azra does to enrichment, monopoly, and Earth's authority; what it does to Earth's poisoned zones; and what happens to the bonded who work the face. The polite threat about the next callers not knocking. Seventy days, and Vaal explains why: a Directorate filing period, flatly, no mystery. Arthur asks a question about drainage tolerances that annoys everyone. **3. The Bond Hall** — Detour. Arthur home; three offers nailed to his door; claim-jumpers surveying his boundary. Halvard, neighbour and old driller, on the water tariff. Arthur goes to the bond hall at Ceraunius to see Mireille: the queue, the chit-stamping, the informal hierarchy in which she is somebody. She doesn't want buying out. A driller's funeral — nine minutes, standing, no ceremony — for a man Arthur didn't know. Commissioner Quill appears at the end, dressed badly, and Arthur takes him for a clerk and is rude to him. **4. An Argument About Lattices** — Sofiya Ambrose, Cavor Institute, wants Arthur's father's logs more than she wants Arthur. The collective-lattice hypothesis: potency scales with contiguous mass; fragmented, yield falls below shipping cost. Her colleague Brakel disputes it by beam and calls it "the Ambrose fallacy." One beautiful wrong theory (Azra as r-process ejecta seeded 900 million years ago, younger than the crust) gets a paragraph and is abandoned. Someone names the ugly application — bone potassium, from orbit, no delivery vehicle required — and nobody follows up. Arthur, being an engineer, asks what it costs to divide the vein and gets the only number that matters. **5. Being Right and Unpersuasive** — Arthur tries to *sell* the fact and fails. Vaal, by beam, is polite and unconvinced; the consortium's Mr. Doust — genial, thick, dangerous — simply doesn't understand and proposes blasting a test face regardless. Quill, whom Arthur now understands is not a clerk, offers nationalisation, a pension, and quiet residence on Earth, and is honest that he'd bury Arthur for the species. Halvard has sold his strip and his testimony: apologetic, unashamed, unpunished. A survey rover is sabotaged and a man Arthur employed dies. Arthur realises he is not a bidder but a commodity. **6. The Instrument** — Arthur drafts, badly, then better, with Ambrose correcting his physics and Quill's own charter clerk unwittingly correcting his law. The reasoning stated plainly: an asset unprofitable to divide cannot be owned, only administered. Terms: beneficial interest to the bonded and freeholders; Antares sole contractor under revocable licence; Earth guarantor and export veto; Institute auditor; Arthur trustee, irrevocably, unsalably, personally. He buys Mireille's bond as a precondition and she is furious. Ambrose tries to publish the lattice data early — for good reasons — and Arthur has to stop her, and does it clumsily and cruelly. **7. The Corridor** — Hearing day, Deimos. The formal proceeding is eleven minutes of theatre; the real work happens in a corridor with Vaal and tobacco. Vaal signs because the Charter's ratification clause revives a two-hundred-year-old Antares grievance against the Directorate and he cannot resist the pleasure. Quill signs because Doust has blasted his test face and killed four men, and the alternative to Arthur is now visibly worse. Kessel-Rhone refuses, litigates, and loses. Ambrose extracts her audit clause. Nobody is convinced by Arthur's argument; they are convinced by each other. **8. Trustee** — Eighteen months on. The plot is under a works complex; Arthur has an office, a chair he likes, and a plaque with his initial wrong. Ceremonial dinners; begging letters; a reputation as a bore. Mireille works for wages and finds him embarrassing. Quill, retiring, says the trust will not last a hundred years and gives his reasons, which are good. Vaal sends tobacco. Closing: a short, pedantic encyclopaedia entry on the Neegan Trust that misspells his surname and credits Ambrose with his insight — then one flat line of Arthur's about the drainage under Sector Nine.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Arthur Neegan **Background.** Born in the Aonia bond camps, 2287, first child born alive in that camp — a fact recited to him so often as a child that he came to hate it. His father, Osric Neegan, was indentured to Kessel-Rhone for twenty-two years on a nine-year bond (interest, equipment charges, water levies), worked off the balance at fifty-one, bought forty hectares of nothing at Sector Nine because it was cheap and adjoined a road, and died three years later of dust-lung with 900 credits and eleven survey ledgers to his name. Arthur was nineteen. He used the 900 credits toward an engineering certification at the Tharsis technical college, which took him six years because he worked nights running a water reclamation loop. He could not afford to buy out both his own and Mireille's bond; he bought his own, on the reasoning — which he explained to her at the time, at length, with figures — that a certified engineer could pay off hers in eight years. That was fourteen years ago. He has never quite got there, and he has never stopped explaining the reasoning. He worked twelve years as a survey engineer for Kessel-Rhone, then for the smaller Tharsis Extractive, then freelance after a disagreement about whether a shaft liner rated for 6 megapascals should be used at 7. He was right. He was also insufferable about it, in writing, to three levels of management. **Personality and flaws.** Arthur is a literalist. He believes documents mean what they say, and this belief survives an astonishing amount of contrary evidence. He is not stupid about people so much as uninterested in them as a system — he can read a load path in a rock face instantly and cannot read a room at all. His great flaw is a pedantry that operates as a nervous tic: under pressure he corrects units, cites clause numbers, and offers unsolicited technical amendments. He does this to men who are threatening him. He does it at funerals. He is also, and he would deny this, vain about being right. Not about credit — about *correctness*. He would rather be proved right and ruined than wrong and comfortable, and he doesn't understand that this is a moral position rather than a neutral one. Physically he is his father's son: 0.4-gravity height, 194 centimetres, thin through the chest, and he has his father's cough on cold mornings, which he does not discuss and monitors privately with a hand pressed flat under his sternum. He has bad teeth from camp water — three replacements, badly matched. He fidgets with a folding rule he keeps in his breast pocket, unfolding and refolding it in threes. **Idiosyncrasies.** Drainage. He is genuinely, boringly fascinated by drainage, subsurface water movement, and the behaviour of Martian regolith under load. He will bring it up. He keeps his father's eleven ledgers in a canvas case and carries them physically to meetings because he does not trust copies. He signs his name *A. Neegan* and is irritated when people spell it *Nigan*, *Negan*, or *Neagan*, and corrects them, and they resent it. **Motives.** In order of the honest truth: to be left alone at Sector Nine; to get Mireille's bond paid off so he can stop thinking about it; to have his father's survey work acknowledged as competent. Nowhere on this list, initially, is anything about Mars, labour, or the future of the species. Those get added late, by argument and attrition, and he never becomes comfortable with them. **Allegiances.** None. This is his actual strategic asset and he doesn't recognise it for most of the story. **Voice.** > "You said 'roughly forty times background.' It was forty-one point three at the face and three point one in the tray, and the discrepancy is the whole of what I came to talk about, so I'd rather we didn't round it." > "I don't want to be famous. I want a shaft liner rated properly and a boundary that nobody surveys without asking. If you can put that in the document I'll sign whatever else you like." > *He had shut the greenhouse valve. He was almost sure. He had been thinking about the valve when the lieutenant handed him the warrant, and he could not now recall whether he had thought about it because he'd shut it or because he hadn't.* --- # Consul Emeric Vaal **Background.** Antares Combine, fourth generation. His great-grandmother ran indenture ships out of Callisto and his family's money is old enough to have been laundered into respectability twice. He is not a diplomat; the Combine's Diplomatic Corps is a chartered armed service with credentials, and Vaal has held plenipotentiary rank for nineteen years. He has personally arranged the transfer of two planetary charters and one small war, and he is proud of the war chiefly because it cost fewer lives than the actuaries projected. He is 63, Earth-raised, and has never adapted to low gravity; he moves in Mars-orbit with a stiff, careful economy and sits down whenever possible. **Personality and flaws.** Charming without warmth, candid as a technique. He tells the truth roughly sixty percent of the time and considers this generous. His flaw is a genuine, consuming grudge: in 2094 the Terrestrial Directorate refused ratification of the Antares Combine's Callisto charter under Article 40 of the Mars Development Charter, applying a provision written for Mars to a Jovian body, and Vaal — who has read every page of the proceedings, who quotes the dissent from memory — regards this as the founding injustice of the modern age. He will bring it up. He brought it up at his own daughter's wedding. Anything that turns Article 40 against the Directorate is, to him, worth more than money, and this is the seam through which Arthur eventually wins. Secondary vanity: tobacco. He grows a specific Rhodesian leaf on a licensed hectare outside Bulawayo, has it cured to his specification, and cannot get it through Martian customs without paying a duty he finds personally insulting. He will talk about this at length before he will talk about business, partly as a power move and partly because he actually cares. **Physicality.** Heavy-set, high-collared, grey at the temples in a way he maintains. Hands very still. He has a habit of aligning objects on a table — decanter, ashtray, cigar case — into a straight line before beginning, and realigning them when someone disturbs them. When he is genuinely interested he stops talking and looks at the middle distance, and people mistake this for boredom. **Motives.** The Combine's interest in Azra is not scarcity — it is *abundance*. Antares owns hulls, not mines. If Azra makes drive-grade fuel cheap, Antares's fleets become the arteries of human commerce and Earth's enrichment monopoly becomes worthless paper. So he wants the vein worked, exported, and above all wants Earth *not* to hold the veto. When Arthur's trust gives Earth a veto but gives Antares the contract and revives Article 40 as a weapon against the Directorate, Vaal makes a trade he knows is bad and cannot resist. **Allegiances.** The Combine, absolutely, in the sense that a man is loyal to his own name. He would sell any individual person in it. **Voice.** > "Mr. Neegan, do you know what the duty is on nine kilos of cured leaf at Deimos transfer? Four hundred and twelve credits. Four hundred and twelve. I have moved a battalion through that port for less. Sit down. Sherry?" > "I am going to be honest with you, which is a thing I do rarely and therefore badly. Sixty thousand men are bonded to the consortia on this planet. When your vein opens, they will work the face, and the face will kill them, and it will kill them at a rate that is calculable and has in fact been calculated. Nobody in this room intends that. It will happen anyway. Do you want the four million or not?" > "In 2094 the Directorate applied Article 40 of a Martian charter to a moon of Jupiter. You will say that is old business. It is. I have a very long memory and no other hobbies." --- # Commissioner Auberon Quill **Background.** Terrestrial Directorate, Office of Colonial Assay and Compliance. Fifty-eight years old, thirty-four in service, posted to Deimos for the last nine, which is a punishment posting and both he and everyone else know it. He was co-author of the Radiological Covenants of 2271 — the document Earth uses to justify its authority over colonial extraction — and he has watched it become a fig leaf, and he authorises the fig leaf every quarter with his own signature because the alternative is worse. He has a wife on Earth whom he sees for six weeks in three years and a son who does not write. **Personality and flaws.** He dresses badly on purpose, having discovered decades ago that people underestimate a shabby man and say more than they should. It has become genuine: he no longer knows whether it is a tactic or that he has stopped caring. He is decent — actually decent, he lies awake about the covenants — and he is also perfectly prepared to have Arthur declared incompetent, sequestered on Earth, and pensioned for life, and he says so out loud without any change of tone, which is the most frightening thing in the story. His flaw is fatalism dressed as realism. He has been in the room for thirty-four years while good arrangements decayed, and he believes all arrangements decay, and so he does not fight quite hard enough for the good ones. He tells Arthur at the end that the trust will not last a century, and gives four specific reasons, and every one of them is correct. **Physicality.** Short, thickening, bad shoes, a grey cardigan under his office coat in a chamber kept at 19 degrees. He keeps paper files in metal cabinets because the Charter requires wet-signature originals and because he likes the noise the drawers make. He eats boiled sweets constantly and offers them to everyone, including men he is about to ruin. Wipes his spectacles on his sleeve, always the same motion, three passes. **Motives.** Prevent proliferation. That's it, and it's not small: Azra means any actor with mine tailings and sixty grams of grey metal is a nuclear power, and Quill has read the Directorate's own projections and cannot unread them. He wants the vein sealed, or held by the only body that has ever restrained itself, which he believes — with reasons, and with shame — is Earth. **Allegiances.** The Directorate, without illusions. The covenants, with grief. **Voice.** > "Boiled sweet? They're not good, they're what the commissary has. — No, I'm not a clerk. It's a reasonable mistake and I'd rather you'd gone on making it, because you were being much more informative." > "I could have you certified. Not maliciously — the finding writes itself, Mr. Neegan, you've been abducted, you're under duress, you've made statements to three parties. Six months' assessment on Earth, a residence at Kew, nine thousand a year, and the vein goes to the Directorate as unadministered colonial asset. I'd be doing it for the species and I'd sleep, more or less. I'm telling you because I'd like you to understand that being right isn't a defence." > "Your document will hold about forty years. Then Antares will have a bad decade, or Earth will have a good one, and someone will find that Clause Nine reads two ways. It always reads two ways. That isn't a criticism. Forty years is a long time. I've never managed more than four." --- # Dr. Sofiya Ambrose **Background.** Cavor Institute, Phobos station, 41. Born Odessa, educated Leiden and Luna, specialist in condensed-matter behaviour under exotic decay conditions — a field with roughly nine practitioners, six of whom hate each other. She has published forty-one papers, been wrong publicly twice, and considers those two the most valuable things she's done. She has no money, no political interest, and no patience, and she is on Mars because Azra is the most interesting object in the solar system and she got there fourteen months before anyone from Earth. **Personality and flaws.** She wants the data. That is the whole of her, and it is both her virtue and the reason she nearly destroys Arthur. Her lattice-coherence hypothesis is real work, contested by her former co-author Brakel (who has publicly named it "the Ambrose fallacy," and whose objection is not stupid), and she needs to publish before he does. When Arthur asks her to sit on it for seventy days she agrees, and then doesn't, and files with the Institute's journal at day thirty-one, because the priority is the priority. She is not sorry. She thinks Arthur's politics are a temporary weather system and the physics is permanent, and on a long enough timescale she's right. She is also funny, in a flat way, and the only person in the story who treats Arthur as a colleague rather than an asset — which is why the scene where he stops her publishing, clumsily and cruelly, costs him more than the assassination attempt. **Physicality.** Small, quick, Luna-raised so she moves well in low gravity and badly on Earth-standard decks. Hair cut short with scissors, by herself, visibly. Wears the same three jumpsuits. Eats standing. When thinking, she draws on any available surface with a wax pencil and does not stop when asked. Her hands are chemically stained at the fingertips. **Motives.** Priority of publication. Understanding the lattice. Access to the vein — she is the only party who wants Arthur's plot for what's *in* it rather than what it's worth. She'll trade an audit clause for sampling rights and think she got the better deal, and she did. **Allegiances.** Brakel, in the way of an old enemy she cannot work without. Otherwise: nothing. **Voice.** > "Your counter isn't faulty. Your counter is the only honest instrument on this planet. Forty-one at the face and three in the tray means the metal doesn't do this by itself — it does it *together*, and when you break it up it stops, and every man who's offered you money for it is buying a very expensive grey brick. Do you have the rest of the ledgers or only these eleven?" > "Brakel calls it the Ambrose fallacy. Brakel called superfluid ordering in mixed lattices the Ambrose fallacy in 2298 and I have his letter framed. He may be right this time. That's not an argument for keeping it quiet, Mr. Neegan, that is precisely the argument for publishing it, and I'd have thought an engineer would understand the difference between a secret and a result." --- # Mireille Neegan **Background.** Born 2291, four years after Arthur, in the same camp. Bonded at sixteen, as everyone was; twenty-nine years old at the story's start with eleven years outstanding on a nine-year bond, which is normal. Deep-face crew at Ceraunius under Kessel-Rhone, and — the thing Arthur has never understood — *good at it*, and something better than good at the bond hall, where she runs the chit queue's unofficial order, arbitrates disputes over shift trades, holds forty-odd people's small money, and is called on for things. She has status. It is not legal status and it cannot be sold, and it is the only thing she has ever owned. **Personality and flaws.** Hard, practical, unsentimental, and — the point — not especially nice. She thinks Arthur is a fool who has confused being clever with being useful. She has not forgiven him for buying his own bond first, not because it was wrong (she has done the arithmetic too, and it was correct) but because he *explained the arithmetic*, at length, and has continued to explain it for fourteen years, and she would have preferred once, badly, in tears. When he buys her out she is genuinely furious: it strips her of the crew, the queue, the standing, and makes her a woman on wages who owes her brother something unrepayable. She says so. She takes the freedom anyway, because she is practical, and she does not thank him, and by the end she is a shift supervisor for the trust and finds him embarrassing at ceremonial dinners. **Physicality.** Shorter than Arthur, broad through the shoulders from face work, hands like a man's, a face-burn scar along the left jaw from a bad seal at nineteen. Sits with her boots out. Laughs loudly and rarely. Has a habit of counting on her fingers under the table — she does everyone's money in her head and checks it with her hands. **Motives.** Her forty-odd people's small money. Her position. Not being anybody's cause. **Allegiances.** The Ceraunius bond hall, absolutely and specifically — not "labour," not "Mars." Individual named people. **Voice.** > "Eleven years. I know it's eleven years, Arthur, I've known it every day for eleven years and you tell me like it's news you've brought me." > "You've bought me. You've bought me and you've put it in a document with the Directorate's seal on it so that everyone at Ceraunius knows I'm the trustee's sister and nobody will trade a shift with me again. Sixty thousand people in your paper and you couldn't manage the one you know." --- # Mr. Doust (Kessel-Rhone, Field Operations) **Background.** Consortium man, forty years on Mars, promoted for reliability rather than judgement. He has read no papers, understands no physics, and has been told by three sets of superiors that the vein is worth an enormous amount, and he intends to open a test face on schedule because his schedule says so. He is the most dangerous person in the story precisely because nothing that is explained to him goes in. **Personality and flaws.** Genial. Enormously genial. Calls Arthur "Art," which nobody has ever done. Genuinely likes people, genuinely does not consider four dead men a reason to change a plan, and would be baffled to be called a villain. Keeps a photograph of his grandchildren on his desk and shows it. His blasting of the test face — which kills four bonded men and vindicates Ambrose's hypothesis by producing three-times-background rubble out of a forty-times-background face — is what actually forces Quill's hand. He is never punished. He is transferred to Ganymede with a commendation. **Physicality.** Broad, red-faced, in shirtsleeves at all times, sweats. Slaps shoulders. Talks over people while nodding as though agreeing. **Voice.** > "Now, Art, I've had all this from the Institute woman and I'll tell you what I told her: there's forty-one times background sitting in that face and I've a schedule that says the fourteenth. Sweet? — Look at that. Six of them. That's the youngest."

Chapter One: The Courteous Arrest The cutter was called *Bellona*, which Arthur thought was a poor name for a diplomatic vessel, and he was thinking about the name because he did not want to think about the greenhouse valve. He was almost certain he had shut it. The valve was a quarter-turn brass gate on the feed line, twelve years old, with a stem that wanted repacking, and he had been standing beside it with his hand on the wheel when the rovers came over the rise. Which meant he had either shut it and then looked up, or looked up and forgotten. If he had forgotten, the tray line would run for eleven days at four litres an hour, the substrate would sour, and he would lose forty onions and a bed of soybean that had taken him two seasons to bring on. Four hundred and twenty-two litres. He worked it out twice because there was nothing else to do. The port beside his couch was set in a brass ring with sixteen bolts, and through it Mars had gone from a floor to a wall to a ball, ochre and hazed, with the Tharsis shields standing out in the low light like knuckles under a blanket. Deimos was somewhere ahead. Acceleration was 0.3 gravities and had been for six hours, and the couch straps were webbing with steel buckles that had been painted and repainted until the paint was thicker than the metal. He was wearing a borrowed jacket. That was the detail he kept returning to, more than the sidearms. Grey worsted, cut for a shorter and broader man, with a Combine sunburst on the pocket. The lieutenant had produced it from a locker and said, courteously, that the Consul kept his rooms at Earth-standard formality and that Mr. Neegan would be more comfortable. Arthur had been wearing a work coverall with a torn knee and eleven days of dust in it. He had let them dress him. He was still turning that over. His father's ledgers were in the canvas case wedged between his hip and the couch frame. Nobody had told him to leave them, and nobody had told him to bring them, and he had brought them because he did not trust copies and because his hands had wanted something to carry. The men had come at 0640, local. There were eight of them, in two rovers, dove-grey with the sunburst on the doors, and they had parked square on his boundary line rather than crossing it, which he noticed and which he understood was meant to be noticed. The lieutenant had walked the last sixty metres on foot. He was perhaps twenty-six, and bored in the way of a man doing a task he had done four times that month, and he had taken off his helmet inside the airlock and asked whether Arthur Neegan was at home. Then he had handed over a warrant. An actual warrant, on paper, folded in three, with a seal of red wax on a foil disc pressed with the Antares device. Arthur had held it and read it twice, standing in his own kitchen with the pump ticking behind him, and it had said that the bearer was authorised and directed to convey Mr. A. Neegan, freeholder, Sector Nine, Aonia, to a conference with the Plenipotentiary Consul of the Antares Combine, and that the said conveyance was to be effected with all courtesy and at the Combine's charge, and that Mr. Neegan's assent was respectfully solicited. "Solicited," Arthur had said. "Yes, sir." "That means asked." "It does, sir." "And if I don't assent." The lieutenant had looked at him with something that was not unkindness. "Then I'd have to signal in, sir, and they'd send somebody senior, and I'd guess they'd get here about the fourteenth. I couldn't tell you who'd get here first." That was the whole of the threat, and it was not even the lieutenant's threat; he was simply reporting the weather. Arthur had folded the warrant along its existing creases and put it in his breast pocket beside his rule, and had gone to get the ledgers, and had come back and said that he wanted it noted that the boundary was not to be surveyed while he was away. "Noted, sir," the lieutenant had said, and had actually written it down. Eighteen months, Arthur thought. That was all it had been. Eighteen months since the Chryse survey had brought up sixty grams of a grey, unremarkable metal from a depth of four hundred metres, and someone at the Cavor Institute had put it in a chamber with a gram of thorium-232 and watched a half-life of fourteen billion years become a matter of a fortnight. Azra. Nobody knew who had coined it and everybody used it. Eighteen months, and there were now forty-one registered extraction leases on Mars where there had been nine, and the bond camps were taking men off Earth at a rate the transports could not honestly service, and the price of drive-grade fuel had fallen eleven percent while the price of hulls had risen forty, and there were three navies quietly rewriting their inventories on the assumption that within a decade enrichment would be a thing a competent chemist could do in a shed. Mars had been worthless. That had been the whole basis of its settlement: a planet no one wanted, developed on borrowed money against future assay, worked by men who signed nine-year bonds at sixteen and served twenty-two. Arthur's father had been one, and had bought forty hectares at Sector Nine because it was cheap and adjoined a road. Arthur had run his own assay in September. Not for anyone; for himself, because his father's ledgers showed an oddity at the four-hundred-metre horizon and Arthur had inherited both the ledgers and the habit. The face had read forty-one point three times background. The tray, with the same sample, three hours later, had read three point one. He had cleaned the counter, replaced the standard, run it again, got the same, and filed a fault report on his own instrument, because that was what a discrepancy of thirteen to one meant: a broken instrument. He had put in for a replacement scintillator. It had not come, and then the offers had started arriving, and then the rovers. He wondered whether the men who had come to his door knew about the tray. He rather thought they didn't. Mireille had eleven years left on her bond. Nine-year bond, taken at sixteen, eleven years still standing at twenty-nine, and Arthur could account for every credit of the interest and had accounted for it to her, more than once. The hatch behind him cycled and a steward came in with a tray of nothing, and said, "Mr. Neegan? The Consul's free now, sir." Arthur unbuckled the webbing and got up carefully in the third-gravity and picked up his father's case. "May I keep the jacket?" he said.
