"Then I'd have to signal in, sir, and they'd send somebody senior, and I'd guess they'd get here about the fourteenth. I couldn't tell you who'd get here first." This is a perfect threat delivered as weather report, exactly as described. **The Tray Discrepancy** The 41.3 vs 3.1 reading, and Arthur's response of filing a fault report on his own instrument, is the chapter's central intellectual hook and it's planted beautifully. The reader understands immediately that this is the key to everything — the vein's potency is collective, not individual — while Arthur has filed it away as an instrument error. This is the kind of dramatic irony Asimov deployed well: the reader is slightly ahead of the protagonist, but not condescendingly so. **Character Consistency** Arthur is exactly as described in the profile: the ledgers carried physically, the boundary notation demanded and written down, the jacket detail (letting himself be dressed, then turning it over). The final line — "May I keep the jacket?" — is perfect. It's funny, it's sad, it shows a man who has been stripped of his context and is trying to hold onto something, and it's entirely in character for someone who would worry about a greenhouse valve while being abducted. **Minor Criticisms** The simile "like knuckles under a blanket" for the Tharsis shields is the one moment where the prose reaches for imagery in a way that slightly violates the register — it's not bad, but it's the kind of thing Asimov wouldn't have written. It establishes voice, character, world, and central mystery with economy and confidence. The Asimov register is maintained almost perfectly. The chapter does what it needs to do without overreaching, and the restraint is itself a form of craft. The small flaws (one metaphor, slightly abrupt Mireille paragraph) are genuinely minor. Chapter Two: Three Offers The room was walnut. Arthur noticed it the way he would have noticed a wall out of plumb. Walnut panelling, floor to ceiling, on a station at Deimos-synchronous orbit, which meant it had been cut on Earth, kilned on Earth, shipped up a gravity well at something like nine hundred credits a kilogram, and then fitted around the curve of a pressure hull by a joiner who had also been shipped. There was a carpet. There was a brass globe of Mars a metre across, on a stand, with the Aonia region facing the door. There was an ashtray of cut glass, and a decanter, and a low table, and behind the table a man in a high-collared coat, sitting, because sitting was easier. A second man stood in the corner and said nothing at all for the entire hour. "Mr. Neegan. Sit down. Do you know what the duty is on nine kilos of cured leaf, at Deimos transfer?" "No." "Four hundred and twelve credits. Four hundred and twelve, on tobacco I grow myself, on a licensed hectare outside Bulawayo, cured to my own specification by a man whose father cured it for my father. I have moved a battalion through this port for less. Sherry?" "I don't drink at 1400." "It's 0300 by this ship. Sit down anyway." Vaal moved the decanter three centimetres to the left, so that it stood in line with the ashtray and a flat silver cigar case. "You'll take a sweet biscuit, I suppose. Nobody on Mars refuses a sweet biscuit. It's the water." "It's the sugar tariff," Arthur said. "The water's eleven credits a kilolitre in Aonia and the sugar's forty-one." Vaal looked at him for a moment with what might have been pleasure. "Yes," he said. "It is. Four million credits." Arthur waited. "That's the offer. Four million credits for the freehold at Sector Nine, forty hectares, mineral rights entire, clean transfer, Combine to bear the registration fee and any Directorate cess. You would be, at a conservative estimate, the eleventh wealthiest private individual on the planet, and you may live anywhere you like except Mars. I'll have the instrument drawn tonight." "No," Arthur said. "You haven't thought about it." "I have. It's not enough." Vaal's hands stayed still on the arm of the chair. "How much would be enough?" "I don't know. That's why it's not enough." Arthur set the canvas case on the carpet beside his foot. "A man who doesn't know what a thing's worth shouldn't sell it. You know what it's worth. That's the whole of the difference between us and it's not a difference four million fixes." There was a pause of perhaps three seconds. "Well," said Vaal. "Good. That was the first offer and I'd have thought less of you for taking it. Cigar?" "No." "Then keep the second one. You keep the freehold." Arthur said nothing. "You keep it," Vaal said. "Title stays in your name, registered, published, uncontested. The Combine takes a development contract — we sink the shafts, we build the works, we haul, we sell, we pay you a royalty which will be nine or ten times four million over your life and I shall argue with you about the figure for a fortnight and enjoy it. And we make you famous, Mr. Neegan. That's not a courtesy, that's the substance of it. Every beam, every ledger, every schoolroom on three worlds knows the name of the man who owns Sector Nine, and knows he's a private citizen, and knows he holds under the Mars Development Charter of 2189, Article 12, freehold vesting in the registered occupier, absolute." "Why does that matter to you?" "Because Earth cannot take a freehold from a private man without amending its own Charter, and it cannot amend its own Charter without publishing a bill, and it cannot publish a bill without every other party in the solar system knowing eighteen months in advance what it means to do." Vaal turned the cigar case a few degrees. "You are a wall, Mr. Neegan. I should like to stand behind you. I am telling you this frankly because you are going to work it out on the transfer home and I would rather you had it from me." Arthur thought about it. "You'd hold the contract and I'd hold the risk." "You'd hold the *title*. The risk is that men come to your door. Men have already come to your door. Mine were polite." "They took my coverall." "They should have burned it. Forty-one times background at the face, Mr. Neegan? You've been standing in it." Arthur looked up. "We read your fault report," Vaal said. "Kessel-Rhone read your fault report. The Directorate read your fault report about ninety minutes after Kessel-Rhone, because their assay office is in the same building and one of the clerks has a second wage. You are the only man on Mars who thinks his instrument is broken." "It reads three in the tray." "I don't care what it reads in the tray." "You should." "Perhaps. I have a fleet, Mr. Neegan, not a laboratory." Vaal reached out and, at last, poured two sherries, and pushed one across the table to a man who had twice declined it. "Now. The third offer, which is not an offer, it's honesty, and I do it rarely and therefore badly, so bear with me. "Azra ends enrichment. That is the whole of it. Enrichment is the thing that makes a nuclear power a nuclear power — the cascades, the plant, the fifteen years, the eleven billion credits, the inspectors. With sixty grams of your grey metal and a heap of mine tailings, a competent chemist in a shed on Callisto is a nuclear power by Thursday. Earth understands this. Earth's entire authority over forty settled bodies rests on being the only party that can make the material. So Earth will want your vein sealed, and it will call that peace, and it will not be entirely lying. "Against which: there are eleven thousand square kilometres of Earth that nobody has stood on since 2140, and Azra ages waste to inertness in a fortnight. So there is a case for opening it that is also not a lie. "And in the middle of these two decencies there are sixty-one thousand men bonded to the consortia on this planet, and when your vein opens they will work the face, and the face will kill them. Not quickly. Calculably. It has in fact been calculated — I've seen the projection, it's forty pages and it's on the Combine's own paper. Nobody in this room intends it. It will happen anyway." The silence went on long enough for Arthur to hear the air plant. "My sister is bonded to Kessel-Rhone," he said. "I know. Ceraunius, deep face, eleven years standing." Vaal set down his glass. "I did wonder whether you'd mention it first or I would." Arthur picked up the sherry, looked at it, and put it down without drinking. "Seventy days," he said. "You said in the warrant you'd want an answer." "Seventy. There's nothing mystical in it — the Directorate's filing period on a disputed colonial asset runs ninety days from first notice and notice was served on the twelfth, and I want twenty days in hand to be cleverer than they are." Vaal shrugged. "Take the seventy. Sit in your greenhouse. Only understand that I am the courteous party, and I shan't be the last to call, and the next people won't knock." Arthur stood, and picked up the canvas case, and said: "The overburden at Sector Nine is one-eighty metres of unconsolidated fines over a caliche horizon. If you sink shafts there without a positive drainage plan you'll have a running-sand failure inside two years, whoever owns it. It's in my father's ledgers. Nobody's ever asked me about the drainage." Vaal regarded him for a long moment. "No," he said. "I don't suppose anybody has."

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of writing that demonstrates a thorough command of the Asimov register and a sophisticated understanding of how to build character, world, and stakes through dialogue and precise observation. The opening paragraph is a masterclass in the "description as measurement" technique outlined in the plan. The walnut panelling is not described for atmosphere but for cost — Arthur notices it as an engineer notices a structural anomaly, and the prose immediately establishes both his character and the economic logic of the world. "Nine hundred credits a kilogram" is exactly the kind of retrofuturist specificity that grounds the scene without becoming a catalogue. Vaal's opening gambit — the tobacco duty — is executed perfectly. It functions simultaneously as a power move, a character revelation, and a piece of world-building, and it lands because the model has given Vaal a genuine grievance rather than a theatrical one. The transition from tobacco to "Four million credits" is abrupt in exactly the right way, mimicking the rhythm of a man who has done this before and finds the preamble tedious. Arthur's refusal of the first offer is beautifully handled: "A man who doesn't know what a thing's worth shouldn't sell it." This is not a clever line in the thriller-protagonist sense; it is the response of a literalist engineer who has genuinely not done the calculation yet. The line is character-true and plot-functional simultaneously. The three-offer structure is executed with discipline. Each offer escalates in complexity and honesty, and Vaal's admission that the third offer is "not an offer, it's honesty, and I do it rarely and therefore badly" is one of the best lines in the chapter — it is self-aware without being cute, and it prepares the reader for the genuine darkness of what follows. The Azra exposition is handled with considerable skill. The information about enrichment, proliferation, and the bonded workers is delivered in Vaal's voice, which means it carries his particular mixture of candor and self-interest. The line "Nobody in this room intends it. It will happen anyway" is genuinely chilling and earns its weight. The mention of Earth's poisoned zones ("eleven thousand square kilometres of Earth that nobody has stood on since 2140") is exactly the kind of compressed world-building the plan called for — a single sentence that implies a century of history. Arthur's mention of Mireille is perfectly timed and perfectly brief. "My sister is bonded to Kessel-Rhone." The response — "I know. Ceraunius, deep face, eleven years standing" — establishes Vaal's surveillance capability and the power differential without any authorial underlining. The closing exchange about drainage is the chapter's best moment. It is funny, it is character-defining, and it is structurally important — it plants the drainage motif that will recur throughout the story. Vaal's final "No. I don't suppose anybody has" is the right note: not warm, not cold, but genuinely interested in a way that is more unsettling than contempt would be. The silent aide in the corner is a nice touch — present throughout, never explained, a reminder that this is a performance with an audience. Minor criticisms: The chapter is almost flawless in execution, which means the criticisms are small. The line "The silence went on long enough for Arthur to hear the air plant" is the one moment where the prose reaches for atmosphere in a way that is slightly at odds with the flat register elsewhere — it is not a failure, but it is a small departure. The sherry business (declined twice, then poured anyway) is a well-worn power-dynamic move and the model executes it competently without transcending the convention. The chapter follows its plan with remarkable fidelity: the walnut panelling, the brass globe, the ashtray, the decanter, the silent aide, the tobacco opening, the three offers in descending dignity, the seventy-day deadline explained flatly, the drainage question at the end. Every element from the plan is present and executed. The characters are entirely consistent with their profiles — Vaal's tobacco grievance, his candor-as-technique, his alignment of objects; Arthur's literalism, his refusal to drink, his pedantic drainage observation. The dialogue is the chapter's greatest strength. It is almost entirely free of exposition-dumping, every line is character-specific, and the rhythm of the exchange — Vaal controlling, Arthur occasionally puncturing — is maintained throughout without becoming mechanical. Chapter Three: The Bond Hall There were three offers nailed to his door. Not slipped under it, not left in the mail box at the road end: nailed, with four-penny nails, through the top edge of each envelope into the frame of the outer hatch. Arthur stood in his own airlock at 0400 local, twelve hours off the transfer, still in the borrowed jacket, and worked them free with the claw of his rule. Kessel-Rhone. Tharsis Extractive. A firm called Halberd Assay & Development that he had never heard of, with a Luna address and no telephone. The greenhouse valve had been shut. He checked it before he opened the envelopes. Somebody had been on his boundary. He found the stakes at first light: four of them, orange fibre, driven on the true line to within half a metre, which meant a proper instrument and a competent hand. The lieutenant had written it down and it had made no difference whatever. "Halberd's Kessel-Rhone," Halvard said. "Registered out of Luna so they can bid against themselves. Drives the price down. Or up. I never work out which way it drives it, but it drives it." He was sitting on Arthur's step with his boots in the dust, seventy-one years old, a driller for thirty-two of them and a neighbour for nineteen. He had a face like something left out over winter. "They've put the tariff up," he said. "The water?" "Eleven to thirteen-fifty. Sector schedule. Effective the first." Halvard spat, precisely, at a stone. "Now you tell me how that works. Eighteen months ago this whole quadrant was worth nothing, and there were nine leases, and water was eleven. Now there's forty-one leases and men coming off the transports four hundred at a time and every one of them drinking, and the price goes *up*. More buyers, more sellers, price goes up. Explain me that." "There's no more water." "There's the same water there always was." "That's what I said." "You said it in a way that's meant to make me feel stupid," said Halvard, without heat, "which is a thing you do, Arthur, and I've never held it against you." He got up, joints audible. "Thirteen-fifty. Your father would have gone up to Ceraunius and shouted at somebody." "Did that ever work?" "No. But he came back cheerful." Arthur went up to Ceraunius on the Thursday, on the ore road, in a hired rover with a bad heater. The bond hall at Ceraunius was four hundred metres long and ten high, sheet-steel over hoop frame, and it had been put up in 2261 as a machine shed. There were benches down one side and a chit counter down the other and the whole of the middle was queue. Sixty-one thousand bonded men and women on Mars, and perhaps eleven hundred of them at Ceraunius, and on a Thursday between shifts something like three hundred of them stood in a line that folded on itself four times to have a card stamped. Arthur had not been inside one for fourteen years. He had forgotten the noise. Not voices — the *stamp*, four clerks working, a flat hard knock every second or so, all day, and under it the ventilators, and under that nothing. He found Mireille at the far end, and she was not in the queue. She was standing at the side of it with a slate and a stub of chalk, and there were nine people around her, and she was saying: "—no. No. Ferrers has your Tuesday and you've got his Saturday, and Saturday's a long shift, so you're up on the trade and you'll stop complaining about it. Ilse. What." "Fourteen credits." "You've got twenty-two in with me." "I know what I've got in with you—" "Then don't ask me like you don't." Mireille wrote something. "Come Sunday. Not Saturday, Sunday, because Saturday I'm on the face and you'll have me woken up." She looked up and saw Arthur, and her expression did not change at all, and she went on working through the nine of them for eleven minutes while he stood there in a jacket with a Combine sunburst on the pocket. Then she came over. "You've got a Combine bird on your coat," she said. "They lent it to me. I'm giving it back." "You're wearing it in the hall." He had not thought of that. He took it off, which was worse, and stood holding it. "Eleven years," he said. "Four hundred and ten thousand, if it's bought clear, and I can get to four-ten inside a year now. Maybe six months." "I know it's eleven years, Arthur." She said it very evenly. "I've known it every day for eleven years and you bring it to me like it's news you've carried up the road." "I'm telling you that I can pay it." "With what?" "With what's under Sector Nine." "So sell it," she said, "and don't come up here and stand in the hall in a Combine coat and *tell* me about it. That's the part I can't stand and it's the part you can never once leave out." "I'm not selling it." "Why not?" "Because I don't know what it's worth." Mireille looked at him for a while. Behind her a clerk stamped, and stamped, and stamped. "Do you know what I am here?" she said. "You run the queue." "I hold forty-one people's money. Nobody made me do it and nobody can take it off me and it isn't in a document anywhere. If you buy me out I'm a woman on wages who's the sister of a man who owns something, and nobody at Ceraunius trades a shift with me again." She put the chalk in her pocket. "You've never once asked me what I've got. You've only ever told me what I haven't." There was a funeral at 1600, in the yard, because a man named Sowerby had come off a ladder in Number Four on the Monday. It took nine minutes. There was no ceremony and no words spoken by anybody official; the crew stood in a block with their helmets under their arms, and a woman read out his name and the number of his bond and the balance outstanding, which was two years and four months, and then everyone went back inside. Arthur stood at the edge because he had not known the man and had no business there and could not think of a way to leave that would not be worse. Afterwards, at the counter, a short thickset man in a grey cardigan and very bad shoes was going through the previous quarter's stamped chits with a pencil, licking his thumb to turn them. "You're in the way of the queue," Arthur told him. "Am I? Sorry." He did not move. "They stamp here. If you want to do that, do it at the end of the bench." "Mm." The man turned another chit. "Boiled sweet?" "No. Look — who are you with? Which office?" "I'm just going through the chits." "Well, you can go through them at the bench. And you can tell whoever files these that the balance column's being kept in credits and the interest column in old marks, which means every one of these people has been read a number that's out by about four percent for two quarters. Somebody ought to know that." The man in the cardigan stopped, with his thumb on a chit, and looked up at Arthur for the first time. "Yes," he said. "Somebody ought." He wrote four words in a notebook. "Four percent. You did that in your head?" "It's not difficult." "No," he said. "Evidently not." He took the sweet out of his own mouth, looked at it, and put it back. "Thank you, Mr. Neegan. Do go on being helpful. You've no idea how few people are." Arthur was halfway down the ore road before it occurred to him that he had not given the man his name.

[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably accomplished piece of Asimov-inflected science fiction prose. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. CRAFT AND VOICE The voice is precisely calibrated to the stated intention: short declaratives, measurement as description ("four-penny nails," "four hundred metres long and ten high," "nine minutes," "two years and four months"), almost no metaphor, and comedy arising from procedure and vanity. The line "He had a face like something left out over winter" is the chapter's one genuine simile, and it earns its place — it's the kind of plain, weathered image that fits the register rather than straining against it. The prose never becomes purple. It stays dry throughout. The retrofuturist texture is present without being labored: nails through envelopes, orange fibre stakes, a hired rover with a bad heater, chit-stamping, a machine shed repurposed as a bond hall. These details accumulate into a world rather than a set. CHARACTERS Arthur's pedantry-as-nervous-tic is beautifully rendered. He corrects the accounting error to a man he's trying to move out of a queue, at a funeral, in a borrowed jacket with a Combine insignia he hasn't thought to remove. The greenhouse valve callback ("He checked it before he opened the envelopes") is a perfect small beat — it resolves the anxiety planted in Chapter 1 with characteristic Arthur flatness, and it's funny without announcing itself as funny. Mireille is the chapter's real achievement. The profile specifies she should be hard, practical, and furious about being reduced to "the trustee's sister," and the chapter delivers this with precision. Her dialogue is exactly right: "I've known it every day for eleven years and you bring it to me like it's news you've carried up the road." The detail of her holding forty-one people's money, running the queue's unofficial order, is rendered in action rather than exposition — we see her working through the nine people before she acknowledges Arthur, and the eleven minutes he stands there holding the jacket is a quietly devastating image. Halvard is economical and effective. His observation about the water tariff — "More buyers, more sellers, price goes up. Explain me that" / "There's no more water" / "There's the same water there always was" / "That's what I said" — is a small gem of dialogue that does worldbuilding, characterization, and comedy simultaneously. The line "You said it in a way that's meant to make me feel stupid, which is a thing you do, Arthur, and I've never held it against you" is exactly the kind of thing a man who has known Arthur for nineteen years would say. Quill's introduction is handled with real skill. The plan calls for Arthur to mistake him for a clerk and be rude to him, and the chapter delivers this through the accounting error scene — Arthur is technically helpful and socially oblivious, Quill is quietly amused and dangerous, and the final beat ("You've no idea how few people are") lands with the right weight. The revelation that Quill knew Arthur's name all along is the chapter's best structural move. THE FUNERAL The funeral scene is exactly what the plan describes: "nine minutes, standing, no ceremony." The detail of the bond balance being read aloud — "two years and four months" — is the chapter's darkest moment, and it's delivered without comment or editorializing. Arthur standing at the edge "because he had not known the man and had no business there and could not think of a way to leave that would not be worse" is precise and true. This is showing rather than telling at its best. FOLLOWING THE PLAN The chapter follows its plan closely: three offers nailed to the door, Halvard on the water tariff, the bond hall visit, Mireille's refusal to be a cause, the funeral, Quill appearing and being mistaken for a clerk. The plan's note that this chapter is "a detour — a bond hall, a water tariff, a funeral — that is not thematically resonant and does not advance the plot much" is somewhat self-deprecating; the chapter does advance character and stakes considerably, but it does so without the machinery of plot, which is the point. WEAKNESSES The chapter is nearly flawless in execution, which makes the few weak moments more visible. The Halberd Assay detail (a Luna address and no telephone) is good, but the parenthetical explanation of why Halvard thinks it's Kessel-Rhone is slightly over-explained — Halvard's reasoning about driving the price up or down is a little muddled and the joke doesn't quite land. The transition from the funeral to the counter scene is slightly abrupt, though the abruptness may be intentional. These are minor complaints. The chapter does not attempt anything it cannot execute. There are no failed metaphors, no purple passages, no moments of unearned sentiment. The darkness is well-earned — the funeral, Mireille's anger, the water tariff — and the lightness (Halvard, the jacket, the accounting error) is equally earned. OVERALL This is a chapter that does exactly what it sets out to do, in a voice that is consistent, controlled, and genuinely funny in the Asimov mode. The characters are rendered with precision and the world accumulates through detail rather than exposition. The Quill reveal is the kind of structural move that rewards rereading. "Here." "Then I'll want the whole eleven and not the four-hundred-metre horizon, because Brakel will say I've selected, and he'll be right to say it even though I haven't." She was small and moved like someone Luna-raised, too much push in the ankle, and she came through his kitchen and put a case on his table and opened it before she had taken her coat off. Inside was a scintillation counter of Institute pattern, a wax pencil, and a folded chart of the Aonia quadrant with three coffee rings on it. "You filed a fault report," she said. "In September." "On your own instrument." "Thirteen to one. That's not a reading, that's a broken counter." "Your counter isn't broken." She had the wax pencil out and was drawing on his table, on the actual wood of it, and did not stop when he moved a cup out of the way. "Your counter is the only honest instrument on this planet, because you're the only man who's bothered to measure the same sample twice in two places. Everyone else measures at the face, gets forty times background, wires their principal, and goes to dinner." "Then what am I looking at?" "You're looking at a collective effect." She drew a lattice: dots, in threes and sixes, badly. "The decay acceleration isn't a property of the atom. It's a property of the arrangement. Azra sets up a coherence across the lattice — a phase relationship, if you want a word, and the word's wrong but it's the one I use in seminars — and the field that comes off it is the *sum*, and the sum goes as something between the square and the cube of the contiguous mass. Not the mass. The *contiguous* mass. Break the lattice and you don't get two half-strength pieces. You get two pieces of grey metal worth their shipping." Arthur looked at the drawing for some time. "Forty-one at the face," he said, "and three in the tray." "Because your tray sample was four hundred grams in a sack and it had been down a hoist. Congratulations, you fractured the most valuable object in the solar system with a rock hammer." She sat down, finally. "Now Brakel says I'm wrong." "Who's Brakel?" "He was my co-author for nine years and he is presently telling the Institute by beam that this is the Ambrose fallacy, and I've had eleven pages of it. His objection is not stupid. He says it's not coherence at all, it's a surface effect — that the acceleration happens in a shell a few microns deep at the interface between Azra and whatever's decaying, and that your tray sample read low because a sack of chips has the wrong geometry and half the surface is chip-on-chip. Which would mean you can cut it up all you like provided you cut it *cleverly*. He's proposing a laminate." "Is he right?" "He may be. He called superfluid ordering in mixed lattices the Ambrose fallacy in 2298 and I have his letter framed, and I was right that time, which is not an argument, it's a grudge." She turned the chart round. "There's a third idea, since you'll hear it eventually. Menotti's. She dates the vein at nine hundred million years, against four billion for the crust it sits in, and says it isn't Martian at all — that it's r-process ejecta, a fragment out of a neutron-star collision, that came in as a slug and went to depth and kept its ordering because it was never melted. It's a beautiful paper. I've read it four times." "Is that right?" "Probably not. The isotope ratios don't quite sit. It doesn't matter." She said this without any regret at all, and Arthur understood that she meant it: an idea could be beautiful and dead and she had space in her head for both. "What matters is the exponent, and to get the exponent I need to measure a mass that's above the knee of the curve, and every sample anyone has ever measured has been under a kilogram, and yours is not." "How much is mine?" Ambrose put her hand flat on the ledger. "On your father's logs, and my three shots off the boundary in November, and taking the caliche horizon as the floor — a contiguous body of between eleven and fourteen thousand tonnes." The pump ticked behind them. "There is no other measured object above a kilogram," she said. "Do you understand what I'm telling you? Every projection anyone has, every navy inventory, every ruined uranium cartel, every one of those forty-one leases — all of that is extrapolated from grams. And the extrapolation is wrong, and I can't prove which way it's wrong until I stand on eleven thousand tonnes." Arthur got up and filled a kettle, because his hands needed it. "Say you're right," he said. "Say it's the lattice. What does it cost to divide it?" "That's not a physics question." "It's the only question. You've told me the yield falls off. Fine. Nobody stops at 'falls off.' Somebody sits down with a pencil and works out whether the fall-off is worse than the haulage." He put the kettle on the ring. "So: nine hundred credits a kilo to lift mass off Mars, call it. What's the yield on a hundred tonnes against eleven thousand?" "On my exponent? Under two percent of the whole. Perhaps one." "Then it's not worth cutting." Arthur said it slowly, hearing it. "Not because it's forbidden. Because the arithmetic's bad. You'd spend the haulage of eleven thousand tonnes to sell the effect of a hundred and forty." "Yes." He gave her the cup with the good handle because his mother had raised him to, and she drank it standing up. "There's one more thing," she said, "and I'll say it once, and then I'd like never to discuss it, because I've discussed it with two men from Earth already and they wrote things down. "The effect doesn't select. It accelerates whatever's decaying. There is potassium-forty in your bones. There is carbon-fourteen in every protein in you. A body of eleven thousand tonnes doesn't need a delivery vehicle, Mr. Neegan, and it doesn't need a warhead, and it doesn't much need a target. It needs a hole in the ground and an argument about who's in range." Arthur stood holding the kettle. "How far?" he said. "I don't know. That's the exponent." She set the cup down. "Now. May I have the other seven ledgers, or are we going to be careful with each other?"

Chapter Five: Being Right and Unpersuasive He tried Vaal first, by beam, at his own expense: forty-one credits for eleven minutes on the Deimos relay, which he could ill afford and which felt, at the time, like the sort of gesture that established seriousness. There was a lag of two and a half seconds, and Vaal used all of it. "Contiguous mass," he said at last. "Between the square and the cube. And your authority for this is a woman on Phobos whose own co-author has publicly named it a fallacy." "He's proposing a laminate. That's an admission the geometry matters." "It is an admission that the geometry matters, which is a very long way from an admission that the vein cannot be cut." The lag. The faint hiss. "Mr. Neegan, I have on this desk a valuation from four separate houses. Every one of them extrapolates from grams, and you are quite right, and I have told my board so, and my board has told me that four houses cannot be wrong, and my board is composed of men who have money. I am not being flippant. I am telling you the actual mechanism by which your fact will be ignored." "You said you'd rather have it from me than work it out later." "I said that about politics. This is physics, and I have a fleet, not a laboratory." A pause that was longer than the lag. "Get Brakel to withdraw. That is not advice, it is the whole of the advice there is. Until the man who says she's wrong stops saying it, she is a woman with a hypothesis, and you are a freeholder with a hypothesis, and the only thing on Mars anybody credits is a number off a face." Mr. Doust came on the Tuesday, unannounced, in shirtsleeves, and sweated in Arthur's kitchen and called him Art. "Now, Art, I've had all this from the Institute woman — she came up to Ceraunius and she gave me an hour and I'll be straight with you, I didn't follow the back half of it." He said this with tremendous good humour. "Lattices. Coherence. Very likely. But here's my position. There's forty-one times background sitting in that face, I've seen the tape, and I've a schedule that says the fourteenth, and if I don't open a test face on the fourteenth then somebody in Luna asks me why not, and 'a woman on Phobos has a theory' is not a thing I can write on a form." "You'd be destroying the thing you're testing." "I'd be taking a sample." "A sample of a collective effect is not a sample. It's like taking a sample of a bridge." Doust laughed, genuinely, as at a good line. "Sweet? — Look at that." He had produced a photograph. "Six of them. That's the youngest. She's at the school at Hellas, they've a proper school there now." "Mr. Doust. If you blast that face, the yield in the rubble will read about three times background, and every party in this system will conclude the vein is worthless, and eleven thousand tonnes of the only object of its kind will be tipped over a spoil bank." "Well," said Doust, standing, slapping Arthur's shoulder on his way past, "then we'll all know, won't we." Commissioner Quill sent a card. An actual card, engraved, with an office on Deimos and no telephone, and on the back in pencil: *the interest column. Still four percent out. Two quarters now three. A.Q.* They met in a room at the Directorate assay office at Ceraunius, kept at 19 degrees, with four steel filing cabinets and a portrait of a president who had died in 2263. "You thought I was a clerk," Quill said. "Yes." "It's a reasonable mistake and I'd rather you'd gone on making it, because you were being a great deal more informative." He was eating a boiled sweet. He offered the bag. "Sit down. I'm going to tell you what I can do to you, and then what I'd like to do for you, and you'll notice they're the same thing, and I'd be grateful if you didn't pretend to be surprised. "I can have you certified. Not maliciously — the finding writes itself. You were removed from your home by an armed retinue of a foreign chartered service. You have been in conference with a plenipotentiary. You've made statements about your own instrument's reliability, in writing, on a Directorate form. Six months' assessment on Earth, a residence at Kew, nine thousand a year for life, and Sector Nine passes to the Directorate as an unadministered colonial asset." He turned the sweet over in his mouth. "I would do it for the species and I would sleep, more or less. I'm telling you so that you understand that being right isn't a defence. It isn't even a factor." "Ambrose says it can't be divided profitably." "I've read her. I've read Brakel and I've read Menotti's dating paper, which is lovely and wrong." Quill took off his spectacles and wiped them on his sleeve, three passes. "It changes nothing for me. Do you know what enrichment is, Mr. Neegan? It's fifteen years, eleven billion credits, forty thousand centrifuges and a building you cannot hide. That is the whole architecture of restraint on forty settled bodies — not treaties, treaties are paper, *plant*. Azra means a man with mine tailings and sixty grams is a nuclear power by Thursday. Whether your vein can be cut or not, the grams exist. Chryse produced grams. The genie is out, and my office is the last office on the list of offices that can put anything at all back in the bottle, and I intend to put your vein in it." "By taking it." "By taking it. Yes." Halvard sold on the Friday. Arthur found out from the stakes: a new line, and a Halberd Assay bulletin wired to his own gate. He walked the eight hundred metres to Halvard's and the old man was sitting on his step with his boots in the dust as he had sat for nineteen years, and he did not get up. "Eight hundred and forty thousand," he said. Arthur said nothing. "Eight hundred and forty thousand credits, Arthur, for eleven hectares of ground that grew nothing but a headache. And a statement." He shrugged. "They wanted a statement about your father's survey. That he cut corners. That the four-hundred-metre horizon in his logs was guesswork." "Was it?" "It was the best work I ever saw a man do with bad gear." Halvard spat at his stone and hit it. "I signed it anyway. I'm seventy-one. I've got dust in me like your father had. I'm going to Hellas where the air's twelve millibars better and I'm going to be warm, and if you want me to say I'm sorry I'll say it, but I'd sign it again in the morning." Arthur stood there. There was nothing to correct. "Thirteen-fifty a kilolitre," Halvard said, to be saying something. "You'll have my share of the tariff now, on top of yours. I never thought of that till Tuesday." On the Sunday a survey rover working Arthur's north boundary lost its steering column on a grade at 40 kph, and rolled, and a man named Tobias Ferrers who had been hired by Arthur at eleven credits an hour to hold a staff was crushed against the roll frame and died before they got him to Ceraunius. The column had been cut, cleanly, on the underside, where a man checking a vehicle looks last. Nobody had wanted Ferrers dead. Ferrers was twenty-four, and had traded a Tuesday for a Saturday with a woman at the bond hall, and the whole of what anyone had wanted was for Arthur Neegan to be in that seat. Arthur sat in his kitchen that night with the eleven ledgers stacked in front of him and the wax-pencil lattice still on the table, going grey where he had wiped at it, and understood a thing he had been refusing for seventy-one days. He had been going about it as a man with something to sell. He was not a man with something to sell. He was the thing being sold. Nobody had made him an offer; they had made offers *about* him, and to each other, and the only reason he was still in the room was that the Charter required a signature and signatures required a hand. Which meant the hand was the only asset he had. He got out paper.

Chapter Six: The Instrument The first draft was four pages and it was worthless, and he knew it was worthless by the end of the second page, but he wrote all four because he had learned as a young man that you cannot see the fault in a structure until you have drawn the whole of it. *I, Arthur Neegan, freeholder,* it began, *do hereby covenant that the body of Azra beneath Sector Nine shall not be divided.* He read it back at 0300 and laughed out loud, alone, in a cold kitchen. A man covenanting with nobody, undertaking nothing, enforceable by no one, and — this was the part that actually made him laugh — a promise to preserve a thing whose preservation was already guaranteed by arithmetic. Nobody was going to cut the vein. Cutting it was stupid. He had spent seventy-one days telling three governments that cutting it was stupid, and the danger had never once been that they would cut it. The danger was that they would take it whole. He went back to the beginning. An asset that cannot profitably be divided cannot be *distributed*. It can be moved from one holder to another entire, and that is all. Which meant it was not, in any useful sense, property. It was territory. It was a jurisdiction with a market value, and the only question ever asked about a jurisdiction is who administers it, and the answer to that question has never in human history been settled by ownership. *So do not own it,* he wrote. *Administer it.* He drew that as a structure, because that was how he thought: four loads and a foundation, and he sat looking at it for an hour and a half, and it did not stand up, because every load path ran through him. Ambrose came down on the Wednesday and read the fifth draft standing at the table, still in her coat. "Clause four's wrong." "Which part?" "'Shall not be extracted.' You can't write that." She had the wax pencil out again. "You'll have Brakel's laminate in eleven months, or Menotti's people will find a second body, or somebody will do something clever I can't presently imagine — and the moment they do, your document forbids the only useful thing anyone might learn. Write 'shall not be extracted save on the certificate of the auditor.' Then when the physics changes, the physics changes, and the paper bends instead of breaking." "Who's the auditor?" "The Institute," said Ambrose, without a flicker. "Me, in practice, for about nine years, and then whoever's most disliked at Phobos." "That's an enormous amount of power." "It's an enormous amount of *work*. Nobody wants it. That's why you'll get it past them." She wrote in the margin. "Also, you're going to give the Institute sampling rights on the working face, in perpetuity, at Institute expense, and you're going to do it in clause nineteen where nobody reads." "You want the exponent." "I want the exponent," she said. "You want a document. I think we can both go home happy, and if you think I'm ashamed of that you've mistaken me for somebody with a career to protect." The law he got, in the end, from a man whose name he never learned. Quill's charter clerk was about thirty, spectacled, and desperately eager to explain, and Arthur went to Deimos on the pretext of filing an objection to the Halberd survey and spent two hours in a corridor outside a records room being educated. "Article 12's freehold, everyone knows Article 12. Article 40's the interesting one." The clerk turned the volume round. "Alienation. A freeholder can transfer to another private person by simple deed. But to a *chartered body* — a consortium, a combine, anything holding a charter — requires ratification by the Directorate, published bill, eighteen months. That's 40(1)." "And a trust?" "A trust isn't a chartered body. A trust isn't a person either." The clerk was delighted. "It's the gap in the drafting. In 2189 nobody imagined a colonial asset large enough to need trustees, so they never wrote the clause, so it falls under 40(3) — *any other disposition* — which requires only that the instrument be lodged with the Commissioner and witnessed by wet signature. Wet signature, in person, on paper. That's why we've still got the cabinets. Nobody's amended it because to amend it you'd have to publish a bill." "And once it's lodged?" "Then it's a fact. The Directorate can dispute it in the colonial court, which sits on Earth, which is four years and eleven months at the current list." He blinked. "Is that useful?" "Yes," said Arthur. He bought Mireille's bond on the eleventh of the month, four hundred and eleven thousand two hundred credits, against a note secured on the freehold that Halberd had valued at nine million and Kessel-Rhone at four and Vaal at rather more, and which he would in eight days not own at all. She came down to Sector Nine to tell him what she thought of it. "You did it Tuesday." "Wednesday. The clearance took—" "Tuesday. It was read out Tuesday afternoon at the counter, with the balance and the number, the way they read out Sowerby, and then Ilse asked me for her twenty-two credits back." Mireille was standing in the middle of his kitchen with her coat on. "Not because she needs it. Because I've got nothing at stake now. That's what the money in my hand *was*, Arthur — it was mine to lose. Forty-one people. That's gone by Friday." "You're free." "Say the rest of it." "There isn't any rest of it." "There's you being right," she said. "You're always right and you're right about this and I'd have gone eleven more years to have had it not read out at the counter, and you'll never understand that, and I've stopped wanting you to." She looked at the papers on the table, the eight drafts, the grey smear of the lattice. "Is that the thing?" "That's the thing." "How many in it?" "Sixty-one thousand bonded. And every freeholder registered before the twelfth." Mireille read the first page standing up, with her lips moving very slightly, the way she did the money. "You've got them in a document," she said. "You couldn't manage the one you knew, and you've got sixty-one thousand in a document." She put it down and squared the edge with her thumb, a habit, and she did not thank him, and she did not stay for tea. Ambrose filed on the thirty-first day. He heard it from Quill, of all people — a card in pencil, *Cavor Institute, Letters, priority claim lodged 31st, embargo 90 days. A.Q.* — and he took a rover to Phobos ferry at four in the morning and found her in a corridor at the Institute with a cup in her hand. What he said was: "You've sold it." What he said after that was worse, and he was aware while saying it that he was reaching for whatever would hurt, and he reached for her career and for Brakel and for the framed letter and for the two papers she had been publicly wrong in, and he said the word *vanity* twice. Ambrose let him finish. She had gone very still. "The embargo's ninety days," she said. "You have eight. I filed for priority, not for publication, because Brakel filed on the twenty-ninth and if I hadn't he'd own the lattice for the next century and be wrong in it." She drank some of her tea. "I told you I'd give you seventy days and I gave you seventy days minus nothing at all, and you have come here and called me vain, which I am, and which is not the same as having broken faith with you. "Now. That was the cruellest four minutes anybody's spent on me in nine years and I shall remember it. Clause nineteen still stands and I still want the exponent and I will still be your auditor, because the work is the work." She turned to go, and stopped. "Do you know, Mr. Neegan, you and Brakel would get on." He sent the notices out that afternoon. Hard copy, by hand, sealed: to the Antares Combine at Deimos-synch, to the Commissioner of Colonial Assay and Compliance, to Kessel-Rhone Extractive, to Halberd Assay & Development at its Luna address with no telephone, and to the bond halls at Ceraunius, Aonia, and Hellas, to be posted at the chit counters where they read out the names. *A hearing, at the Directorate assay office, Deimos, on the seventieth day, at 1000 hours. Wet signature. In person.*

Chapter Seven: The Corridor The hearing took eleven minutes. It was held in the assay office on Deimos, a room kept at nineteen degrees, with four steel cabinets, a portrait of a president dead forty-seven years, and eleven chairs that had been carried in from somewhere and did not match. Quill sat at the head with the register open in front of him and a paper bag of boiled sweets beside it. Vaal sat, because sitting was easier, in a high-collared coat, with the silent man standing behind him. Ambrose sat with a slate on her knee. A young advocate for Kessel-Rhone sat with two clerks and eleven volumes, and a Halberd man sat apart and said nothing whatever and wrote everything down. Mr. Doust was not there. Mr. Doust had opened a test face at Sector Nine on the fourteenth. Arthur read out the instrument. He read the whole of it, twenty-two clauses, in the voice he used for shaft specifications, and it took nine minutes, and by the fourth clause he understood that nobody in the room was listening to the argument. They were listening to each other. "Objection to the whole," said the Kessel-Rhone advocate, when he had finished. "Article 40(1). The disposition is in substance an alienation to a chartered body — the Combine, which takes the contract — and requires ratification by published bill." "It's 40(3)," Quill said. "A trust isn't a chartered body." "A trust isn't anything." "Precisely the difficulty," said Quill, and wrote something. "Your objection's noted and it's arguable and it's four years and eleven months on the colonial list. Anything else?" The advocate said a great deal else, for six minutes, competently, and Quill let him do it and then closed the register. "Instrument lodged, pending signature. Adjourned to 1400." He unwrapped a sweet. "I'd suggest everybody take some air. Not that there is any." The real business was done in the corridor outside the records room, which was two metres wide, floored in ribbed steel, and cold. Vaal was smoking. He had brought the cigars himself and paid four hundred and twelve credits' duty on nine kilos of leaf to do it, and he offered one to Arthur, who refused, and to Quill, who took it and did not light it and put it in his cardigan pocket. "Clause fourteen," Vaal said. "Which part?" "'Sole contractor, licence revocable on the certificate of the auditor.' You have given me the entire work of the largest extraction on Mars — shafts, works, haulage, forty years of it — and you have made the whole of it revocable by a woman on Phobos with a grudge against her co-author." "Yes." "And the Directorate holds a veto on export." "On export. Not on work." "So I may build it, and I may run it, and I may never own a gram of it, and Earth may forbid me to ship what I do not own." Vaal considered the end of his cigar. "It is the worst commercial proposition that has ever been put to me in nineteen years and I include a Callisto ferry monopoly in 2301." "It's better than nothing, which is what you get if Earth takes it." "It is not better than nothing. It is *approximately* nothing." Vaal turned his hand over. "Tell me about clause nine." "Nine's the ratification recital." "Read me the words." Arthur read them. "'Whereas the within disposition is made under Article 40(3) of the Mars Development Charter of 2189, and whereas ratification under Article 40(1) is not required in respect of a disposition to trustees, the same not being a chartered body—'" Vaal held up one finger, and Arthur stopped, and Vaal sat with the cigar in his hand and looked at the middle distance for what Arthur later measured, from the corridor clock, as fifty-one seconds. "In 2094," Vaal said, "the Directorate refused ratification of the Antares Combine's Callisto charter under Article 40, applying a provision written for the surface of Mars to a moon of Jupiter, on the reasoning that 40(1) governed *all* colonial dispositions whatsoever and admitted no other category. Mr. Justice Ahearn dissented. He said that 40(3) existed, that it must mean something, and that a court which held it meant nothing was amending a charter it had no power to amend. He was overruled six to one and he died in 2101 and nobody has cited him since." Vaal tapped ash onto the ribbed steel floor. "Your clause nine cites him. In a lodged instrument. Which the Directorate's own Commissioner will countersign and file in his own cabinet." "I didn't know about Callisto," Arthur said. "The clerk told me about 40(3), not—" "Do not," said Vaal, "explain to me that you did it by accident. I have spent nineteen years pretending things were intended. Allow me the courtesy in return." He got up, stiffly, and put out the cigar against the wall. "The Combine will sign. Not for the contract; the contract is a humiliation and my board will have my head for it. It will sign because in one hundred and ninety-two years no man has been able to make the Directorate write down in its own hand that Article 40(1) is not the whole of the world, and I am going to be able to do it before dinner." He went four paces and stopped. "You should understand what you are making of yourself," he said. "Not the trust. Yourself. Clause twenty-one: trustee irrevocable, non-alienable, personal. You cannot sell it, you cannot resign it, you cannot be bought out of it, and it is worth nine million credits a year to eleven parties that you go on breathing. There is no cage in the solar system as strong as being *useful*, Mr. Neegan. I have been in one for nineteen years. The tobacco is very good and one gets used to the bars." Quill signed at 1412 because of Doust. Arthur had not known until that morning. The test face had gone in on the fourteenth, four charges on the four-hundred-metre horizon, and the shot had brought down a hanging wall nobody had drained for — one hundred and eighty metres of unconsolidated fines over a caliche horizon, running sand, exactly as it was written in Osric Neegan's ledgers in a hand that Halvard had sworn was guesswork — and four bonded men had gone into it and were still in it, and would stay in it, because the sequence could not be re-entered. The rubble at the spoil bank read three point one times background. "Three point one," Quill said. He had the assay slip in his hand and he had been holding it since 1000. "Forty-one at the face. Three at the bank. Your Dr. Ambrose is right, and the entire commercial world will now conclude that Sector Nine is worthless, and in about nine months somebody in Luna will work out that it isn't, and in the interval the only body that can lawfully touch it is a trust with your name on it." He wiped his spectacles, three passes. "I was going to have you certified. I had the finding drafted. It's in the third cabinet." "Why not?" "Because Doust is genial and has six grandchildren and will be transferred to Ganymede with a commendation, and because there are four men in that sequence, and because I have signed the Radiological Covenants every quarter for nine years knowing what they were worth." He signed. It took him about two seconds. "Your document will hold about forty years, and I'll tell you why in a moment, and it isn't a criticism. Forty years is a long while. I've never managed more than four." Kessel-Rhone did not sign. Kessel-Rhone lodged its objection, and litigated it, and four years and eleven months later the colonial court on Earth held for the trust, six to one, and cited Ahearn. Ambrose signed as auditor at 1431 and had clause nineteen read aloud into the register first, and got her sampling rights in perpetuity at Institute expense. Arthur signed last, in wet ink, with a Directorate pen that leaked. He was, at 1436 on the seventieth day, the owner of nothing at all.

Chapter Eight: Trustee Eighteen months on, they gave him an office at the Sector Nine works with a window, and the window looked out over four hundred hectares of gantry, spoil, hoist house, tank farm, dormitory blocks, and a rail loop, and somewhere under the north end of it, under a maintenance shed, was where his kitchen had been. They had asked him where the greenhouse had stood, so as to put a marker on it. He had told them not to. It would have been eleven metres inside the ore road and men would have driven round it for forty years. He had the onions in a tray on the sill. They did not do well; the office was kept at Earth-standard humidity for the Combine engineers, and onions want it drier than that, and he had said so in writing to a maintenance section that answered to a subcontractor of the trust of which he was the sole trustee, and nothing had happened. He had a chair he liked. He had gone to some trouble over the chair. On the wall by the door was a plaque, brass, screwed on before he was consulted: THE NEEGAN TRUST ESTABLISHED 2313 A. NEEGAR, TRUSTEE He had raised it once, with the works secretary, who had been apologetic and had written it down. That was fourteen months ago. The dinners were the worst of it. There were four a year at Ceraunius and two on Deimos and he was obliged to attend them all because his attendance was a term of the Combine's licence — clause fourteen, sub-clause four, which he had drafted himself in a cold kitchen at three in the morning and had thought at the time was a way of keeping a hand on the contractor. He sat at the head of tables and was toasted, and men who had never gone below a hundred metres explained the drainage to him, and he corrected them, and a small hardness would come into the room and pass. He had been asked to speak at the school at Hellas. He had spoken for fifty-one minutes on subsurface water movement in unconsolidated fines, with figures, and it had been, he was later told, not what they had wanted. The letters came at about forty a week. Some of them wanted money. Some of them wanted a lease. A woman in Aonia wrote every month about a boundary dispute that had nothing to do with the trust and Arthur answered every one, at length, with the relevant clause numbers, and she wrote back angrier each time. Mireille came up on the Thursdays because the trust's shift schedule went out on the Thursdays and she was a supervisor now, at nine hundred and forty a month, on the second sequence. "Twenty-two men short on the Tuesday." "The bond hall said—" "The bond hall said forty and it'll be twenty-two, because there's a transport in at Aonia and the Aonia hall's paying a bonus and yours doesn't." She put the slate on his desk. "You'll want to write to somebody about that. You like writing to people." "Sit down." "I've got the second sequence at four." She stood. She always stood. "That plaque's still wrong." "I know." "Are you going to have it done?" "I've asked twice." "Ask a third time or stop mentioning it," said Mireille. "You do this. You'll take four hundred thousand off your own name for sixty-one thousand people you've never met and then you'll go on for eighteen months about a brass plate. Nobody can help you with the plate, Arthur. It's a plate." She got as far as the door. "Ilse's back at Ceraunius," she said. "She's holding the money now. Forty-four of them. She's not as good at it as I was and she'd tell you so herself." A shrug that was not quite a shrug. "It goes on. That's all I came to say and I'm not saying it again." Quill retired in the March. He came to Sector Nine on his way to the Earth transport, in a grey cardigan, with very bad shoes, and stood at the window looking out at the tank farm and eating a boiled sweet. "Forty years," he said. "I said forty. You never asked me why." "I assumed you'd tell me." "Four reasons and they're all dull. One: clause nine cites Ahearn, and a citation is a hostage — the day the Directorate has a court it likes better, it will read Ahearn the other way, and it will be able to, because dissents can always be read two ways. Two: your auditor is a person and not an office, and Ambrose is fifty-one, and whoever follows her will want something, and they will be offered it. Three: the beneficial class is 'bonded persons and freeholders registered before the twelfth,' and in forty years there will be no bonded persons on Mars, and a class that empties out is a class that a clever man can argue has lapsed." He turned round. "Four: it works. That's the serious one. It will pay, and go on paying, and nobody destroys an arrangement that is failing — they destroy the ones worth taking." "Then it should have been drafted better." "It should have been drafted by six men over two years and it was drafted by an engineer in a fortnight, and it is the best-drafted instrument I have lodged in thirty-four years, and I have lodged some very good ones." Quill put the paper twist of his sweet in his pocket. "Don't fish. It doesn't suit you." "Vaal sends tobacco," Arthur said. "At Christmas. Nine kilos, duty paid." "Yes. He'll go on doing that. He'll go on doing it long after he's stopped meaning anything by it, and one year it will arrive after he's dead, because he'll have set up a standing order, and you will smoke it, because you don't smoke and you will have kept it all." Quill put out his hand. "Nobody was persuaded by you, Mr. Neegan. I want you to know that, because you'll have people telling you otherwise for the rest of your life. Vaal signed out of a grudge, I signed because Doust killed four men in a face your father had drained on paper thirty years before, and the Institute signed for a sampling clause. Not one of us was moved by the argument." "Does that matter?" "No," said Quill. "That's the whole of the trick and nobody ever believes it. Goodbye. Mind the onions, they want it drier than that." --- *From the* Encyclopaedia of the Settled Worlds*, 14th edition (2417), vol. IX:* **NEEGAR TRUST** (also *Neegan Trust*): the administrative instrument governing the Sector Nine azraic body, Aonia, Mars, lodged with the Terrestrial Directorate 2313 and upheld in *Kessel-Rhone Extractive v. the Trustee* (2318). Its central provision — that a lattice-coherent mass may not be divided without loss of effect, and is therefore susceptible of administration but not of ownership — is generally credited to the physicist **Sofiya Ambrose** (2272–2341), whose "Notes on Contiguity" of 2312 established the exponent. The trustee, an engineer, appears to have been an intermediary of some kind. The Trust is commonly cited as the origin of the export veto system, under which no fewer than nine general wars are held by the standard authorities to have been deferred, and by revisionist authorities merely postponed. It was dissolved by consent in 2361, the beneficial class having been held to have lapsed. --- That evening, before the second sequence came up, the works secretary caught him in the corridor with a slate. "Sir — the drainage under Sector Nine, the maintenance section have queried the standing instruction. They want to know why we're pumping a horizon that's been dry for eleven years." Arthur stopped. "Because it isn't dry," he said. "It's caliche over fines. It's dry until it isn't, and then it's a hundred and eighty metres of running sand and four men you don't get back. Tell them it's in the ledgers. Tell them it's been in the ledgers since 2281." "Whose ledgers, sir?" "Neegan's," he said, and went in to look at the onions.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 8)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of writing that demonstrates rare discipline and craft. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. **Voice and Style** The chapter executes the Asimov-inflected retrofuturist register with remarkable consistency. The prose is built from short declaratives, measurements, and procedural specificity: "nine hundred and forty a month, on the second sequence," "forty a week," "fifty-one minutes." There is almost no metaphor, and what little figurative language exists is embedded in character observation rather than authorial decoration. The line "a small hardness would come into the room and pass" is the closest thing to a poetic gesture, and it earns its place precisely because it is understated and accurate. The writing never reaches for effect; it achieves effect through restraint. **Character Consistency** Arthur's pedantry-as-nervous-tic is rendered perfectly throughout. He corrects the drainage men at dinner. He answers the Aonia woman's letters with clause numbers. He has written to the maintenance section about the humidity. He has asked twice about the plaque and will not ask a third time but will keep mentioning it — and Mireille calls this out with devastating precision: "You do this." The folding rule is absent but the behavioral tic is present in every scene. His final line — "Neegan's," and going to look at the onions — is exactly right: the name correction, the deflection into the practical, the refusal of sentiment. Mireille is rendered with equal fidelity. She stands. She always stands. She is not grateful, not warm, not reconciled — she is practical and slightly contemptuous and she tells him the one thing she came to say and says she won't say it again. "It goes on. That's all I came to say and I'm not saying it again" is a perfect line for her character. The detail about Ilse holding the money now, and not being as good at it, and Mireille knowing she'd say so herself — this is exactly the character as profiled: her allegiance is to specific named people, not to sentiment. Quill's four reasons for the trust's forty-year lifespan are delivered in his exact register: flat, specific, fatalistic, and correct. "It works. That's the serious one. It will pay, and go on paying, and nobody destroys an arrangement that is failing — they destroy the ones worth taking." This is the best line in the chapter and possibly in the story. His observation about Vaal's tobacco — that Arthur will keep it all and smoke it after Vaal is dead because he doesn't smoke — is a small, precise, slightly cruel piece of characterization that lands completely. **The Encyclopaedia Entry** This is a masterstroke of execution. The plan called for a pedantic, slightly wrong entry that credits Ambrose and misspells Arthur's name, and the chapter delivers it with perfect comic timing. "The trustee, an engineer, appears to have been an intermediary of some kind." The dissolution note — "the beneficial class having been held to have lapsed" — vindicates Quill's third reason exactly. The misspelling "NEEGAR" in the header, then "Neegan" in the body text, is a nice additional touch of institutional carelessness. **The Final Scene** The drainage question as the closing beat is exactly right. It is not symbolic — or rather, it refuses to be symbolic while being quietly resonant. The father's ledgers, the 2281 date, the four men you don't get back — these echo the story's concerns without announcing themselves. "Neegan's," he said, and went in to look at the onions" is an ending that earns its flatness completely. **Emotional Engagement** The chapter is emotionally engaging in the way the plan intended: through accumulation of small, precise, unsentimentalized details rather than through declared feeling. The plaque with the wrong initial. The onions that don't do well. Mireille standing. These work. The reader feels the texture of Arthur's life without being told how to feel about it. **Weaknesses** There are very few. The chapter is perhaps slightly long — the Quill scene is the emotional and intellectual climax, and the encyclopaedia entry and final scene both work, but the piece might be marginally tighter without one of them. However, the plan called for all three beats and they all execute well, so this is a minor observation. The line "He had gone to some trouble over the chair" is the one moment where the prose risks preciousness, but it recovers immediately. The chapter follows its plan with extraordinary fidelity: the wrong plaque, the ceremonial dinners, Mireille as shift supervisor finding him embarrassing, Quill's four reasons, Vaal's tobacco, the encyclopaedia entry crediting Ambrose and misspelling the name, the drainage line at the end. Every planned element is present and executed with craft rather than mere competence. This is writing that knows exactly what it is doing and does it without flinching. Final Piece Evaluation

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of science fiction writing that demonstrates genuine mastery of the Asimov mode while transcending mere pastiche. Let me examine it carefully across all dimensions. **Craft and Voice** The prose is controlled, precise, and deeply characteristic of a certain strain of classic SF — the retrofuturistic bureaucratic-procedural mode that Asimov perfected. The voice is consistent throughout all eight chapters, which is a significant achievement for a long-form generation. The opening gambit — Arthur worrying about a greenhouse valve while being effectively arrested — is a masterstroke of characterization through displacement anxiety. It establishes him immediately as a man whose mind works in practical, quantifiable terms, and this characterization never wavers. The prose style is deliberately spare and functional, which suits both the character and the genre. Sentences like "He was wearing a borrowed jacket. That was the detail he kept returning to, more than the sidearms" demonstrate economy and psychological acuity simultaneously. The writing earns its occasional lyrical moments rather than reaching for them. **World Building** The Asimovian big-and-small-picture worldbuilding is executed with genuine skill. The detail about enrichment — "fifteen years, eleven billion credits, forty thousand centrifuges and a building you cannot hide" — is exactly the kind of concrete, consequential worldbuilding that makes SF feel real. The bond system, the water tariff, the Directorate's charter provisions, the relay lag on communications — all of these accumulate into a coherent and textured world without ever feeling like an info-dump. The encyclopaedia entry at the end is a perfect Asimovian touch, and the misspelling of "Neegan" as "Neegar" in the plaque and then in the encyclopaedia is a quietly devastating joke about institutional indifference. **Characters** Arthur Neegan is a genuinely nuanced protagonist. He is right about almost everything and yet consistently fails to understand the human dimensions of his rightness — his sister's speech about the money being "hers to lose" is the most emotionally complex moment in the piece, and it lands because it has been earned. Mireille is the most fully realized secondary character: her refusal to be grateful, her understanding of social capital that Arthur cannot grasp, her final line about Ilse — all of this is excellent. Vaal is a superb antagonist-ally, the kind of morally complex figure who is simultaneously self-serving and honest about it. His speech about the cage of being useful is one of the finest passages in the piece. Quill is also well-drawn — the boiled sweets, the cardigan, the spectacles wiped three times — and his final speech about nobody being persuaded by the argument is thematically central and beautifully delivered. Ambrose is perhaps slightly thinner than the others, but her function is partly structural (she represents the pure scientific interest) and she has enough personality — the wax pencil on the table, the framed letter, the unapologetic self-interest of clause nineteen — to feel real. **Plot and Structure** The plot is genuinely clever. The central insight — that the vein cannot be profitably divided, therefore cannot be owned, only administered — is the kind of elegant SF premise that Asimov would have been proud of. The legal mechanism (Article 40(3), the trust, the Ahearn citation) is worked out with real care and feels plausible within the world's logic. The Doust subplot — the test face, the four men lost, the three-point-one reading — is both plot-functional and morally weighted without being melodramatic. The Ferrers death (the cut steering column) is handled with appropriate restraint. It's not dwelt upon, which is correct — Arthur processes it as information that changes his understanding of his situation, not as a sentimental moment. **Dialogue** The dialogue is consistently excellent. The Chapter Two meeting with Vaal is the standout — the three offers structure is elegant, and the exchange about the drainage at the end ("Nobody's ever asked me about the drainage") is perfectly placed. The Mireille scenes are also strong, particularly her speech about the money and her final visit to the office. The dialogue is never expository in a clumsy way; information is conveyed through character voice and conflict. **Pacing** The pacing is well-managed across eight chapters. The story accelerates appropriately — the early chapters are more expansive and atmospheric, the middle chapters more pressured, and the final chapter achieves a quiet, elegiac tone that suits the material. The encyclopaedia entry is a perfect structural choice, providing both closure and irony (the trustee "appears to have been an intermediary of some kind"). **Weaknesses** The piece is not without flaws. The Ambrose confrontation in Chapter Six — where Arthur says cruel things and then immediately regrets them — is the one moment that feels slightly rushed. The emotional beat is real but the resolution comes quickly. The "unearned transformation" risk is low throughout, but this is the one scene where the emotional work could have been done more thoroughly. The Halvard subplot, while well-observed, is slightly underdeveloped — his signing of the false statement and Arthur's non-response to it is interesting but the thread doesn't quite resolve. This may be intentional (life doesn't resolve neatly) but it leaves a small loose end. The man with the bad shoes / Quill reveal is perhaps slightly telegraphed — the reader will likely identify him before Arthur does — but this is a minor issue and the scene works regardless. **Metaphor and Poetry** The piece is notably restrained in its use of metaphor, which is appropriate to the voice. When metaphors appear — "Mars had been worthless. That had been the whole basis of its settlement" — they are functional and precise. There is no purple prose, no forced lyricism. The one extended metaphor (Vaal's cage of being useful) is earned by character and context. **Faithfulness to Prompt** The prompt is followed with great fidelity. The story begins aboard the transfer vessel, the meeting with Vaal is primarily dialogue with vivid scene-setting, the hints of larger intrigue are present throughout, and the Asimovian retrofuturistic vibe is sustained. The story goes well beyond the prompt's requirements in developing a complete and satisfying narrative arc. **Overall Assessment** This is a genuinely excellent piece of science fiction writing — not merely competent pastiche but a story with its own ideas, its own emotional register, and its own earned wisdom. The final line ("Neegan's," he said, and went in to look at the onions) is quietly perfect. The piece has the quality of a story that knows what it's about and executes that knowledge with discipline and intelligence.
